                                PRESENTATION


      The book Perspectives and Analyses of Educational Research stands as
a relevant contribution to understanding the different approaches and
interpretations in the field of educational research. With a broad perspective, the
work brings together reflections that support theoretical and methodological
development, considering the complexity of educational processes.


      By emphasizing the connection between theory and practice, the book
encourages the development of critical and well-grounded analyses, which are
essential for knowledge production in education. The work includes multiple
perspectives that enrich academic debate and promote the development of more
consistent and contextualized research.


      This book is recommended for professors, students, and professionals in
the field of education and related areas, as well as for anyone interested in
expanding their knowledge of educational research. It is a work that fosters
learning, reflection, and the improvement of investigative practices.

CHAPTER 1
 CHALLENGES AND PRACTICES IN
 PEDAGOGICAL COORDINATION IN A
 PUBLIC SCHOOL: A CASE STUDY AT PINTO
 MARQUES STATE SCHOOL

ABSTRACT: This article critically analyzes the experience of a supervised
internship in pedagogical coordination carried out at Pinto Marques State School
in Belém, Pará, Brazil. Based on field observations, document analysis, and
conversa-tions with school professionals, structural, administrative, and relational
as-pects that directly influence school management were identified. The chal-
lenges faced, such as lack of resources, centralized management, and teacher
demotivation, are discussed in light of contemporary educational literature. The


                                                                                 11

study highlights the importance of democratic management, active listening, and
collaborative work as strategies to promote quality public education. The
methodology adopted was qualitative, with an emphasis on critical analysis of the
lived experience. The conclusion is that, despite adversities, there are sig-nificant
experiences of resistance and commitment to social transformation within the
school context.

KEYWORDS: pedagogical coordination, democratic management, supervised
internship, public education.

RESUMO: Este artigo analisa criticamente a experiência de estágio
supervisionado em coordenação pedagógica realizada na Escola Estadual Pinto
Marques, em Belém-PA. A partir de observações de campo, análise documental
e conversas com profissionais da escola, identificaram-se aspectos estruturais,
administrativos e relacionais que influenciam diretamente a gestão escolar. As
dificuldades enfrentadas, como a escassez de recursos, a gestão centralizada e
a desmotivação docente, são discutidas à luz da literatura educacional
contemporânea. O estudo destaca a importância de uma gestão democrática, da
escuta ativa e do trabalho colaborativo como estratégias para a promoção de
uma educação pública de qualidade. A metodologia adotada foi qualitativa, com
ênfase na análise crítica da prática vivenciada. Conclui-se que, apesar das
adversidades, há experiências significativas de resistência e compromisso com
a transformação social no contexto escolar.

PALAVRAS-CHAVE: coordenação pedagógica, gestão democrática, estágio
supervisionado, educação pública.




                                                                                  12

1 INTRODUCTION


       The reality of Brazilian public schools, especially those located in
peripheral urban areas or socially vulnerable contexts, reveals a complex
landscape    in   which      pedagogical   resistance,   structural   precariousness,
institutional conflicts, and constant challenges to democratic management
coexist. In this context, the pedagogical coordinator plays a central role as a
liaison between the school’s political-pedagogical project, the guidelines of the
Department of Education, and everyday teaching practices (Lück, 2009; Paro,
2012). However, this professional does not always find adequate conditions to
perform their role, frequently being subjected to overwork, improvisation, and
institutional devaluation.
       The supervised internship in pedagogical coordination, as a mandatory
component of teacher and educational administrator training, constitutes a
unique opportunity for the articulation of theory and practice, fostering critical
observation of school dynamics and the experience of the real challenges that
permeate everyday educational life. According to Freire (1996), there is no
transformative pedagogical practice without a critical reading of reality, and the
internship, in this sense, must transcend the logic of mere technical application,
taking on the character of a formative, investigative, and political experience.
       This article presents and analyzes the results of the supervised internship
experience conducted at the Pinto Marques State School, located in the city of
Belém (PA), in 2016. Through immersion in the daily school routine, it was
possible to observe structural, administrative, and cultural tensions that directly
impact the performance of pedagogical coordination and school management as
a whole. Among the most evident elements are: the centralization of decision-
making by the administration, the marginalization of strategic functions such as
the school office, the precarious state of teaching and learning resources, the
overburdening of coordinators, episodes of gender discrimination, and practices
of explicit religiosity in public educational spaces.
       The choice of a qualitative approach is justified by the investigative nature
of the internship, whose objective was to understand, describe, and problematize
lived situations from a critical and formative perspective. Participant observation,
document analysis, and informal interviews with teachers, coordinators, and


                                                                                   13

school staff were employed. Through this, the study sought to analyze not only
pedagogical practices but also the meanings and values that permeate the
institution’s daily life.
        This study is grounded in the perspective that the internship should not be
a passive rite of passage, but rather a moment for questioning school structures,
actively listening to those engaged in the practice, and producing knowledge
about the actual functioning of public schools. We start from the understanding
that schools are not mere spaces for normative reproduction, but contested
territories where antagonistic visions of society and education coexist (Freire,
1996; Dubet, 2004; Lück, 2000).
        Thus, the central objective of this article is to critically analyze the
experience of the supervised internship in pedagogical coordination, identifying
the limits and possibilities of this professional’s role in a public school
environment marked by material, symbolic, and political challenges. The intention
is, thereby, to contribute to the debate on initial , and continuing teacher
education, the valorization of educational work, and the urgency of implementing
democratic management practices within Brazilian public schools.


2. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK


2.1 DEMOCRATIC MANAGEMENT AS A POLITICAL AND PEDAGOGICAL
PRINCIPLE


        Democratic management of public schools constitutes one of the pillars of
quality education, as provided for in Article 3 of the Law on Guidelines and Bases
for National Education (LDB – Law No. 9,394/96), which establishes “the
democratic management of public education” as one of the principles of
education in the country. However, despite its centrality in law and discourse, the
implementation of democratic practices in schools faces historical resistance
related to the hierarchical culture of public administration, the inadequate training
of administrators, and the persistence of authoritarian structures in everyday
school life (Ferreira; Oliveira, 2010; Paro, 2012).
        According to Paro (2012), democratic management is not limited to the
direct election of principals or the creation of school councils, but requires a


                                                                                  14

profound change in the power relations that structure the educational
environment. It involves understanding the school as a public space, where
decisions must be shared among its stakeholders—teachers, coordinators,
students, families, and staff—within a framework of shared responsibility and
effective participation. Although many schools espouse the rhetoric of
democracy, their practices reveal a concentration of power in the hands of the
administration, fragmentation among sectors, and a lack of genuine mechanisms
for listening and dialogue.
      Lück (2009) reinforces this understanding by arguing that democratic
management implies not only the decentralization of decisions but also the
formation of an organizational culture guided by ethics, cooperation, and
collective commitment. However, the author warns that this construction depends
on processes of ongoing training and the willingness of administrators to be open
to criticism, to a diversity of perspectives, and to ongoing negotiation with the
school community . Democratic management, therefore, is not a ready-made
model, but a political and pedagogical process in constant construction.


2.2 PEDAGOGICAL COORDINATION AS MEDIATION BETWEEN PROJECT
AND PRACTICE


      The role of the pedagogical coordinator occupies a strategic position within
the school’s structure: it is the coordinator who links the Political-Pedagogical
Project (PPP) with teaching practices, monitors teaching-learning processes,
mediates conflicts, and promotes teachers’ continuing professional development.
However, as Oliveira (2007) and Lück (2000) point out, this role is often stripped
of meaning in public schools, being confused with bureaucratic tasks or the
supervision of teaching work.
      In Brazil, the role of pedagogical coordination has been constructed in an
ambiguous manner. On the one hand, it is recognized as essential to the
educational process, but on the other, it faces obstacles such as a lack of
autonomy, an overload of duties, and institutional ambiguity regarding its role.
Often, coordinators are appointed on an ad hoc basis due to functional
restructuring or administrative convenience, without the proper training to perform
the role (Lück, 2009).


                                                                                15

       In this regard, Libâneo (2001) argues that the school’s pedagogical
function cannot be fully realized without a body for critical and dialogic
coordination that promotes systematic monitoring of teaching work and collective
reflection on the school’s objectives and methods. The author argues that the
pedagogical coordinator should be a training agent, capable of fostering research
within the school, articulating knowledge, and contributing to overcoming the
pedagogical difficulties faced by teachers and students.
       This view is corroborated by Veiga (2008), who understands coordination
as a space for collective construction, rather than supervision. For the author,
pedagogical coordination must break away from technical formalism and position
itself as a space for listening, collaboration, and the construction of transformative
practices. This function gains even greater relevance in contexts of social
exclusion and the deterioration of school conditions, in which the coordinator can
serve as a fundamental link between pedagogical aspirations and the concrete
reality of school stakeholders.


2.3   THE       PRECARITIZATION      OF    EDUCATIONAL         WORK      AND     THE
CONTRADICTIONS OF PUBLIC SCHOOLS


       Another fundamental aspect for understanding the reality experienced
during the internship is the precariousness of working conditions faced by
education professionals. Esteve (1999) uses the term “teacher malaise” to
describe the sense of frustration and discouragement that afflicts teachers and
coordinators in the face of the system’s demands, the lack of institutional
recognition, and the daily difficulties in performing quality work.
       In the case of Brazilian public schools, this malaise is exacerbated by
factors such as the lack of teaching and pedagogical resources, the dilapidated
state of school buildings, low salaries, an overload of duties, and the symbolic
violence that permeates the daily lives of education professionals. According to
Dubet (2004), schools today face a crisis of legitimacy, as they are held
accountable for results they cannot achieve on their own, and professionals, in
turn, are blamed for structural problems that go beyond their individual
capabilities.



                                                                                   16

         The imposition of administrative, pedagogical, and social demands on
coordinators and teachers without adequate institutional support characterizes a
neoliberal accountability model that shifts the blame for the system’s failure onto
individuals (Shiroma; Campos; Garcia, 2005). In this model, the pedagogical
coordinator ceases to be a facilitator and becomes an executor of fragmented
and poorly implemented policies.
         Despite these difficulties, authors such as Freire (1996) insist on the
possibility of reinventing public schools based on educators’ ethical commitment
to social transformation. For the author, even under the most adverse conditions,
the educational act can be a space for hope, dialogue, and resistance. This
perspective is essential for thinking about initial teacher education and the role of
the internship as a critical experience, and not merely as a way to fulfill required
hours.


3. METHODOLOGY


         The research underlying this article falls within the qualitative approach,
grounded in the critical-reflective perspective of the supervised internship as a
space for investigation, training, and analysis of the educational context.
According to Bogdan and Biklen (1994), qualitative research seeks to understand
the meanings that subjects attribute to their experiences, based on the premise
that the social world is constructed through daily interactions and practices. This
approach proves particularly suitable when the objective is to interpret complex
phenomena, such as the dynamics of management and pedagogical coordination
in public schools.
         The supervised internship was conducted at the Pinto Marques State
School, located in the city of Belém, PA, from June 22 to September 28, 2016,
totaling 49 hours and 30 minutes of in-person activities. During this period, it was
possible to directly observe the school routine during the morning shift (from 7:30
a.m. to 12:00 p.m.), under the supervision of Professor Dr. M. S. Coelho, from
the Federal University of Pará (UFPA). The school is situated in a historic and
central neighborhood of the city, featuring a diverse physical structure, but with
evident signs of disrepair and lack of maintenance.



                                                                                  17

       Data collection was carried out through three main strategies: (1)
participant observation, (2) document analysis, and (3) informal interviews.
Participant observation allowed the intern to become part of the school’s daily life,
experiencing formal and informal moments of interaction among administrators,
coordinators, teachers, staff, and students. This mode of observation is not
restricted to the passivity of an external gaze but involves direct and reflective
engagement with the observed reality (André, 1995). School events, meetings,
conflict situations, and daily practices were recorded, which enabled an
understanding of the institutional culture and the school’s modes of operation.
       The documentary analysis consisted of examining the school’s Political-
Pedagogical Project (PPP), internal regulations, pedagogical plans, and
administrative documents. The critical reading of these materials aimed to verify
the alignment between the school’s formal principles and the practices actually
carried out in daily life. It was found, for example, that the PPP had been outdated
since 2012, which already indicates a disconnect between planning and
pedagogical implementation.
       Finally, informal interviews and spontaneous conversations were
conducted with members of the school community, including pedagogical
coordinators, teachers, administrative assistants, and a special education
teacher. These conversations, though unstructured, revealed relevant aspects of
the professionals’ perceptions regarding school management, the role of
coordination, working conditions, and the challenges faced in daily life. The
statements were recorded in a field journal and organized by thematic themes for
subsequent analysis.
       The triangulation of these sources—observation, documents, and
statements—allowed for a more consistent understanding of the school’s reality,
highlighting the contradictions between institutional discourse and lived practices.
Rather than presenting a static portrait of the school, the methodology adopted
sought to interpret the processes, tensions, and disputes that permeate the
educational environment, based on the involved perspective of the intern-
researcher.




                                                                                  18

4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS


       The data collected throughout the supervised internship reveal the
complexity of public school dynamics, marked by contradictions between legal
principles and the actual mechanisms of management and pedagogical practice.
Based on the analysis of observations, institutional documents, and informal
conversations with professionals at Pinto Marques State School, four major
analytical categories were organized to account for the main tensions and
possibilities identified: (1) centralized school management and the crisis of
participation; (2) pedagogical coordination under conditions of overload and the
erasure of institutio ; (3) exclusionary practices and challenges to democratic
culture; and (4) solidarity and micro-resistance as educational potential.


4.1 CENTRALIZED SCHOOL MANAGEMENT AND THE CRISIS OF
PARTICIPATION


       During the supervised internship, direct observation and staff reports
revealed a school management model excessively centered on the principal, with
visible traits of authoritarianism and low adherence to democratic principles of
leadership and collegiality. Although the principal’s personal dedication and her
frequent presence on campus are acknowledged, these characteristics do not
automatically translate    into   effective   pedagogical leadership or broad
participatory processes.
       The accounts gathered indicate that decisions of a pedagogical,
administrative, or disciplinary nature are concentrated exclusively with the
principal, without prior consultation with other departments. Pedagogical
coordinators, for example, reported that they are often not consulted in the
development of the school calendar, the organization of institutional events, or
the definition of internal guidelines, and are frequently informed only afterward,
once the actions have already been decided. This practice relegates the
pedagogical team to a role of execution rather than conception, undermining the
collegial nature of school management advocated by Brazilian educational
legislation.



                                                                               19

       The LDB (Law No. 9,394/96, Art. 14) establishes that education systems
must ensure democratic forms of management in public schools, involving the
participation of the school and local community in decision-making processes.
However, this guideline often fails to materialize in the concrete reality of
institutions. As Paro (2012) analyzes, democratic management requires a shift
from authority as imposition to authority as mutual recognition. This means that
school leadership should not be based on unilateral orders, but on continuous
processes of listening, negotiation, and collective decision-making.
       The model observed in the analyzed school still appears to be strongly
influenced by the logic of technocratic school administration, inherited from the
bureaucratic-corporate paradigm of the 1990s, in which the principal assumes
the role of a manager, and the other school stakeholders become operational
staff, often without a voice or active participation. This vertical structure also
contradicts the views of Lück (2009) and Ferreira and Oliveira (2010), who assert
that democratic management implies the strengthening of dialogic and horizontal
practices among school segments, allowing individuals to recognize themselves
as co-authors of the educational project.
       Another indication of the participatory crisis is the absence of institutional
channels for listening and debate. During the observation period, no regular
meetings of the school council, student council, or collective planning forums
involving all school sectors were identified. The lack of time allocated to joint
planning and the informality in communication between administration,
coordination, the school office, and teachers reinforce the fragmentation of
management. According to Libâneo (2001), this fragmentation hinders the
construction of a solid institutional identity and compromises coordination among
the different levels and functions of school work.
       There is also a relevant symbolic dimension: silence as a management
tool. Some staff members avoid expressing disagreements or making
suggestions because they fear subtle retaliation, such as the non-renewal of
certain assignments or the public exposure of mistakes. This creates an
institutional climate of passivity and conformity, where dissent is viewed as a
threat rather than a contribution. Such practices resemble what Dubet (2004)
defines as institutionalized symbolic violence, in which individuals are led to
accept the rules of the institutional game as if they were natural or inevitable.


                                                                                    20

       This authoritarian culture, as it perpetuates itself, tends to discourage the
active involvement of various school stakeholders, particularly teachers and
coordinators, who end up limiting their roles to the mechanical fulfillment of
operational duties. As a result, the pedagogical dimension of management—
which should serve as a cross-cutting axis linking educational practices—is lost.
       The lack of opportunity for the intern to gain a comprehensive
understanding of management practices is also telling. The intern’s lack of
involvement in administrative activities—not even as a close observer—
reinforces the logic of information control and restricted access to certain aspects
of the institution, as if there were off-limits zones of power that could not be
touched. This not only compromises the initial training of future professionals but
also violates the principle of transparency and the collective construction of
educational knowledge.
       Thus, the school management of the observed unit presents serious
limitations regarding the promotion of a participatory, horizontal, and formative
culture. Such limitations cannot be attributed solely to the individual figure of the
administrator but are also the result of an authoritarian tradition and an
institutional culture that still resists the full realization of democracy within public
schools. Overcoming this logic requires more than just changing individuals: it
requires modifying structures, establishing permanent spaces for dialogue, and
investing in the ethical, political, and pedagogical training of all school
stakeholders.


4.2 PEDAGOGICAL COORDINATION UNDER CONDITIONS OF OVERLOAD
AND INSTITUTIONAL MARGINALIZATION


       The school’s pedagogical team consists of three coordinators: two who
have been reassigned from other roles and one resource room teacher. Although
these professionals play fundamental roles in organizing the pedagogical routine,
their work is frequently undervalued, rendered invisible, or misunderstood within
the institution. In informal conversations, they reported feeling overburdened,
working without support from the administration, lacking even minimal material
resources, and frequently covering basic expenses to keep projects running.



                                                                                     21

      The role of pedagogical coordination, as argued by Lück (2000) and Veiga
(2008), should be understood as a space for articulating the school’s political-
pedagogical project with teaching practice—a place for training, listening, and
mediation. However, in the observed practice, coordinators accumulate
bureaucratic functions, disciplinary responsibilities, and tasks that go beyond
their role, without formal recognition or adequate working conditions.
      In material terms, the lack of resources is alarming: there is a shortage of
paper, printer ink, basic materials for teaching activities, and minimal
infrastructure in support rooms. According to reports, part of the pedagogical
projects relies on donations or voluntary contributions from the staff members
themselves. This situation constitutes what Esteve (1999) called “teacher
malaise,” a feeling of frustration and helplessness that emerges when the
educator’s commitment is systematically hindered by the objective conditions of
the system.
      The precarious nature of pedagogical work, as pointed out by Shiroma,
Campos, and Garcia (2005), is part of the process of the state shirking its
responsibilities, transferring to frontline professionals the task of keeping the
school running, even without adequate resources. In this model, coordinators
cease to be strategic agents of pedagogical transformation and come to play an
almost technical-administrative role, focused on resolving urgent issues.
      Despite this, it was possible to observe practices of everyday resistance
and emotional engagement among the coordinators, especially in their
relationships with students. These micro-resistances, as described by Dubet
(2004), do not negate institutional suffering, but demonstrate that the school
remains a place of meaning, where bonds, memories, and hopes are built.


4.3 EXCLUSIVE PRACTICES AND CHALLENGES TO DEMOCRATIC
CULTURE


      During the supervised internship, it was observed that daily life at Pinto
Marques State School, although governed by an institutional discourse of
commitment to inclusion and citizenship, reproduces exclusionary practices and
values that contradict the foundations of a democratic and pluralistic school.
Participant observation revealed instances of gender discrimination, signs of


                                                                               22

religious intolerance, and symbolic exclusion of certain individuals and groups
within the school, demonstrating that building a democratic culture goes far
beyond drafting official documents or formal adherence to legislation.
       One of the most emblematic incidents occurred when a student was
addressed by a teacher in a harsh tone, hearing the phrase: “Go sweep a house,
do the laundry.” This statement, laden with sexist content, normalizes the
association between the female figure and domestic work, devaluing the
student’s presence in the school setting and revealing a conservative and sexist
view of gender roles. Such an attitude, in addition to being offensive, reproduces
what Saffioti (2004) and Louro (1997) call institutionalized patriarchy, in which the
school, instead of combating, ends up reinforcing stereotypes and inequalities.
       The reproduction of discriminatory discourse in the school environment
directly undermines the right to quality education and the full development of
individuals. The school, as a public space for ethical, intellectual, and civic
education, has a duty to act in confronting society’s structural inequalities,
including those related to gender, race, sexual orientation, and religion (BRASIL,
2012). When practices such as the one observed are ignored or downplayed, the
symbolic exclusion of historically marginalized groups is legitimized, undermining
the principle of equity.
       Another critical aspect observed was the conspicuous presence of
religious symbols in administrative offices, hallways, and educational settings.
Even though the majority of the staff professes the same faith, the public display
of Catholic religious icons in a public educational space contradicts the
constitutional principle of the secular nature of the State (CF, Art. 19, item I). As
Saviani (2008) argues, public schools must guarantee universal access to
knowledge and ensure that no belief or doctrine takes precedence over the right
to learn and coexist in diversity.
       This symbolic imposition, even when unintentional, can cause discomfort
and subjective exclusion among students and staff who do not share the same
religious orientation, reinforcing what Dubet (2004) calls forms of silent
institutional violence—those that manifest in absences, silences, and everyday
normalizations.
       In parallel with this, there was a lack of systematic training initiatives on
human rights, diversity, and the culture of peace. Although the school participates


                                                                                  23

in specific projects, such as environmental initiatives or prevention and “ ”
campaigns, there is no institutionalized program that promotes critical discussion
of prejudice and discrimination. The absence of an educational policy in this
regard undermines the progress established by legal frameworks such as
Resolution CNE/CP No. 1/2012 (National Guidelines for Human Rights
Education), which establishes the need for these themes to be integrated across
all stages of basic education.
       Building a democratic culture in schools requires more than the
formalization of school councils or the existence of internal elections. It demands
a daily pedagogy of listening, respect for differences, and the active promotion of
social justice. As argued by Veiga (2008) and Freire (1996), the school must be
a space of emancipation rather than domination, a place where individuals feel
recognized in their multifaceted humanity.
       Finally, it is important to highlight that, in contrast to these exclusionary
practices, it was possible to observe the actions of individuals—particularly
special education teachers and pedagogical coordinators—who seek to
challenge these logics and create spaces of welcome and care. These actions,
though still scattered and lacking effective institutional support, demonstrate that
resistance to exclusion and the normalization of inequality also manifests itself in
small, everyday gestures and commitments, as we will see in the following
section.


4.4 SOLIDARITY AND MICRO-RESISTANCE AS EDUCATIONAL POTENTIAL


       Despite the countless challenges faced by the school staff—ranging from
a scarcity of material resources to the rigidity of authoritarian structures—the
supervised internship also revealed significant manifestations of commitment,
affection, and solidarity in the daily life of Pinto Marques State School. These
actions, though often overlooked by institutional discourse, function as forms of
micro-resistance and a reaffirmation of the ethical meaning of educational
practice.
       During school events such as the June festival, Student Day, and the
environmental project, the involvement of various segments of the school
community was notable. Teachers, coordinators, administrative staff, students,


                                                                                 24

and even local merchants actively participated in the organization, donating
materials, time, and volunteer labor to ensure the activities took place. On these
occasions, the school seemed to suspend—albeit temporarily—the structural
tensions that mark its daily life, becoming a space for collective celebration,
belonging, and cultural expression.
       Far from being trivial, these experiences represent what Dubet (2004)
refers to as forms of moral commitment on the part of individuals to the school
institution. According to the author, even in contexts where the organizational
structure is fragile and working conditions are precarious, individuals find ways to
maintain a symbolic bond with the school, engaging in actions that reaffirm its
social legitimacy. These are everyday gestures that sustain the public school not
merely as a structure, but as a collective life project.
       Pedagogical coordinators, in particular, stood out as central figures in this
process of mobilization and care. In informal conversations, they reported that
even in the face of a recurring sense of professional devaluation and task
overload, they find motivation in interacting with students, especially when
witnessing the success stories of former students who now hold positions in
higher education or the formal labor market. This type of symbolic recognition—
though often not institutionalized—serves as an element of re-enchantment in
educational work, as Esteve (1999) highlights.
       Such practices demonstrate that public schools endure, in large part,
thanks to the ability of their professionals to sustain relationships of care, trust,
and affection, even in environments marked by precariousness. Freire (1996) had
already warned that hope is not passive waiting, but an active stance in the face
of reality. In the case of the school, this takes the form of an education that does
not give up on others, that believes in the potential of each individual, and that
refuses to accept exclusion or failure as inevitable.
       Another aspect observed was the role of affection in pedagogical
mediation. In many situations, teachers and staff compensated for the lack of
resources with creative strategies, improvised materials, and, above all,
empathetic listening. The pedagogical coordination office, for example, was
frequently occupied by students seeking emotional support, guidance, or simply
a place to be heard. This informal space of welcome contrasts with the



                                                                                  25

bureaucratic model that often organizes public schools and reveals a subjective
and ethical dimension of pedagogical work that cannot be overlooked.
       Finally, the continuation of these practices depends on an institutional
policy that goes beyond the goodwill of individuals. Although resistance and
innovation can be found in everyday life, it is essential that the state ensure
objective conditions so that the commitment to public education is
sustained in a structured manner. These micro-resistances need to be
recognized, valued, and strengthened by public policies that ensure adequate
funding, continuing professional development, democratic management, and the
recognition of education professionals.
       It can thus be concluded that the power of public schools lies in the
people who build them daily, in the small gestures and everyday commitments
that keep their social function alive. In times of institutional discredit, this daily life
of solidarity and resistance reaffirms the school as one of the last spaces for the
collective construction of the future


5. CONCLUSION


       The supervised internship in pedagogical coordination at Pinto Marques
State School provided an intense, critical, and formative experience, allowing for
a concrete understanding of the complexity involved in pedagogical work in public
schools. Far from being a mere curricular requirement, this experience proved to
be a powerful space for investigation, reflection on educational practices, and
awareness— —of the structural, political, and subjective challenges that
permeate school management.
       Throughout the process, it was possible to identify four major axes of
analysis that structured the reflection: (1) the centralization of power in school
management and the fragility of democratic participation; (2) the institutional
overload and marginalization of pedagogical coordination; (3) the reproduction of
exclusionary practices, particularly regarding gender and religiosity; and (4) the
forms of solidarity and micro-resistance that sustain the public purpose of the
school. These categories are not watertight but are continuously intertwined and
in tension within the school’s daily life, revealing profound contradictions between



                                                                                        26

official educational norms and the concrete practices experienced by those within
the school.
        The analysis demonstrated that, although Brazilian legislation establishes
clear guidelines on democratic management, teacher training, and equity, the
implementation of these principles in public schools still faces historical and
structural obstacles. The absence of mechanisms for listening, the authoritarian
institutional culture, the lack of material resources, and the lack of professional
recognition create an environment hostile to the development of emancipatory
educational practices. At the same time, the resistance of the participants, the
daily dedication of the professionals, and the emotional bond with the students
show that the public school remains a space of contestation, invention, and
potential.
        It is essential to recognize that pedagogical coordination plays a strategic
role in mediating between the intent of the pedagogical project and the concrete
reality of the classroom. To this end, it is necessary to ensure not only adequate
training but also objective working conditions, institutional time for planning,
management support, and active participation in the school’s decision-making
processes. Without this, the pedagogical coordinator risks being reduced to a
technical-administrative agent, distanced from their role as an educator and
facilitator.
        From the perspective of teacher training, the internship demonstrated that
it is essential to move beyond a technical and passive view of educational
practice. The intern should not merely be an observer but a subject involved in
the process— —capable of critically interpreting reality, engaging in dialogue with
school stakeholders, and constructing knowledge through experience. As Freire
(1996) states, teaching requires courage, ethics, and hope—qualities that must
also be present in initial teacher training.
        Finally, this article reaffirms the importance of valuing public schools as
spaces for social transformation, but warns of the urgency of public policies that
ensure dignified conditions for their operation. Quality education cannot depend
solely on the resilience of professionals but must be a collective responsibility of
the state and society. May this internship report contribute, albeit modestly, to the
strengthening of a public, democratic, and socially grounded education system.

ABSTRACT: This article explores ““Caminhos Afetivos no Processo de
Construção do Sa-ber” and highlights the importance of sensitive research and
sensitivity in hu-man interactions. The proposal is to recognize that the
construction of knowle-dge transcends the mere collection of data,
encompassing the emotions, stori-es and relationships that shape the
experiences of individuals. By integrating affective elements into the research,
we promote a space for listening and res-pect, which is essential for the formation
of more collective and transformative knowledge. We have tried to detail the
experience of entering the Professional Master's in Sociology, highlighting the
welcoming faculty and the importance of research methodology as a field of
exploration. Research is presented not just as a technical process, but as a
practice that involves the subjectivity of the researcher and the participants,
highlighting the need for an empathetic and inclusive approach. Finally, we
consider that sensitive research transforms the construction of knowledge into a
relational act, where affectivity plays a crucial role. This approach not only sheds
light on human experiences, but also pro-motes a more meaningful and
welcoming learning environment, emphasizing the importance of cultivating
sensitivity in investigative processes.

KEYWORDS: construction, knowledge, affectivity, reception.

RESUMO: Este artigo explora os “Caminhos Afetivos no Processo de
Construção do Sa-ber”, e destaca a importância da pesquisa sensível e da
sensibilidade nas inte-rações humanas. A proposta é reconhecer que a
construção do conhecimento transcende a mera coleta de dados, englobando as
emoções, histórias e rela-ções que moldam as experiências dos indivíduos. Ao
integrar elementos afeti-vos na pesquisa, promovemos um espaço de escuta e
respeito, essencial para a formação de um conhecimento mais coletivo e
transformador. Procuramos detalhar a experiência de ingresso no Mestrado
Profissional em Sociologia, ressaltando a acolhida do corpo docente e a
importância da metodologia de pesquisa como campo de exploração. A pesquisa
é apresentada não apenas como um processo técnico, mas como uma prática
que envolve a subjetividade do pesquisador e dos participantes, ressaltando a
necessidade de uma abor-dagem empática e inclusiva. Por fim, consideramos
que a pesquisa sensível transforma a construção do conhecimento em um ato
relacional, onde a afeti-vidade desempenha um papel crucial. Essa abordagem
não apenas ilumina as experiências humanas, mas também promove um
ambiente de aprendiza-gem mais significativo e acolhedor, enfatizando a
importância de cultivar a sensibilidade nos processos investigativos.

PALAVRAS-CHAVE: construção, saber, afetividade, acolhimento.

1. INTRODUCTION


                                                                            THE STEPS
                                                Don’t walk down the steps of the dream
                                                         Lest you awaken the monsters.
                                                    Do not climb into the attics—where
                                                          The gods, behind their masks,
                                                                 Hide their own enigma.
                                                       Don’t go down, don’t go up, stay.
                                                            The mystery lies in your life!
                                                And this world of ours is a mad dream...
                                                                          Mário Quintana


      We begin this writing with a poem by Mário Quintana, which makes us
reflect on our dreams and the steps we will take to achieve them. We live
dreaming of many things, and often, as we dream and strive to make them a
reality, we think only of the joys they might bring us. But does this pursuit bring
only joy? Of course not! Soon come the setbacks; after all, the path of
knowledge—just like any quest for something we wish to be or do—is full of
challenges: sometimes linear, sometimes winding."
      This article is titled “Affective Pathways in the Process of Knowledge
Construction” and aims to engage in a dialogue with the references presented to
us throughout the research methodology course in the Professional Master’s
Program in Sociology within the National Network—PROFSOCIO—at UNEMAT
(Mato Grosso State University).
      We must be willing to overcome the difficulties that may arise, for it is a
journey requiring great self-sacrifice, focus, and determination, overcoming fears
and anxieties. It is part of a teacher’s professional journey to be in constant
motion in their development. Along this path, we encounter people with different
ways of being, acting, and thinking, who build knowledge and affective memories
with us. The importance of this professional development lies in the fact that
society is in a state of constant transformation, which directly impacts the
educational landscape.
      New knowledge, discoveries, and innovations emerge regularly, requiring
teachers to stay up to date to better meet students’ needs, integrate new
pedagogical approaches, and utilize new teaching methods that promote
meaningful learning consistent with current reality. Thus, as Freire tells us:
“Teaching requires conscious decision-making” (1996, p. 122).



                                                                                       32

       Seeking new knowledge is a conscious decision-making process. At some
point in our lives, a sense of restlessness arises that drives us to seek something
more to enhance our professional development, and this search involves various
participating actors, since “the search is an internal desire, a unique movement,
and at the same time, one that provokes interference in the environment, for the
mobilization of one will always involve the other; hence the importance of
relationships” (Oliveira and Silva, 2016, p. 50). Every movement in search of
something new— —generates another, in everything and everyone around us.
       Through this approach, we aim to highlight the value of sensitivity in
research, demonstrating how emotions and affections can enrich and transform
educational practice. The support of friends, the understanding of coworkers, and
the patience and affection of family are essential. All are part of a vast web of
relationships that are absolutely necessary for the learning and improvement
process to unfold as smoothly as possible.


2. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK


       When we entered the Professional Master’s Program in Sociology
Education in the National Network (PROFSOCIO), our expectations of what we
would encounter and experience were intense and worrisome, as we were
beginning to explore an unknown world of scientific knowledge—one that,
according to what many had told us, would be very difficult, tense, stressful, and
lonely, potentially even leading to mental health issues.
       The first meeting of the 2024/01 class, held in March of this year, shattered
several paradigms by welcoming us so warmly. The professors, with their
distinguished doctoral degrees, demonstrated humility and warmth in every
gesture, word, and even in the way they dressed. This warm welcome made us
feel instantly part of that world, as if we had been there for a long time.
       Within the complexity of the academic world, the discipline of research
methodology emerges as a fertile field for exploring the diverse facets of
knowledge. The tireless work of artists of the word—as our professor of this
discipline says, deeply rooted in the tradition of cordel literature—invites us to a
sensitive and poetic reflection on the practice of educational research.
       The integration of sensitivity into educational research requires a paradigm


                                                                                 33

shift that goes beyond traditional methodologies. The texts compiled by Débora
Alves Feitosa et al. in the work *O Sensível e a* *Sensibilidade na Pesquisa em
Educação* (2016) point to paths for this transformation, as they propose
sensitivity and affectivity as legitimate and necessary components of the
investigative process. By incorporating these dimensions, research becomes a
space where subjectivity is valued, promoting a richer and more multifaceted
understanding of educational phenomena:


                      The gaze that scrutinizes produces the world that produces it. What is
                      seen of the world is perceived by a gaze, already informed by the
                      (re)connection and relationship with the world seen, steeped in
                      cognitive and intellectual reasons, emotions, sensations, and intuitions.
                      It is a gaze overflowing with ethical, aesthetic, and affective dispositions
                      (Dorneles, 2003, p. 32, cited in Dorneles; Arenhaldt, 2016, pp. 31–32).


       In our journey through “Investigative Paths III: Risks and Possibilities of
Researching at the Frontiers” (2005), a work edited by Marisa Vorraber Costa
and Maria Isabel Edelweiss Bujes, we encounter the urgency of recognizing
subjectivity as an ally in the construction of knowledge. In contemplating the
nuances of affective paths, we highlight the importance of an investigative stance
that values both feeling and thinking, and that promotes an epistemology that
embraces the wholeness of the human being in the construction of knowledge.
In this way, we hope to contribute to a more holistic and humanized
understanding of educational research, where sensitivity is not merely an
accessory but an essential guide on this journey in search of knowledge.
       Research is not limited to a mere technical process, but extends into a
practice that incorporates the hearts, thoughts, and experiences of both
researchers and research participants. Becoming emotionally engaged with the
subject of study fosters a deeper and richer relationship, in which knowledge is
constructed within a web of multiple, interconnected meanings. Thus, the
researcher becomes not merely an observer, but an active participant, whose
emotional and intellectual journey intertwines with their field of research.
       The texts we explored during the Research Methodology course,
especially the works “The Sensible and Sensibility in Qualitative Research in
Education” (2016) and “Investigative Paths III: Risks and Possibilities of
Researching at the Frontiers” (2005), serve as pillars in this theoretical



                                                                                               34

framework, offering us a unique perspective on the relationship between research
and affect. These readings inspire us to reevaluate our methodologies and to
recognize the value of affect, personal histories, and human connections as
fundamental elements in the production of knowledge.
       As we embark on affective paths in the process of knowledge construction,
we discover the possibility of proposing a methodology that is more inclusive and
representative of the diverse dimensions of human experience. It is an invitation
to recognize the richness that comes from vulnerability, empathy, and sensitivity,
creating a research space where emotional and intellectual bonds mutually
reinforce one another, which enables a deep and transformative understanding
of the world around us.


2.1 THE INTEGRATION OF SENSITIVITY INTO EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH


       But after all, what motivates academic research in the humanities,
particularly in the teaching of Sociology? All research stems from a sense of
unease, which propels us toward an undefined path, for to research is to immerse
oneself in an infinite universe of possibilities, bringing new meaning to the specific
object of study; there is a starting point, and the paths are unpredictable; and on
this journey of discovery, research may present itself in a less pragmatic way.
The sensitivity of the scientific gaze brings multiple possibilities that go beyond
what is presented to it.
       The researcher must shed prejudices and predefined notions to extract
from the depths a new facet, a new perspective on what, a priori, seemed
immutable. Following solid and well-established theoretical frameworks becomes
necessary to lend credibility and robustness to the concepts that will become the
pillars of future research. The researcher must leave their mark on the research
with their identity so that it does not become a mere reproduction of previously
researched writings, for “reality can be understood through phenomenology in
diverse forms, as many as there are understandings and interpretations, and
thus, innumerable” (Gil, 2008, cited in Almeida, 2021, p. 15). A solid foundation
serves to consolidate what one proposes to reinterpret, for times change,
concepts evolve, and writing must be dynamic, not static.



                                                                                   35

                      When we use an author in academic writing, we in a way rewrite them;
                      we appropriate them and continue their work; we challenge the concept
                      they created; we subject a theory to discussion, because we immerse
                      it in the empirical, in the study of an object we have selected, which
                      goes beyond the objects the chosen author selected, precisely because
                      our history is different, our places and times are different. To rewrite an
                      author, to appropriate them, is to sift through their theoretical
                      formulations, a meeting point with ourselves, with what we have chosen
                      as our object, with what we have invested in—our life, our work, our
                      thought—has to do with a commitment, our commitment to a theme, to
                      an object, to a way of thinking, which we embrace as researchers
                      (Fischer, 2005, p. 120).


      Writing, in this context, becomes an art, for through words the researcher
reinvents themselves, questions, agrees, and disagrees, recording their
existence and essence. This process is an intentional search for answers to the
concerns that trouble them. Thus, “this is the great challenge, this is the great
exercise of what I here call the conversion of the gaze in academic writing,
understood as self-care, a writing of the self, and an expression of the art of
existence” (Fischer, 2005, p. 125).
      Academic discourse can be seen as a defense of an existential discourse,
reflecting our beliefs and aspirations to transform both our personal reality and
the world around us, observed through a particular lens. We mobilize the
concerns that drive us to become researchers, using science to deepen our
investigations. This process allows us to rediscover our own trajectory, fostering
critical self-reflection on the reality we seek to understand. What motivates us to
engage in research can stem from various factors: pain, violence, abuse,
repression, neglect, among many other possibilities. How can we address such
themes without being carried away by passion and personal feelings? It is
precisely at this moment that we must approach the subject with lightness and
remain open to listening, attentive to every detail within the complexity that
surrounds our object of study. In Ficsher (2005), we read that:


                      When we write and think, we separate ourselves from ourselves, from
                      our origins, from our legacies; we die a little, and in that very instant we
                      appear, we reveal, we cast a fleeting light on something that concerns
                      us, on something that pains us in our time, on something that is beautiful
                      in these times and places and perhaps is not being sufficiently spoken
                      of (Fischer, 2005, p. 131).


      Research can be conducted with a light touch; we are thus invited to
understand the importance of methods in the scientific realm, filled with


                                                                                               36

challenges, experiments, evaluations, and intense learning. In this universe, we
are driven by a constant search for answers, experiences, and challenges that
lead us to the new. As historical agents, we are biographical bodies, and our
bodies speak for us through everything we have stored in our life journey (Oliveira
e Silva, 2016); we produce an ethical-affective learning process, where we are
our own object of study, seeking to understand who we are, how we became who
we are, and what we can still become.


                      Our researched-researcher bodies bring forth/speak of trajectories,
                      choices, energies, lacks, absences, and images of imaginary states. It
                      is also in this group space, as a training device, that biographical
                      bodies—understood as the matter in which human memories resulting
                      from lived experiences are imprinted—meet and amplify energies,
                      negatively or positively [...] (Oliveira and Silva, 2016, p. 58).


      The meaning of the gaze—the way we approach our concerns—provides
new perspectives. Through research and inquiry, including experiments,
challenges, impartiality, and impersonality, we enter the field of the humanities
and social sciences, transforming desires and fostering a reinterpretation of
ourselves. The lightness of research guides us toward a deep understanding of
differences and diversities, allowing for a critical exploration of reality. It is
essential to analyze the contexts in which these take shape within the various
forms of human relations; thus, academic constructs become drivers of change
in the issues under investigation.
      One of the main challenges in adopting this approach is the need to
reconnect reason with emotion. In the positivist tradition, there is a tendency to
value objectivity and measurability, often excluding affective and subjective
nuances. However, it is precisely this richness of human experiences that can
offer deeper and more transformative insights.
      By approaching the methodology with sensitivity, the researcher is invited
to create an empathetic and inclusive research environment. This can be seen in
the way interviews are conducted, in interactions with participants, and in the way
data is interpreted. For example, in research investigating the impact of
pedagogical practices on students’ emotional development, attention to personal
accounts, narratives, and life stories offers a more complete understanding of the
context and experiences of the individuals involved.



                                                                                         37

       The research process should be viewed as a dynamic and evolving
journey, where the researcher and the subject of study interact continuously and
reciprocally. This implies an ethical commitment to participants, where
confidentiality, respect, and active listening play fundamental roles. By respecting
and valuing the experiences and voices of participants, we create a space for
dialogue where knowledge is collaboratively co-produced.
       In addition, sensitivity in research requires constant self-reflection on the
part of the researcher. This means being aware of one’s own emotions, biases,
and perspectives, and how these elements can influence both the research
process and the interpretation of data. This critical self-analysis is vital to ensuring
that observation remains authentic and respectful of human complexities and
diversities.
       Adopting a sensitive and affective approach also leads us to reconsider
traditional forms of knowledge dissemination. Academic writing can benefit from
a more narrative and poetic style that reflects the depth and richness of the
human experiences involved. Such an approach not only makes knowledge more
accessible but also more engaging and meaningful to a broader audience.
       By exploring affective pathways in the construction of knowledge, we are
not only broadening our methodological horizons but also reaffirming the
importance of an education that is, at its core, human and holistic. By valuing
sensitivity and emotion in research, we contribute to a more inclusive, empathetic,
and transformative field of inquiry, where knowledge is a collaborative and
effectively engaged construction, though one that may, perhaps, give rise to
conflicting situations. Carlos Drummond de Andrade, in his poem “Pedras No
Meio do Caminho,” tells us:


                       In the middle of the road there was a rock. There was a rock in the
                       middle of the road. There was a rock. In the middle of the road there
                       was a rock. I will never forget that moment. In the life of my weary eyes.
                       I will never forget that in the middle of the road. There was a rock. There
                       was a rock in the middle of the road. In the middle of the path there was
                       a stone (Andrade, 1967, p.16).


       The poem “In the Middle of the Road” offers a powerful metaphor about
the obstacles and discoveries along that journey. The stones described in the
verses can symbolize life’s obstacles, prompting us to reflect on what we choose



                                                                                               38

as our goal from a professional perspective. It is up to us to decide whether we
will use the stones as excuses to give up, or whether we will move forward with
persistence and resilience, overcoming the various challenges and obstacles a
researcher may encounter. Just as in Drummond’s poem, these obstacles cannot
be ignored or underestimated. In fact, it is often these “stones” that define the
trajectory and depth of the research. This brings us to Bedin (2016), who states
that “poets always have something to say, with new expressions that prompt us
to feel and rethink recurring questions” (Bedin, 2016, p.71).
       Sensitive research is an approach that values empathy, ethics, and
attention to the subjective and emotional nuances of participants. This method is
particularly suited to capturing human complexities and challenges, going beyond
numbers and statistics to understand what truly matters to the people involved.
       For a sensitive researcher, every stumbling block represents an
opportunity for learning and reflection. It may be a methodological challenge,
such as adapting a questionnaire to respect the cultural diversity of participants,
or an emotional barrier, such as dealing with the painful personal stories that
emerge during interviews. Attention to these difficulties, and the way the
researcher interacts with them, can transform ordinary research into a profound
and meaningful study.
       Drummond shows us that the stone is not merely an obstacle, but also an
indelible mark on the memory: “I will never forget this event in the life of my weary
retinas.” Similarly, a sensitive researcher must never forget the challenging
moments that shaped their research. These difficulties are not meant to be
forgotten, but rather remembered and analyzed, for it is through them that true
growth occurs.
       “In the Middle of the Road” teaches us that it is our relationship with
obstacles—the stones—that defines the journey. In sensitive research, the way
challenges are faced and understood can lead to profound and valuable
discoveries, both for the researcher and for the study participants. The stones,
then, become not only difficulties to be overcome, but also significant milestones
that enrich our understanding of the world and human experiences.




                                                                                  39

3. CONCLUSION


      “Affective Pathways in the Process of Knowledge Construction” reminds
us that knowledge is the result of complex human interactions, shaped by
affections, experiences, and individual histories. Throughout this article, we have
explored how sensitive research stands out as a fundamental approach in this
construction, recognizing that emotional and empathetic relationships between
researchers and participants are central to a deep and truly meaningful
understanding.
      Sensitivity is an essential element in this context: it invites us to pay
attention not only to quantitative data and objective analyses, but also to the
subjective narratives and emotions that permeate each interaction. The
commitment to sensitive research implies a conscious effort to listen to, welcome,
and reflect on the experiences of others, fostering a space where all voices can
be heard and respected.
      By integrating affectivity into the process of knowledge construction, we
are able to transform the way we understand and interpret human experiences.
Sensitive research not only illuminates these experiences but also enriches the
epistemological repertoire, allowing us to address complex issues with greater
ease and new perspectives. In this process of knowledge construction, affectivity
plays a crucial role because it refers to the emotions, feelings, and bonds that
permeate the entire path of knowledge construction, fostering a more welcoming
and safe learning environment and more meaningful and lasting learning.
      By adopting an approach that integrates sensitivity, ethics, and critical
reflection, we are not only broadening the methodological horizon but also
reaffirming the importance of research that acknowledges the complexity of
human experience. This commitment not only enriches the field of the humanities
but also invites us to be more conscious, empathetic, and transformative
researchers, capable of constructing knowledge that resonates with the realities
and aspirations of society.
      The affective paths we have taken and/or will take throughout our research
reveal that the pursuit of knowledge is, in fact, a relational act. By adopting a
sensitive and affective stance, we not only broaden our theoretical understanding
but also become agents of social transformation, capable of recognizing and


                                                                                40

valuing the differences that enrich our journey. Therefore, as we look toward the
future of research, may we always remember the importance of cultivating
sensitivity in research processes, for it is in this that the true essence of
knowledge construction resides.

ABSTRACT: This study investigates the Foucauldian concept of apparatus and
its applica-tion to the analysis of the National High School Exam (Enem),
understood as a mechanism of control within the educational environment.
Established by the Ministry of Education (MEC) in 1998, the exam has become a
fundamental tool for accessing public and private higher education in Brazil,
especially after the implementation of educational policies such as SiSU, ProUni,
and FIES. The objective is to analyze Enem as a dispositif of power that regulates
and disci-plines the educational process. Based on bibliographic and
documentary re-search, the analysis is grounded in Michel Foucault’s notion of
apparatus, supplemented by the contributions of Giorgio Agamben and Gilles
Deleuze. The study also considers official documents and uses as its corpus the
Partici-pant’s Guide – Understand Your Score in the Enem (Brasil, 2021). Based
on the idea of the apparatus as a set of discourses, practices, and institutions
that shape subjectivities and regulate behaviors, it is argued that Enem, beyond
its evaluative function, materializes as a technology of power. Its adaptive as-
sessment model adjusts to individual and social differences, mobilizing subtle
forms of control that directly affect the constitution of subjects. In this sense, the
configuration of Enem as an apparatus makes it possible to understand the exam
as an essential instrument in the maintenance and reproduction of pow-er and
exclusion dynamics within Brazilian education.

KEYWORDS: education, discourse, apparatus, enem, higher education.



                                                                                   43

RESUMO: O estudo investiga o conceito de dispositivo foucaultiano e sua
aplicação na análise do Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio (Enem),
compreendido como um mecanismo de controle no ambiente educacional.
Instituído pelo Ministério da Educação (MEC) em 1998, o exame consolidou-se
como uma ferramenta fundamental para o acesso ao Ensino Superior público ou

educacionais, como o SiSU, o ProUni e o FIES. O objetivo é analisar o Enem
como um dispositivo de poder que regula e disciplina o processo educativo.
Partindo de uma pesquisa bibliográfica-documental, a análise fundamenta-se no
conceito de dispositivo de Michel Foucault, complementado pelas contribuições
de Giorgio Agamben e Gilles Deleuze. A análise também contempla documentos
oficiais e toma como corpus o Guia do Participante – Entenda a sua nota no
Enem (Brasil, 2021). Com base na noção de dispositivo como conjunto de
discursos, práticas e instituições que moldam subjetividades e regulam
comportamentos, defende-se que o Enem, para além de sua função avaliativa,
se concretiza como tecnologia de poder. Seu modelo de avaliação adaptativa
ajusta-se às diferenças individuais e sociais, mobilizando formas sutis de
