1. INTRODUCTION


       Over the past few years, the National High School Exam (Enem) has
established itself as one of the primary assessment and selection tools for
admission to higher education in Brazil. Created in 1998 by the Ministry of
Education, the exam has undergone several reforms, expanding its influence and
becoming a central component of the country’s educational policies. Beyond its
evaluative function, the Enem can be understood as a mechanism that articulates
knowledge and power, shaping pedagogical practices, subjectivities, and life
trajectories.
       In contemporary Brazilian education, the Enem serves as the primary
mechanism for accessing higher education, whether through the competition for
spots via the Unified Selection System (SiSU) at public universities, or through
obtaining scholarships from the University for All Program (ProUni) or financing
from the Student Financing Fund (FIES) at private institutions. Given the exam’s
importance in the academic lives of millions of students, reflecting on its
configuration as a mechanism allows us to examine the subtle modes of control
and regulation that permeate the educational field.
       Starting from the question of how the Enem functions as a device for
access to higher education, this study aims to analyze its constituent elements
within the educational field. To this end, we investigate the history of the exam’s
creation, the concept of the device, and the materialization of this logic in the
Participant’s Guide – Understand Your Enem Score (Brazil, 2021). The
methodology adopted combines bibliographic and documentary research. The
bibliographic research allowed for a theoretical deepening based on the
assumptions of Michel Foucault (1969; 1977; 1995; 1998; 1999; 2000; 2008;
2014; 2022), Giorgio Agamben (2005; 2009), and Gilles Deleuze (1992; 1996),
whose contributions are fundamental to understanding the device as a
technology of power. The documentary research, on the other hand, consisted of
an analysis of official documents from the Ministry of Education (MEC) and the
Anísio Teixeira National Institute for Educational Studies and Research (INEP),
with a focus on the corpus comprising the aforementioned Participant’s Guide.
       Based on this approach, we have organized the article into three parts.
The first presents the history of the creation and development of the Enem, its


                                                                                45

reformulations over the years, and the process of systematizing the Participant’s
Guide. The second part discusses the notion of the “device” from a Foucauldian
perspective, drawing on the contributions of Agamben and Deleuze, situating its
configuration within the context of the Enem. Finally, the third part proposes a
discursive analysis of what is said and what is left unsaid in the Participant’s
Guide, highlighting the effects of power produced by this discursive apparatus.


2. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK


2.1 THE ENEM IN PERSPECTIVE: FROM THE CREATION TO THE
SYSTEMATIZATION OF THE PARTICIPANT’S GUIDE


      The 1990s were a period of great challenges for education in Brazil. The
national landscape was characterized by stark socioeconomic and regional
inequalities, high rates of school dropout and grade repetition, low-quality
education, limited public funding, as well as educational reforms and pressures
stemming from globalization and the demands of the labor market. In response
to these challenges, the Ministry of Education (MEC) created the ENEM as an
tool to assess the quality of secondary education in the country and provide a
benchmark for student self-assessment. The creation of the exam was formalized
through Ministerial Ordinance No. 438, dated May 28, 1998, signed by then-
Minister Paulo Renato Souza. This ordinance established the Enem as an
instrument for assessing the performance of high school graduates, with the aim
of contributing to the improvement of basic education, as described below:


                     Ministerial Ordinance No. 438, dated May 28, 1998
                     THE MINISTER OF STATE FOR EDUCATION AND SPORTS, in the
                     exercise of the powers conferred upon him by Article 87, sole
                     paragraph, item II, of the Constitution, hereby resolves:
                     Art. 1 To establish the National High School Exam (ENEM) with the
                     following objectives:
                     I - To assess student performance at the end of basic schooling;
                     II - To inform public policies aimed at improving the quality of basic
                     education;
                     III - To contribute to improving the quality of secondary education,
                     vocational education, and higher education;
                     IV - To promote certification upon completion of high school;
                     V - To support selection processes for admission to higher education
                     (Brazil, 1998).




                                                                                        46

      The first edition of the Enem took place in 1998, with 157,221 registered
participants, of whom 115,575 actually took the exam on August 20. Of the total,
83% were exempt from the R$20.00 registration fee. That year, although the
Enem results were accepted by only two higher education institutions, the exams
were administered in 184 cities across the country. The exam consisted of 63
multiple-choice questions and an essay, covering the areas of languages, codes,
and their technologies; humanities; natural sciences; and mathematics (Inep,
2020). The main objective was to serve as a benchmark for self-assessment and
contribute to the improvement of teaching in schools, based on an
interdisciplinary and contextualized approach that encouraged the practical
application of acquired knowledge.
      In 2009, following a major overhaul, a new Enem was introduced, which
became the primary means of admission to various public universities with the
implementation of SiSU. The exam replaced traditional entrance exams,
complementing ProUni, created in 2005 to offer scholarships for “ ” programs at
private institutions. This new version of the Enem included 180 multiple-choice
questions—45 for each subject area—and an essay, administered over two days.
It also began to serve as certification of high school completion. The exam’s
Reference Matrices were adjusted based on the Encceja competency
certification. In 2009, 4,138,025 candidates registered for exams held in 1,830
municipalities. That edition was marked by a leak of the exam, which led to the
development of a new monitoring mechanism.
      According to data released by Inep (2020), other changes were
implemented starting in 2010, aimed at improving the exam and addressing the
“challenges of national education.” Between 2010 and 2013, security and
logistical measures were strengthened, such as having police forces escort the
exams; specialized support for candidates with disabilities was expanded; Enem
results became a criterion for student financing through FIES; and most federal
institutions began adopting it as a selection method. The exam score also
became a criterion for awarding scholarships under the Sciences Without
Borders program.
      Continuing these changes, from 2014 to 2016, new guidelines were
established. In terms of social inclusion, a quota system was instituted for
students from public schools, Black and mixed-race individuals, Indigenous


                                                                             47

people, and people with disabilities. Regarding accessibility, exams were made
available in Braille, with enlarged fonts, and with sign language interpreters. Also
noteworthy are: the recognition of social names, the identification of “cheaters,”
the collection of biometric data, and the acceptance of the ENEM by some
Portuguese universities.
         As noted by Inep (Brazil, 2020), in 2017, following a public consultation,
the exam schedule was modified: it shifted from two consecutive days (Saturday
and Sunday) to two Sundays in a row, allowing for a longer rest period between
exams. Another new feature that year was the debut of a personalized test
bearing the participant’s name and registration number. In 2018, upon reaching
its 20th anniversary, the Enem received a new logo, a commemorative historical
document, and a series of mini-documentaries about its history. Requests for
exemption from the registration fee began to be made prior to the exam, and high
school certification became the exclusive responsibility of Encceja.
         Between 2019 and 2023, the Enem underwent further changes,
particularly due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Notable among these was the 2019
launch of Enem Digital as a pilot project, to be implemented in 2020, with a focus
on modernizing the exam administration. During this period, challenges arose,
such as: the postponement of exams in 2020; health protocols in 2021; the
expansion of Enem Digital and adjustments to the National Curriculum Guidelines
in 2022; and the return to the regular format only in 2023.
         Since its inception in 1998, and with its growing role as a pathway to higher
education at both public and private institutions, there has been a need to provide
clear information to applicants. In 2012, the Participant’s Guide was created,
followed by the Enem Participant’s Handbook. The guide was not created in
response to specific legislation, but is part of the efforts by Inep and MEC to
increase transparency and facilitate access to information. The guide provides
details on the structure of the exams, grading criteria, essay-writing guidelines,
and study suggestions. The booklet, in turn, complements the guide with rules of
conduct, logistical guidelines, and examples of top-scoring essays. The booklet
was formalized by Ordinance No. 1,021, dated December 19, 2013, as noted
below:




                                                                                   48

                     Ordinance No. 1,021, dated December 19, 2013
                     THE MINISTER OF EDUCATION, in the exercise of the powers
                     conferred upon him by Article 87, sole paragraph, item II, of the
                     Constitution, and in view of the provisions of Articles 205 and 214 of the
                     Constitution, hereby resolves:
                     Art. 1 The National High School Exam (ENEM) Participant’s Handbook
                     is hereby established, with the objective of providing candidates with
                     detailed information about the exam.
                     Art. 2 The Participant’s Handbook shall contain, among other
                     information:
                     I - A detailed description of the subject areas assessed in the ENEM:
                     Languages, Codes, and their Technologies; Mathematics and its
                     Technologies; Natural Sciences and their Technologies; Human
                     Sciences and their Technologies.
                     II - Guidelines on the ENEM essay, including grading criteria, examples
                     of essays that received top marks, and topics from previous essays.
                     III - Study and preparation tips, study strategies, time management, and
                     relaxation techniques.
                     IV - Instructions regarding the day of the exam, including what to bring,
                     schedules, security procedures, and permitted and prohibited conduct.
                     Art. 3 The Participant’s Handbook shall be prepared and published
                     annually by the Anísio Teixeira National Institute for Educational
                     Studies and Research (INEP).
                     Art. 4 This Ordinance enters into force on the date of its publication
                     (Brazil, 2013).


      In 2021, INEP published on its website an update to the Participant’s Guide
– Understanding Your ENEM Score, with the aim of clarifying participants’
questions regarding exam scores, specifically the test-scoring methodology, the
Item Response Theory (IRT). To achieve this goal, the Participant’s Guide is
organized in a didactic manner and is divided into six sections: “Calculating the
Score,” “Understanding Other Aspects of the IRT Model,” “Grading Procedures,”
“Question Development Process,” “Common Questions About the ENEM Score,”
and “Technical Understanding of the IRT Score.” According to Inep (Brazil, 2021),
this document does not address the grading of the essay, as it has its own
methodology, detailed in the Participant’s Handbook.
      To complement this set of materials, the MEC and Inep publish the Enem
announcement annually in the Federal Official Gazette, including the schedule,
guidelines, rules, and deadlines for participation. The announcement stipulates
that candidates, before registering, must carefully read the document and the
regulatory acts referenced therein, in order to confirm their acceptance of all
conditions and requirements necessary to take the exam (Brazil, 2024).
      From this historical perspective, we observe that the Enem is a tool that
goes beyond the function of a mere selective exam. Created as a response to
the challenges faced by Brazilian education in the 1990s, it plays a significant


                                                                                            49

role in democratizing access to higher education, assessing the quality of basic
education, encouraging study, promoting social inclusion, and fostering academic
mobility in both public and private institutions. At the heart of this assessment
policy, we highlight the Participant’s Guide, whose structure, content, and
communicative function demand a more in-depth analysis. To this end, in the next
chapter, we propose to investigate the guide as an expression of a modern
pedagogical apparatus, grounded in Michel Foucault’s theoretical framework.


2.2 POWER AND KNOWLEDGE: THE CONFIGURATION OF A FOUCAULTIAN
DISPOSITIVE IN THE ENEM


       In order to understand how the Participant’s Guide fits into the fabric of
power-knowledge that structures the ENEM, it is necessary to draw upon the
notion of “device,” formulated by Michel Foucault. This concept, established as
an analytical tool in this study, was developed by Foucault in his work The History
of Sexuality, specifically in “The Will to Knowledge.” In this context, during an
interview with the International Psychoanalytical Association (IPA), the author
highlights this theoretical framework as a case of a more generalized “episteme,”
defined as:


                      [...] a decidedly heterogeneous set that encompasses discourses,
                      institutions, architectural organizations, regulatory decisions, laws,
                      administrative measures, scientific statements, philosophical, moral,
                      and philanthropic propositions. In short, the said and the unsaid are the
                      elements of the dispositif. The dispositif is the network that can be
                      woven between these elements (Foucault, 2000, p. 244).


       Given this definition, it is necessary to understand the relationships woven
between these elements to construct a discursive network capable of establishing
power and control. According to Foucault (2008), this weaving, at its origin,
requires two strategic planes: one for choosing the object and the other for its
fulfillment, thus composing the entire dynamism of the dispositif. From this
perspective, if the apparatus fails to meet pre-established economic and social
aspirations, other forms of knowledge are produced with the aim of filling the gaps
so that the dominant dynamic may prevail. Thus, it is evident that, in this strategy,




                                                                                            50

there is no single strategist, but rather a combination of power relations that
ultimately take on a practical meaning and culminate in a punitive society.
       In contemporary education, this notion is fundamental to understanding
how different elements combine to produce and control knowledge. Given this, in
light of the educational challenges faced in the 1990s, there was a need to rethink
school dynamics and propose a new mechanism that would maintain the
relationships between knowledge and power. To this end, the Ministry of
Education (MEC) created the ENEM, which can be analyzed as a mechanism
that standardizes and evaluates students’ academic performance, but also
establishes antagonistic standards of excellence and insufficiency that directly
influence access to higher education. Thus, the provisions contained in
Ministerial Ordinance No. 438, dated May 28, 1998, confirm this antagonism.
       For Foucault (2014), discourse is a concept that extends beyond its
monological function but encompasses metalinguistic factors. Discourses, as well
as those who produce them, convey positions and interests even when these are
underlying linguistic/phonetic codes. Thus, the author asserts that “discourses as
we can hear them, as we can read them in the form of text, are not, as one might
expect, a pure and simple interweaving of things and words” (Foucault, 2022, p.
59), but a linguistic strategy that articulates relations of power and domination.
Based on this conception, the ENEM, by encompassing a “set of rules” imposed
on participants, effectively qualifies this “discursive practice.”


                       These rules define not the silent existence of a reality, not the canonical
                       use of a vocabulary, but the regime of objects. “Words and Things” is
                       the—serious—title of a problem; it is the—ironic—title of the work that
                       modifies its form, displaces its data, and reveals, after all, an entirely
                       different task, which consists of no longer treating discourses as sets of
                       signs (signifying elements that refer to contents or representations), but
                       as practices that systematically form the objects they speak of
                       (Foucault, 2022, p. 60).


       As pointed out by Foucault (2022), the set of rules established since the
creation of the ENEM is what defines the regime of its practical application.
Teaching and assessment methods, in this context, function as devices for
regulating behavior and knowledge. In the school environment, pedagogical
practices and curricular content are frequently adjusted to align with the exam’s
criteria, transforming it into an instrument of control that guides both teaching and



                                                                                               51

learning. Foucault (1977) also argues that educational institutions operate in a
manner similar to prisons, as they employ surveillance and disciplinary
procedures to shape student behavior—such as the administration of
assessments that follow the exam’s required standards—thereby monitoring
student performance. Thus, “the exam combines the techniques of the hierarchy
that surveils and those of the sanction that normalizes” (Foucault, 1977, p. 185).
       According to Chignola (2014, p. 7), “a device is, therefore, first and
foremost, the point of connection between heterogeneous elements: discourses,
yes, but also regulations, architectural solutions, administrative decisions,
philosophical and moral propositions, and technologies.” From this perspective,
this point of connection is essential for achieving the intended strategic goal.
Schools, for example, are “fueled” by the applicability of this practice. This,
according to the author, generates consequences that can enhance this point of
connection, but also highlight the hierarchy of power that exists, implicitly, within
the educational system.
       Building on the more generalized notion of “episteme” developed by
Foucault, Agamben (2005, p. 11) emphasizes that this network established
among the distinct constituent elements of the apparatus possesses a dominant
strategic function based on its enunciative practices, which refer to “mechanisms
(at once linguistic and non-linguistic, legal, technical, and military) aimed at
addressing an urgency and achieving an effect.” In the case of the ENEM, “this
urgency to achieve an effect” manifests itself in the political changes and
educational crises that drive adaptations to the exam, often announced as
provisional but which, over time, end up becoming permanent. An example of this
practice was the implementation of stricter security and logistical measures,
including the escorting of exam materials by police forces in 2010, due to the leak
of exam questions that occurred in the 2009 edition.
       That said, Agamben (2005, p. 13) defines a “device” as follows:


                      I shall literally call a device anything that in some way has the capacity
                      to capture, guide, determine, intercept, shape, control, and ensure the
                      gestures, behaviors, opinions, and discourses of living beings. Not only,
                      therefore, prisons, asylums, the panopticon, schools, confessions,
                      factories, disciplines, legal measures, etc., whose connection to power
                      is in a certain sense evident, but also the pen, writing, literature,
                      philosophy, agriculture, the cigarette, navigation, computers, cell
                      phones, and—why not—language itself, which is perhaps the oldest of



                                                                                             52

                      these devices, in which thousands and thousands of years ago a
                      primate—likely without realizing the consequences that would follow—
                      had the unconsciousness to allow itself to be captured.


      Based on all this capacity that Agamben attributes to the device, three
fundamental characteristics defined by Foucault (2008) are revealed:
heterogeneity, security through relations of force and power, and the strategic
function that serves as an apparatus to resolve an urgency. In this sense, the
ENEM becomes an adaptable device that perpetuates new forms of control and
regulation within the educational system. Thus, this relationship is established in
a space that is not always physical, but which can “correlate the device with
discourse” (Moruzzi, 2017, p. 289), for, according to Veyne (2009), discourse is
a “formal framework” through which the materialization of disciplining objects is
presented to us.
      Moruzzi (2017) points out that “a civilization is formed when individuals
begin to speak in accordance with the device of the moment, without there
necessarily being an effort or physical violence; individuals come to constitute
themselves within these devices.” That is, the device is what shapes the subject
in all their subjective dimensions of self, belonging to a civilization where power,
thought, and freedom operate. According to the author, this device “has a
productive relationship in society, just like power” (Moruzzi, 2017, p. 290). Thus,
by analyzing the discourse present in Ministerial Ordinance No. 438, which
established the exam as an instrument for evaluating the performance of students
completing high school, with the aim of contributing to the improvement of the
quality of basic education, one can understand this relationship between
productivity and power in contemporary society.
      In line with the concepts presented by Agamben, Deleuze (1996) observes
that devices are constituted by lines of visibility and enunciation—that is,
mechanisms that operate “making see” and “making speak”—sustained by lines
of force that, at any moment, can be diverted or transformed into lines of flight.
These lines, therefore, are not fixed but subject to variations and displacements.
Deleuze (1996, p. 1) defines this dynamic by stating that the lines do not “delimit
or enclose homoge y systems on their own, such as the object, the subject,
language, etc., but follow directions, trace processes that are always in
disequilibrium, and that now approach and now move away from one another.”


                                                                                       53

In this sense, considering the ENEM as a standardized apparatus, these “lines”
not only delimit a homogeneous system of assessment but are also in constant
“variations and derivations” to meet educational, social, and cultural demands.
       In the context of this study, Foucault’s notion of the “device,”
complemented primarily by the perspectives of Agamben and Deleuze, allows us
to understand the dynamics of power and control present in contemporary
education by identifying how this concept of the device is configured in the ENEM.
To delve a little deeper into the research, we propose a discussion of the linguistic
aspects present in the ENEM Participant’s Guide—the document that “dictates”
or “does not dictate” the set of rules applied in the exam.
       Given this conceptual framework built upon the works of Foucault,
Agamben, and Deleuze, we understand that the ENEM functions as a dispositif
that operates in the production and regulation of subjectivities through
normalizing discursive practices. In this sense, it is essential to analyze the Enem
Participant’s Guide, a document that embodies, in normative and prescriptive
language, what is expected of exam participants. It is within this discursive space
that the apparatuses of power that regulate behavior and the silenced
meanings—the said and the unsaid—are simultaneously revealed, thus
constituting a privileged field for the critical analysis of language as a technology
of control.


3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION


       Continuing the reflection on the Enem as a Foucauldian device, this
section proposes a critical analysis of the Participant’s Guide – Understand Your
Enem Score, based on the theoretical assumptions of Foucault, Agamben, and
Deleuze. The analysis is grounded in the notion of discourse as a practice that
produces knowledge and power, seeking to understand how the guide’s linguistic
con t operates not only through what it explicitly states, but also through strategies
of silencing, exclusion, or naturalization of meanings. By highlighting the tension
between what is stated and what is omitted, the aim is to demonstrate how the
guide contributes to the consolidation of a governmental rationality, establishing
a mechanism for controlling access to higher education in the contemporary era,



                                                                                   54

while simultaneously legitimizing evaluation criteria and desirable behaviors,
rendering conflicts, disputes, and contradictions present in the process invisible.
      In The Genealogy of Power, Foucault (1969) offers a powerful tool for
deconstructing traditional ways of understanding history and power relations, as
he helps us understand how norms, institutions, and subjects are historically
constituted and politically conditioned. To apply Foucault’s concept of “the said
and the unsaid” to the ENEM Participant’s Guide, it is important to highlight how
Foucault understands the relationship between what is explicitly stated (the said)
and what is implicit or omitted (the unsaid) in discourses. According to him, power
and knowledge are exercised not only through what is articulated, but also
through omissions, implied structures, and the rules governing what can be said;
that is, “what is said is determined by what is not said; it is structured against a
background of the unsaid” (Foucault, 1969, p. 112).
      Since the creation of the Enem, the Inep has sought to fulfill the exam’s
objectives, which entailed the need to establish criteria that would ensure an
assessment considered fair by the participants. From this perspective, several
questions have become recurrent among candidates: “How is my Enem score
calculated? Why did I answer more questions correctly this year than last year,
yet my score is lower? What is the weight of each question on the Enem? Why
don’t those who answer all questions correctly receive a score of 1000, or why
don’t those who get all questions wrong receive a score of 0?” (Brazil, 2021, p.
5). In response to these questions, in 2012, Inep implemented the Participant’s
Guide – Understanding Your Enem Score, updated in 2021, with the purpose of
explaining the test scoring methodology—the TRI—through an educational
framework designed to guide candidates.
      Given this theoretical framework, which conceives of discourse as a field
of forces in which both the spoken and the unspoken operate, we now turn to an
analysis of the Participant’s Guide – Understanding Your ENEM Score (2021).
Below, we will explore the explicit statements present in the document, seeking
to identify how they relate to the strategies of control and normalization described
by Foucault, Agamben, and Deleuze.




                                                                                 55

3.1 VOICES IN FOCUS: UNVEILING THE SAID IN DISCOURSES


       The 2021 ENEM Participant’s Guide – Understand Your Score provides a
detailed explanation of how scores are calculated using Item Response Theory
(IRT). According to the document, “to measure is to evaluate something using a
measuring instrument and compare it to a standard” (INEP, 2021, p. 7). However,
when this notion of “measurement” is applied to an abstract field such as
knowledge—represented by the skills described in the ENEM Reference
Matrices—it becomes necessary to resort to a concrete element that allows for
this measurement: the test. Thus, the assessment is structured based on a
standardized proficiency scale, which enables its pedagogical interpretation, as
demonstrated in the figure presented in the guide itself.


                           Figure 1. ENEM Proficiency Scale




                              Source: Brazil, 2021, p. 10.


       This scale is fundamental to understanding how candidates are assessed,
and there is one for each area of knowledge. The questions are divided into easy
and difficult and are positioned at the bottom and top of the scale, respectively.
According t (Brazil, 2021), this is the key distinguishing feature of the TRI, as both
the questions and the participants are positioned on the same scale and use the
same proficiency scale.
       For Foucault (2000), the device is defined as a heterogeneous network
that includes discourses, institutions, laws, and administrative measures
coordinated to address a specific emergency. In this case, the guide is part of an
educational device that, by placing students on “a single scale and using the
same proficiency scale,” standardizes and regulates participants’ performance at




                                                                                   56

the national level. Thus, this positioning “generates a process of the modern
state’s governmentalization” (Gonçalves, 2013, p. 109), understood as a


                      set consisting of the institutions, procedures, analyses and reflections,
                      calculations, and tactics that enable the exercise of this very specific
                      and complex form of power, which targets the population, primarily
                      through political economy and essential technical instruments, namely
                      security devices (Foucault, 1998, p. 291–292).


       From this perspective, the guide’s explicit discourse on the objectivity and
precision of the TRI, which employs “procedures, calculations, and tactics,” is a
clear example of how assessment practices are standardized, naturalized, and
ensure security. Thus, it becomes clear that “the apparatus is always inscribed in
a power play” (Foucault, 1995, p. 244), and, in the context of the ENEM, this
power is exercised through standardized assessment. Agamben (2009, p. 28)
emphasizes that, once a device is naturalized, its propagation becomes
imperceptible and at the same time compliant in the eyes of the government; that
is, “the device is always linked to a strategy of power.” Thus, it is undeniable that
the way the guide structures participants’ relationship with the exam—through
rigorous and detailed norms—creates a disciplined subjectivity in harmony with
the demands of the educational system.
       On the other hand, according to Deleuze (1992), devices embedded in a
society of control shape a constant labor. The TRI, for example, “models the
probability of a participant correctly answering a test item, based on the item’s
parameters and the participant’s proficiency” (Brasil, 2021, p. 24). We can affirm,
based on Deleuze (1996, p. 2), that this statement distributes “variables defined
by the regimes they give rise to,” such that “they are neither subjects nor objects,
but regimes that must be defined through the visible and the enunciable, with
their derivations, their transformations, and their mutations.” Thus, by detailing
how the TRI operates, the ENEM guide reveals the “visible regime” of control that
arises from the constant adaptation of assessment practices, shaping
participants’ expectations and behaviors in a subtle yet effective manner.
       In short, the analysis of the statements in the 2021 Enem Participant
Guide, relating them to the concepts of the “device” as proposed by Foucault,
Agamben, and Deleuze, demonstrates the functionality of this document as a
mechanism of power. In addition to regulating, disciplining, and modulating the


                                                                                            57

subjectivity of participants, it also promotes a vision of objective assessment at
the institutional level that is presented as fair on a national scale.


3.2 HIDDEN VOICES: REVEALING THE UNSPOKEN IN DISCURSIVE
STATEMENTS


       Beyond what is explicitly stated in the discursive statements of the 2021
ENEM Participant’s Guide – Understand Your Score, it is important to analyze
what is not said, exploring the document’s subtext and thus relating it to the
concepts of the “dispositif.” By revisiting the objective of creating the ENEM as a
fundamental instrument in democratizing access to higher education, in
assessing the quality of basic education, in encouraging students’ study and
preparation, in promoting social inclusion, and in facilitating academic mobility—
whether public or private—participants are consequently attributed a sense of
happiness when they achieve the desired success on the exam. According to
Agamben (2009, pp. 43–44), this happiness is part of the constitution of the
dispositif, for “at the root of every dispositif lies, in this way, an all-too-human
desire for happiness, and the capture and subjectivation— —of this desire, in a
separate sphere, constitute the specific power of the dispositif.”
       In this context, it is essential to realize that this “power” that generates the
subjectivation of the “desire for happiness” among participants does not reach
everyone. When they are measured by the same yardstick and use the same
proficiency scale modeled by the TRI for calculating scores, existing differences
in access to quality education in the country are not taken into account. For
Foucault (1977), the exercise of power will always be greater than its possession.
It is a fact that the guide includes a set of rules that demonstrate objectivity and
transparency; however, the structural inequalities that afflict the lives of
candidates during the exam preparation process are concealed.
       In the words of Bourdieu (1999, p. 75),


                       to the extent that the cultural capital embodied in the instruments of
                       production grows (and, for the same reason, the time required for its
                       embodiment for objective intent, its purpose, its function), the collective
                       power of the holders of cultural capital would tend to grow, if the holders
                       of the dominant form of capital were not in a position to pit the holders
                       of cultural capital against one another (who, incidentally, are inclined



                                                                                               58

                       toward competition by the very conditions of their selection and
                       training—and, in particular, by the logic of academic competition and
                       the entrance exam).


       The author helps us understand that the logic underlying the “competition”
of the exam establishes a selection of cultural capital—in this case, the
participants—originating from the holders of the instruments that produce it.
According to Agamben (2009), this is a strategy of power that produces
subjectivities and ways of life that constitute the apparatus. In the guide, the
pressures and anxieties that candidates face due to this logic of performance and
competition create subjectivities that discipline and shape them. In accordance
with the exam’s objectives, this takes the form of an unspoken element that
implicitly reinforces power and control within the official discursive statements.
       Related to this control, Deleuze (1992) argues that the adaptations and
adjustments made so that the “holders of the instruments” remain in power follow
a constant pattern, evident when observing changes in the exam’s historical c t
over the years. Thus, the TRI is presented in the guide as a fair and accurate tool,
that is, “a reliable method widely used in educational assessments and exams in
various countries” (Brazil, 2021, p. 13); however, what is left unsaid masks the
reality that students from diverse social and economic backgrounds face
difficulties in realizing their “desire for happiness.”
       Thus, the analysis of what is left unsaid in the Participant’s Guide shows
how the ENEM, by normalizing the TRI as a fair method, conceals social
inequalities that affect students. This silence is part of the mechanism that
produces subjectivities conformed to the exam’s criteria, reinforcing the logic of
power and control.


4. FINAL CONSIDERATIONS


       Since its creation in 1998, and as it has evolved significantly over the
years, the ENEM has become a very important tool for accessing higher
education in Brazil, particularly following the introduction of programs such as
SISU, ProUni, and FIES. This evolution demonstrates that Brazilian educational
policies have come to value a standardized national assessment as a means of
democratizing access to universities, both public and private.


                                                                                         59

       However, this assessment has also presented many challenges to the
educational system regarding equity and inclusion, as it does not account for
Brazil’s regional and socioeconomic inequalities, and this has a profound impact
on student performance. The unilateral application of the exam as a standardized
measure of knowledge is based on a meritocratic notion that lacks the depth to
assess students’ diverse subjectivities, as well as the hardships to which they are
subjected. Consequently, it is clear that there is an urgent need to implement
public policies that guarantee equal opportunities for all students.
       By understanding the concept of the “dispositif” as elaborated by Foucault,
and also debated by Agamben and Deleuze, we observe that this concept is
configured within the context of the ENEM, which also allows us to identify how
this exam functions as a mechanism of power and control within the Brazilian
educational context. As Foucault points out, the dispositif is a heterogeneous set
of correlated elements—discourses, institutions, norms, laws—that regulate and
discipline individuals. Thus, the centralized and standardized assessment
imposed by the ENEM acts as a dispositif that shapes the behavior and
subjectivity of participants.
       Agamben, in turn, also associates the device with the production of
subjectivities and ways of life, as he asserts that it not only controls but also
delineates the existence of subjects by “capturing” them. From this perspective,
the ENEM is not limited to merely assessing students’ knowledge but encourages
them to adapt to the idea of a meritocratic competition within the selection
process. Deleuze, on the other hand, defines devices as composed of lines of
visibility and enunciation, subject to variations and derivations. These “lines,”
when applied to the exam, demonstrate the existence of a rigid mechanism of
power, as over the years, the Enem has constantly adjusted to diverse conditions
to remain up-to-date and regulate educational practices.
       During the analysis of the Participant’s Guide, in light of the concepts
listed, we understand that the guide employs a well-planned criterion in the
constitution of power and control over students. Clearly, it offers a detailed
explanation of how scores are calculated using the TRI and its unique approach
to placing questions and participants on the same scale and using the same
proficiency scale, regardless of the educational conditions from which they
originate. The Participant’s Guide contains provisions that students perceive not


                                                                                60

merely as instructions, but as requirements for adaptation, that is, ordinances
requiring unilateral adherence. For Foucault, power manifests itself both in what
is said and in what is not said; thus, we observe that the guide explicitly states
the evaluation criteria but conceals the structural conditions unfavorable to
participants’ performance, such as regional and socioeconomic inequalities,
which are responsible for maintaining the hierarchies established by power.
      Based on this study, by analyzing the configuration of the ENEM as a
device in light of the concepts of Foucault, Agamben, and Deleuze, we identify
the exam- s a fundamental mechanism for the maintenance and reproduction of
the dynamics of power and exclusion in Brazilian education. Considering the
interrelationship between knowledge and power present in these concepts, an
important reflection emerges: why does the Ministry of Education (MEC)
guarantee the provision of basic education to students, yet simultaneously use
an instrument of control—the Enem—to select and determine access to higher
education? Could this be a strategy to prevent access to “knowledge” from
threatening or destabilizing the “power” exercised by dominant discourses?

ABSTRACT: This study explored the organization and memories of
pedagogical spaces in Professional and Technological Education (EPT),
addressing the challenge of adapting these environments to contemporary
educational demands and the needs for inclusion and innovation. The main
objective was to analyze how the configuration of these spaces influences the
teaching-learning process and contributes to the construction of institutional
identity. The methodology was based on aliterature review, examining
previous studies on the topic, relevant public policies, and examples of
innovative pedagogical practices. Results showed that pedagogical spaces
in EPT play a crucial role in promoting integrated and meaningful learning,
facing challenges related to technological updates and the maintenance of
an infrastructure that supports active learning methodologies. The final
considerations highlighted the need for continuous investments and effective
management for pedagogical spaces toevolve in a way that meets the
requirements of a qualified professional education aligned with labor market
and societal demands.

KEYWORDS: professional and technological education, pedagogical spaces,
educational innovation, institutional identity, inclusion.

RESUMO: Este estudo investigou a organização e memórias de espaços
pedagógicos na Educação Profissional e Tecnológica (EPT), abordando o
desafio de adaptar esses       ambientes    às    demandas     educacionais
contemporâneas        e    às necessidades de inclusão e inovação. O
objetivogeral foi analisar como a configuração desses espaços influencia o
processo de ensino-aprendizagem e contribui para a construção da identidade
institucional. A metodologia adotada baseou-se em uma revisão de literatura,
explorando estudos anteriores sobreo tema, políticas públicas relevantes e
exemplos de práticas pedagógicas inovadoras. Os resultados indicaram
que os espaços pedagógicos na EPT desempenham um papel fundamental
na promoção de uma aprendizagem integrada e significativa, enfrentando,
contudo, desafios relacionados à atualização tecnológica e à manutenção
de uma infraestrutura que suporte metodologias ativas de aprendizagem.
As considerações finais destacaram a necessidade de investimentos
contínuos e de uma gestão eficaz para que os espaços pedagógicos
evoluam de forma a atender às exigências de uma educação profissional
qualificada e alinhada com as demandas do mercado de trabalho e da
sociedade.

PALAVRAS-CHAVE: educação profissional e tecnológica, espaços

1. INTRODUCTION


       The organization and memories of pedagogical spaces in Professional and
Technological Education (PTE) represent a field of study that has gained
prominence in educational literature, given its importance for the development of
educational practices that respond to contemporary needs for technical and
technological training. This topic involves the analysis of the physical and
organizational structure of learning environments, as well as how these spaces
contribute to the construction of institutional memory and influence the
educational process.
       The rationale for choosing this topic lies in the growing demand for
qualified professionals in various technical fields, which highlights the need for
educational spaces that not only foster the development of specific skills but also
promote the integration of theoretical knowledge with practice. Furthermore, the
organization of these spaces and the memories they help to build play a
fundamental role in shaping the identity of vocational and technical education
(VTE) institutions, influencing both the perceptions of students and faculty as well
as the image of these institutions in society.
       The issue arises when observing that, despite the relevance of
pedagogical spaces in vocational and technological education, there are
significant challenges in their organization and in the way the memories of these
spaces are constructed and maintained. Issues such as the adequacy of
infrastructure to teaching-learning methodologies, resistance to change in
pedagogical practices, and the need to preserve institutional memory in the face
of rapid technological and curricular transformations are aspects that require in-
depth analysis.
       In this context, the objectives of this research are: first, to identify and
analyze the main characteristics of educational spaces in technical and
vocational education (TVE), taking into account their physical and pedagogical
organization; second, to understand how these spaces contribute to the
construction of institutional memory and the formation of the identity of TVE
institutions; and, finally, to investigate the challenges faced by institutions in
managing these spaces and preserving their memories. By achieving these
objectives, we hope to make a significant contribution to the literature on


                                                                                 66

professional and technological education, providing insights for the improvement
of pedagogical practices and the effective management of educational spaces.
      The following section provides a theoretical review that outlines the state
of the art regarding Professional and Technological Education in Brazil, the
organization of spaces pedagogical spaces and the importance of the memory
and identity of these spaces. The methodology employed is described with an
emphasis on literature review as a tool for compiling existing knowledge. The
results and discussions emerge from the analysis of the collected data, exploring
the pedagogies and teaching methods applied to VET, the impact of pedagogical
spaces on the teaching-learning process, challenges faced, and future
perspectives. Finally, the concluding remarks summarize the study’s key findings,
underscoring the need for effective management of these spaces to meet the
demands of contemporary education. This structural format aims to facilitate
readers’ understanding of the investigated aspects, allowing for a fluid and
informative reading experience.


2. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK


      The theoretical framework of this study is structured to provide a cohesive
and informative theoretical basis for the main themes that comprise the research.
It begins with a historical and contextual analysis of Professional and
Technological Education (PTE) in Brazil, highlighting the regulatory milestones
and public policies that have influenced its development. This is followed by a
discussion of the organization of pedagogical spaces in VTE, examining the
physical and pedagogical structures that support the teaching-learning process.
Additionally, the relevance of memory and identity in pedagogical spaces is
addressed, reflecting on how these dimensions contribute to the perception and
value of VTE institutions. This section is grounded in previous studies,
educational theories, and practical examples that illustrate the dynamics between
educational spaces, learning, and institutional identity. This organization aims to
establish a clear understanding of key concepts and the existing literature, laying
the groundwork for data analysis and subsequent discussions in the text.




                                                                                67

3. VOCATIONAL AND TECHNOLOGICAL EDUCATION (VTE) IN BRAZIL


       Vocational and Technical Education (VTE) in Brazil has undergone
significant transformations over the years, reflecting changes in social, economic,
and technological demands. The evolution of VTE in the country can be
understood by examining its history and the regulatory milestones that have
shaped its public policies.
       The history of EPT in Brazil has been marked by a series of ups and
downs, with periods of expansion alternating with periods of stagnation.
According to Machado (2008), “teacher training for EPT has been a constant
challenge, reflecting changes in the world of work and the need to adapt curricula
to new technologies and production methods.” This quote highlights the
importance of EPT’s constant adaptation to social and technological changes.
       Regarding regulatory frameworks and public policies, Brazilian legislation
on EPT began to take a more concrete form starting in the 1990s, with the Law
on Guidelines and Foundations of National Education (LDB), Law No.
9,394/1996, establishing the legal foundations for the organization of national
education, including vocational education. Fernandes (2009) points out that “the
management of Federal Institutes represents a significant challenge, especially
considering the goal of integrating vocational education into secondary
education, thereby promoting a more comprehensive and coordinated
education.”
       The expansion of the network of Federal Institutes, beginning in 2008,
represents a significant milestone in the history of EPT in Brazil. Pacheco (2010)
argues that “Federal Institutes constitute a revolution in vocational and
technological education by offering quality education aligned with the demands
of sustainable regional development.” This statement highlights the importance
of Federal Institutes in promoting vocational education that meets local and
regional needs, contributing to economic and social development.
       The importance of the political-pedagogical foundation in the organization
of EPT is emphasized by Pacheco (2015), who advocates for the need for
"guidelines toward a transformative vocational and technological education,
capable of promoting not only job readiness but also the civic and critical



                                                                                68

education of students." This perspective underscores the role of VET in
promoting a comprehensive education that goes beyond technical skills.
      Finally, the production of knowledge about VET and its configuration as a
field of study has been the subject of analysis, as highlighted by Ciavatta (2016):
“The production of knowledge regarding the configuration of the field of vocational
and technical education reflects a growing academic and political interest,
marking VET as a relevant field of research and intervention.” This lengthy
quotation illustrates the growing recognition of VET as a field of study and the
importance of research for the development of innovative educational policies
and practices.
      Therefore, VET in Brazil is characterized by a history of continuous
evolution, marked by challenges, adaptations, and innovations. Regulatory
frameworks and public policies have played a crucial role in defining the contours
of VET, aiming not only to meet the demands of the labor market but also to
promote a holistic and civic-minded education.


4. ORGANIZATION OF LEARNING SPACES IN VET


      The organization of pedagogical spaces in Professional and Technological
Education (EPT) plays a fundamental role in the teaching-learning process,
directly reflecting on the quality of the education provided. The concept of
pedagogical spaces in VTE encompasses not only traditional classrooms but also
laboratories, workshops, libraries, and other environments that enable the
conduct of practical and theoretical activities, integrating technical and
technological knowledge.
      The importance of physical and technological infrastructure for the
effectiveness of the educational process is widely recognized. As Pacheco (2015)
states, “the political-pedagogical foundations of federal institutes must consider
infrastructure as a key element for promoting transformative vocational and
technological education.” This perspective highlights the role of infrastructure not
merely as a support but as an integral part of the pedagogical strategy, directly
influencing the quality of teaching and the students’ learning experience.
      Different models and practices for organizing learning spaces have been
explored in vocational and technical education (VTE) institutions, seeking to


                                                                                 69

adapt to the specific needs of the courses offered and the characteristics of the
student body. Ciavatta (2016) highlights that "the production of knowledge
regarding the configuration of the field of professional and technological
education reflects the need for spaces that foster the integration of theory and
practice, promoting more meaningful learning." This extended quote emphasizes
the need for pedagogical spaces that facilitate the practical application of
theoretical knowledge, a fundamental aspect of VET.
       The diversity of models and practices observed in the organization of
pedagogical spaces in VTE reflects the search for environments that are both
inclusive and conducive to the development of specific competencies. According
to Machado (2008), “teacher training for VET requires spaces that stimulate
creativity, innovation, and critical reflection, both on the part of teachers and
students.” This perspective points to the need for spaces that promote not only
the acquisition of technical knowledge but also the development of cognitive and
social skills.
       In short, the organization of pedagogical spaces in Professional and
Technological Education is a key element that directly influences the
effectiveness of the teaching-learning process. Physical and technological
infrastructure, combined with innovative pedagogical models and practices, are
fundamental to meeting the demands of an education system that seeks to
prepare students for the challenges of the labor market and contemporary society.


5. MEMORIES AND IDENTITY OF EDUCATIONAL SPACES


       The memories and identity of educational spaces play an essential role in
defining and recognizing Professional and Technological Education (PTE)
institutes. The construction of these institutes’ identity is intrinsically linked to the
memories shared by students, teachers, and the community, reflecting not only
the educational history but also the experiences lived within these spaces.
       The role of memories in building the identity of VTI institutions is
highlighted by Pacheco (2010), who states: “Federal institutions, throughout their
history, have accumulated a set of memories that contribute to the formation of
their unique identity, which is a reflection of pedagogical practices, community
interactions, and the innovations implemented.” This quote underscores the


                                                                                      70

importance of collective experiences in shaping the perception and value
attributed to EPT institutes.
       An analysis of case studies reveals how changes and continuities in
educational spaces influence institutional memory. A significant example can be
seen in the evolution of laboratories and workshops, which, as they advance
technologically, remain fundamentally committed to practical and applied
learning—a core value of TPE. As González Arroyo (2019) points out, “the
evolution of pedagogical spaces in EPT institutes reflects changes in social and
technological demands, while preserving the mission of providing an education
that effectively integrates theory and practice.”
       This duality between change and continuity is essential to understanding
how memories contribute to the identity of EPT institutes. The preservation of
certain traditional aspects, such as the emphasis on technical education and the
close relationship with the local productive sector, coexists with the
implementation of pedagogical and technological innovations, highlighting a
continuous process of identity renewal.
       Ciavatta (2016) offers a comprehensive perspective on this phenomenon,
noting that “The production of knowledge regarding the configuration "The field
of vocational and technological education is a testament to the constant quest to
balance tradition and innovation, an effort that is reflected in the way educational
spaces are organized and experienced." This lengthy quote underscores the
complexity of managing educational spaces, which must take into account both
current needs and historical legacy.
       In short, the memories and identity of pedagogical spaces at EPT are
fundamental elements that influence how the institutes are perceived and valued
by the educational community and society. Through the analysis of case studies,
it becomes evident that transformations in educational spaces contribute to the
dynamic construction of institutional identity, reflecting an ongoing commitment
to educational excellence and innovation.

       Data collection for the literature review involves identifying relevant
sources, including scientific articles, books, theses, dissertations, and research

       Finally, the methodology adopted in this study aims to synthesize the

8. PEDAGOGY AND DIDACTICS APPLIED TO VET


      In Professional and Technological Education (PTE), pedagogical
approaches and didactic strategies play a fundamental role in promoting teaching
that meets the specific needs of the productive sector and contemporary society.
Adapting teaching methodologies to incorporate both technical knowledge and
technological skills becomes essential in this context.




                                                                                75

      Pedagogical approaches in VET emphasize the integration of theory and
practice, an essential aspect of professional training. Machado (2008) highlights
the importance of this integration, arguing that “the training of teachers for
Vocational and Technical Education requires a commitment to adopting
pedagogical practices that promote the application of knowledge in practical
contexts.” This perspective reinforces the need for teaching strategies that
facilitate the connection between classroom learning and its application in the
workplace.
      With regard to innovative teaching strategies, the use of digital
technologies and multimedia resources has proven effective in improving
teaching-learning process. Ciavatta (2016), in an analysis of the configuration of
the EPT field, observes that "the production of knowledge and pedagogical
innovation are fundamental to responding to the challenges posed by the
information society, requiring an educational environment that incorporates new
technologies and active learning methodologies." This lengthy quotation
highlights the need for constant updating of pedagogical practices to incorporate
the technological and methodological innovations that characterize today’s
society.
      The application of innovative teaching strategies in EPT educational
settings is not limited to the use of technologies but also includes active
methodologies, such as project-based learning, collaborative learning, and
problem-based learning. These approaches promote greater interaction between
students and teachers and stimulate the development of critical and reflective
skills. Pacheco (2015) underscores the relevance of these methodologies, stating
that "the political-pedagogical foundations of Federal Institutes must include
teaching strategies that engage students in the learning process, making them
protagonists of their own education."
      Therefore, pedagogy and teaching methods applied to EPT require
constant reflection and adaptation to new educational and productive realities.
The incorporation of integrative pedagogical approaches and innovative teaching
strategies into educational settings is essential to prepare students for the
challenges of the job market and to promote vocational training that is at once
technical, technological, and humanistic.



                                                                               76

9. IMPACT OF PEDAGOGICAL SPACES ON THE TEACHING-LEARNING
PROCESS


       The impact of pedagogical spaces on the teaching-learning process is a
topic of growing interest in Professional and Technological Education (PTE).
Research analysis reveals that both the physical and organizational
environments exert a significant influence on learning, affecting not only the way
students absorb knowledge, but also how they interact with one another and with
educators.
       The physical environment—including classroom layout, lighting, thermal
comfort, and the availability of technological resources—can either enhance or
limit learning opportunities. According to Pacheco (2015), “the configuration of
educational spaces should be designed to promote interaction and collaboration,
creating an environment conducive to the development of skills relevant to
technical and technological training.” This perspective highlights the need for
spaces that are flexible and adaptable to different teaching and learning
modalities.
       Beyond the physical aspect, the organizational environment—which
includes institutional culture, pedagogical practices, and school management—
plays a crucial role in the educational process. The way in which educational
spaces are managed and activities are organized directly influences student
engagement and motivation. Ciavatta (2016) addresses this issue by stating that
“the production of knowledge regarding the configuration of the field of
professional and technological education reflects the importance of creating
learning environments that stimulate curiosity, experimentation, and critical
reflection.” This lengthy quote underscores the need for spaces that foster the
construction of meaningful knowledge, in an environment that encourages
students’ active participation.
       Examples of successful practices in designing educational spaces that
promote learning include the implementation of well-equipped laboratories for
conducting practical experiments, classrooms that allow for reconfiguration of the
space to accommodate different educational activities, and common areas that
encourage collaborative study and interaction among members of the school
community. Fernandes (2009) illustrates this approach by noting that “the


                                                                               77

administration of Federal Institutes faces the challenge of integrating physical
spaces and pedagogical practices in a way that reflects the institution’s
educational objectives, fostering a dynamic and inclusive learning environment.”
      Therefore, the impact of pedagogical spaces on the teaching-learning
process is multifaceted, involving physical and organizational aspects that, when
properly coordinated, contribute to a richer and more effective educational
experience. The creation of environments that support active learning,
collaboration, and innovation is essential to meet the demands of contemporary
professional and technological education, preparing students for the challenges
of the labor market and society.


10. CHALLENGES AND FUTURE PROSPECTS


      The organization and maintenance of innovative and inclusive learning
spaces in Professional and Technological Education (PTE) face significant
challenges, which require constant attention and collaborative efforts from
administrators, educators, and the educational community. Among the main
challenges is the need to adapt physical infrastructure to new pedagogical and
technological demands, ensuring that all students have equal access to learning
opportunities.
      One of the challenges mentioned by Pacheco (2015) is "the need to align
political and pedagogical principles with educational practices, so as to foster a
professional and technological education that is truly transformative and
inclusive." This quote highlights the complexity of integrating educational policies
and pedagogical practices in a way that meets the needs of a diverse student
population, within a context of rapid technological and social change.
      Furthermore, maintaining pedagogical spaces that keep pace with
technological innovations represents another challenge. Ciavatta (2016)
highlights that “constant technological evolution necessitates frequent updates to
teaching resources and physical infrastructure, in order to provide a learning
environment that is in tune with contemporary practices in the world of work.” This
statement underscores the importance of continuous investment in material and
technological resources, so that educational settings can effectively prepare
students for the professional challenges they will face.


                                                                                 78

      As for the future prospects for learning environments in EPT, there is an
expectation of increasing integration of digital technologies and innovative
pedagogical approaches, such as project-based learning and gamification, which
promote student engagement and active participation in the learning process.
Fernandes (2009), in discussing the challenges for the management of Federal
Institutes, suggests that “the incorporation of active methodologies and emerging
educational technologies can transform pedagogical spaces into dynamic and
adaptive learning environments, capable of responding to the educational and
professional needs of a society in constant transformation.”
      Therefore, the challenges in organizing and maintaining innovative and
inclusive pedagogical spaces are complex and multifaceted, requiring a holistic
approach that considers both the physical and pedagogical dimensions of
education. Future prospects point toward greater flexibility in learning spaces,
with a focus on personalizing education and preparing students for an
increasingly technological and globalized job market. Overcoming these
challenges and realizing these prospects require an ongoing commitment to
innovation, inclusion, and sustainability within the context of EFA.


11. FINAL CONSIDERATIONS


      The concluding remarks of this study on the organization and memories of
educational spaces in Professional and Technological Education (PTE) reflect on
the importance of such spaces in the teaching-learning process and in the
construction of institutional identity. The analysis conducted, based on a thorough
literature review, identified the challenges faced in designing educational
environments that are simultaneously innovative, inclusive, and conducive to the
development of skills relevant to the labor market.
      It has been shown that educational spaces in early childhood education
play a significant role not only in the transmission of knowledge but also in
promoting active and meaningful learning. The integration of theory and practice,
essential for professional and technological training, requires spaces that are
adequately equipped and organized to stimulate interaction, creativity, and critical
thinking. The challenges associated with technological updates and the



                                                                                 79

adaptation of pedagogical practices to new educational and professional
demands require attentive management and adequate resources.
       Furthermore, the memory and identity of educational spaces contribute to
a sense of continuity and belonging among students and teachers, reinforcing the
institution’s value and mission. Preserving these memories, combined with the
ability to innovate and adapt to change, is crucial for maintaining the relevance
and effectiveness of T&V institutions in the face of contemporary challenges.
       Future prospects point to a trend toward greater flexibility and
personalization of learning spaces, with the incorporation of advanced
technologies and pedagogical methodologies that foster an education more
closely aligned with students’ individual needs and the demands of the workforce.
The creation of educational environments that foster collaborative and
interdisciplinary learning, as well as civic and ethical education, emerges as a
fundamental element in training qualified professionals who are aware of their
role in society.
       It can therefore be concluded that organizing and maintaining appropriate
learning environments in EPT are complex tasks that require a constant
commitment to educational quality and innovation. Overcoming the identified
challenges and realizing future prospects will depend on joint efforts by
administrators, educators, students, and the community, in a continuous process
of evaluation and adaptation to social and technological dynamics. By shedding
light on crucial aspects of pedagogical spaces in EPT, this study aims to provide
insights for reflections and actions that strengthen vocational and technological
education in the country, making it more effective, inclusive, and aligned with the
demands of the 21st century.

ABSTRACT: This qualitative study, designed as action research, aimed to
analyze how the use of base ten blocks, integrated into a planned
pedagogical proposal, can contribute to the learning of quadratic equations in
the final years of elementary school. The investigation was carried out with a 9th-
grade class in a public school through four lessons that comprised a
methodological teaching plan. The activities integrated the use of base ten
blocks with the traditional algebraic approach, allowing students to move from
concrete representations to symbolic records. Data collection took place
through observations conducted during the implementation of the proposal.
The results indicated that the use of base ten blocks favored the conceptual
understanding of quadratic equations, stimulated students’ interest and
participation, and contributed to the development of meaningful learning.
However, it was found that the resource requires intentional teachermediation so
that its manipulative aspect does not override the learning objective. It is
concluded that base ten blocks, when used in a planned and reflective
way, constitute a powerful learning tool and an effective strategy to make
the teaching of quadratic equations more meaningful and engaging.

KEYWORDS: mathematics teaching, quadratic equations, base ten blocks,
meaningful learning, pedagogical proposal.

1. INTRODUCTION


       The teaching of quadratic equations is still, in many contexts,
characterized by mechanical and unmeaningful approaches (Pereira, 2017),
which contributes to students’ learning difficulties (Silva, 2017). In light of this, this
study proposes a methodological teaching plan that seeks to overcome such
difficulties through the use of golden material, promoting conceptual
understanding and meaningful learning.
       The research, which is qualitative in nature and characterized as action
research, was guided by the following question: How can a pedagogical approach
that integrates the use of golden material with the teaching of quadratic equations
contribute to learning in the resolution of these equations? Thus, we aim to
analyze how the use of golden material, integrated into a planned pedagogical
proposal, can promote conceptual understanding and meaningful learning of
quadratic equations in the final years of elementary school.
       To this end, we developed a pedagogical proposal inspired by didactic
transposition (Chevallard, 1991; Brasil, 2006), applied in a 9th-grade elementary
school class.
       The stages of theoretical review and analysis of textbooks, presented in a
previous study (Soares et al., 2022), formed the basis of this research, which
focuses on the development, implementation, and evaluation of the pedagogical
proposal.
       The following sections present the methodological approach, a description
of the proposal, and an analysis of the results obtained during the pedagogical
intervention.


2. METHODOLOGY


       This study is qualitative in nature (Minayo, 2002) and is classified as action
research, as it seeks to address the difficulties observed in learning “quadratic
equations” by promoting the joint participation of researchers and students
(Thiollent, 1997). The research was conducted in a spiral cycle, in which the
planning was constantly reevaluated and adjusted according to the reality of
pedagogical practice and the needs of the participating group.


                                                                                       84

           This type of research comprises four stages: exploratory, planning, action,
   and evaluation (Thiollent, 1997). The exploratory stage, focused on the analysis
   and diagnosis of the effects of using concrete materials in teaching the
   mathematical concept in question, was addressed in a previous study (Soares et
   al., 2022). The remaining stages are presented in this paper and summarized in
   Table 1, which describes the roadmap of the pedagogical intervention.

  introduce the mathematical concept of “equations , linking it to the use of the

golden ratio. Through a dialogic approach, the teacher-researcher facilitated

        Next, we presented the golden material and explained the correspondence

        Lesson Topic: Solving quadratic equations with the golden material
        Duration: 50 minutes Objectives:
        Use the golden material to factor and solve quadratic equations with

3.2.1 Methodological procedures, analysis, and discussion


        The objective of Lesson 2 was to apply the core concepts to solving
quadratic equations. The teacher-researcher began the lesson with the following


                                                                                 88

questions: “Why do we solve a quadratic equation? What are we trying to find?”
One of the students replied: “To find the solution.” Another question was then
asked: “What is the solution to a quadratic equation?” The students were unable
to answer, so the teacher-researcher formalized the answers to the questions
posed to the students. In addition, the relationship between the roots and the
coefficient of the equation was mentioned.
       Building on the concepts from the previous class, the example 3x2+
