meaningful understanding of the equation-solving process, attributing meaning to
the construction of the solutions. According to Francisco et al. (2019, p. 6),
“algebraic solving is supported by geometric solving, giving greater meaning to
the former and streamlining the equation-solving process.”




                                                                                            95

       We emphasize, however, that the use of the golden material presented
challenges. The manipulative nature of the resource sometimes diverted the
attention of some students, who began to use it in a playful manner, as illustrated
in Figure 7.


                     Figure 7. Students playing with the golden material




                               Source: Ramos et al., (2023).


       Upon observing the behavior of some students, the teacher-researchers
reinforced the objective of the activity and the educational nature of the golden
material, redoubling their attention to ensure that its use remained focused on
learning, as advised by Nacarato (2005).
       With this final lesson, we have completed the implementation of the
pedagogical approach, confirming that the “golden material” promotes
meaningful learning and an understanding of quadratic equations, even though it
has limitations and presents challenges, requiring careful instructional planning
(Lorenzato, 2006).

4. SUMMARY OF THE LESSONS




                                                                                96

       The implementation of the pedagogical proposal, structured into four
lessons, allowed us to observe the students’ progress in understanding quadratic
equations and in using the golden material as a resource for mediating
mathematical knowledge.
       In the first lesson, the focus was on raising awareness and revisiting prior
knowledge, establishing the difference between first- and second-degree
equations and introducing the geometric representation of coefficients using the
golden material. The students demonstrated curiosity and engagement,
recognizing the resource’s potential for visualizing abstract concepts.
       The second class was dedicated to solving quadratic equations with the
golden material, promoting the collective construction of reasoning and the
development of intellectual autonomy. The dialogue between teacher-
researchers and students showed that the manipulative method promoted
engagement and understanding, although specific doubts arose in situations
involving negative coefficients.
       In the third class, the work focused on the formalization of knowledge,
revisiting Bhaskara’s formula and the relationship between the discriminant and
the roots of the equation. This stage revealed that some students identify more
with algebraic methods, while others maintain an affinity for concrete approaches,
indicating the importance of methodological diversification.
       Finally, the fourth class proposed the practical and comparative application
of the two methods—the golden material and Bhaskara’s formula—in problem-
solving situations. Group discussions, the exchange of strategies, and the
sharing of solutions demonstrated that the golden material fosters meaningful
learning, although it requires constant guidance to ensure the focus does not get
lost in the playful aspect.
       Overall, the four lessons showed that the use of golden material
constitutes a powerful tool for the didactic transposition of the mathematical
object “quadratic equations,” promoting engagement, conceptual understanding,
and reflection on the problem-solving process. However, they revealed the need
for careful instructional planning to balance the manipulative nature of the activity
with the goal of formal learning

equations” has often been associated with a mechanical and meaningless
approach to teaching (Pereira, 2017), and that such an approach tends to lead to
learning difficulties (Silva, 2017), this study aimed to propose a methodology
capable of overcoming these limitations through the manipulative use of golden
material. In this sense, we sought to understand, in a qualitative study, how a
coordinated teaching methodology

CHAPTER 6
 PERSONAS: THEORY AND PRACTICE IN
 TEACHING ACTION


Rita de Cássia Spréa
Master's Degree in Child and Adolescent Health
Universidade Federal do Paraná (UFPR)
E-mail: ritaspreapsicologia@gmail.com


ABSTRACT: The "Personas Methodology" was developed as an active and agile
strategy to respond to changes in teaching and learning and the new demands
of the edu-cational environment, characterized by the coexistence of digital and
analog spaces. The objective was to improve the academic and clinical
performance of Psychology students, in addition to developing essential soft skills
for profes-sional practice. The methodology was applied in the course "Clinical
Practice: Behavioral and Cognitive Approaches" in the 7th semester at Tuiuti
University of Paraná, using the Flipped Classroom, clinical simulations inspired
by the OSCE model, and the development of treatment plans based on
"personas" constructed based on scientific literature and clinical cases. The
evaluation pro-cess included formal exams, guided studies, and the production
of digital mate-rials for scientific dissemination. The results initially revealed
student resistance, attributed to the difficulty adapting to active methodologies,
but over the semes-ter, improved scores, increased autonomy, development of
critical skills, negotia-tion skills, and crisis management. It was also observed that
night classes, de-spite the workload, achieved high performance. The conclusion
is that the "Per-sonas Methodology" proved effective, contributing to the
comprehensive devel-opment of students and can be replicated in other
disciplines and courses, pro-vided it is accompanied by flexible teaching and
dialogue with students.

KEYWORDS: active methodologies, agile methodologies, personas, teaching
and learning.

RESUMO: A “Metodologia Personas” foi desenvolvida como estratégia ativa e
ágil para responder às transformações no ensino-aprendizagem e às novas
demandas do ambiente educacional, caracterizado pela convivência entre
espaços digitais e analógicos. O objetivo foi aprimorar o desempenho acadêmico
e clínico de estudantes de Psicologia, além de desenvolver soft skills essenciais
para a prá-tica profissional. A metodologia foi aplicada na disciplina “Prática
Clínica: Abor-dagens Comportamentais e Cognitivas”, no 7º período da
Universidade Tuiuti do Paraná, utilizando a Sala de Aula Invertida, simulações
clínicas inspiradas no modelo OSCE e elaboração de planos de tratamento a
partir de “personas” construídas com base em literatura científica e casos
clínicos. O processo avali-ativo incluiu provas formais, estudos dirigidos e
produção de materiais digitais para divulgação científica. Os resultados


                                                                                  101

evidenciaram inicialmente resistência dos alunos, atribuída à dificuldade de
adaptação às metodologias ativas, mas ao longo do semestre verificou-se
melhora nos escores, maior autonomia, desen-volvimento de competências
críticas, capacidade de negociação e gerenciamen-to de crises. Observou-se
ainda que turmas noturnas, mesmo com a sobrecarga do trabalho, obtiveram

em outras disciplinas e cursos, desde que acompa-nhada de flexibilidade
docente e diálogo com os discentes.

1. INTRODUCTION


       In recent decades, social, cultural, and technological changes have brought
about profound transformations in the way individuals relate to knowledge and
construct understanding. The educational environment, situated within this context,
is also impacted by contemporary society, characterized by the coexistence of digital
and analog spaces, instant communication, and unrestricted access to information
(VALENTE; ALMEIDA; GERALDINI, 2017). This reality demands new pedagogical
approaches from higher education institutions, since, according to the Brazilian
Association of Distance Education, “it is urgent and necessary that the paradigms
underpinning pedagogical practice adapt to the new student and the new reality in
which we live” (ABED, 2016, p. 9).
       However, teaching practice in undergraduate programs, particularly in
Psychology, still relies heavily on traditional methodologies, which are often
insufficient to prepare students for the complexities of clinical practice. This
scenario highlights the following research question: how can active and agile
methodologies contribute to the development of the technical and socio-
emotional competencies necessary for clinical training in Psychology?
       The rationale for this investigation is grounded in the need to innovate the
teaching-learning process, fostering autonomy, critical thinking, and the
development of soft skills—such as assertive communication, decision-making
under pressure, frustration tolerance, and crisis management—which are
indispensable competencies for future psychologists. In this sense, the creation
of the “Personas Methodology” seeks to address gaps observed in previous
semesters, proposing a mechanism to bridge the gap between theory and clinical
practice through simulation, case studies, and active methodologies.
       Thus, this study aims to: Describe the creation, implementation, and
application of the Personas Methodology in the course “Clinical Practice:
Behavioral and Cognitive Approaches” in the Psychology program at Tuiuti
University of Paraná; To analyze the impact of the methodology on the
development of technical skills (diagnosis, hypothesis formulation, clinical
management) and socio-emotional skills (soft skills); To evaluate the results
obtained in the “ ” course in terms of academic performance and student
engagement, verifying its effectiveness for the teaching-learning process; and


                                                                                 103

discuss the possibility of replicating the methodology in other disciplines and
undergraduate programs.


2. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK


       Active methodologies, often grounded in Piaget’s constructivism and
Vygotsky’s sociocultural perspective, have been identified as promising
approaches to making learning more meaningful and responsive to students’
needs (VALENTE; ALMEIDA; GERALDINI, 2017). Authors such as Freire (1996)
emphasize the importance of problematizing and dialogic education, as opposed
to the banking model of teaching, highlighting that knowledge must be
constructed through interaction and not unilaterally imparted by the teacher. In
this field, there is consensus on the relevance of student-centeredness in the
learning process. However, the literature also points to challenges: student
resistance, teacher overload in planning, and the institutional difficulty of breaking
with traditional paradigms (SOARES; FERRAZ, 2007).
       Agile methodologies, in turn, although originating in the technology sector,
have been progressively explored in higher education, particularly in health
education. They promote values such as simplicity, flexibility, assertive
communication, and continuous feedback (ASFORA, 2009). The international
literature reinforces that these principles are useful for preparing professionals in
environments of uncertainty and constant change, favoring adaptive learning.
However, gaps still exist regarding the systematization of hybrid models that
integrate agile and active methodologies in a cohesive and replicable manner in
clinical contexts, especially in Psychology.
       In psychology education, the literature highlights efforts to bridge theory
and practice through clinical simulations, case studies, and flipped classroom
methodologies (MEDEIROS et al., 2013; ANDRADE; MADEIRA; AIRES, 2013).
Such strategies have proven effective in fostering technical skills and developing
clinical reasoning. However, there are contradictions between the recognition of
their importance and the concrete difficulty of implementing them on a large scale,
due to factors such as infrastructure, reduced course loads, and a shortage of
faculty members trained to conduct these approaches.



                                                                                  104

          A critical analysis of the literature reveals that, although there is consensus
on the need for pedagogical innovation, there are still gaps in empirical studies
that systematically evaluate the impacts of integrating active and agile
methodologies into clinical training in Psychology. Research is predominantly
conducted in the fields of Medicine and Nursing, but there is a smaller number of
studies applied to the teaching of Psychology. Furthermore, it is observed that
the discussion regarding the development of soft skills—such as communication,
negotiation, decision-making under pressure, and frustration tolerance—is still in
its infancy in studies on mental health training, despite these being crucial
competencies for professional practice.
          Thus, this study is part of an effort to fill these gaps by proposing and
evaluating the “Personas Methodology” as a pedagogical model that combines
principles of active and agile methodologies, applied specifically to clinical
training in Psychology. In doing so, it seeks to contribute not only to the literature
on educational innovation but also to teaching practice, offering a replicable
model that engages with the contemporary reality of higher education and the
demands of the professional market.

3. METHODOLOGY


      This study is characterized as applied research of a qualitative and quan-
titative nature, as it sought both to understand the process of implementing the
proposed methodology and to evaluate its measurable impacts on students’ ac-
ademic performance. The design adopted was that of a pedagogical intervention
study, conducted in the context of higher education in Psychology.
      The sample consisted of students regularly enrolled in the course “Clinical
Practice: Behavioral and Cognitive Approaches,” offered in the 7th semester of
the Psychology program at Tuiuti University of Paraná. Two classes participated,
totaling approximately 60 students, with diverse profiles in terms of age, profes-
sional experience, and study shifts (day and night). Volunteers from advanced
semesters of the program also collaborated, having been previously trained to
act as simulated patients during the assessments.
      Data collection was conducted using various instruments and procedures.
First, the Flipped Classroom methodology was employed, in which students had
prior access to selected chapters from the book Clinical Manual of Psychological
Disorders: Step-by-Step Treatment (2016). In the classroom, each topic was op-
erationalized using a “clinical persona,” constructed based on demographic and
behavioral characteristics, to simulate patients with specific needs.
      Formal assessment took place at two bimonthly intervals (AV1 and AV2),
inspired by the OSCE (Objective Structured Clinical Examination) model, which
consists of structured clinical simulation stations. Trained volunteers portrayed
cases of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder and Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder in
the first two-month period, and different diagnoses drawn from the book Clinical
Cases of the DSM-5 (2015) in the second. Students completed structured as-
sessment forms ( ) containing diagnostic items, identification of core beliefs and
cognitive distortions, choice of treatment protocol, and selection of techniques.
Quantitative analysis was performed using the scores assigned on the forms,
which were recorded and compared with scores obtained in previous semesters
when the methodology was not used.
      In addition to formal assessments, the Directed Studies (ED1 and ED2)
constituted another source of data. In the first two months, students presented
treatment plans developed based on the personas studied in class. In the second,


                                                                              106

they produced scientific outreach materials in digital formats (videos, podcasts,
cards, or blog posts), based on scientific articles, using language accessible to
the general public. These products were analyzed for clarity, scientific accuracy,
and innovation, providing qualitative evidence of the methodology’s impact.
       The analyses were conducted on two levels. Quantitatively, assessment
scores were compared across classes and shifts, with attention to differences in
performance. Qualitatively, we observed student engagement, initial adaptation
difficulties, reports of resistance, and, subsequently, progress in the development
of technical and socio-emotional competencies, particularly soft skills such as
communication, decision-making, and frustration tolerance.
       Regarding ethical considerations, the research followed the principles es-
tablished by Resolution No. 510/2016 of the National Health Council, which reg-
ulates studies in the Humanities and Social Sciences. All participants were in-
formed about the objectives of the pedagogical project, and their participation
was voluntary, with no academic repercussions for those who chose not to col-
laborate in specific activities. The cases used for simulation were adapted from
public or literary materials, without identifying real patients, thereby safeguarding
confidentiality and professional ethics.
       Finally, some limitations of the study are acknowledged. The intervention
took place in only one course, which limits the generalizability of the results. Fur-
thermore, the observation period was limited to one academic semester, making
it impossible to assess long-term effects. Despite these limitations, the method-
ology was described in detail, ensuring the possibility of replication in other edu-
cational contexts and allowing for the expansion of evidence regarding the effec-
tiveness of the integration of active and agile methodologies in psychology edu-
cation.


4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION


       The implementation of the Personas Methodology yielded positive results
in both students’ academic performance and the development of socio-emotional
skills. Regarding formal assessments, a significant improvement in scores was
observed    compared     to   previous     semesters   in   which   only   traditional
methodologies were used. In particular, in the evening classes, although the


                                                                                  107

literature indicates that students in this shift tend to perform less well due to work
overload and sleep deprivation (ARAÚJO; ALMONDES, 2012), the results
revealed superior performance, suggesting that the methodological approach
fostered motivation and engagement, even under adverse conditions.
       In the first two months, students demonstrated greater difficulty adapting
to the OSCE-inspired assessment model, especially regarding the reduced
response time and the requirement for synthesis in simulated situations. This
initial resistance was accompanied by manifestations of anxiety and insecurity,
as described by Soares and Ferraz (2007) when addressing the defense
mechanisms mobilized in contexts of pedagogical change. However, over the
course of the semester, a progressive reduction in these barriers was observed,
with increased autonomy, greater clarity in diagnostic formulation, and
confidence in proposing therapeutic protocols.
       The Directed Studies (DS1 and DS2) also revealed significant gains. In
the first, the treatment plans showed progress in the integration of theory and
clinical practice, demonstrating the ability to integrate prior knowledge with the
demands presented by the personas. In the second, the production of scientific
outreach materials—videos, podcasts, cards, and texts—indicated not only
conceptual mastery but also creativity and the ability to translate academic
language for the lay public, an aspect still largely unexplored in traditional
psychology education. This practice aligns with the literature on university
extension and scientific communication, which advocates for bringing academia
closer to society as a means of bridging the gap between technical knowledge
and social demands (FREIRE, 1996).
       The qualitative analysis showed that, in addition to cognitive and technical
gains, there was development of soft skills, such as assertive communication,
teamwork, frustration tolerance, and decision-making under pressure. These
results align with research indicating the effectiveness of clinical simulation-
based learning in fostering complex competencies among health science
students (MEDEIROS et al., 2013; ANDRADE; MADEIRA; AIRES, 2013). At the
same time, the need to adjust the pace of implementation—moving from one case
per class to one case every two or three classes—highlighted the challenge of
balancing pedagogical innovation with students’ capacity for absorption, pointing



                                                                                  108

to a gap in the literature regarding the optimal dosage of simulation workload in
psychology programs.
       In terms of limitations, it should be noted that the intervention was
conducted in only one course and over a limited period (one semester), restricting
the generalizability of the findings. Furthermore, the absence of a formal control
group precludes comparison under equivalent conditions, although historical data
from previous classes served as a reference point. Despite these limitations, the
results obtained offer relevant contributions to teaching practice, demonstrating
that the integration of active and agile methodologies can enhance the teaching-
learning process in Psychology, particularly in the development of clinical and
socio-emotional competencies.
       The implications of this study reinforce the need for greater institutional
investment in innovative pedagogical approaches and point to avenues for future
research. Among these, the expansion of the application of the Personas
Methodology to other disciplines within the Psychology program, replication at
different higher education institutions, and the conduct of longitudinal studies
evaluating the medium- and long-term impact on the professional practice of
graduates stand out.


5. CONCLUSION


       The present study aimed to describe the creation, implementation, and
evaluation of the Personas Methodology, applied in the course “Clinical Practice:
Behavioral and Cognitive Approaches” in the Psychology program at Tuiuti
University of Paraná, as well as to analyze its impacts on the development of
students’ technical and socio-emotional competencies. Through the application
of this pedagogical approach, it was possible to observe a significant
improvement in academic performance, greater student engagement, and
progress in the ability to integrate theory and clinical practice.
       The results showed that the use of clinical personas, combined with active
methodologies and agile principles, fostered student autonomy, improved
diagnostic formulation, and strengthened soft skills such as assertive
communication, frustration tolerance, and decision-making under pressure.
Although there was initial resistance on the part of the students, the process


                                                                              109

demonstrated that adapting to innovative methodologies helps overcome barriers
and enhance academic and professional maturity.
       From a practical standpoint, the Personas Methodology proved effective
in bridging the gap between academic training and clinical reality, offering future
psychologists a safe space for experimentation and reflection. From a theoretical
perspective, the study contributes to the debate on the integration of active and
agile methodologies in psychology education, filling existing gaps in the literature.
While acknowledging the limitations regarding the scope of the intervention and
the observation period, the findings reinforce the importance of expanding future
research to explore its replication across different disciplines, institutions, and
educational contexts.
       Thus, it is concluded that the Personas Methodology represents an
innovative and replicable pedagogical strategy, capable of enriching the
teaching-learning process and training professionals who are more critical,
autonomous, and prepared for the challenges of contemporary clinical practice.

CHAPTER 7
 STORIES BETWEEN THE LINES OF SCHOOL
 NOTEBOOKS


Eliane Küster
Master of Education
Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Paraná
E-mail: likuster@yahoo.com.br

Alboni Marisa Dudeque Pianovski Vieira
Doctor of Education
Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Paraná
E-mail: alboni@alboni.com


ABSTRACT: The article analyzes the school notebooks of a third age student in
the context of school, social and cultural practices and guidelines, in a Youth and
Adult Education (YLE) class, in the Municipal Education Network of Curitiba, from
2003 to 2004. Considering the school notebooks as research sources and the
EJA as a learning opportunity, we tried to identify its different uses and possible
meanings. This bibliographical, documental and field research was based on the
studies of Chartier (1990), Oliveira (2008), Grinspun (2008), Viñao-Frago (2008)
and Julia (2001). As a result, it was possible to reflect on the school notebooks,
their use and what they represent in the school's daily life, as their own spaces
of expression of the student's individuality.

KEYWORDS: active methodologies, agile methodologies, personas, teaching
and learning.

RESUMO: O artigo analisa os cadernos escolares de uma aluna da terceira
idade no contexto das práticas e pautas escolares, sociais e culturais, em uma
classe de EJA - Educação de Jovens e Adultos, na Rede Municipal de Ensino de
Curitiba, no período de 2003 a 2004. Considerando os cadernos escolares como
fontes de pesquisa e a EJA como oportunidade de aprendizagem, procurou-se
identificar seus diferentes usos e possíveis significados. A pesquisa, de caráter
bibliográfico, documental e de campo, apoiou-se nos estudos de Chartier (1990),
Oliveira (2008), Grinspun (2008), Viñao-Frago (2008) e Julia (2001). Como
resultado, foi possível refletir sobre os cadernos escolares, sua utilização e o que
representam no cotidiano da escola, como espaços próprios de expressão da
individualidade da aluna.

PALAVRAS-CHAVE: história cultural, história da educação, EJA - educação de
jovens e adultos, cadernos escolares.




                                                                                113

1. INTRODUCTION


      This article examines school notebooks as documentary sources within
the field of cultural history (CHARTIER, 1990). It is well known that school
notebooks constitute “a significant material artifact of the contemporary school,
the study of which proves to be an excellent source of research” (OLIVEIRA,
2008, p. 129). In this regard, Grinspun (2008) notes that “each notebook bears
the mark of each of us, of our preferences and the way those preferences were
addressed,” adding that “each person put into their [notebook], beyond what was
requested, copied, or created, a unique way of interpreting what existed”
(GRINSPUN, 2008, p. 261).
      Not everything, however, is recorded in the notebooks. Viñao-Frago
(2008) states that the notebooks “remain silent; they say nothing about the oral
or gestural interventions of the teacher and students, about their significance and
the way they occur and manifest themselves, or about the atmosphere or climate
of the classroom” (VIÑAO-FRAGO, 2008, p. 25). Seeking out these interventions
and the environment in which they occurred justifies this study of school
notebooks. As Oliveira (2008) observes in this field, the subjects of the school
are also considered:


                       In the case of school notebooks, the subjects to be examined by the
                       study are, primarily, the students to whom they belonged, but not
                       exclusively. The study offers a glimpse into some of the other school
                       subjects—such as teachers, their practices, and thus their pedagogical
                       affiliations—school content and the methodology in use, the institution’s
                       epistemological and methodological commitments, and even the
                       general rules of current educational policy (OLIVEIRA, 2008, p. 130).


      The general objective of the study was, therefore, to investigate what the
school notebooks of a senior citizen student revealed in the context of school,
social, and cultural practices and norms during the time she attended a class in
the EJA (Youth and Adult Education) program at a school in the Curitiba
Municipal Education Network from 2003 to 2004. The specific objectives were
established as follows: to consider school notebooks as research sources; to
present Adult Basic Education (ABE) as a learning opportunity; and to examine
the school notebooks of an ABE student, exploring their various uses and
possible meanings.


                                                                                            114

       The study made it possible to “employ multiple research strategies”
(RIBEIRO, 2003, p. 287), including literature review, documentary research, and
field research.
       The theoretical framework of this study is rooted in cultural history
(CHARTIER, 1990), with foundational authors including Oliveira (2008), Grinspun
(2008), Viñao-Frago (2008), Razzini (2008), and Julia (2001), among others.
       For the documentary research, printed sources were used, specifically two
school notebooks, materials that, according to Gil (2010, p. 31), are also capable
of “verifying a fact or event” and are considered documentary sources.
       In addition to bibliographic and documentary research, field research was
employed, drawing on oral history procedures—a methodology that “can be used
in research on recent topics, within the scope of the interviewees’ memories,
involving events that occurred over a period of approximately 50 years,” as Vieira
(2015, p. 372) aptly explains.
       Oral history, according to Alberti (2014), “consists of conducting interviews
[...] with individuals who participated in, or witnessed, events and circumstances
of the past and present,” a fact that allows “access to ‘stories within History,’
broadening the possibilities for interpreting the past” (ALBERTI, 2014, p. 155).
       Constantino (2004) clarifies that in addition to “capturing much more than
just some data,” through oral history it is possible to “capture the narrators’
experiences, their traditions, myths, perhaps fictional narratives that lay deep in
memory, as well as the beliefs existing within their group” (CONSTANTINO,
2004, pp. 63–64).
       The study was divided into three chapters: the first presents school
notebooks as research sources for the History of Education; the second
describes Adult Basic Education (ABE) as a learning opportunity for those who
did not complete their studies at the standard age; and the final chapter presents
a analysis of the records of a senior citizen who attended adult education classes.


2. SCHOOL NOTEBOOKS: RESEARCH SOURCES FOR THE HISTORY OF
EDUCATION


       School notebooks, like other materials, have come to be recognized as
significant documentary sources since the advent of cultural history (CHARTIER,


                                                                                115

1990). Grinspun (2008) notes that “research into school notebooks provides an
inexhaustible source of knowledge” (GRINSPUN, 2008, p. 259).
       According to Viñao-Frago (2008), studies conducted on the focus, themes,
and uses of school notebooks have demonstrated that they were used as: a
source for understanding images and social representations, instruments of
written acculturation, vehicles for transmitting values and attitudes, a means of
ideological and political indoctrination, a medium for studying the curriculum and
various school subjects and activities, an educational innovation within the New
School movement, and an instrument of personal and subjective expression for
students.
       Viñao-Frago (2008, p. 18) further highlights that, from the moment school
notebooks began to be considered historical sources, interest also arose in “the
study of their material aspects (format, dimensions, layout of graphic spaces,
etc.), their iconography (interiors and covers, whether printed or created by the
student), and their various uses,” with the aim of “developing a typology that
organizes and classifies the various types of notebooks,” as well as
understanding the possibilities and limitations that this study allows.
       The study of school notebooks can contribute to the contextualization of
school practices, “here understood as part of what has been historically defined
over the last decade as school culture” (RAZZINI, 2008, p. 92), which, according
to Julia (2001), is “a set of norms that define knowledge to be taught and
behaviors to be instilled, and a set of practices that enable the transmission of
this knowledge and the incorporation of this knowledge” (JULIA, 2001, p. 10).
       In light of this understanding, Viñao-Frago (2008) considers the notebook
as a product of school culture, explaining that:


                      Whether one considers the history of childhood, written culture, or
                      education, one must never lose sight of the fact that, ultimately, the
                      notebook is a product of school culture—of a specific way of organizing
                      classroom work, of teaching and learning, and of introducing students
                      to the world of academic knowledge and to the rhythms, rules, and
                      norms of school life.
                      As a school product, the notebook reflects the specific culture of the
                      grade level, stage, or educational cycle in which it is used (VIÑAO-
                      FRAGO, 2008, p. 22).


       Grinspun (2008) explains that “the notebook involves visible and invisible
issues, ideas, and content that go beyond what we see and touch,” that is, school


                                                                                         116

notebooks have meanings that go beyond what is written in them, “allowing us to
reflect on learning processes, the curriculum, memories, life stories, records of
taught and assessed content, and communication between parents and
guardians” (GRINSPUN, 2008, p. 264). Thus, studies on school notebooks “make
it possible to examine educational trajectories, learning records, corrections, and
even the student’s interest in lived learning” (GRINSPUN, 2008, p. 259).
      Furthermore, according to Viñao-Frago (2008), “school notebooks should
be situated as a historical source within the context of the school, social, and
cultural practices and norms of their time; their use must be supplemented and
combined with other historical sources” (VIÑAO-FRAGO, 2008, p. 27). In this
sense, Grinspun (2008) adds that the richness of the notebook “transcends the
teaching-learning process to become part of both the training of the
teacher/educator and the expectations and interests of the students”
(GRINSPUN, 2008, p. 259).
      For Grinspun (2008, pp. 259–260), the preserved notebooks also record
the memory of an era, hold incredible stories of a past that will never return, and
allow us to glimpse the rhythms of daily life at that time across different periods,
emphasizing that:


                      If we consider that the notebook is the living history of a particular
                      educational experience, of a particular school or teacher, and if we are
                      interested in understanding how this education takes place, we are
                      faced with a new life lesson. It is enough to observe what the pages say
                      or do not say, the blank pages found on some pages, the retained
                      silences that no writing will ever be able to convey (GRINSPUN, 2008,
                      p. 263).


      Faced with the inexhaustible source of knowledge that research on
Regarding the insights provided by school notebooks, Grinspun (2008) states:
“The more I delve into them, the more I discover about who taught and who
learned” (GRINSPUN, 2008, p. 259). This statement is corroborated by Viñao-
Frago (2008), who notes that there is no object, phenomenon, event, or subject
that, when viewed from different perspectives, does not reveal previously
unnoticed aspects. “Everything depends, therefore, on the position adopted by
the observer. The place from which one looks conditions not only what is seen,
but also how what is seen is perceived” (VIÑAO-FRAGO, 2008, p. 15).




                                                                                          117

      For these reasons, this study on school notebooks, as historical sources
in the context of teaching and learning practices, as well as in the context of
academic, social, and cultural frameworks, was conducted in conjunction with
other historical sources, including information derived from oral history.


3. ADULT BASIC EDUCATION (ABE): AN OPPORTUNITY FOR LEARNING


      With the enactment of the Law on Guidelines and Foundations of National
Education (Law No. 9,394/96), Youth and Adult Education (EJA) came to be
considered a distinct form of Basic Education, “intended for those who did not
have access to or were unable to continue their studies in elementary and
secondary school at the appropriate age” (BRAZIL, 1996, p. 18). In Article 37,
      § 1, Law No. 9,394/96 establishes that:


                      § 1 Educational systems shall provide, free of charge, appropriate
                      educational opportunities to young people and adults who were unable
                      to pursue their studies at the regular age, taking into account the
                      characteristics of the student body, their interests, and their living and
                      working conditions, through courses and examinations (BRAZIL, 1996,
                      p. 18).


      As a result of these legal provisions, on May 10, 2000, the National
Curriculum Guidelines for Youth and Adult Education, developed by the National
Education Council, were enacted, and on January 9, 2001, the Federal
Government included EJA in the National Education Plan (BRAZIL, 2001).
      This form of education is characterized by the diversity of its learners’
profiles (adolescents, young people, adults, and the elderly), “in terms of age,
current level of schooling, socioeconomic status, and “cultural background,
occupations, and the motivation that drives them to seek out school” (PARANÁ,
2006, p. 27).
      Understanding the profile of the EJA learner requires:


                      [...] knowing their history, culture, and customs, understanding them as
                      individuals with diverse life experiences who, at some point, left school
                      due to social, economic, political, and/or cultural factors. Among these
                      factors, the following stand out: early entry into the workforce, school
                      dropout, or grade repetition (PARANÁ, 2006, p. 29).




                                                                                            118

       EJA, therefore, “must include specific pedagogical actions that take into
account the profile of young, adult, and elderly learners who did not receive
schooling or did not continue their studies due to factors often beyond their
control” (PARANÁ, 2006, p. 30).
       Thus, one of the groups deserving special attention in the EJA educational
process is the elderly, who have a specific timeline in the learning process: “they
seek school to develop or expand their knowledge, as well as to engage in other
opportunities for social interaction and personal fulfillment” (PARANÁ, 2006, p.
30). The adolescents, young people, adults, and older adults who seek out EJA
bring with them a wealth of knowledge from other social contexts, “life
experiences that are significant and must be considered in the development of
the school curriculum, which employs a distinct methodology because it
       exhibits characteristics different from those of regular education”
(PARANÁ, 2006, p. 30).
       According to the Curriculum Guidelines for Youth and Adult Education in
the State of Paraná (2006), EJA, as an educational modality, has as its aims and
objectives “a commitment to human development and access to general culture,
so that learners enhance their critical awareness and adopt ethical attitudes and
political commitment for the development of their intellectual autonomy”
(PARANÁ, 2006, p. 27).
       EJA has the responsibility to provide the necessary support so that its
students become active, critical, creative, and democratic individuals, within a
framework that encompasses different cultures, forms of knowledge, and
specificities to be prioritized. It also plays a fundamental role in the socialization
of individuals, “incorporating elements and values that lead them toward
emancipation and the affirmation of their identity “cultural” (PARANÁ, 2006, p.
29).
       According to the Curriculum Guidelines for Youth and Adult Education in
the State of Paraná (2006):


                      Youth and Adult Education (EJA) must have a flexible structure and be
                      capable of incorporating innovations that offer meaningful content.
                      From this perspective, there is a differentiated learning timeline rather
                      than a single timeline for everyone. The limits and possibilities of each
                      learner must be respected; therefore, it is a challenge [...] to present




                                                                                           119

                      viable proposals so that the learner’s access, retention, and success in
                      studies are ensured (PARANÁ, 2006, p. 28).


       It is necessary to foster the involvement of EJA students in school
practices, with access to knowledge in its various forms. “Such practices must be
closely aligned with their needs, expectations, and life trajectories, and must
serve as an incentive for them to continue their studies,” so that, in this way, they
become active participants in the construction of knowledge “through an
understanding of the processes of work, creation, production, and culture”
(PARANÁ, 2006, p. 28).
       The Curriculum Guidelines (2006) also emphasize issues related to
students attending EJA and their relationship with time, content, perspectives,
and life plans:


                      The time a student spends in EJA has its own intrinsic and significant
                      value; therefore, the school must move beyond encyclopedic teaching,
                      which focuses more on the quantity of information than on the
                      qualitative relationship with knowledge. As for the specific content of
                      each subject, it should be grounded in reality, taking into account its
                      socio-historical dimension, linked to the world of work, science, new
                      technologies, among others.
                      With regard to students’ perspectives and their life plans, EJA can help
                      them expand their knowledge critically, enabling reflection through the
                      pursuit of rights to improve their quality of life (PARANÁ, 2006, p. 29).


       Each student who seeks out EJA “brings with them a lived social and
school experience, which implies the need to reorganize the curriculum, school
schedules, and spaces in pursuit of their emancipation,” and [...] “it can be said
that learners have lived and continue to live through individual and collective
times, which encompass the stages of childhood, youth, and adulthood within the
context of multiple social relationships.” It is also worth noting that “the
organization of school times and spaces influences the formation of learners,
whether “to shape or to generate other practices of meaning” (PARANÁ, 2006, p.
33).
       Many students, upon entering adult education, bring with them internalized
models of school experiences or other experiences. “In these models, the idea of
a traditional school predominates, where the educator plays the role of the holder
of knowledge and the learner that of a passive recipient of that knowledge”; for




                                                                                           120

this reason, “many assume that the school is responsible for their learning”
(PARANÁ, 2006, p. 30).
      The role of the EJA educator stands out during the educational process,
stimulating students’ intellectual autonomy so that they may continue their
studies. “It is the educator’s role to encourage the constant pursuit of knowledge
produced by humanity, found in other sources of study or research,” as well as to
stimulate individual study, which is necessary “when it comes to managing the
student’s time spent at school and is important in building autonomy” (PARANÁ,
2006, p. 29).
      According to the Curriculum Guidelines (2006), this intellectual autonomy
must be built so that students become active participants in the educational
process:


                      Human emancipation will result from the development of this autonomy
                      achieved through school education. The exercise of democratic
                      citizenship by EJA students will reflect a cognitive, critical, and
                      emancipatory process, based on values such as mutual respect,
                      solidarity, and justice (PARANÁ, 2006, p. 29).


      The challenge of developing processes of human formation, linked to
socio-historical contexts, in order to reverse exclusion and guarantee learners
access, retention, and success at the start or upon their return to basic schooling,
thus forms the foundation of EJA’s pedagogical work.


4. SCHOOL NOTEBOOKS: A STUDENT’S RECORDS IN ADULT BASIC
EDUCATION (ABE)


      Forgotten for some time were two school notebooks that belonged to an
elderly woman and were used during 2003 and 2004, when she attended an adult
education class at a school in the Curitiba/PR Municipal School System. These
school supplies—or rather, these historical artifacts—were found at the end of
2016, at the back of an old wooden bookshelf, among other documents.
      Upon finding these school notebooks, somewhat by chance, during a
renovation of the property where this woman lives, the desire arose to continue
preserving them, initially with the sole intention of caring for the physical items,
without expecting that one day they might be useful for any reason, as well as for


                                                                                      121

the significance they held, the sentimental value, and the memories they brought
and represented for her—who today is still an independent and hardworking
woman, an active homemaker, seventy-five years old, full of life, and who strives
every day to achieve her goals.
      After observing these materials a few times, it became clear how much
historical data a more detailed analysis of them could provide. Given this
situation, an interest arose in conducting this research, with the aim of capturing
more than just some printed data, but rather attempting to capture the
significance of these notebooks in this woman’s life story. To this end, the oral
history methodology was employed, through interviews with the author of the
notebooks herself, with due ethical care, from the “invitation and assignment of
rights regarding the testimony for use of the data in the research” (VIEIRA, 2015,
p. 372), to transcription and feedback of the data to the interviewee.
      During the interviews, the woman reported that she had a very humble
childhood and was unable to pursue her studies at the typical age. From a very
young age, she had already contributed to the household’s livelihood, helping her
parents with farmwork and at sawmills in the municipality of Faxinal, in northern
Paraná, and thus had not had the opportunity to attend school regularly.
      For a time, around the age of seven or eight, she had studied in a multi-
grade classroom at a rural school located on the grounds of a sawmill. The
conditions for studying at that time, she explained, were very precarious, as her
home was on a farm far from the school. According to the interviewee, she and
her younger sister had to walk about three kilometers to reach the rural school,
without proper shoes, poorly dressed, unaccompanied by their guardians, and
exposed to all kinds of dangers along the way (animal attacks, encounters with
herds of cattle, bad weather, accidents, etc.). Sometimes, she added, hunger and
the physical exhaustion caused by that long journey also took their toll on the two
girls, so they had to stop along the way to rest and eat the snacks they prepared
at home and stored in makeshift lunchboxes, which were old margarine tins.
      Even while facing such difficulties in getting to school, the interviewee
fondly recalled that time, noting that she loved studying and felt proud when her
teacher asked her to help her classmates with their work or to look after the
classroom.



                                                                               122

       Despite her efforts to attend school, even if only for a short period during
her childhood, the woman did not possess a diploma, certificate, transcript, or
any other document proving her education, which she regretted.
       In 2003, however, a group of elderly women living in the Alto Boqueirão
neighborhood of Curitiba, Paraná—whose life stories were similar to the
interviewee’s—learned about an Adult Education (EJA) course being offered at
one of the schools in the Municipal Education Network. They decided to form a
group to resume their studies and invited her to join them. Right at the beginning,
she recounted, she had been a little scared, reluctant to accept the invitation, as
she didn’t believe she was capable of going back to school. After much
encouragement from family and friends, however, she decided to take on the
challenge.
       The course was held at a school near her home. The group of women met
every night, from 7:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m., and one classmate encouraged the
other. They attended EJA classes during 2003 and 2004, with a common goal: to
obtain the long-awaited diploma for grades 1 through 4.
       During the analysis of the two school notebooks used by the interviewee,
it was possible to reflect on the use of these school materials as a source for
research, focused on the study of daily school life and what exists within it that
differs from what is expected and standardized. By delving into her notebooks,
traces of her uniqueness were discovered, which contributed to a reflection on
how she expressed knowledge, feelings, and uncertainties. Her relationships with
elements of effective pedagogical work regarding school content and official
school activities, as well as social roles, among other things, were observed.
       These two school notebooks were also analyzed in terms of their physical
characteristics: they are of the university-style type, intended for a single subject,
without dividers, spiral-bound; both have the same vertical format, measuring 203
x 280 cm, with 96 sheets each, and simple covers illustrated with images of young
athletes. The first notebook has a thin cardboard cover, while the second
notebook has a hardcover made of thicker cardboard. According to the
interviewee, they were purchased randomly, without any consideration of the
listed characteristics, simply because the notebooks were basic items she
needed to attend classes. The notebook covers bore no identification with the
student’s name or the class to which she belonged.


                                                                                  123

       The records revealed routine use of ballpoint pens, alternating between
blue and black ink, as well as pencils and erasers. The use of colored pencils,
crayons, and colored pens was observed only very sporadically. The use of a red
ballpoint pen was exclusive to the teacher, during individual corrections and to
record some praise at the end of the exercises, such as: “Congratulations! Very
good!”, which leads one to believe that this practice was likely just a result of rules
established in the classroom.
       Written in clear handwriting, her records showed almost no erasures,
demonstrating that they were completed with care. It was evident that the student
was concerned about not making mistakes and about organization, neatness,
attention to detail, efficient use of space, and discipline in the use of materials,
likely following aesthetic standards that had been imposed on her in the past. All
the notes recorded by the interviewee in her notebooks were dedicated
exclusively to the content covered in class.
       The student demonstrated seriousness in her studies and a concern to do
everything that was requested. Texts, activities, prompts, and exercises were
recorded in full, completed, and corrected, with almost no embellishments or
other details, always in a legible, clear, and organized manner.
       The marked presence of interdisciplinarity in the development of the
lessons is evident. The content was taught within projects. Based on themes such
as: Heart-shaped cake; The history of money; Papyrus; Folklore; Historical
sources; Work in Brazil; Learning about the history of coffee; Building a healthy
environment; Christmas, its meaning and symbols; among others, the teacher
presented the projects by linking them to the content of the subjects Portuguese,
Mathematics, History, Geography, Science, and Art, drawing on information that
was meaningful to her students, which made sense and related to their life
experiences.
       During the development of the “Heart-Shaped Cake” project, for example,
it is noted that the teacher presented the project proposal based on emotional
connection and leveraging the bonds of friendship within that group to primarily
stimulate the production and interpretation of texts, while also incorporating
research and analysis of other cake recipes, accentuation, fractions, the
measurement system, problem-solving situations, healthy eating, modes of
production, etc.


                                                                                   124

        With the “History of Money” project, the teacher introduced topics such as:
measures of value, the monetary system, Brazilian currency, decimal numbers,
ascending and descending order, writing numbers in words, text production and
interpretation,    problem-solving        situations    involving     addition,    subtraction,
multiplication, and division, fractions, prices, and goods, drawing connections
between the types of currency that had served as monetary standards in Brazil
and which of these the students in that class had encountered.
        In the project “Work in Brazil,” the teacher presented the types or forms of
labor: slave labor, servile labor, and wage labor, also bringing to the discussion
issues regarding indigenous labor, immigrant labor, women’s labor, child labor,
compensation, workers’ hours, significant changes in labor relations in Brazil,
labor laws, workers’ rights and duties, rural workers’ organizations, and the
relationship between educational attainment and the labor market, using
problem-solving scenarios, drawing, painting, captions, text production and
interpretation, graph interpretation and creation, percentages, etc. The photos
below are examples illustrating some of the connections between the “Work in
Brazil” project and the interviewee’s life experiences:


   Figure 1: The description of the activity proposed in the project “Work in Brazil” outlines the
research objective: “To determine, through job advertisements, what the labor market’s current
  requirements are in terms of educational attainment” and the procedure used: “We collected
100 job advertisements from the newspaper and classified the requirements sought by the labor
 market, as shown in the chart below: High school diploma; middle school diploma; incomplete
                            middle school education” (SILVA, 2003).




                                      Source: The authors

blue: incomplete elementary school; red: completed elementary school; light blue: high school;
  green: higher education; brown: no education required (Research results from the “Work in
                                Brazil” project) (SILVA, 2003).




                                     Source: The authors

Figure 3: Text production: Conclusion regarding the graph on the level of education required by
            the labor market (Results of the “Work in Brazil” project) (SILVA, 2003).




                                     Source: The authors


       One of the notebooks analyzed provides some insight into how the teacher
encouraged interactive processes among her students, how interpersonal
relationships developed, and how these interactions took place.
       It was possible to perceive the student’s difficulty—or perhaps simply her
insecurity—in producing texts. Records regarding this are minimal, and some of


                                                                                            126

the fictional characters were given the names of family members or classmates,
with almost no connection to reality.
       It became evident that half of one of the notebooks was designated for
“remedial work,” specifically set aside for the subject of Mathematics. The
multiplication table featured prominently on the back cover; the activities and
exercises were not linked to interdisciplinary projects, and various exercises were
recorded, completed, and corrected in a more mechanical manner.
       Also noteworthy was the presence of a large section with blank pages,
resulting from a period when the student had not attended classes because her
daughter was hospitalized with a serious health issue.
       During the study, therefore, it was possible to gain a deeper understanding
of this student’s academic behavior, her relationship with the school, and with the
curriculum. It was also possible to observe some of her unique traits as she
interacted with these materials, which served as spaces for expressing her
individuality and some of her criteria and values.


5. CONCLUDING REMARKS


       Given the expansion and diversity of documentary sources fostered by
cultural history, school notebooks have come to be recognized as such,
representing a vast field for research in the history of education. From this
perspective, this study analyzed visible and invisible issues discernible in school
notebook records, highlighting the potential for using these materials as historical
sources.
       The context studied was that of EJA—Youth and Adult Education, a form
of education considered an alternative learning opportunity for those who did not
complete their studies at the standard age, characterized by the diversity of its
students’ profiles (adolescents, young adults, adults, and seniors), who bring with
them a wealth of knowledge from other social contexts. EJA is responsible for
providing the resources for its students to become active, critical, creative, and
democratic individuals, taking into account different cultures, forms of knowledge,
and specificities that need to be prioritized in the socialization of these individuals.
       Based on the analysis of two notebooks used by a student who attended
an EJA class at a school in the Curitiba/PR Municipal Education Network during


                                                                                    127

the 2003–2004 academic year, it was possible to contextualize school practices,
reflecting on the use of these artifacts and what they represent in daily school life,
in the relationship between the prescribed and the standardized. The research
also brought to light issues related to content, subjects, and the relationships
between them, perceived by delving into the lines and between the lines of the
studied material.
       By analyzing these notebooks, it was possible to uncover traces of their
uniqueness and the way in which the student expressed knowledge, feelings, and
uncertainties. Her relationships with elements of effective pedagogical work, with
school content and official school activities, as well as with social roles, were
observed.
       During the course of the research, evidence emerged that could be directly
related to the reality in which the student was embedded: information about daily
school life, the subjects, the norms, the school environment, its practices, and its
objectives.
       In short, the study of school notebooks allowed for a deeper understanding
of school notebooks, their use, and what they represent in the daily life of the
school, as spaces for the expression of the student’s individuality.

CHAPTER 8
 TEACHING TISSUE ENGINEERING
 THROUGH PROJECT-BASED LEARNING: AN
 EXPERIENCE REPORT FROM A TEACHING
 AND PEER-TUTORING PROJECT

ABSTRACT: Tissue engineering is a rapidly evolving field focused on the
development of biological substitutes in laboratory settings. Its inherently
interdisciplinary nature requires pedagogical strategies capable of integrating
biomedical and technological concepts in a cohesive and meaningful way. The


                                                                           131

course Fundamentals of Tissue and Organ Engineering, offered at the Federal
University of Rio Grande do Norte (UFRN), Brazil, has no prerequisites and
therefore attracts students from diverse health and technology programs,
enriching multiprofessional discussions. This experience report describes the
implementation of project-based learning combined with a teaching and peer-
tutoring initiative during academic semesters from 2023.1 to 2025.2, with the aim
of enhancing teaching quality and student performance. At the beginning of each
semester, students were challenged to design a tissue or organ and progressively
refine their projects as new theoretical concepts were introduced. This dynamic
required continuous supervision and fostered active discussion, conceptual
consolidation, and clarification of questions. Teaching assistants played a central
role by developing educational materials, supporting digital learning activities,
and providing guided assistance under faculty supervision. This experience
suggests that close integration among faculty members, teaching assistants, and
students is essential for knowledge consolidation and for promoting a dynamic,
collaborative, and motivating learning environment. This experience contributed
to students’ academic development, strengthened the pedagogical training of
teaching assistants, and reinforced the teaching–learning process in tissue
engineering.

KEYWORDS: tissue engineering, project-based learning, peer tutoring, teaching
assistants, higher education, health profession education.




                                                                               132

1. INTRODUCTION


         Tissue engineering is an interdisciplinary field that integrates principles
from engineering and life sciences to develop in vitro biological substitutes for
damaged or lost tissues and organs (Langer, 2000). Although its conceptual roots
have extended back centuries, tissue engineering became more firmly
established as a biomedical field in the late twentieth century, driven in part by
the growing demand for innovative strategies to repair or replace injured tissues
(Levin et al., 2019; Zhang & Yelick, 2018). This global context has intensified the
need to train professionals capable of navigating the scientific, technological, and
ethical complexities that characterize the field.
         With respect to undergraduate education, however, teaching tissue
engineering presents important challenges. Because the field draws on
knowledge from anatomy, histology, embryology, cell biology, biochemistry,
biomaterials, scientific methodology, and bioethics, students are required to
integrate concepts that are traditionally taught in separate disciplinary domains.
Conventional teaching approaches may therefore be insufficient to support
meaningful learning in such a dynamic and multifaceted area (Marques et al.,
2021).
         At the Federal University of Rio Grande do Norte (UFRN), Brazil, the
course Fundamentals of Tissue and Organ Engineering is offered as an elective
by the Department of Morphology for undergraduate students in biomedicine,
biological sciences, and dentistry. Because the course has no prerequisites, it
also attracts students from other health- and technology-related programs,
including biomedical engineering, medicine, pharmacy, and physical therapy.
This academic diversity creates valuable opportunities for interdisciplinary
exchange while also increasing the need for pedagogical strategies that promote
engagement, conceptual integration, and collaborative learning.
         To address these demands, project-based learning was adopted as the
core teaching strategy in the course. In health and biomedical education, this
active-learning approach has been recognized for its potential to connect theory
with practice, promote student autonomy, and foster the development of scientific
and professional competencies (Pranjol, Oprandi, & Watson, 2024). Its
successful implementation, however, depends on sustained guidance, close


                                                                                133

monitoring of group work, and structured support throughout the learning process
(Kokotsaki, Menzies, & Wiggins, 2016). In this setting, the peer-tutoring initiative
played a key pedagogical role by supporting students’ progress, facilitating
interaction between faculty and students, and contributing to the educational
development of the teaching assistants themselves (Souza & Oliveira, 2023;
Sanday, Silva, & Mocellin, 2024).
      Against this background, this chapter reports the experience of
implementing project-based learning in association with a peer-tutoring initiative
in tissue engineering education during academic semesters from 2023.1 to
2025.2. Specifically, it describes the pedagogical strategies adopted, examines
their contributions to the teaching–learning process, and discusses their impact
on the academic and pedagogical development of teaching assistants.


2. EDUCATIONAL AND CONCEPTUAL FOUNDATIONS


      As a field within regenerative medicine, tissue engineering is supported by
three fundamental pillars: a cell source capable of forming the target tissue, a
biocompatible scaffold that provides structural support and a favorable
environment for cell growth, and bioactive molecules or growth factors that direct
cellular proliferation and differentiation (Langer & Vacanti, 2016). The success of
tissue engineering strategies depends on multiple interconnected factors,
including the appropriate selection of cell sources and methods for cell collection,
isolation, and stimulation (Lira et al., 2024); the choice of biomaterials and
scaffold synthesis and functionalization techniques that favor cell adhesion,
migration, and differentiation (Bakhshandeh et al., 2017); and the identification of
effective agents capable of stimulating cellular activity (Sabino et al., 2020). In
addition, the field involves discussion of in vitro and in vivo evaluation methods,
as well as ethical and translational issues. For this reason, tissue engineering
education requires an interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary approach capable of
integrating scientific, technological, and ethical perspectives (Sarvazyan, 2020;
Bateman & Sherman, 2025).
      This need becomes even more relevant when considering the profile of
students currently entering higher education. Recent cohorts, particularly those
commonly described as belonging to Generation Z, have been associated with


                                                                                134

strong familiarity with digital technologies, preference for practical and immersive
experiences, expectation of rapid feedback, appreciation of autonomy, and
interest in collaborative and meaningful learning processes (Chaudhuri, 2020).
Such characteristics help explain why many students tend to engage more
effectively when they participate actively in knowledge construction rather than
remaining limited to the passive reception of content.
       In this context, active-learning methodologies become especially relevant.
Rather than emphasizing the accumulation of information, these approaches
prioritize knowledge construction and skills development, with instructors creating
meaningful learning situations that promote initiative, participation, and student
responsibility (Monteiro, Caires, & Almeida, 2025). Active learning may therefore
be understood as an approach that encourages students to assume a central role
in their own education by engaging critically in the search for, analysis of, and
application of knowledge (Moran, 2018). It also supports the development of
essential professional competencies by integrating theory and practice and
fostering critical thinking and decision-making (Silva et al., 2025).
       Among active-learning methodologies, project-based learning (PBL)
stands out as a student-centered approach that emphasizes engagement,
collaboration, and critical thinking through the exploration of real-world
challenges (Kokotsaki, Menzies, & Wiggins, 2016; Guo et al., 2020). Grounded
in constructivist principles, PBL positions students as active participants in the
learning process and values their prior knowledge, experiences, and
perspectives (Revelle et al., 2020). By introducing authentic and complex
problems that resemble professional situations, this methodology encourages
students    to     formulate    questions,   conduct     investigations,   and   develop
collaborative solutions (Jones, 2019; Almulla, 2020; Warr & West, 2020).
       In health profession education, PBL has been shown to promote
knowledge        integration,   interdisciplinary   collaboration,   and   adaptability—
competencies that are increasingly important in a rapidly changing global context
(Shah, Patel, & Chhatriwala, 2021; Si, 2020). It also strengthens essential abilities
such as critical thinking, problem solving, and teamwork while increasing student
motivation and engagement (Chang et al., 2022). More recently, PBL has gained
further relevance through digital technologies, especially in the post-COVID-19
educational landscape, in which virtual learning environments and collaborative


                                                                                     135

software have expanded opportunities for teamwork, problem solving, and joint
project development (Samala et al., 2024).
      The effectiveness of PBL, however, depends on systematic follow-up and
continuous pedagogical support. In the context of Brazilian higher education, this
support is often provided through institutional teaching assistantship programs,
which have been recognized in educational policy since Law No. 5.540/1968 and
reaffirmed by the Law of Directives and Bases of National Education (LDB No.
9.394/1996) as activities that promote integration among teaching, research, and
extension (Sanday, Silva, & Mocellin, 2024). More than being an auxiliary
resource, such programs have increasingly been understood as formative
educational practices that benefit both the students receiving support and the
teaching assistants themselves. Studies indicate that teaching assistants can act
as mediators between faculty and students, fostering collaborative learning, self-
regulation, and student agency (Frison, 2016). This horizontal interaction
contributes to a more accessible and participatory learning environment in which
knowledge exchange and joint problem solving strengthen conceptual
understanding and student confidence (Oliveira & Vosgerau, 2021).
      From an institutional perspective, teaching assistantship programs
represent a strategic resource for improving teaching quality, stimulating critical
reflection on educational methodologies, and strengthening a culture of academic
cooperation (Sanday, Silva, & Mocellin, 2024; Santos & Silva, 2025). With respect
to teaching assistants, the experience provides an opportunity for early
pedagogical development by expanding their understanding of the educational
process, strengthening communication and instructional skills, and often
stimulating interest in an academic career (Silva et al., 2021; Souza & Oliveira,
2023; Kavalek & Pessoa, 2023). This formative dimension extends beyond
technical support to the instructor and becomes relevant to the construction of
the teaching assistant’s professional and pedagogical identity. By collaborating
with faculty, teaching assistants may participate in the planning, implementation,
and evaluation of educational activities, thereby consolidating theoretical and
practical knowledge about teaching and learning while developing mediation,
empathy, pedagogical responsibility, and professional confidence (Silva et al.,
2021; Souza & Oliveira, 2023; Kavalek & Pessoa, 2023).



                                                                               136

       Taken together, these educational and conceptual foundations suggest
that integrating project-based learning with structured teaching assistantship and
peer-tutoring support is a coherent pedagogical strategy for teaching complex
and interdisciplinary content such as tissue engineering. From this perspective,
the course Fundamentals of Tissue and Organ Engineering at UFRN provided an
appropriate setting for the implementation and consolidation of these approaches
and served as the foundation for the teaching and peer-tutoring project reported
in this chapter.


3. METHODOLOGY


       This experience report describes the implementation of an instructional
strategy integrating project-based learning and a peer-tutoring initiative in the
course Fundamentals of Tissue and Organ Engineering at the Federal University
of Rio Grande do Norte (UFRN), Brazil, between academic semesters 2023.1
and 2025.2. Over this period, the course was offered in seven sections—five in
the afternoon and two in the evening—with a total enrollment of 255
undergraduate students. Each year, the project involved two teaching assistants
working within the peer-tutoring initiative under the supervision of the same
faculty member. The chapter is based on a reflective account of the pedagogical
process supported by qualitative evidence gathered during the implementation of
the activities.
       At the beginning of each semester, students were challenged to propose
the in vitro development of a tissue or organ. This task functioned as the
organizing framework for the course and guided the integration of theoretical and
practical content. As new concepts were introduced, student groups
progressively refined and expanded their proposals by articulating biomedical
and technological knowledge. The project-based learning activities were
designed by the instructional team, which included the faculty supervisor, the
teaching assistants, and a graduate student engaged in a supervised teaching
practicum, to ensure alignment with the course learning objectives.
       The course was delivered in person and combined synchronous and
asynchronous activities. Synchronous sessions included interactive lectures,
roundtable discussions, and thematic analysis of scientific articles. Asynchronous


                                                                              137

activities were offered through the university’s virtual learning environment,
allowing additional time for project development and collaborative group work.
Students had access to all essential learning materials and submitted
assignments for each stage through the university’s electronic academic
management platform, the Integrated Academic Activities Management System
(SIGAA).
       The project-based learning strategy was organized into five stages—
preparation, implementation, presentation, evaluation, and revision—following
the framework proposed by Taiebine, Al Hassani, and Nejjari (2024). Across the
semester, the student projects were developed through six sequential thematic
axes, each with specific objectives and guiding strategies (Table 1).


Table 1. Thematic axes guiding the development of student projects on in vitro tissue or organ
                                       construction
