                                                        to animal experimentation
                                  Source: Prepared by the authors.


       Within each thematic axis, the five stages of project-based learning were
operationalized through guiding challenges delivered via the institutional
platforms SIGAA and Multiprova. Students who worked in small groups
completed the activities with direct support from the teaching assistants, whose
role was central to pedagogical mediation and methodological guidance. The
assignments submitted at each stage were reviewed by the instructional team,
which included the faculty member, the teaching assistants, and the graduate
student, and formative feedback was provided to support revision before
progression to the next thematic axis.




                                                                                                 138

       Because the methodology required sustained pedagogical support,
students were followed continuously by the instructional team throughout the
semester. To facilitate communication, a WhatsApp group was created to allow
rapid interaction between students and staff. Weekly goals were also established
to promote steady progress and prevent the accumulation of tasks.
       This follow-up was intended not only to clarify conceptual and
methodological issues related to tissue engineering but also to encourage
student progression across the different stages of project development. In
parallel, the approach fostered creativity, autonomy, and decision-making;
strengthened collaborative learning; and contributed to the pedagogical
development of the teaching assistants.


4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION


       The implementation of project-based learning (PBL) in association with the
peer-tutoring initiative in tissue engineering education yielded positive outcomes
in terms of student engagement, meaningful learning, and the development of
cognitive and socioemotional competencies. Among the 328 students enrolled in
the course sections included in this project, 317 passed, corresponding to a pass
rate of 96.6%. Although pass rates alone do not fully capture the quality of
learning, this high rate, combined with the strong adherence of students to the
proposed activities, suggests a favorable academic environment marked by
motivation and sustained engagement, in line with the observations of Almulla
(2020). As students were challenged to design and progressively develop an in
vitro tissue or organ project, they became more active in discussions and
demonstrated increasing intellectual autonomy throughout the semester. This
pattern reinforces the potential of PBL to promote student agency and active
learning, as highlighted by Kokotsaki, Menzies, and Wiggins (2016) and Chang
et al. (2022).
       Group-based activities encouraged collaboration among students from
different academic backgrounds and supported the integration of multiple
domains of knowledge, reflecting the interdisciplinary nature of tissue
engineering. In this context, students were able to articulate concepts from cell
biology, materials engineering, bioethics, and scientific methodology in response


                                                                              139

to the proposed challenges, demonstrating a broader and more integrated
understanding of course content. The progressive development of the projects
was therefore essential not only for intellectual growth but also for the
strengthening of practical competencies applicable beyond the classroom. This
close connection between theory and practice is consistent with the findings of
Pranjol, Oprandi, and Watson (2024), who describe PBL as an effective strategy
for developing scientific and professional competencies in complex and
interdisciplinary educational settings. In our experience, the integration of active
learning, critical reflection, and collaborative problem solving confirmed the
pedagogical value of PBL as a transformative strategy in higher education, as
also emphasized by Lee, Yoon, and Hwang (2024).
       Continuous follow-up by the teaching assistants and the faculty member
proved to be a key element in consolidating the methodology. The pedagogical
support provided by the teaching assistants was particularly important because it
facilitated communication between faculty and students, promoted the
clarification of conceptual and procedural questions, and contributed to a more
accessible and collaborative learning environment. As noted by Frison (2016)
and Silva et al. (2021), teaching assistants can play an important mediating role
in the learning process by fostering self-regulation and autonomy among their
peers. In the present experience, this role became evident in the monitoring of
weekly tasks and goals, as well as in the mediation of conceptual difficulties and
interpersonal challenges within the groups. These contributions strengthened the
pedagogical relationship between students and the instructional team and helped
maintain continuity across the different stages of project development.
       Another relevant finding was the formative impact of the initiative on the
teaching assistants themselves. Participation in PBL activities expanded their
pedagogical, communicative, and organizational competencies, offering early
teaching experience in a real educational context. By monitoring group progress,
preparing instructional materials, and participating in assessment and feedback
processes, the teaching assistants developed greater capacity for planning,
empathy, and critical reflection on teaching and learning. This experience
supports the contributions described by Silva et al. (2021), Souza and Oliveira
(2023), and Sanday, Silva, and Mocellin (2024), who characterize teaching
assistantship as a formative practice that can foster initial pedagogical


                                                                                140

development and consolidate educational knowledge. Constant interaction with
both faculty and students also appeared to promote professional maturation, in
agreement with Kavalek and Pessoa (2023) and Santos and Silva (2025), who
identify these experiences as meaningful spaces for the construction of teaching
identity.
       Overall, the findings suggest that the integration of PBL with a peer-
tutoring    initiative   strengthened   the   teaching–learning   process    in   the
Fundamentals of Tissue and Organ Engineering course by promoting a dynamic,
collaborative, and student-centered environment. The methodology stimulated
scientific curiosity, intellectual autonomy, and students’ sense of responsibility
while also contributing to the pedagogical development of the teaching assistants
and to reflective teaching practices. Taken together, these results indicate that
the combination of active-learning methodologies and structured teaching
assistants can be a viable and effective strategy for teaching complex and
interdisciplinary content, contributing to the quality of academic training and to
the consolidation of a collaborative learning culture in higher education.


5. CONCLUSION


       The experience reported in this chapter demonstrated that the integration
of project-based learning (PBL) with a peer-tutoring initiative constitutes an
effective strategy for teaching complex and interdisciplinary content such as
tissue engineering. The implementation of this approach fostered a dynamic,
collaborative, and student-centered learning environment in which knowledge
was constructed progressively and in a meaningful context. The organization of
the projects into thematic axes, together with continuous follow-up by the
teaching assistants and the faculty member, supported the consolidation of
theoretical content, the development of practical skills, and the strengthening of
teamwork and problem-solving competencies.
       The participation of the teaching assistants proved essential to the
success of the proposal, functioning both as pedagogical support for students
and as a formative space for early teaching development. This experience
contributed to the improvement of the teaching assistants’ communicative,
reflective, and instructional skills, promoting the construction of their teaching


                                                                                  141

identity and strengthening their commitment to educational practice in higher
education.
       Overall, the initiative proved relevant not only for improving the quality of
tissue engineering education but also for fostering the development of critical,
creative, and engaged future professionals and educators committed to
innovation and interdisciplinarity in the health sciences.

CHAPTER 9
 MOLECULAR STRUCTURES IN
 ACTION: USING GAME TO ASSIST
 IN LEARNING THE FUNDAMENTALS
 OF ORGANIC CHEMISTRY

Karlos Alexandre Martins
Master's Degree in Chemistry
Universidade Federal do Triângulo Mineiro (UFTM)
E-mail: karlosalexandremartins@gmail.com

Alexandre Rossi
Doctor in Organic Chemistry
Universidade de São Paulo
E-mail: alexandre.rossi@uftm.edu.br

Evandro Roberto Alves
Doctor in Analytical Chemistry
Universidade de São Paulo
E-mail: evandro.alves@uftm.edu.br


ABSTRACT: Teaching Chemistry has been a challenging task for the subject
teacher, who must stimulate learning and spark students' interest in the content
in an engaging way. Organic Chemistry is considered complex by high school
students, as it is abstract and requires memorization of formulas and
nomenclature, in addition to understanding the representations of the three-
dimensional molecular structures of organic compounds. Several factors have
been identified as responsible for the lack of success in learning Organic
Chemistry, such as the use of traditional teaching methodologies which include
demotivating classes that disregard students' everyday experiences, resulting in
a lack of interest in the subject. The playful game "Molecular Structures in Action"
(MSA) was designed to assist high school Chemistry teachers in their classroom
work, making it easier for students to review and understand key concepts of
Organic Chemistry, enhancing learning. MSA is composed of pieces similar to a
puzzle, made of colored acrylic and designed to represent the atoms of the main
chemical elements that form organic compounds. The colors of the pieces follow
the CPK standardization. After the implementation of MSA for a class of 37 3rd-
year high school students, the review and consolidation of Organic Chemistry
fundamentals were evaluated by high school teachers as positive and engaging,
as it minimized the abstraction of the content. Students also found MSA to be an
interesting teaching approach, suggesting that teachers from other subjects could
also use this method of teaching.



                                                                                146

KEYWORDS: organic chemistry, gamification, game, chemistry teaching.

RESUMO: Lecionar Química tem sido uma tarefa desafiadora para o professor,
que deve estimular a aprendizagem e despertar o interesse dos alunos pelos
conteúdos de forma atrativa. A Química Orgânica é considerada pelos alunos do
Ensino Médio como complexa, por ser abstrata e exigir a memorização de fór-
mulas e nomenclaturas, além do entendimento das representações das estrutu-
ras moleculares tridimensionais dos compostos orgânicos. Alguns fatores foram
apontados como responsáveis pelo insucesso da aprendizagem de Química Or-
gânica, tais como o uso de metodologias tradicionais de ensino que contemplam
aulas desmotivadoras que desconsideram a vivência cotidiana dos alunos, re-
sultando no desinteresse pela disciplina. O jogo lúdico “Estruturas Moleculares
em Ação” (EMA) foi concebido com o objetivo de auxiliar o professor de Química
do Ensino Médio durante o seu trabalho em sala de aula e facilitar a revisão e
assimilação dos conteúdos fundamentais da Química Orgânica, fortalecendo a
aprendizagem. EMA é composto por peças semelhantes às de um quebra-ca-
beça, confeccionadas em acrílico colorido e idealizadas para representar os áto-
mos dos principais elementos químicos formadores dos compostos orgânicos.
As cores das peças obedeceram a padronização CPK. Após a aplicação do EMA
para uma turma de 37 alunos do 3º ano do Ensino Médio, a revisão e a consoli-
dação dos fundamentos de Química Orgânica foram avaliadas pelos professores
das escolas de Ensino Médio como positiva e engajada, tendo minimizado a abs-
tração dos conteúdos. Os alunos avaliaram o EMA como uma proposta interes-
sante de ensino, mencionando que os professores de outras disciplinas também
poderiam utilizar essa maneira de ensinar.

PALAVRAS-CHAVE: química orgânica, gamificação, jogo, ensino de química.




                                                                            147

1. INTRODUCTION


       Teaching chemistry has been a challenging task for chemistry teachers,
who must stimulate learning in an engaging way and spark students’ interest in
content that is often abstract, given that most students are no longer interested
in classes taught in the traditional format (Carbo et al., 2019; Silva, Loja, & Pires,
2020; Pinheiro, Cardoso, 2022; Lima, 2024). Traditional teaching is often based
on pedagogical activities that require memorization, intensifying abstraction and
hindering the development of critical and scientific learning (Vieira; Silva, 2017;
Assai et al.,   2018; Rossi et al., 2024). Abstraction and the emphasis on
memorizing symbols, formulas, and the nomenclature of organic compounds
make the content even more complex, resulting in tiring and uninteresting
classes.   Teaching    processes     that   rely   on   memorization    mechanisms
disconnected from students’ everyday reality can inhibit their ability to
comprehend new information and demotivate them during learning (Capellato;
Ribeiro; Sachs, 2019; Delou; Albano, 2023).
       Although Organic Chemistry is present in our daily lives at all times and in
various forms, the content is considered difficult by high school students due to
the abstraction involved and the diversity of similar organic functions, which often
cause confusion (Pereira; Fernandes; Bizerra, 2020; Delou; Albano, 2023). Given
the importance of knowledge related to Organic Chemistry, mastery of the
fundamental basic concepts of this subfield of Chemistry is relevant and
indispensable for understanding everyday phenomena, as well as the chemical
properties and reactivity of its compounds.
       A lack of interest in learning Organic Chemistry may be related to a lack of
understanding and the disconnect between the content and everyday life, as it
does not establish a close connection to students’ reality (Pricinotto; Primo, 2020;
Almeida, 2022; Silva et al., 2024). In everyday life, there are various chemical
transformations involving organic compounds; however, most students do not
know how to associate them with chemical knowledge.
       The traditional approach to teaching has been considered incompatible
with contemporary needs (Cunha, 2012; Souza; Cantero, 2024). In this context,
educational games have been gaining prominence in the teaching and learning
process, as they incorporate motivational elements that spark students’ interest


                                                                                  148

and enthusiasm. Recreational games value creativity, interaction, and
imagination (Conde et al., 2021; Arnaud, 2024).
       According to Ferreira et al. (2012), engaging in a playful activity produces
satisfaction and entertains the participant. If there are rules for carrying out this
activity, it can be considered a game, provided that it fosters closeness and
interaction among participants. Playful activities provide an engaging experience
through the use of dynamic and mechanical elements (Ortiz; Dorneles, 2018).
Thus, playful games become educational when used in the classroom,
considering that playfulness stimulates students’ ability to analyze, think, and
develop their logical reasoning (Bezerra; Silva, 2024).
       Cunha (2012) notes that educational games can be used to present and
illustrate relevant aspects of content, assess previously taught material, review
and synthesize chemical concepts, and organize and integrate topics in an
interdisciplinary and contextualized manner. Franco et al. (2018) report various
benefits of games when applied in the classroom as a teaching strategy,
highlighting the development of self-esteem, improved interaction between
teacher and student, student and peers, as well as student and community. They
also foster the development of cognitive skills, autonomy, self-reflection,
creativity, self-assessment, increased attention, concentration, and the ability to
complete schoolwork. The same authors emphasize that respect, boundaries, the
incorporation of values, the expansion of logical reasoning and motor
coordination, and the development of spatial organization and a spirit of
cooperation were also observed during the application of this pedagogical tool.
       In light of the above, this study aimed to develop the educational game
“Molecular Structures in Action (EMA)” as a low-cost educational resource
designed to assist teachers in the classroom during the review of fundamental
concepts in Organic Chemistry. During EMA games, students manipulated the
physical game pieces, stimulating touch, sight, and imagination, in order to
facilitate the process of cognitive construction and the review of concepts and
content.




                                                                                 149

2. METHODOLOGY


      This study was conducted in stages involving the conception, construction,
and implementation of the EMA educational game with 37 11th-grade students
from Public High Schools A, B, and C, located in the city of Uberaba (MG).
      The EMA aimed to attract students’ attention to the learning of introductory
Organic Chemistry content, using an innovative, attractive, and interesting
pedagogical tool with dynamics distinct from those found in traditional teaching
(Saleem et al., 2022; Bezerra, 2024). Below is a description of the stages of
development of the EMA educational game:
      Stage 1 (Analysis of responses to a questionnaire administered to
chemistry teachers to design the EMA educational game): The teachers
interviewed in this stage answered 8 multiple-choice questions regarding the
teaching methodology and digital resources they use in their classes, the profile
of the student groups they teach, and the reasons for their students’ lack of
interest in the subject of chemistry. The questions were created on the Google
Forms platform, with the aim of clarifying for the teacher-researcher what type of
activity should be adopted to facilitate the teaching of introductory Organic
Chemistry content in an engaging and stimulating manner.
      Stage 2 (Development of the EMA educational game): The EMA
educational game was developed based on a preliminary analysis of the
structures of organic compounds covered in the initial phase of Organic
Chemistry studies, taking into account the types of chemical bonds between
atoms, molecular geometry, organic functions, as well as the responses provided
by the teachers interviewed in Stage 1.
      Stage 3 (Application of the EMA educational game and analysis of
results). To implement the EMA, the teacher-researcher divided the classes into
groups of 4 students, who received instructions on how to play the games via a
video created by the researcher and integrated into the game.          The video
displayed cards containing instructions on how to assemble the structures of
organic compounds, information regarding types of carbon chains and the
number of carbons they contain, types of chemical bonds (saturated or
unsaturated chains), the nature of the atoms present (homogeneous or
heterogeneous     carbon    chain),   the   closure    of   the   carbon     chain


                                                                               150

(open/acyclic/aliphatic or closed/cyclic or aromatic), and the arrangement of the
atoms (linear or branched chain). During the rounds of the EMA game, students
were qualitatively assessed regarding enjoyment, prior knowledge of organic
chemistry, mastery of fundamental organic chemistry concepts, teamwork, and
interest in the proposed methodology (gamification). The teacher-researcher also
interviewed teachers from schools A, B, and C involved in the study, asking them
to report whether the EMA educational game could be considered a teaching
resource that facilitates the teaching and learning process of fundamental organic
chemistry concepts.


3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS


      The responses provided by each of the teachers from Schools A, B, and
C interviewed during the first stage helped the teacher-researcher in designing
the EMA educational game, particularly in understanding the students’ learning
difficulties in the subject of Chemistry. Furthermore, the responses clarified the
type of appropriate activity that should be planned as a strategy for reviewing the
fundamental content of Organic Chemistry. When asked about the reason for
students’ failure to learn Organic Chemistry content, 70% of the interviewed
teachers cited the spatial abstraction of organic compound structures as the
content with which students have the greatest difficulty learning. The other
responses cited were a lack of understanding of natural phenomena at the
macroscopic and microscopic levels (18%) and a failure to contextualize the
content within students’ daily lives (12%). In another question, which addressed
the use of active methodologies by teachers in their teaching practice, it was
found that 40% of them use blended learning, gamification, the flipped classroom,
problem-based learning, and peer instruction, albeit infrequently. Among the 60%
of respondents who have never used active methodologies, three reported being
unaware of the meaning of the term, eight had heard of it ( ), seven intend to use
it, and one has no intention of doing so. School teachers were also asked in which
area of Chemistry they used gamification, with 67% and 53% of respondents
citing the application of this methodology in Organic Chemistry and Physical
Chemistry content, respectively. The higher percentage of gamification use in
Organic Chemistry is likely due to the fact that students consider this area of


                                                                               151

chemistry to be “difficult” and because it depends on understanding prior content,
such as molecular geometry, chemical bonds, and compound nomenclature,
which are easy to gamify.
       The choice of gamification was justified because it is an engaging
methodology that differs from traditional teaching activities, in addition to
facilitating student learning by stimulating curiosity and a desire for challenge.
These responses provided by the interviewed teachers are corroborated by the
authors Cleophas; Soares, 2018; Silva; Pires, 2020; Eugenio, 2024.
       The second stage involved the development of the EMA educational
game. Figures 1 and 2 show, respectively, the plastic packaging for the
instruction cards and the colored EMA pieces, in accordance with the CPK model
convention developed by Corey, Pauling, and Koltun (1965), which uses
standardized colors to distinguish atoms of different chemical elements.
       The cards containing the game instructions, as well as the methane and
ethane structures assembled according to the EMA game instructions—to
illustrate how they should fit together—are shown in Figures 3 and 4.


Figure 1. Packaging for the EMA educational game, containing the instruction cards and pieces.




                              Source: Prepared by the authors.

    Figure 2. Pieces of the EMA educational game with the colors of the chemical elements
 standardized according to the IUPAC convention . (The colors of the pieces represent carbon
  (black), hydrogen (white), oxygen (red), nitrogen (blue), sulfur (yellow), fluorine (turquoise),
chlorine (green), bromine (burgundy), iodine (purple-blue), and the types of chemical bonds that
 must occur between carbon atoms to form the carbon chain (single, double, and triple covalent
                                 bonds represented in white).

      Figure 3. Sample letter of instructions for the rounds of the EMA educational game.

              Figure 4. Pieces assembled to form methane and ethane molecules.




                              Source: Prepared by the authors.


          Made of colored acrylic at a local print shop and designed to represent the
main chemical elements that form organic compounds, such as carbon,
hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur, and halogens (chlorine, bromine, and iodine),
the pieces of the EMA educational game were produced at a cost of R$ 80.00.
Round in shape and featuring openings for the joints designed to resemble
molecular geometry, the pieces were constructed according to the color of each
chemical element (Figure 2). Sticks representing single, double, and triple
covalent chemical bonds were also produced in acrylic to facilitate their
interlocking , ensuring greater durability and a better demonstration of carbon
chain formation.
          Analysis of the results, following the administration of the EMA educational
game to the students participating in the study during Stage 3, demonstrated their
improved understanding regarding the fact that carbon’s tetravalence can be
established through single, double, or triple covalent bonds. This insight enabled
them to comprehend the formation of different types of carbon chains and their
classification.
          The students mentioned that the instructions for the EMA games
presented in the video were clear, easy to understand, and presented in a logical
sequence. They reported that the EMA game facilitated the review and learning
of fundamental content, expressing their views as follows: “If we had more
classes like this, we would learn a lot”; “More classes like this to learn more”; “It
was very good for better understanding the content”; “We should have it more
often!”
          The teachers responsible for the Chemistry course at Schools A, B, and C
observed high student engagement during classes, as well as greater interest
and motivation in reviewing introductory Organic Chemistry content when playing


                                                                                  154

the EMA games. The concepts of the subject were revisited and learned more
easily through the use of the interactive and challenging elements of the game,
which aided in building knowledge as a team. EMA encouraged cooperation,
which facilitated content comprehension and learning. The way the pieces were
configured, respecting the positioning of the joints and the colors of the chemical
elements, facilitated students’ visualization of the valence and composition of
each type of carbon chain (cyclic or acyclic, normal or branched, saturated or
unsaturated, homogeneous or heterogeneous), minimizing abstraction. The
same teachers considered that the EMA demonstrated its potential as a teaching
resource that facilitates the teaching and learning process of the fundamental
concepts of Organic Chemistry.


4. CONCLUSION


       The proposal to develop a playful activity aimed at helping students review
and understand the fundamental concepts of Organic Chemistry was
successfully implemented and broke the paradigm of uninteresting and
demotivating classes when conducted in the traditional teaching format.
       The EMA game, structured as an educational resource, minimized the
difficulty faced by teachers seeking to teach abstract concepts of Organic
Chemistry to their students, thereby emphasizing that gamification is an
attractive, dynamic, and enjoyable teaching methodology. The stimulation of the
human senses, particularly sight and touch, through colors and the manipulation
of 2D pieces representing each chemical element forming the carbon chains of
organic compounds, served as crucial resources for minimizing abstraction and
strengthening learning.
       The review of basic and fundamental concepts in Organic Chemistry was
facilitated by the exchange of knowledge and insights among the student players,
who were engaged during the rounds of the EMA game, demonstrating that it is
a relevant and effective activity in the teaching and learning process.
       Public school teachers viewed the EMA as an important educational tool
that helped students review and learn the fundamentals of organic chemistry.
Furthermore, given that the colored pieces symbolically represented the chains
of organic compounds, as well as the different types of chemical bonds involved,


                                                                               155

these game elements contributed to its evaluation as an effective educational
resource in the teaching and learning process.
      For future studies, it is suggested that the EMA educational game be used
as an assessment tool and applied to the teaching or review of other topics in
Organic Chemistry, such as the recognition of types of carbon chains and the
chemical bonds involved, the nomenclature of organic compounds, and the
geometric arrangement of atoms in organic structures and functions.

ABSTRACT: The school environment frequently presents itself as a setting of
crises for students with Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD), where emotional
dysregulation severely impacts learning and social coexistence. The complexity
of BPD challenges traditional pedagogical approaches, demanding an
understanding that transcends the isolated biological or the purely subjective.
The objective of this article is to propose emotional regulation strategies within
the school context through a hybrid neuropsychoanalytic perspective, articulating
the neurobiology of emotions with Freudian technique and Lacanian topology.
The methodology adopted was a theoretical essay, integrating data on
frontolimbic circuits with a reading of the subject based on free association and
the structure of the Borromean Knot. The results indicate that instability in BPD
can be understood as a failure in the knotting between the Real, the Symbolic,
and the Imaginary, correlated with amygdala hyperactivation. The discussion
points out that pedagogical listening, inspired by dream interpretation and free
association, can act as a symbolic buffer, aiding in the stabilization of the knot
and, consequently, in neural modulation. It is concluded that the hybrid approach
offers innovative tools for school inclusion, allowing the educator to act not as a
therapist, but as a facilitator of the circulation of speech, reducing the impact of
emotional short-circuits and promoting a sustainable learning environment.

KEYWORDS: neuropsychoanalysis, borderline personality disorder, borromean
knot, emotional regulation, school inclusion, psychoanalysis, classroom.

1. INTRODUCTION


       The contemporary educational landscape faces the pressing challenge of
incorporating perspectives that go beyond the boundaries of traditional
pedagogies. Among these, Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) stands out not
only for its prevalence but also for the disruptive impact that emotional
dysregulation has on the learning environment.
       The phenomenon presents itself as a coin with two inseparable sides.
Neurobiologically, these students exhibit hyperactivation of the amygdala
correlated with hypoactivation of the prefrontal cortex, resulting in emotional
responses that “hijack” cognition. In parallel, psychoanalysis describes this same
dynamic as a failure in tying the Borromean Knot—where the Real (nameless
anxiety) invades the scene without the mediation of the Symbolic.
       However, current literature often operates in isolation: neuroscience
focuses on the brain, while psychoanalysis focuses on the subject. This
dichotomy creates a gap in pedagogical practice: the purely biological reading
offers no tools for relational management to the teacher, and the purely
psychoanalytic reading may seem too abstract for the urgency of the classroom.
       Faced with this impasse, this article is structured as a Theoretical Essay
to answer the following Research Question: How can a hybrid perspective, which
articulates the regulation of frontolimbic circuits with the topology of the
Borromean Knot, underpin effective pedagogical strategies for students with
PDD?
       The relevance of this study lies in translating clinical knowledge into
education without turning the teacher into a therapist. The central thesis defended
here is that access to neural modulation (calming the amygdala) can be facilitated
through symbolic intervention (pedagogical listening). It is proposed that, by
welcoming the student’s disordered discourse via adapted free association, the
educator erects a ‘symbolic barrier’ capable of preventing emotional short-
circuiting.




                                                                               163

1.1 GENERAL OBJECTIVE


      To analyze how the integration of the neurobiology of emotions and
Lacanian psychoanalytic topology can inform pedagogical practices of emotional
regulation for students with Borderline Personality Disorder.


1.2 SPECIFIC OBJECTIVES


    ● To articulate the neurobiological correlates of dysregulation (amygdala-
      prefrontal axis) with their implications for learning;
    ● Relate the instability described by neuroscience to Lacan’s clinical concept
      of the “unknotted knot,” establishing a transdisciplinary vocabulary;
    ● To establish guidelines for “pedagogical listening” and the construction of
      causal narratives as devices for emotional regulation in school settings.


2. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK


2.1 THE NEUROBIOLOGICAL SUBSTRATE: THE “FLESH” OF EMOTION


      For Roberto Lent, emotion is not an ethereal event, but the product of
precise neural orchestration. He defines the stage where this phenomenon
occurs, describing the Limbic System not merely as a location, but as a
coordination system.
      “The limbic system refers to the set of structures in the central nervous
system that participate in the subjective and behavioral coordination of emotions
[...] including the hypothalamus, the amygdala, and the cingulate cortex” (LENT,
2010, p. 257).
      From this perspective, the “flesh” of emotion is composed of subcortical
circuits that ensure survival. The amygdala, for example, acts as a sentinel,
processing emotional salience even before full consciousness. Lent argues that
without this anatomical substrate, the subjective experience (“the feeling”) would
lack a physiological anchor to trigger autonomic and motor responses.
      However, the mere activation of limbic structures would result in
uncontrolled behavior. This is where Morais intervenes, introducing the cortical


                                                                              164

and functional layer. For Morais, the anatomy described by Lent needs to be
managed so that it fulfills its evolutionary role. He emphasizes that emotion is not
noise in the cognitive system, but part of its learning mechanism.
       "Executive functions and emotions are mechanisms responsible for the
evolution and adaptation of individuals in society. [...] Human behavior is directly
influenced by executive functions and emotions, with emotional regulation being
crucial for learning" (MORAIS, 2020, Ch. 3).
       Morais argues that the “standard anatomy” necessarily includes the
connection pathways to the prefrontal cortex. Emotional health, therefore,
depends on the ability of these executive functions to modulate limbic intensity,
transforming instinctive reactions into socially adjusted behavior.
       The clinical counterpoint is provided by Mauro Hegenberg. While Lent
describes the system and Morais describes its ideal regulation, Hegenberg
describes the collapse of this circuit in the figure of the Borderline patient. In such
cases, the “flesh” of emotion seems to be raw, lacking the psychic skin of
regulation mentioned by Morais.
       Hegenberg illustrates how the failure to integrate these structures results
in unbearable psychic pain, where the anatomy of emotion manifests as
destructive impulsivity.
       "The borderline individual has explosive and impulsive reactions precisely
because of the fear of losing the object of support. [...] There are generally chronic
feelings of emptiness and a propensity to engage in intense and unstable
relationships" (HEGENBERG, 2000, p. 53).
       For Hegenberg, the physiology of emotion in the borderline state is marked
by excessive intensity. The “neurobiological substrate” ceases to be a warning
system (as proposed by Lent) or an adaptation system (as proposed by Morais)
and becomes a source of suffering, revealing a functional disconnection where
the intensity of affect (amygdala/hypothalamus) overpowers the capacity for
containment (cortex/executive functions).
       The “standard” anatomy of emotions, therefore, does not reside in an
isolated structure, but in the integrity of the circuit that connects limbic reactivity
(Lent) to executive regulation (Morais). When this circuit fails, the raw and
painful “ ” face of emotion described in the clinical presentation of borderline
states (Hegenberg) is revealed, confirming that the biological substrate is


                                                                                   165

inseparably the foundation of both mental health and pathology.
       Western pedagogical tradition has often operated under the premise that
learning is a strictly cognitive phenomenon, where emotion figures as a noise to
be silenced in favor of reason. However, contemporary neuroscience, grounded
in the work of António Damásio, subverts this logic by demonstrating that
rationality is not self-sufficient. In Descartes’ Error, Damásio posits the Somatic
Marker Hypothesis, arguing that the decision-making process—essential for
academic learning—depends on bioregulatory signals from the body.
       Damásio demonstrates that the ability to reason and plan for the future is
drastically compromised in the absence of emotional feedback. “Pure reason,”
disconnected from the affective substrate, becomes ineffective. The author
describes how emotion acts in the selection of biological and social options,
stating that:
       "Feelings guide us in the right direction, leading us to the appropriate place
within the decision-making space where we can make use of the tools of logic"
(DAMÁSIO, 2012, p. 238).
       Therefore, “academic reason”—the ability to focus, decide to study, and
block out distractions—does not exist without the foundation of emotion. If the
somatic marking system fails, the architecture of rational decision-making
collapses.


2.2 THE TOPOLOGY OF THE SUBJECT: THE UNLEASHED “SYMBOLIC”


       If the previous section demonstrated that the biology of the Borderline
student operates in a state of neurophysiological “short-circuit,” it is now
appropriate to question the programming that precedes the body. Why does
biology fail? To answer this question without falling into organicist reductionism,
it is imperative to move from anatomy to topology. The hypothesis put forward
here is that limbic dysregulation is the somatic echo of an unraveling in the
subject’s structure. Where neuroscience sees a hyperactive amygdala,
psychoanalysis identifies a failure in the function of the word.
       Understanding this dynamic requires a return to Jacques Lacan’s *The
Seminar, Book 11: The Four Fundamental Concepts of Psychoanalysis*. In
contrast to the * * intuitive notion of a “deep” or instinctual “place,” Lacan posits


                                                                                 166

the unconscious as a structure homologous to language. The healthy subject is
one capable of capturing the drive (the Real of the body) within the networks of
the signifier (the Symbolic).
         However, in the Borderline phenomenon or in a student’s outburst in the
classroom, we observe the breakdown of this mechanism. Lacan warns that the
absence of symbolic mediation condemns the subject to “show” what they cannot
“say.”
         "The unconscious is structured like a language [...] but when the subject
cannot constitute himself in speech, he plunges into the act. Acting out is the
display of that which cannot be recalled in words" (LACAN, 1979, p. 129 [approx.
in the Zahar Ed.]; see also the concept of passage to the act).
         The student who attacks or cries convulsively is not merely “out of control”;
he is exposing the precariousness of his Borromean Knot. In late Lacanian
topology, mental health depends on the firm entanglement between the Real
(organism/drive), the Symbolic (language/law), and the Imaginary (ego/body).
The aggressive act is evidence that the ring of the Symbolic has come loose,
allowing the Real of the drive to invade the body without any barrier or mediation.
Biology fails because the Symbolic has come undone.
         Moving toward a contemporary and pioneering perspective, we ask: what
causes this symbolic unraveling? Why does this specific subject fail to constitute
the word? Here, we engage with Galit Atlas and her work Emotional Inheritance.
Atlas proposes that many of the “disorders” we diagnose individually are, in fact,
manifestations of traumas not processed by previous generations.
         The key concept here is the “radioactivity” of the family secret. Atlas argues
that what was not resolved in the parents’ psyche returns as a symptom in the
children’s bodies.
         "The people we love and those who raised us live within us; we feel their
pain, we dream their memories [...] We literally carry our parents’ secrets and
unprocessed traumas" (ATLAS, 2022, p. 1-2).
         From this perspective, the Borderline student brings to school not only their
own regulatory deficit, but the “ghosts” of a traumatic family history. The “ghost in
the classroom” is the invisible presence of unresolved grief, silenced violence,
and unspeakable pain that surrounds the child.
         The “failure in the constitution of the subject” occurs, therefore, because


                                                                                   167

the child has been designated to bear the weight of their parents’ traumatic Real,
without having received the symbolic tools to narrate it. The child’s developing
brain is flooded by an anguish that does not entirely belong to them, yet which
they are forced to process. Biological dysregulation (excess cortisol, executive
dysfunction) is the physiological response to this intrusion of a massive,
unsymbolized emotional legacy.
       The integration of these theoretical vectors allows for a revolutionary
reading of disruptive behavior. The student is not merely a “defective brain”
(Lent/Morais) or an “undisciplined” child. He is the bearer of an unbound
Symbolic (Lacan) due to an Emotional Inheritance (Atlas) too heavy to be
articulated.
       Pedagogical and clinical intervention, therefore, must aim to “re-tie” the
knot. It is not merely a matter of containing behavior (the Imaginary) or medicating
the brain (the Real), but of offering a space where words can circulate,
transforming the “phantom” into history and the raw act into a shared narrative.


3. THE HYBRID SYNTHESIS IN THE SCHOOL CONTEXT


       The articulation between the neurobiology of emotions and Lacanian
topology should not serve merely for diagnosis, but should underpin a new ethics
of classroom management. If, as seen, the student with PD suffers from an
overactivation of the amygdala correlated with a disengagement of the Symbolic
register, the pedagogical intervention must act as a temporary prosthesis for this
failed function. Three lines of action are proposed here that constitute the “hybrid
approach”: the Teacher as Symbolic Shield, Decompressive Pedagogical
Listening, and Narrative as Cortical Modulation.
       The first challenge in crisis management is “imaginary capture.” When the
student explodes in aggression or tears, they summon the teacher to a mirror
duel (Imaginary). Neurobiologically, the student’s brain is in survival mode,
seeking in the other a reaction that confirms the danger (feeding back to the
amygdala). If the educator reacts with anger or excessive authoritarianism, they
validate the dysregulation.
       The “Symbolic Shield” approach requires the educator not to respond to
the provocation (content level), but to embrace the distress (structural level). The


                                                                                168

teacher must lend their own prefrontal regulation to the student. This means
maintaining a monotone voice and a non-threatening posture, acting as the
missing link for the student. By refusing to enter into the symmetry of aggression,
the educator introduces an “interval” between the impulse (Real) and the action,
allowing the neural alert circuit to begin cooling down due to the absence of
threatening feedback.
       The technique of free association, fundamental in clinical practice, can be
adapted to the school context not as an investigative method, but as an outlet. In
pre-crisis moments, it is observed that the speech of the Borderline student
becomes fragmented or accelerated.
       "Pedagogical Listening" consists of allowing the student to verbalize the
disordered flow of thoughts without the immediate demand for logic or
pedagogical coherence. Unlike the traditional classroom, which requires silence
for learning, the crisis requires speech for regulation. By offering a safe space for
“disordered speech” to flow, the teacher facilitates what neuroscience calls
labeling (naming the emotion). Studies show that the act of transforming emotion
into words engages the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, inhibiting amygdala
reactivity. The educator does not interpret “family trauma”—a role for the
therapist—but bears witness to the speech, validating the subject’s existence
beyond their disruptive behavior.
       After the acute phase of dysregulation, the hybrid pedagogical approach
focuses on reconstructing historical context. The student with BPD lives in an
“eternal present” of emotional intensity, unable to access the temporal
perspective necessary for planning (executive function).
       The strategy here is to help the student construct a causal narrative about
the event: “What happened before? What did you feel? What did you do?” This
Socratic questioning is not punitive, but structuring. It forces the recruitment of
the hippocampus (memory) and the prefrontal cortex (logic), helping to “re-tie”
the Real of the drive with the Symbolic of the explanation. By transforming the
impulsive act into a story with a beginning, middle, and end, the student ceases
to be a hostage to pure biological discharge and begins to inhabit language,
restoring— , albeit precariously—the stability of the Borromean Knot necessary
for learning.



                                                                                 169

4. CONCLUSION


       This study sought to demonstrate that the pedagogical challenge posed
by Borderline Personality Disorder cannot be overcome by a one-dimensional
interpretation. Neither neurobiology alone, which risks reducing the student to a
synaptic deficit, nor pure psychoanalysis, which might ignore the urgency of
executive dysfunction, is sufficient. The “hybrid” perspective proposed here
proves not only viable but necessary.
       It is concluded that the “untied knot” in the classroom—the explosive crisis
or deep apathy—is the behavioral correlate of a dual failure: limbic (biological)
hyperactivation and the insufficiency of symbolic (psychic) binding. In this
scenario, the teacher’s role transcends that of a mere content transmitter to
assume the function of a regulatory buffer. By lending their own prefrontal stability
and offering the spoken word as a mediating resource, the educator acts directly
on the student’s neural plasticity and subjective structure.
       The proposal is not that schools should become clinics, but that pedagogy
should incorporate clinical intelligence to fulfill its social function. The adoption of
strategies such as “decompressive listening” and “causal narrative” allows
students with PD to move from being held hostage by their emotions to becoming
active participants in their own learning. Ultimately, tying this knot means
ensuring that school inclusion is not merely the physical presence of the body at
a desk, but the symbolic inscription of the individual within the social bond.

ABSTRACT: A positive classroom climate has been recognized as an important
factor in strengthening learning, academic engagement, and student well-being
in the contemporary educational context. This study aimed to analyze the impacts
of a positive classroom climate on students’ academic, emotional, and social
development, highlighting the relevance of humanized pedagogical practices and
social-emotional competencies in the educational process. This is an integrative
literature review conducted in the ERIC, SpringerLink, Latindex, and SciELO
databases, considering articles published between 2020 and 2026 in Portuguese
and English. The results showed that welcoming, collaborative, and emotionally
safe school environments foster greater student participation, strengthen
interpersonal relationships, improve academic performance, and reduce school
conflicts. Furthermore, it was found that participatory methodologies, social-
emotional learning, and welcoming practices significantly contribute to promoting
emotional safety and a sense of belonging. It is concluded that a positive
classroom climate represents an essential pedagogical strategy for the holistic
education and healthy development of students.

KEYWORDS: learning, student well-being, school climate, social-emotional
education, academic engagement.

1. INTRODUCTION


       The creation of a positive classroom climate has established itself as an
indispensable contemporary pedagogical strategy for strengthening teaching and
learning processes, especially in light of the social, emotional, and technological
transformations permeating the current educational context. More than just a
physically organized environment, the school climate involves healthy
interpersonal relationships, respectful communication, emotional security, a
welcoming atmosphere, and pedagogical practices capable of promoting active
participation, motivation, and the holistic development of students. In this context,
the school comes to be understood not only as a space for the transmission of
knowledge, but also as an environment for human and socio-emotional
development (Martinsone et al., 2023).
       Recent studies demonstrate that a positive classroom climate directly
influences academic performance, student engagement, and students’ emotional
well-being.   According    to   (García-Peinado,      2023),   welcoming      school
environments foster children’s emotional development, strengthening skills such
as empathy, self-regulation, and social interaction. Similarly, (Nazilah, Hayati &
Azizah, 2025) emphasize that the teacher’s role is fundamental in building a
classroom culture based on respect, dialogue, and cooperation—factors that
contribute to more meaningful and participatory learning.
       Furthermore, contemporary methodologies centered on meaningful,
conscious, and enjoyable learning have reinforced the need for humanized and
motivating pedagogical practices. As evidenced by (Feriyanto & Anjariyah, 2024),
approaches that promote joyful and reflective learning experiences enhance
students’ interest and increase their participation in the educational process. In
this context, strengthening teachers’ pedagogical competencies also becomes
essential for creating inclusive and emotionally safe environments (Susmawati &
Sukinah, 2025).
       However, despite the relevance of the topic, many institutions still face
difficulties related to indiscipline, student demotivation, interpersonal conflicts,
and weaknesses in teacher-student relationships, compromising the school
climate and educational outcomes. As Guedes (2021) points out, students’



                                                                                 174

perceptions of the school environment exert a significant influence on their sense
of belonging and academic participation.
       Given this, this study is justified by the need to understand how a positive
classroom climate can serve as a contemporary pedagogical strategy capable of
fostering learning, engagement, and student well-being. Thus, the objective of
this study is to analyze the impacts of a positive classroom climate on students’
academic, emotional, and social development, highlighting the importance of
humanized pedagogical practices in promoting more inclusive, participatory, and
healthy educational environments.


2. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK


       A positive classroom climate has been widely discussed in contemporary
educational literature as a fundamental element for students’ academic,
emotional, and social development. Understanding this concept goes beyond the
idea of organizing the physical space, encompassing relational, emotional, and
pedagogical factors that directly influence learning experiences. In this regard,
Júnior et al. (2023) state that positive learning environments foster active student
participation, strengthen motivation, and contribute to the development of
healthier interpersonal relationships in the school setting.
       The literature shows that strengthening social-emotional competencies is
one of the main pillars for promoting a healthy school climate. According to
Durlak, Mahoney & Boyle (2022), school programs focused on social-emotional
learning have significant impacts on academic performance, the reduction of
problematic behaviors, and the development of skills such as empathy, self-
control, and cooperation. The authors emphasize that such skills are essential for
the holistic development of students and for building more welcoming and safe
educational environments.
       Complementing this perspective, Brush et al. (2022) highlight that social-
emotional learning must be incorporated into pedagogical practices in a
continuous and contextualized manner, allowing students to develop skills in
social interaction, conflict resolution, and collective participation. This approach
reinforces the need for humanized teaching practices capable of promoting a
sense of belonging and valuing the unique qualities present in the classroom.


                                                                                175

       In the context of contemporary pedagogical practices, the teacher’s role
takes center stage in fostering a positive classroom climate. According to
Contreras & Maussa (2025), pedagogical strategies based on dialogue, active
listening, and participatory methodologies strengthen the bond between teachers
and students, promoting greater engagement and meaningful learning. Similarly,
Holanda & Beranger (2025) argue that contemporary teaching requires flexible,
collaborative, and student-centered methodological practices, taking into account
the emotional and social demands present in today’s school environment.
       Collaborative leadership is also identified as a key factor in improving the
school climate. As Mondal (2020) analyzes, building cooperative relationships
among administrators, teachers, and the school community contributes to more
democratic environments, strengthening collective participation and institutional
commitment to educational quality. This perspective highlights that fostering a
positive climate does not depend exclusively on the teacher, but on the
coordination among different educational stakeholders.
       Furthermore, recent studies demonstrate that the classroom climate has a
direct influence on student engagement and academic self-efficacy. According to
Khuhro (2024), welcoming and emotionally safe school environments foster
greater student confidence in their abilities, stimulating participation, persistence,
and improved academic performance. Similarly, Majumder & Beri (2024) found
that a positive classroom climate significantly influences academic performance,
especially in the process of learning English, reinforcing the relationship between
emotional aspects and educational performance.
       Another relevant aspect concerns the promotion of well-being and
emotional safety in the school environment. As highlighted by Guimarães et al.
(2025), pedagogical interventions focused on teacher mediation and the
strengthening of interpersonal relationships contribute to reducing tensions,
improving social interaction, and enhancing learning. In the same vein, Marques
(2026) emphasizes that acceptance and a sense of belonging are fundamental
pillars for building a positive school climate, fostering inclusion and valuing
students.
       Finally, positive education has been identified as a relevant strategy for
reducing conflicts and strengthening school relationships. According to Silva et
al. (2026), pedagogical practices grounded in empathy, respect, and emotional


                                                                                  176

development contribute to more harmonious and collaborative environments.
Furthermore, Aguiar et al. (2026) argue that social-emotional learning represents
an essential tool for promoting student well-being and inclusive educational
planning, highlighting the importance of pedagogical practices committed to the
holistic development of students.


3. METHODOLOGY


       This study is characterized as an integrative literature review, a research
method that allows for the collection, analysis, and synthesis of results from
scientific studies on a specific topic, contributing to the construction of knowledge
and the identification of evidence relevant to educational practice. This type of
review enables a broad understanding of the positive classroom climate as a
contemporary pedagogical strategy, considering different methodological
approaches and theoretical perspectives.
       The integrative review was developed through the following stages:
definition of the theme and the guiding question, establishment of inclusion and
exclusion criteria, selection of databases, search and organization of studies,
critical analysis of scientific literature, and synthesis of the findings.
       The research was guided by the following research question: “What are
the impacts of a positive classroom climate on learning, engagement, and student
well-being in the contemporary educational context?” Defining the research
question allowed us to direct the selection of scientific studies related to the
investigated topic.
       The literature search was conducted in the ERIC (Education Resources
Information Center), SpringerLink, Latindex, and SciELO databases, chosen for
their academic relevance in the fields of education, educational psychology, and
social-emotional development. Articles were collected from publications available
in Portuguese and English.
       The following search terms were used, combined using the Boolean
operators “AND” and “OR”: “classroom climate,” “positive classroom climate,”
“school climate,” “student engagement,” “student well-being,” “social and
emotional learning,” “clima escolar,” “clima positivo em sala de aula,”
“engajamento      estudantil,”   “bem-estar      estudantil,”   and    “aprendizagem


                                                                                 177

socioemocional.” The search strategy aimed to broaden the identification of
studies related to the influence of school climate on the teaching-learning process
and on students’ emotional development.
       The inclusion criteria adopted included: full-text scientific articles available
for free; studies published between 2020 and 2026; research in Portuguese and
English; studies related to positive classroom climate, learning, student
engagement, emotional well-being, and contemporary pedagogical strategies; as
well as studies presenting results relevant to the educational context. Quantitative
and qualitative studies, systematic reviews, and mixed-methods research were
included.
       As exclusion criteria, we disregarded duplicate articles in the databases,
incomplete studies, simple abstracts, final course projects, dissertations, theses,
editorials, book chapters, and publications that had no direct relation to the
proposed theme. We also excluded studies published outside the established
time frame and articles in languages other than those selected.
       The selection of studies occurred in three stages: reading of titles, analysis
of abstracts, and full reading of potentially eligible articles. After applying the
inclusion and exclusion criteria, the selected studies were organized into
spreadsheets for descriptive analysis and thematic categorization, allowing for
the identification of the main findings related to the impact of a positive classroom
climate on learning, engagement, and student well-being.
       The selection process for the articles used in this integrative review is
illustrated in Figure 1, which is based on the stages of identification, screening,
eligibility, and inclusion of the scientific studies analyzed.




                                                                                   178

        Figure 1 – Flowchart of the study selection process for the integrative review.




                           Source: Authored by the authors (2026)


       Since this is an integrative review based on secondary data in the public
domain, there was no need to submit it to the Research Ethics Committee, in
accordance with the guidelines established for research that uses exclusively
material already published in scientific journals.

20 scientific studies published between 2020 and 2026, in Portuguese and
English, were selected. These studies addressed positive classroom climate and
its impacts on student learning, engagement, and well-being. The analyzed
studies include qualitative and quantitative research, systematic reviews, and
mixed-methods studies, allowing for a comprehensive understanding of the

       The results showed a predominance of studies focused on the influence
of interpersonal relationships and humanized pedagogical practices in the
creation of more welcoming and participatory educational environments. In this
context, Nazilah, Hayati & Azizah (2025) identified that teachers who use
strategies of dialogue, cooperation, and positive mediation contribute significantly
to the formation of a more organized, participatory, and emotionally safe




                                                                                           181

classroom culture. The authors emphasize that the teacher’s attitude has a direct
influence on students’ motivation and behavior.
       Regarding emotional development, García-Peinado (2023) demonstrated
that a positive classroom climate fosters the strengthening of socio-emotional
skills in childhood, particularly aspects related to empathy, emotional self-
regulation, and social interaction. Similar results were observed by Aguiar et al.
(2026), who highlighted social-emotional learning as an essential strategy for
promoting student well-being and reducing emotional vulnerabilities in the school
environment.
       The studies also revealed a strong relationship between a positive school
climate and academic performance. As noted by Majumder & Beri (2024),
welcoming and organized school environments foster higher academic
achievement, particularly in English language learning, due to increased student
participation and confidence. Corroborating these findings, Khuhro (2024) found
that students in emotionally safe environments exhibit greater self-efficacy,
academic persistence, and engagement in school activities.
       Another recurring aspect in the analyzed studies concerns the importance
of contemporary student-centered methodologies. According to Feriyanto &
Anjariyah (2024), pedagogical approaches grounded in meaningful, conscious,
and enjoyable learning promote greater student engagement and enhance
knowledge construction. Similarly, Contreras & Maussa (2025) observed that
participatory teaching practices strengthen teacher-student interaction and foster
active learning.
       In the context of school management and organization, Martinsone et al.
(2023) emphasized that the sustainable promotion of a positive school climate
depends on the integration of institutional policies, teacher training, and the
strengthening of interpersonal relationships. Furthermore, Mondal (2020) noted
that collaborative leadership has a significant impact on improving the school
environment, fostering communication, cooperation, and conflict resolution.
       The importance of pedagogical training was also widely highlighted. As
demonstrated by Susmawati & Sukinah (2025), learning communities focused on
teacher professional development strengthen pedagogical competencies related
to inclusion, welcoming students, and emotional management in the classroom.
In this regard, Holanda & Beranger (2025) emphasize that the challenges of


                                                                              182

contemporary teaching require teachers prepared to handle increasingly complex
emotional, social, and cognitive demands.
       Furthermore, the studies analyzed revealed that practices of welcoming
and belonging are fundamental factors for building healthy school environments.
According to Marques (2026), students who feel valued and that they belong in
the school environment demonstrate greater participation, motivation, and
engagement with the learning process. Similar results were found by Júnior et al.
(2023), who demonstrated that positive environments contribute to strengthening
trust, social interaction, and student retention.
       The reduction of school conflicts also emerged as one of the main benefits
associated with a positive classroom climate. As noted by Silva et al. (2026),
positive education strategies based on empathy, active listening, and emotional
support foster more harmonious relationships between students and teachers.
Complementarily, Guimarães et al. (2025) found that teacher-mediated
pedagogical interventions contribute to greater emotional security, reduced
tensions, and improved learning.
       Finally, there was consensus among the studies regarding the need for
integrated, inclusive, and emotionally supportive pedagogical practices to
promote students’ holistic development. The results demonstrated that a positive
classroom climate represents an essential element for strengthening learning,
academic engagement, and student well-being, establishing itself as an
indispensable pedagogical strategy in the contemporary educational context.
       The findings of this integrative review highlight that a positive classroom
climate represents one of the key elements associated with the quality of the
contemporary educational process, simultaneously influencing academic
performance, student engagement, and emotional well-being. The analyzed
literature demonstrates consensus regarding the need for welcoming,
collaborative, and emotionally safe school environments as a fundamental
condition for meaningful learning and for students’ holistic development.
       In this context, there is agreement among the studies in pointing out that
the relational dimension of the school environment has a direct impact on student
participation and on the construction of more effective pedagogical bonds.
Nazilah, Hayati, and Azizah (2025) argue that teaching practices based on
dialogue, respect, and cooperation foster the creation of a positive school culture


                                                                               183

capable of encouraging greater student involvement in educational activities. This
perspective aligns with the reflections of Contreras and Maussa (2025), who
emphasize    that        participatory   methodologies    strengthen    teacher-student
interaction, fostering more democratic and collaborative environments.
      The relevance of social-emotional competencies also appears repeatedly
among the authors analyzed. Durlak, Mahoney, and Boyle (2022) state that
social-emotional learning programs contribute significantly to improving students’
behavior, social interaction, and academic performance. In line with this
approach, Brush et al. (2022) highlight that integrating social-emotional education
into pedagogical practices enhances skills related to empathy, self-regulation,
and conflict resolution, fostering healthier interpersonal relationships within the
school setting.
      Furthermore, studies demonstrate that a positive school climate is directly
associated with promoting students’ emotional safety. García-Peinado (2023)
emphasizes        that    welcoming      environments    foster   children’s   emotional
development, allowing students to express feelings, build trust, and develop
social skills essential for school life. Similarly, Guimarães et al. (2025) identify
that pedagogical interventions mediated by welcoming practices and active
listening contribute to reducing tensions and strengthening students’ emotional
balance.
      Another relevant aspect concerns the relationship between school climate
and academic engagement. The findings of Khuhro (2024) show that students in
positive environments exhibit greater self-efficacy and persistence in the face of
academic challenges, which leads to better educational outcomes. This analysis
is reinforced by Majumder and Beri (2024), who demonstrate that school climate
directly influences academic performance, especially in contexts that require
active participation and constant interaction between students and teachers.
      The authors also agree in recognizing that contemporary social and
educational transformations require new pedagogical approaches on the part of
teachers. For Holanda and Beranger (2025), contemporary teaching demands
methodological practices that are more humanized, flexible, and centered on
students’ emotional and cognitive needs. From this perspective, the teacher
ceases to act merely as a transmitter of content and begins to play a mediating
role in building more inclusive and participatory pedagogical relationships.


                                                                                     184

       Teacher training thus emerges as an essential element for consolidating
positive school environments. According to Susmawati and Sukinah (2025), the
development of pedagogical competencies related to inclusion, sensitive
listening, and emotional management fosters more welcoming and effective
educational practices. This understanding aligns with the contributions of
Martinsone et al. (2023), who advocate for the need for institutional policies aimed
at the sustainable promotion of a positive school climate, integrating continuing
education, institutional support, and the strengthening of interpersonal
relationships.
       Another point widely discussed in the literature concerns the sense of
belonging in the school environment. Marques (2026) argues that pedagogical
practices grounded in acceptance and individual recognition strengthen student
identity and foster greater academic participation. This analysis is supported by
the findings of Júnior et al. (2023), who highlight the importance of positive
learning environments for strengthening motivation, social interaction, and school
retention.
       Additionally, the reduction of school conflicts is one of the main benefits
associated with a positive classroom climate. Silva et al. (2026) demonstrate that
positive education strategies promote more harmonious relationships among
students, reducing aggressive behaviors and strengthening practices of
respectful coexistence. These results indicate that emotionally safe environments
contribute not only to learning but also to the promotion of mental health and a
culture of peace in the educational context.
       Thus, the analysis of the studies shows that a positive classroom climate
cannot be understood as a secondary element of the educational process, but
rather as a structural component of contemporary pedagogical practice. The
integration of a welcoming environment, social-emotional skills, participatory
methodologies, and teacher training proves fundamental for promoting
educational environments that are more inclusive, motivating, and capable of
fostering students’ academic, emotional, and social development.




                                                                                185

5. CONCLUSION


      This study has shown that a positive classroom climate constitutes a
fundamental contemporary pedagogical strategy for strengthening student
learning, engagement, and well-being. Based on the analysis of the selected
studies, it was possible to identify that welcoming, participatory, and emotionally
safe school environments foster not only academic performance but also
students’ social-emotional development. Thus, the research answered the
guiding question by demonstrating that a positive classroom climate directly
influences the quality of educational experiences and the relationships
established within the school context.
      The results demonstrated that pedagogical practices based on dialogue,
respect, acceptance, and active participation contribute significantly to the
development of healthier bonds between teachers and students. Furthermore, it
was observed that student-centered methodologies associated with the
development of social-emotional competencies foster greater motivation,
confidence, school retention, and engagement in educational activities. These
aspects reinforce the importance of understanding the school environment as a
space for holistic education, in which emotional and relational factors have a
direct impact on the teaching-learning process.
      Another relevant finding concerns the role of teachers and school
administration in fostering a positive classroom climate. The reviewed literature
highlighted that teacher training, pedagogical mediation, and the implementation
of inclusive strategies are essential elements for creating more democratic,
collaborative, and humanized environments. In this sense, it was found that the
teacher’s role extends beyond the transmission of content, assuming a mediating
function in students’ emotional, social, and academic development.
      Additionally, the studies showed that strengthening socio-emotional
competencies and positive education practices contributes to reducing school
conflicts, increasing emotional security, and promoting a culture of peace in the
educational environment. Thus, it is concluded that valuing interpersonal
relationships and a sense of belonging is an indispensable factor for consolidating
school environments that are more inclusive, healthy, and conducive to human
development.


                                                                               186

      Finally, we suggest that future research focus on the practical analysis of
the implementation of pedagogical strategies related to a positive school climate
across different educational levels and sociocultural contexts. Longitudinal
studies investigating the impacts of these practices on academic performance,
mental health, and school retention could deepen our understanding of this topic
and contribute to the development of more human-centered and effective
educational policies.
