ABSTRACT: Professional burnout is one of the major issues relating to quality
of life and working conditions. It can affect the health of workers and organizations
as well. In recent years, the higher education sector in Algeria has experienced
major constraints, especially with the implementation of new reforms. All these
constraints have put more pressure on teachers, making their work more stressful
than before. This situation has led to psychosocial risks such as burn-out, and to
occupational illnesses (overwork, depression, etc.). In this work, we are
interested in measuring the degree of burnout among university teachers. We are
trying to make the links between burnout and this new change and to see the
pedagogical performance of university teachers both in the classroom and in
scientific research. As a case study, we chose the Faculty of Science and
Technology at the University of Constantine1, Algeria, with a population of 314
teachers. This study, the first of its kind in Algeria, enabled us to unfold the
relationship between burnout and the academic environment. The results showed
that a large number of teachers suffer from this syndrome, resulting in reduced
job satisfaction, demoralization, impaired health, and permanent stress. This had


                                                                                 190

an impact on teaching performance and increased the cost of work stoppages
due to teacher illness. These impacts justify the objective of this research, namely
to propose an analysis of teachers' health and identify which department is most
affected by burnout and the influence of burnout on teacher health in order to
increase their performance and thus create a sustainable university.

KEYWORDS: professional burnout, university teaching, measurement, stress,
sustainable university.

RESUMO: O esgotamento profissional é um dos principais problemas
relacionados à qualidade de vida e às condições de trabalho. Ele pode afetar a
saúde dos trabalhadores e também das organizações. Nos últimos anos, o setor
de ensino superior na Argélia passou por grandes restrições, especialmente com
a implementação de novas reformas. Todas essas restrições colocaram mais
pressão sobre os professores, tornando seu trabalho mais estressante do que
antes. Essa situação levou a riscos psicossociais, como o esgotamento, e a
doenças ocupacionais (excesso de trabalho, depressão etc.). Neste trabalho,
estamos interessados em medir o grau de esgotamento entre os professores
universitários. Estamos tentando estabelecer as ligações entre o esgotamento e
essa nova mudança e observar o desempenho pedagógico dos professores
universitários tanto na sala de aula quanto na pesquisa científica. Como estudo
de caso, escolhemos a Faculdade de Ciências e Tecnologia da Universidade de
Constantine1, na Argélia, com uma população de 314 professores. Esse estudo,
o primeiro desse tipo na Argélia, nos permitiu desdobrar a relação entre o
esgotamento e o ambiente acadêmico. Os resultados mostraram que um grande
número de professores sofre dessa síndrome, resultando em redução da
satisfação no trabalho, desmoralização, saúde debilitada e estresse permanente.
Isso teve um impacto no desempenho do ensino e aumentou o custo das
interrupções de trabalho devido a doenças dos professores. Esses impactos
justificam o objetivo desta pesquisa, ou seja, propor uma análise da saúde dos
professores e identificar qual departamento é mais afetado pelo burnout e a
influência do burnout na saúde dos professores, a fim de aumentar seu
desempenho e, assim, criar uma universidade sustentável.

PALAVRAS-CHAVE: esgotamento profissional, ensino universitário, medição,
estresse, universidade sustentável.

1. INTRODUCTION


      Teacher professional well-being and teaching quality are two key aspects
of teaching research that have been rarely studied together (Klusmann et al.,
2008). Previous research has shown that teachers' professional knowledge and
motivation are closely linked. Teachers' symptoms of stress and burnout (e.g.
emotional exhaustion) are also thought to influence teacher performance, but no
empirical studies have tested this prediction (Klusmann et al., 2016). The Algerian
higher education sector has undergone significant changes in recent years,
especially with the implementation of the new LMD (License, Master, doctorate)
reform. This reform has created new constraints for some scientific
establishments, such as the number of subjects to be taught each semester, the
large number of students in charge, teaching tasks, and hybrid teaching (face-to-
face and distance "tele-teaching"), especially after the advent of the Covid 19
pandemic and its consequences on teacher burnout (Klusmann et al., 2023);
(Baeriswyl et al., 2021), and also scientific research: the new teaching system.
All these constraints have put more pressure on teachers, making their work more
stressful than before. These constraints have triggered a number of changes that
have had repercussions on the teaching profession, and as a result, professional
pathologies (stress, overwork, and depression) have set in. It's natural to assume
that these changes to teachers' work have had a negative effect on their well-
being at work. This is worrying, as teachers were already perceiving their
profession as stressful and reporting high levels of burnout prior to these changes
(Klusmann et al., 2023); (Herman et al., 2020); (Iriarte Redín and Erro-Garcés,
2020). Moreover, teacher burnout is linked to their health, retention in the
profession, teaching quality, and student achievement (Klusmann et al., 2016);
(Klusmann et al., 2023); (Arens and Morin, 2016); (Klusmann et al., 2022).
      Burnout originates from work-related stress, which can be defined as a
negative psychological state with cognitive and emotional components that affect
both individual and group health (HASSARD J., 2011). It occurs when a person
realizes that he or she lacks the physical or mental strength or resources to cope
with excessive demands and pressures (Iriarte Redín and Erro-Garcés, 2020).
Burnout is a widespread concept, used to express a widespread malaise,
increasingly perceived through the prism of medical and psychological


                                                                               192

knowledge (Loriol. Marc, 2000). The current state of the university and burnout
are now closely linked (Verquerre, 2006).
      Given the complexity and scope of this syndrome, which is unfortunately
experienced by so many individuals from a wide range of professional
backgrounds, we felt it was vital to understand work in order to transform it and
to take the broadest possible view of this syndrome (Brühlmann, 2010).
Measurement and control activities are central to the establishment of
sustainable development practices.        To achieve the targeted objectives, the
problem will be tackled along three main axes (Maslach and Leiter, 2008) :
    • Burn-out from the point of view of the individual, with a focus on risk factors
      prior to and following health problems, and individual prevention;
    • Burn-out from the point of view of the collective, and the link with work
      organization, by investigating what prevention is put in place at this level;
    • Burn-out from an economic and political point of view, i.e. on a general
      structural level, by exploring the gradual deterioration in working
      conditions, and drawing a parallel between changes in the world of work
      and the increase in stress, and therefore the possible increase in burn-out.
      Today, no one disputes that the main symptom of burn-out is exhaustion
and that it can affect all human dimensions (cognitive, emotional, motivational,
and physical exhaustion). The result is depersonalization (we are no longer
ourselves, others perceive us as more distant, more negative, sometimes cynical)
and reduced performance, figure 1 (Bertels, D.S., 2010.). However, exhaustion
in the form of loss of energy is just as much a central symptom of depression
(despondency, sadness, impoverished thinking, loss of interest, loss of initiative).


                 Figure 1. Burn-out characteristic symptoms in sequence.




                              Source: Bertels, D.S., 2010.




                                                                                 193

      The sustainability movement now involves aspects parallel to the safety
and business ethics movements of years passed. Research in these fields
indicates that organizations need to implement a diverse set of practices, to fully
implement the desired changes (DIDRY Pascal, s. d.). As the choice is so vast,
we determined from the outset which population we would be most focused on.
As our field of application, we chose teachers from the Faculty of Science and
Technology at Constantine1 University, Algeria.


2. WORKING METHODOLOGY


      Our objective is to measure the level of professional burnout and provide
a strategic decision-making aid for the management of risks faced by teaching
staff. These risks have caused a number of changes that have had an impact on
the teaching profession, resulting in the emergence of professional pathologies
(stress, burnout, and depression). For this reason, this work is intended to be a
tool for measuring, raising awareness, and mobilizing for better prevention within
our universities. The working method consists in designing a questionnaire based
on dependent variables and their indicators linked to the hypotheses and
objectives of our work. It includes open-ended, closed-ended, and direct
questions to gather information likely to verify the hypotheses formulated. These
various elements provide guidelines for prioritizing improvement actions as part
of an overall program (Maslach and Leiter, 2008). The proposed approach will
therefore make it possible to unfold the relationship between this pathology and
the university environment, and even to identify the most influential factors in the
burnout of university teachers, to assess their job satisfaction and their degree of
burnout, and even to propose effective actions to improve the weaknesses
identified. We chose the teaching staff of the Faculty of Science and Technology
at Constantine University1 as our field of application. Our survey was carried out
in the various departments of the faculty, as well as in taleau1.

3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION


       To carry out this work, we distributed a questionnaire to all teachers
(N=314) in the Faculty of Science and Technology, i.e. a rate of 100%. However,
only 164 teachers returned our questionnaire, representing a response rate of
52.30%.
       The questionnaire used in our study is the most commonly used for
measuring burnout syndrome. We have based ourselves primarily on the MBI:
Maslach Burnout Inventory (Maslach, C. et al., 1996) in its original version (MBI-
human services survey MBI-HSS). This is an easy-to-use instrument whose
psychometric qualities have been extensively studied and is highly satisfactory,
both in terms of the original scale (Maslach, C. et al., 1996); (Massou et al., 2013)
and its French version (Massou et al., 2013); (Dion and Tessier, 1994). The scale
comprises 22 items, each representing a facet of the evaluation of one's work.
The frequency with which each symptom is experienced is described on a 7-point
Likert scale (Dion and Tessier, 1994). The tool is subdivided into three sub-scales
such as:
    • Emotional exhaustion;
    • Depersonalization;
    • Professional fulfillment.




                                                                                                                                                             195

      We will now describe the socio-professional situation of teachers in the
Faculty of Science and Technology. The main component is males (65%), and
they are considered to be young, ranging in age from 30 to 40, with a percentage
approaching 40%. The majority of teachers surveyed are married (71%), with no
more than 10 years of service in the teaching profession. Lecturers Class B and
assistant lecturers Class A are the two grades held by the majority of teachers,
with percentages of 38% and 47% respectively.

      To study the burnout of teachers, we looked at the relationship between

the working atmosphere was limited. As a result, we noted that teachers are
reserved and keep their distance from everyone, both horizontal (among
themselves) and transversal (management and students). This can lead to
considerable stress, coping and even depersonalization. It can also be said that
the nature of teachers' jobs makes them prone to burnout.

      Based on the work of Demerouti et al (Bakker, A. B. Demerouti, E. et al.,
2003), we have identified five configurations using cluster analysis:
    • A non-exhausted group;
    • A burnout group and;
    • Three other groups called "incomplete burnout", each characterized by the
      presence of only one of the three burnout symptoms.




                                                                                        197

          Based on the graphical curves and the results of the SEP, SD and SAP
calculations for each teacher, we applied a methodology in our analysis that
involved first grouping together the three "incomplete burnout" groups, and then
the "burnt-out" group. We then grouped the four groups together under the
heading of "burnt-out teacher", with the remaining group referred to as "non-
exhausted teacher".
          The results were as follows: 127 staff in the faculty are burnt out out of a
total of 164, i.e. a rate of 77% figure 5. This shows that the level of stress in this
faculty is high, as well as from what we found earlier that the majority of reserved
teachers are subject to burnout.

      We note that the most burned-out teachers reached all the scales of total
burnout.        The         trajectory of                      this      burnout           is        typical:    from    burnout     to
depersonalization, once teachers feel depersonalized, they experience low levels
of professional accomplishment, making their performance and output
inadequate. The main causes of this total burnout are that teachers have higher


                                                                                                                                    199

levels of stress, anxiety, fatigue or sleep disorders, confirmed by the results found
by studies on stress in teachers established by Concha (Iriarte Redín and Erro-
Garcés, 2020). In addition, burnout highlighted the effect of high job demands on
poor health, work engagement also showed the effects of job resources on
organizational commitment, and finally burnout mediated the effects of lack of
resources on low commitment (Hakanen et al., 2006). Burnout is linked to work
demands and resources. Work demands refer to aspects of work that are
associated with physical and/or psychological costs because they require effort
or skill over long periods of time (Klusmann et al., 2023). Work resources are the
characteristics of a work environment that facilitate the achievement of work
objectives and stimulate personal growth, learning and development (Klusmann
et al., 2023).

       According to the results obtained in the different departments, we found that

as well as the working conditions (heavy workload, internal conflicts between
teachers and also teacher-management, many copies to correct,....). We can't
overlook the fact that teachers in this department (core curriculum) are also involved
in teaching in their home department. For the other departments, this exhaustion is
related to working conditions (supervision, certain illnesses, etc.).

       It is also interesting to note that teachers in burnout at the end of their
training evolve towards a profile of emotional exhaustion at the beginning of their
professional life. In this way, they experience an improvement in their level of
depersonalization and self-fulfillment, and emerge from a "complete" burnout
(Admiraal and Kittelsen Røberg, 2023). Our empirical observations provide us
with some answers to this question: trainees often complain that they are
overworked, given the amount of time they are given to do the work they are
asked to do, or that the training is incoherent, with contradictory views on the job,
or that their relationship with tutors is poor. And the reform of the teaching system,
which juxtaposes Master's studies and preparation for a competitive examination,
has undoubtedly only amplified this work overload.


6. DISCUSSION AND RECOMMENDATIONS


       The results show that, despite being young and less experienced,
assistant lecturers are in burnout in certain departments, which is explained by
the efforts they make to demonstrate their skills, and therefore to do too much,
which leads to burnout right from the start of their careers. This category of
teachers therefore needs to be supervised, oriented and guided in the
performance of their duties.
       Based on our findings, we propose a number of areas for improvement in
order to alleviate the situation of burnout teachers and prevent other teachers
from falling into burnout.
    1. Improve teacher well-being;
    2. Raise awareness of the risk of burnout;
    3. Improve the working environment;
    4. Improve the relationship between teachers and their colleagues;
    5. Improve the relationship between teachers and management;
    6. Reduce teachers' workload (avoid excessive numbers of students);
    7. The use of more advanced technology, such as data shows and
       microphones in lecture theaters, to protect teachers' health;
    8. Replace all old blackboards with new ones that use markers instead of
       chalk;
    9. Motivate teachers to avoid depersonalization and negativism;


                                                                                  204

  10. Special action needs to be taken for teachers suffering from burnout,
       especially professors, by reducing their teaching load and leaving them to
       focus solely on scientific research and supervising doctoral students.


7. CONCLUSION


       In this study, we addressed an issue that poses a critically important risk
to the health of university teachers and the quality assurance of university
teaching: burnout and its influence on teacher performance. It's a subject that
affects all sectors of activity, including the university. This study is based on the
Maslach Burn out Inventory (MBI) model. We explored several axes, such as
emotional exhaustion, depersonalization and professional fulfillment. Following
this, we classified the teachers into three main categories: totally burnt-out
teachers, partially burnt-out teachers and, finally, non-exhausted teachers. When
we analyzed the results, we found that, from now on, an exhausted teacher
cannot perform well in his or her job, for a variety of reasons: stress,
disengagement, fatigue, absenteeism...
       We have found that physical, behavioral, emotional, intellectual and
experiential disorders are all factors in teacher burnout. These disorders have
varying degrees of impact on teachers' health.
       The department most affected by burnout is Electronics, followed by Civil
and Mechanical Engineering.
       In order to build on the results obtained in our study, we propose a number
of areas for improvement in order to alleviate the situation of burnt-out teachers
and prevent other teachers from falling into burnout.
       This study was carried out only in the Faculty of Engineering, so for future
work, we recommend extending the burnout study to other faculties and
identifying more teachers, in order to give further recommendations for
minimizing teacher burnout and increasing their performance and health.
       In this work, we have attempted to address an issue which is of vital
importance to the health of university teachers and the quality assurance of
university teaching. It is a subject that affects all sectors of activity, including the
university. The issue is burnout and its influence on teacher performance.



                                                                                    205

      Today's burnt-out teachers are unable to perform at their jobs, for a variety
of reasons: stress, disengagement, fatigue, absenteeism, etc.
      We have found that physical, behavioral, emotional, intellectual and
experiential disorders are all factors in teacher burnout. These disorders have
varying degrees of impact on teachers' health.

CHAPTER 13
 PREVENTIVE SCHOOL
 COEXISTENCE FACILITATED BY
 ICT: A PATH TOWARD A SOCIAL
 ENVIRONMENT OF COEXISTENCE
 AND PEACE


Jairo Soledad
Master's Degree (candidate) in ICT Applied to Education

Alex Puertas González

Ariel-Adolfo Rodriguez-Hernandez

ABSTRACT: This study designs a multimedia program to serve as a
technological tool for improving students’ understanding of school rules through
a dynamic pedagogical strategy focused on socialization and the internalization
of school regulations. Due to the pandemic, the study utilized a sample of 30 high
school students from a public school in Duitama. Based on a nested research
design, descriptive approach, comparative design, and deductive method, a
diagnostic survey was administered covering the following topics: legal
foundations of school regulations, school democracy, students’ rights and
responsibilities, and due process, to conduct an initial assessment of the level of
understanding of the school regulations outlined in the student handbook. a
multimedia program with case studies was then implemented to disseminate the
regulations, and finally, the virtual educational tool was introduced, with the task
of measuring the change in the students’ understanding of school regulations.
The results showed that participating students are drawn to this type of
technology, and it surpasses their interest in traditional methods of disseminating
and studying coexistence rules. It was also determined that economic, cultural,
and social factors affect coexistence, in addition to the instructional, restrictive,
and punitive approach that traditionally governs school coexistence.

KEYWORDS: peaceful coexistence, rules, social environment, communication
technology.



                                                                                 209

RESUMO: Com o presente trabalho, desenha-se um programa multimédia que
serve de ferramenta tecnológica para melhorar o nível de apropriação das regras
de convivência com uma estratégia pedagógica dinâmica nas tarefas de
socialização e apropriação dos regulamentos escolares. No desenvolvimento,
por motivos de pandemia, foi utilizada uma amostra de 30 alunos do ensino
médio de uma instituição de ensino oficial em Duitama. Com base em uma
pesquisa aninhada, abordagem descritiva, desenho comparativo e método
dedutivo, aplicou-se uma pesquisa diagnóstica com os temas: fundamentos
jurídicos do regulamento escolar, democracia escolar, deveres e direitos dos
alunos e devido processo legal, para fazer uma mensuração inicial do nível de
apropriação do regulamento escolar consagrado no manual de convivência,
depois foi implementado um programa multimédia com estudos de caso para
socializar o regulamento e por fim a ferramenta didática virtual foi partilhada,
deixando a tarefa de medir a mudança na apropriação do regulamento escolar.
Os resultados mostraram que os alunos participantes são atraídos por esse tipo
de tecnologia e seu interesse ultrapassa os métodos tradicionais de divulgação
e estudo das regras de convivência. Também foi possível constatar que existem
fatores econômicos, culturais e sociais que afetam a convivência, aliados à
abordagem instrutiva, restritiva e sancionatória que tradicionalmente rege a
convivência escolar.

PALAVRAS-CHAVE: coexistência pacífica, norma, mídia social, tecnologia da
comunicação.




                                                                            210

1. INTRODUCTION


      Most educational institutions in the city of Duitama face problems with
school coexistence, manifested in various forms of aggression and rule-breaking.
Schools establish mandatory regulations and raise standards in an effort to
improve the school environment, but community support is insufficient to
overcome this problem. School regulations are a legal requirement that schools
must comply with to obtain accreditation and maintain the institution’s internal
and external relationships with the community (Mendoza & Barrera, 2018)
      Given the low level of parental involvement and students’ lack of interest
in activities aimed at socializing the rules of coexistence. It is necessary to
implement communication channels to increase participation in the dissemination
of school regulations. It is essential to foster unity or collaboration among
members of the educational community to achieve interpersonal development
across various aspects of school life (Acuña, Concha, De la Fuente, & Medina,
2018) .
      Teachers and administrators at the school have used various means to
invite the community to participate in activities aimed at disseminating school
regulations, seeking to improve the level of ownership in school life; however,
parents often respond with evasiveness and excuses. To achieve healthy
coexistence, it is necessary to simultaneously advance simple, consultative,
projective, and meta-participation, as these are not mutually exclusive but
complementary (Ochoa & Pérez, 2019)
      The task is not to assign blame and shift the responsibility for school
violence onto others, but rather to identify which sector of the educational
community needs to take action to promote the adoption of institutional policies
and improve the level of ownership regarding school coexistence. School
coexistence must be approached in a preventive and ongoing manner.
      Members of the educational community must properly address the
fundamental aspects of school regulations, such as: legal foundations, school
democracy,   rights   and   responsibilities, disciplinary offenses and their
consequences, and due process. Additionally, they must have a clear
understanding of the concepts of school coexistence, the coexistence handbook,
classroom agreements, and the use of ICT for mediation in students’ educational


                                                                            211

processes.   The    assertive   handling   of   basic   concepts   facilitates   the
comprehension and internalization of content. Vocabulary reveals meaning and
provides greater textual understanding (Olivares, 2018)
      Regarding the implementation of communication channels with the
educational community, a program of multiple representations is proposed. The
purpose is to facilitate and energize the dissemination of school regulations so
that students can internalize them and improve the school’s experiential
environment. This program is based on the analysis and resolution of coexistence
cases, in which students must give their opinion and choose the solution they
consider appropriate.
      The social and economic issues present in the community under study
create challenges in managing school coexistence. Therefore, motivation and the
creation of spaces for the socialization and internalization of institutional
regulations are required. School coexistence, as manifested in the interactions of
the educational community, impacts students’ ethical, social, psychological, and
academic spheres (Cerda, Salazar, Guzman, & Narvaez, 2018)
      The integration of technological development into the socialization and
adoption of school coexistence not only minimizes the occurrence of violence but
also impacts students’ academic performance and retention. The use of ICT as
a means to carry out continuous and preventive work innovates and motivates
the understanding of regulations. Furthermore, it allows for the development of
educational and inclusive actions in all areas of school life; teachers must
incorporate them in a creative, inclusive, and democratic manner into their
pedagogical practice (Navarro & Ricardo, 2018)
      This section covers the conceptualization of key themes for this research,
theoretical foundations from previous studies, and the historical background of
similar research conducted by authors, along with their corresponding
bibliographic references.
      It contains the most relevant concepts to be addressed in this study, as
the thematic focus depends on their interpretation and situates us within the
context of the research topic, namely the level of adherence to school regulations
among students at the Simón Bolívar Municipal Technical School.




                                                                                 212

1.1 SCHOOL COEXISTENCE


        Coexistence is interpreted as the peaceful coexistence of members of the
educational community. It implies a positive interrelationship among them and
enables the fulfillment of educational objectives in an environment that fosters the
holistic development of students. Similarly, it is defined as the act of living
alongside others in the school setting in a peaceful and harmonious manner.
(Ministry of National Education, 2014)
        Positive coexistence is life in common within the school community ,
composed of parents, students, and teachers. It involves living with one another
through respect and commitment; agreeing on relationship norms that facilitate
and improve social interactions; addressing the emergence of conflicts;
preventing potential acts of violence; and mediating to resolve them (Aragón,
2017)
        In a broad sense, coexistence refers to the different ways in which human
beings interact; hence, the aim is for relationships to be as harmonious as
possible, that is, respecting differences, rights, and duties. When discussing
school coexistence, the emphasis is on the positive environment that must be
maintained in schools and colleges, grounded in legality and legitimacy, where
the members of the school community come together, each bearing the
responsibility to prevent and mitigate factors that affect the school climate
(Redondo & Jaramillo, 2019)


1.2 SCHOOL COEXISTENCE AGREEMENT


        It is the set of rules developed by consensus among the members of the
educational community. Once approved, they regulate the behavior of students
and teachers in the school environment, academic performance, and student
participation in representative roles. The school coexistence pact reflects the
lived experience of the educational community; therefore, it must be developed,
disseminated, and embraced by the community members themselves. It is a
pedagogical, didactic, and political strategy used by students and parents to
adhere to and determine commitments, duties, and rights (Caicedo, Garcia, &
Quintero, 2018)


                                                                                213

       The classroom pact is more than an agreement between students and
teachers, as it involves not only the exchange of knowledge, the negotiation of
learning, and the sharing of individual or collective understandings, conceptions,
and ideals about life that shape them as social, cultural, and rights-bearing
subjects, but also the recognition of the social context in which the classroom is
embedded (Rivera & Mejia Correa, 2019) It is an agreement between two or more
parties seeking to benefit from a joint decision that generally aims for the greater
good. In the context of school life, the family cannot be dismissed as an influential
and determining factor in social behavior (Gallardo, Hernandez, Monsalve, &
Barrientos, 2019)


1.3 SOCIAL ENVIRONMENT OF PEACE


       A social environment of peace is conceived as the set of conditions
enabling a human group to live in a context free from manifestations of violence,
intolerance, exclusion, and injustice, and under the protection and respect of
human rights. The social environment of peace is a cultural construct based on
participatory agreements that determine a social experience of widespread well-
being (Arcia, Pilar, Añaños, & Medina, 2020)
       Citizen competencies regarding peace and coexistence stem from
recognizing others as human beings and from the pursuit of addressing and
resolving problems in their environment through nonviolent means, as well as
creating a new way of thinking, feeling, and acting in the face of the reality of their
environment (Adame, García, & Gómez, 2017)
       Conflicts are inherent to social dynamics; therefore, they cannot be
eradicated but must be addressed assertively to channel that energy and
generate circles of coexistence that strengthen social bonds. In social circles of
peace and coexistence, regardless of age, educational level, or cultural
background, they function as a framework to maintain a safe environment for
dialogue (León, 2019)
       Promoting a harmonious school environment is a responsibility of the
educational community that extends to the broader social context; the family
plays a decisive role in creating peaceful and harmonious environments. It
provides the foundational parenting guidelines that shape students’ behavior and


                                                                                   214

is also affected by school-related issues, making it both a source and a recipient
of matters concerning social interaction. For this reason, families seek balance
and the fairest solutions to problems, although currently, due to media influence
and the manipulation of their children, parents act in a protective manner; they do
not seek to mitigate conflicts but rather to justify the actions of their children, and
in this way, school problems spill over into society with negative impacts. School
is the setting for the formation of values and the preparation of children for life in
society and, therefore, has the responsibility to create social spaces for
coexistence (Sinisterra, 2019)


1.4 MULTIMEDIA PROGRAMS


        Multimodal or multimedia programs are defined as digital tools that engage
the senses—such as sight and hearing—to convey an effective message that
fosters interest, communication, self-learning, and visuomotor development,
while capturing the student’s attention (Senevoa & Alex, 2005) They are also
defined as technologies that have facilitated the integration of various media,
such as text, graphics, sound, voice, and video, with full motion or animation in a
computer application (Amaya, 2010)
        The incorporation of multimedia resources, thanks to the support of
information and communication technologies in the work of educational
institutions, demonstrates the desired pedagogical shift; it is a trend that
contributes to the teaching-learning process, enabling students to be active
participants and protagonists in the development of school activities (Tomalá,
2018)


2. METHODOLOGY


        The research design is nested, with a quantitative focus, because the
objective is to verify the impact of developing and implementing a multiple
representations program on the adoption of coexistence norms and the reduction
of school violence. It is characterized by the use of both quantitative and
qualitative components and seeks to apply or utilize acquired knowledge while
simultaneously acquiring new knowledge, after implementing and systematizing


                                                                                   215

research-based practice. The use of knowledge and research findings results in
a rigorous, organized, and systematic way of understanding reality (Delgado,
Gadea, & Vera, 2018)
       However, research work        cannot be limited to the development of a
technological tool or the measurement of data; rather, it must reflect an attitudinal
change in students, which is qualitative in nature, since qualitative research
encompasses the study, use, and collection of a variety of empirical materials—
case studies, personal experiences, interviews, surveys, and direct visual
observation—that describe problematic moments and their meanings in
individuals’ lives (Otero, 2018)
       This research is designed with a descriptive or diagnostic approach, as it
seeks to characterize a specific phenomenon or situation by highlighting its most
distinctive or differentiating features. The purpose is to understand prevailing
situations and attitudes through the precise description of activities, objects,
processes, and people; it is not limited to data collection but extends to predicting
and identifying existing relationships. The research is not merely a tabulation of
data; rather, it gathers information based on a hypothesis or theory, and the
results are then thoroughly analyzed to extract meaningful generalizations that
contribute to knowledge and the implementation of actions (Arantzamendi,
López, Carole, & Carrasco, 2016)
       Following the quantitative component, the study begins with an
assessment of the current situation regarding the educational community’s
knowledge of school regulations, interest in transforming the school environment,
the community’s legal knowledge regarding the design of regulations, as well as
their willingness to undertake tasks related to revising the handbook, socializing,
and adopting school regulations on coexistence. This requires the design and
administration of surveys, analysis of institutional statistical data, accounts from
members of the educational community, meeting minutes, and bibliographic
sources to help measure the educational community’s perception of the school
environment and the adoption of coexistence rules.
       Qualitatively, the study will consider personal and attitudinal progress
before and after the implementation of the multiple representations program in
the socialization of institutional regulations.



                                                                                 216

       The study is designed using a comparative methodological approach;
consequently, since it seeks to compare two moments in institutional life
regarding the adoption of the norms enshrined in the coexistence manual, these
moments will be defined by the implementation of a multiple representations
program in the socialization of institutional norms.
       Comparative hypotheses are designed in research aimed at establishing
comparisons between groups and moments to determine whether there is
difference. Additionally, they explain the reasons for these differences based on
their causes or reasons; thus, they are classified as hypotheses of explanatory
studies (Balcazar, 2019)
       It falls within the deductive method, given that this research does not seek
to establish universal laws but rather to conduct an experimental test on a specific
population to collect data, process it, and interpret the effect of implementing a
multiple representations program on reducing rates of school violence.
       The deductive method, in terms of its linguistic roots, means to lead or
extract; it is based on reasoning, just like the inductive method. However, it is
entirely different, as in this case it allows one to move from general principles to
specific facts. It essentially involves analyzing the general principles of a specific
topic to be tested, verified, and applied to particular contexts. The deductive
method is grounded in specific theoretical foundations, ultimately leading to the
configuration of particular facts or practices (Prieto, 2017)
       In developing the assessment of the state of school coexistence within the
educational institution, the premises are outlined upon which actions are
developed to ensure that the educational community of the institution, the Simón
Bolívar Municipal Technical School, embraces the rules of school coexistence
through a socialization phase that includes a program of diverse representations
designed to facilitate and energize the understanding of the normative content
and encourage the adoption and adherence to the school coexistence manual.


2.1 UNIT OF ANALYSIS


       The study population is a defined, limited, and accessible set of cases that
will serve as the reference for sample selection. It is necessary to clarify that when
referring to a study population, the term does not refer exclusively to human


                                                                                  217

beings; it may also correspond to animals, files, objects, families, organizations,
or institutions; for the latter, it might be more appropriate to use an analogous
term, such as study universe (Otzen & Carlos, 2017) .
       Due to the effects of the pandemic, the study population or universe
consisted of lower secondary students at the Simón Bolívar Municipal Technical
School, with priority given to those with internet access and electronic devices
capable of running multimedia programs.
       All students are digital natives with an interest in new technology. Their
situation reflects their families’ demographic conditions; however, a significant
number are, due to their parents’ occupations or family issues, under the care of
a private caregiver or a relative other than their parents. Their ages range from
11 to 16; there are students outside the typical age range for these grades, but
due to exceptional circumstances, they are admitted into the regular education
system despite this being a factor that influences aggression. There are also
students with special educational needs who require individualized support, but
who, due to economic circumstances, do not receive assistance, and whose
behavior affects the school environment.


2.2 SAMPLE


       The sample is a subset of the population to which we have access and
must be representative of it, because it is on this sample that the relevant
measurements are made (López & Fachelli, 2017) .
       Due to the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, the population sample for
this study had to be limited to lower secondary students who had access to
technological   devices,    permission from      their   legal   guardians,   internet
connectivity, and a willingness to participate in the required activities. A sample
of 36 students from the seventh, eighth, and ninth grades at the Simón Bolívar
Municipal Technical School was obtained, representing a variety of ages,
genders, academic levels, and socioeconomic backgrounds. Teaching staff were
also involved, but in the role of facilitators for the dissemination of information.




                                                                                   218

2.3 PROCEDURES


      To achieve this objective, the project was carried out in three stages:
diagnosis or data collection; implementation or program design and documen ;
and a stage of sharing and operationalizing the dynamic tool to disseminate and
foster ownership of school regulations.


2.4 IDENTIFICATION OF THE LEVEL OF KNOWLEDGE REGARDING
SCHOOL COEXISTENCE RULES


      To identify the level of knowledge, a Likert-type survey was administered
online to a sample population of small groups of high school students at the
Simón Bolívar Municipal Technical School. The survey covers three topics related
to school coexistence: school democracy, students’ rights and responsibilities,
and due process. Each topic includes questions rated on a scale of one to three,
corresponding to the categories of disagree, partially agree, and fully agree.
      During the diagnostic phase, data from the Likert-scale survey was
compiled, using a 1-to-3 rating scale and three variables: school democracy,
rights and responsibilities, and due process. This information was entered into a
statistical table in Excel, where the median, mode, mean, and percentage of
correct and incorrect responses were calculated to identify weaknesses in the
adoption of school regulations. Based on this, the multiple representations
program was implemented as a teaching tool using ICT mediation to disseminate
and promote the school coexistence manual (see Table 1).

2.5 IMPLEMENTATION OF A MULTIPLE REPRESENTATION PROGRAM
WITH VIRTUAL PEDAGOGY


       Once the information from the diagnostic phase was analyzed, we
proceeded to study the feasibility of a multiple representations program to
disseminate the school regulations contained in the coexistence manual. We took
into account aspects such as free access, accessibility, reusability, novelty, and
appeal to students.
       Following this analysis and experimentation with various platforms, we
opted to develop a program using NPM, JavaScript, and Node.js technology. This
program presents hypothetical scenarios of coexistence involving different types
of misconduct, which students must observe and use to answer questions that
place them within the context of school coexistence. The presentation of each
case includes both text and graphics to engage and motivate students in reading
and observing the content


2.6 IMPLEMENTATION OF A MULTIPLE REPRESENTATION PROGRAM TO
TEACH SCHOOL COEXISTENCE RULES THROUGH DYNAMIC PEDAGOGY


       Once the implementation phase of the multimedia program was complete,
a program of multiple representations was delivered to the educational institution
to be used as a tool in the tasks of socialization and internalization of school
regulations, through a dynamic strategy that combines graphics, dialogues,
examples, and fundamental concepts for managing school coexistence.

        After studying these results, certain concepts were identified regarding the

        After organizing and evaluating the diagnostic phase, we proceeded to
 select and implement the teaching tool, opting for the development of a


                                                                                                                        221

multimedia program using NPM-JavaScript technology, due to its ease of use
across students’ various devices. The program is based on case studies of
coexistence, using illustrated dialogue scripts with textual and graphic content,
which students observe and then complete the initial survey to measure their level
of improvement. (See Figure 1)


            Figure 1. Example of an illustrated dialogue. Created by the author

      After implementing the program and testing the application with students,
it was observed that participants showed greater interest in the virtual materials
than in traditional physical documents. It was also observed that the level of
comprehension and understanding of the content was facilitated more effectively
through ICT-mediated learning than through documents and lectures.
      The instructional materials were delivered to the educational institution to
be used as a technological resource in the dissemination, socialization, and
adoption of school regulations regarding coexistence.


4. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS


      This study sought to implement ICT-mediated teaching materials to serve
as a technological tool for disseminating, socializing, and fostering the adoption
of school regulations. In the first stage of development, the level of knowledge



                                                                                  222

regarding school coexistence rules among the selected students was identified
through the use of data collection instruments. It was found that students do not
like their parents to participate in school governance, that they are familiar with
the coexistence manual but do not apply it, confuse mandatory rules with
voluntary ones, and are unaware of the procedures and protocols of due process.
       Our results are similar to those reported by (Penalva, 2018) , which notes
the low level of community participation in the dissemination of rules and,
consequently, their limited knowledge of them—a fact that leads to difficulties in
communication and assertive conflict resolution. In a different scenario, this
contrasts with the findings presented by (Troyer et al., 2018) , which refers to
rules developed by consensus within the educational community and the
availability of resources to carry out training activities on coexistence with the full
commitment of teachers.
       Regarding the implementation and sharing of the tool, we found that
students show greater interest and, consequently, better grasp of the material
when technological mediation is used and various forms of presenting
information—such as graphics, color, text, and sound—are combined. Traditional
dissemination methods like books, brochures, and meetings do not generate the
same level of interest, and their impact is limited.
       These findings are consistent with the arguments presented by (Cabello,
2019) , where the author explains how ICTs have facilitated the dissemination
and socialization of peace-related issues. The author also describes how
technological strategies have been integral to social and cultural changes,
accelerating the pace of learning and transformation. However, this contrasts with
certain sections of the work by (Navarro T., 2019) , which highlights how ICTs
facilitate misconduct such as bullying and other related behaviors that violate
school regulations and lead to problematic situations within educational
institutions.
       Students grasp messages better through audiovisual means than through
text, and the use of ICT as a teaching strategy contributes to improved adherence
to school rules
       The implementation of the multimedia program with case studies
demonstrates progress in the adoption of rules of coexistence



                                                                                   223

      Adherence to rules of conduct improves interpersonal relationships and
fosters a pleasant school environment that extends to the broader social context.

CHAPTER 14
 MANAGEMENT OF EDUCATIONAL
 TECHNOLOGY IN HIGHER
 EDUCATION: THE CASE OF
 INTEGRATING SIMULATORS INTO
 EDUCATION


Ariel Adolfo Rodriguez-Hernández
Doctor in Educational Technology
Universidad Pedagógica y Tecnológica de Colombia
E-mail: ariel.rodriguez@uptc.edu.co

Fanny Avella-Forero
Master of Business Administration
Universidad Pedagógica y Tecnológica de Colombia
E-mail: fanny.avella@uptc.edu.co

Juan Sebastián Rodríguez Avella
Agricultural Engineering Student
Universidad Nacional de Colombia
E-mail: jurodrigueza@unal.edu.co


ABSTRACT: The objective of this paper is to present reflections on the
university’s experience in incorporating simulators into teaching and learning in
the fields of physics, chemistry, and electronics, as well as the theoretical
frameworks that led to the incorporation of these technologies. The project began
with a diagnostic and identification phase focused on open-source and free-to-
use simulators, aiming to identify and document the state of development of
open-source simulators. The goal was to define a methodological model for the
use of simulators within educational processes and a guideline model for their
implementation in the classroom. After analyzing this diagnostic phase and
constructing the methodological model, proprietary software solutions were
analyzed, and finally, investments were made in proprietary software licenses,
which were combined with the use of open-source software. The project presents
a description of the educational methodological model for the use of simulators,
outlining the characteristics the model must possess, which are grounded in
learning theories (active learning, problem-based or real-world case-based
learning, incremental development of competencies, and ICT support) in order to
make effective use of this type of IT solution within education. The project’s
results revealed the existence of open-source simulation software developments,
which offer an easily accessible, low-cost, and high-quality alternative for
improving educational processes in institutions. It also identified high-quality,
valuable proprietary simulation software solutions for education.



                                                                             227

KEYWORDS: simulation in education, educational simulation software,
interactive learning resources.

RESUMO: O objetivo deste trabalho é apresentar as reflexões sobre a
experiência da universidade na incorporação de simuladores no ensino e
aprendizagem nas áreas de física, química e eletrônica. Bem como os
referenciais teóricos que levaram à incorporação dessas tecnologias. Partiu de
uma fase de diagnóstico e identificação em primeira instância de simuladores
para uso livre e aberto, onde se procurou identificar e documentar o estado do
desenvolvimento de simuladores em software livre. Buscou-se definir um modelo
metodológico para o uso de simuladores nos processos educacionais e um
modelo guia para sua implementação em sala de aula. Após a análise dessa
fase de diagnóstico e construção do modelo metodológico, foram analisadas as
soluções de software proprietário e, por fim, foram feitos investimentos em
licenças de software proprietário e combinado o uso de software livre. A
descrição do modelo metodológico educacional para uso de simuladores é
apresentada dentro do projeto, são descritas as características que o modelo
deve ter, que são baseadas em teorias de aprendizagem (aprendizagem ativa,
aprendizagem baseada em problemas ou casos da realidade, desenvolvimento
de habilidades incrementais e suporte de TIC para o uso efetivo deste tipo de
soluções computacionais na educação. Os resultados do projeto revelaram a
existência de desenvolvimentos de simuladores de software livre, que oferecem
uma alternativa de fácil acesso, baixo custo e excelente qualidade para melhorar
os processos educacionais nas instituições , além de soluções proprietárias de
simuladores de software de grande qualidade e valor para a educação.

PALAVRAS CHAVE: simulação na educação, software educacional para
simulação, recursos interativos de aprendizagem.




                                                                            228

1. INTRODUCTION


      This project arose from the university’s need regarding virtual laboratories,
particularly in the fields of physics and chemistry for distance education students.
      Its rationale stems from the need to identify and understand the current
state of development of simulators for educational purposes.
      This research explores and identifies the state of the art in this field; I
sought to identify as many educational simulators as possible, with an initial
requirement that their development or distribution model be open-source
software. I then sought to identify proprietary software. The project began with
two questions:
    • Are there simulators for educational use in physics, chemistry, and
      electronics?
    • If such resources exist, what is their use and dissemination within the
      educational community, and how can they be incorporated into an
      institution’s educational activities?
      To organize the information, a categorization system was defined, which
included: development language type, distribution license type, and area within
physics. (Esquembre, 2004).
      Once the solutions were identified, we proceeded to identify or define a
methodological model for incorporating simulators into education, which included
the design of work guides.



2. METHODOLOGY FOR INCORPORATING SIMULATORS INTO HIGHER
EDUCATION


      To address this project, the following phases were generally defined:
    • Identify simulation systems for physics, chemistry, and electronics
      laboratories,   both    open-source     and     proprietary,   including    their
      characteristics,   functionality,   technical   information,    source     code,
      executables, and costs.
    • Identify a methodological model for education that supports the use of
      simulation systems for laboratories.



                                                                                   229

    • Define and design guidelines for implementing a simulator in an actual
      course.
    • Validate the use of simulators and the defined educational methodology in
      a course.
    • Conduct an assessment to identify strengths, weaknesses, and
      opportunities for improvement that will enable more efficient use of this
      type of material in the classroom.
    • Implement a simulator solution for educational purposes at the university
      as part of the Strategic Plan for ICT Integration, within the project
      “Methodological Modernization and Integration of ICT and Virtual Learning
      in the Faculty of Distance Studies and its Regional Centers.” (UPTC, 2010)


2.1 DEVELOPMENT PHASES


2.1.1 Identification and documentation of software resources


      We searched for and identified educational software solutions of the
simulator type for physics, chemistry, and electronics laboratories developed
using open-source or proprietary software at the national and international levels.
This stage or phase involved identifying the characteristics, functionality,
technical information, source code, and executables—to the extent possible—for
each solution found that had been developed in the last ten years, or, failing that,
the website from which it can be used or is sold. (Fernández, 2004).
      These     resources   were    classified   following   an   analysis   of   the
characteristics they must meet in terms of the subject matter they address, which
was developed based on the content taught in the Physics, Chemistry, and
Electronics courses of undergraduate programs. In particular, these resources
must provide computational treatment of the simulation of phenomena related to
these subjects. (Martínez, 2016).
      At the same time, this phase included a review of studies on the didactic
challenges of experimental learning in Physics, Chemistry, and Electronics, with
the aim of identifying the most important pedagogical aspects that a simulation
system must fulfill for educational use (theoretical content, virtual experiences,



                                                                                  230

skill-building tasks, learning activities, and methodologies for developing
simulator-based practices). (Franco & Álvarez, 2008).


2.1.2 Identification of the educational methodology and design of
implementation guides


       It was necessary to define an educational methodology to validate the
educational use of simulators in a real course. The course population, level, and
educational modality were defined.
       The Physics I course in the Civil Engineering Technology program at the
Faculty of Distance Studies of the Pedagogical and Technological University of
Colombia was selected as the pilot group.
       At the same time that this educational methodology was identified, an
implementation guide for the simulator as educational material in a real course
was developed. This guide is intended to help students practically carry out a
series of physics experiments using the selected simulator, with the aim of
validating the strengths, weaknesses, and opportunities for improvement that will
allow for more efficient use of this type of material in higher education classrooms.
       Similarly, indicators were defined to assess the educational use of
simulators and their impact on education.


2.1.3 Application


       In this phase, these resources were incorporated into teaching practice as
a complementary tool in the planning of laboratory work for courses in the first
years of undergraduate engineering programs (Kofman, 2003)
       The use of simulators was then validated. We also sought to analyze the
influence of these computer applications and complementary teaching materials
on the learning process carried out by students through laboratory experiences,
evaluating the reports from the work sessions conducted with the software
(Kofman, 2000).




                                                                                 231

2.1.4 Assessment of the use of simulators in teaching


      Here, the aim was to assess the validation of simulator use in education
and identify the strengths, weaknesses, and opportunities for improvement that
would allow for more efficient use of this type of material in the classroom
(Rosado & Herreros, 2005).


2.2 METHODOLOGICAL APPROACH


      This project sought to describe the current state of the field by identifying
developments in simulators through descriptive research, with the primary
purpose of establishing the current state of development regarding the
educational use of simulators. Keeping this in mind is essential for understanding
the results presented.
      Since one of the objectives is to create a database that identifies and
presents developments in simulator-type software based on free or proprietary
software, this led to establishing the characteristics of the information analysis
regarding the topic and defining the general framework for the research. The
characteristics defined for data identification, processing, and analysis are:
      Type of software: a characteristic focused on the types of free software or
the conditions a software must meet to be classified as free software. The
criterion used is that it must comply with at least one of the freedoms¹ defined in
the concept of free software.
      Software distribution license: it was necessary to identify this characteristic
in order to present the results more robustly.
      Programming language: the aim was to determine which languages lead
the development of simulators in free software.
      Platform or Operating System: to determine on which operating system the
identified software can be used.
      Field of knowledge: although the project is limited to physics, chemistry,
and electronics, fundamental subfields were identified, and each result was
associated with one of these areas.




                                                                                 232

      Once the characteristics for collecting information were identified, it
became necessary to categorize each one, define variables, and establish
indicators to evaluate the results, as shown in Table 1. Research Variables.

2.3 POPULATION UNIVERSE AND SAMPLE OR UNIT OF ANALYSIS


      The study population is limited in terms of time, as the projects identified
must have been developed within the last ten years.
      Furthermore, although the aim was to identify projects developed in
Spanish, it was deemed prudent for the sake of objective analysis to include other


                                                                               233

languages in order to obtain results that would lead to a more comprehensive
study.
         In terms of sample size, the primary aim was to identify developments
carried out in educational institutions worldwide and in organizations related to
physics, chemistry, and electronics, as well as within the free software
communities and universities.
         It was not possible to establish a fixed sample, as the degree of uncertainty
regarding the subject did not allow for the definition of a population; instead, the
characteristics of the target to be identified were defined.


2.4 DEVELOPMENT, SELECTION, AND DESIGN OF INSTRUMENTS


         Given that free software communities and universities are organized on a
global scale, and based on the characteristics and variables to be identified in the
information-gathering process, a spreadsheet-style table was created containing
the elements necessary to identify existing developments and projects.
         The instrument used was a results record sheet, which was employed in
the identification process and enabled the analysis and processing of the data
obtained according to the needs and objectives defined by the project.


2.5 PILOT TEST AND VALIDITY


         The pilot test was conducted over five months and required sending the
form to educational and research networks to quickly identify potential sources of
information.
         In addition, an Internet search was conducted to identify existing projects
and developments.
         To ensure validity, it was mandatory that the projects be referenced and
available on the Internet, in order to verify existing developments and thus
guarantee the availability of resources.




                                                                                  234

2.6 PLAN FOR PRESENTING RESULTS


       To present the results, the information was consolidated, tabulated, and
organized according to the defined characteristics and variables.
       The summary of the results is presented in terms of quantities,
percentages, and graphical representations. Highly relevant projects are briefly
described in the full document.


3. RESULTS OF THE DIAGNOSTIC FOR THE INCORPORATION OF
SIMULATORS


       It is important to note that we sought to identify the development language,
finding that the largest percentage of projects are developed in Java, with a
smaller percentage developed in C or C++, and Python.

trends regarding software types.

over the Internet, and their robustness for mathematical operations. The
languages used for these simulations are Java and Flash (the executable is
distributed for free, but not the source code).

      The identified applet-type simulators developed in Java allow users to

      Regarding executable-type applications, it was found that the vast majority

developments into its distribution. This project originated in the Republic of
Argentina and integrates more than 15 simulation solutions for multiple areas of
scientific knowledge.


3.2 IDENTIFICATION OF RESOURCES BY DEVELOPMENT LANGUAGE


      As part of the research and project survey process, the programming
language in which each project was developed was identified. The purpose of
this analysis is to establish trends in programming languages for simulator
development and to identify the reasons for their use.
      In conclusion, this analysis shows that Java is the most widely used
language for simulator development, followed by Flash, C++, and Python. The
latter language is being tested in the SimPy = Simulation in Python system, a
project that has created a solution for developing simulators. See Table 3.




                                                                              236

              Table 3. Classification of simulators by programming language

       Java is the most widely used language because it is cross-platform. This
makes it portable and scalable. Its APIs for mathematical and graphical
processing in 2D and 3D integrate and handle the complex operations and
graphics that physics requires to simulate events. Furthermore, the ability to run
an applet in a web browser makes its distribution and use straightforward.
       A special case is the topic of simulators developed in Flash; it is one of the
development systems with the best graphics processing and is versatile when it
comes to integrating with the Internet.
       The key difference between developments in Java, C++, and Python
compared to Flash is that the first three languages offer the four freedoms
established for free software, while Flash only grants freedoms 1 and 3: execution
and distribution.

Freeware—as software that offers a free trial version for evaluation but does not

       In conclusion, freeware (57.1%) is the most common way to publish and

license ranks second with 32.7%

3.5 DESIGN OF THE PROTOTYPE GUIDE FOR THE EDUCATIONAL USE OF
PHYSICS SIMULATORS


       Once the different simulators have been identified, it becomes necessary
to design the respective guides for the educational use of these systems within a
physics course at the higher education level.
       This led to the definition of a prototype guide for the educational use of
simulators. On this topic, there is a postdoctoral thesis titled MODELLUS:
Learning Physics with Mathematical Modeling, developed by Teodoro, V. D. in
2003 at the University of Nova in Lisbon, Portugal (Teodoro, 2003). The final
result was the project titled MODELLUS: Interactive Modeling with Mathematics,
which defines software developed in Java for simulation and the methodology for
implementing that software in education.
       In Chapter Six, “Use of Modellus,” the author describes the theoretical
frameworks for the educational use of simulators and defines the general
structure of the guidelines required to use this simulation software solution.
       After reviewing and analyzing this experience—which, within the scope of
the research conducted, is the most comprehensive and well-documented project
regarding the educational use of simulators in education—the general structure
of the guide for the educational use of simulators has been defined, and it is
designed to be compatible with any other simulator.
       The guide model has been used in the development of practical exercises
within the Physics I courses at the Faculty of Distance Learning, with satisfactory
results.
       This prototype must undergo constant review, evaluation, and updating,
and depending on the simulator used, its components must be adjusted as
deemed appropriate.



                                                                                 239

3.5 SWOT ANALYSIS OF LEARNING USING SIMULATORS


           To validate the educational use of the selected simulators, the Physics I
course was used, specifically Group 550 with 26 students and Group 551 with
29. Both groups are part of the Civil Engineering Technology program in the
distance learning format.
           To begin these courses, students were provided with training to familiarize
them with the simulators, covering both the installation and usage processes.
Guided by the instructor, they learned about the simulator and how to interact
with it.
           The experimental group consisted of two groups of students: the first group
(550) used the Modellus simulation environment, and the second group (551)
used the Physlets project simulators and the Uninorte circular motion simulator.
           Each environment is very different, as Modellus is an integrated simulation
design and development system in which the user can change not only the
variables but also the simulation conditions; in fact, from a single example, they
can create an entirely new simulation. Physlets are applets with pre-designed
simulations in which the student only changes variables and then runs the
simulation with those variables.


3.5.1 Advantages and strengths


     • The use of simulators makes all physics experiments accessible without
           requiring complex and highly expensive laboratories. It also allows
           students to have a practice environment right in their own homes.
     • Simulators allow for the reproduction of natural phenomena that are
           difficult to observe directly in reality for various reasons: risks, costs, time
           scale, spatial scale
     • Students test their prior ideas and knowledge about the simulated
           phenomenon by formulating their own hypotheses, which leads to greater
           autonomy in the learning process and the development of constructivist
           and meaningful learning.




                                                                                       240

    • Students can modify the various parameters and initial conditions that
      appear in the physical model provided by the simulator, which helps them
      draw their own conclusions based on different scenarios.
    • Simulation provides students with a wide variety of relevant data,
      facilitating the qualitative and quantitative verification of laws and scientific
      principles across different fields of science.
    • Simulators display real-time graphs of various quantities, giving students
      a much more realistic sense of the simulated phenomena.


3.5.2 Disadvantages and challenges


      In general, no disadvantages as such have been identified; rather, the
issues arising from the use of simulators stem from certain challenges:
    • When students first begin using simulators, they sometimes modify
      variables of the simulated phenomenon that are not relevant to testing their
      hypotheses and that can cause errors in the program’s execution. To
      prevent this, adequate training in the use of simulators and clearly defined
      guidelines are required. (Rodríguez, 2010).
    • The most effective simulation systems from a didactic standpoint are those
      that implement a sufficient variety of physical models, with varying levels
      of complexity, as is the case in the Modellus simulation environment. In
      this environment, each physical model implemented is associated with a
      specific informational interface for the student, such that the sequence of
      proposed tasks requires the student


4. INTEGRATION OF EDUCATIONAL SIMULATION INTO THE UNIVERSITY’S
STRATEGIC PLAN FOR ICT INCORPORATION


      After confirming that simulators are a viable solution for the development
of physics, chemistry, and electronics laboratories, the project for the acquisition
and implementation of a hardware architecture for the institutional integration of
simulators was presented to the Strategic Plan for ICT Integration Committee.




                                                                                   241

This architecture would align with the university’s operations and complement the
existing physical laboratories.
       This research effort ultimately led to the implementation of an IT solution
for integrating simulators into physics, chemistry, and electronics laboratories.
The following activities were carried out for this project:
    • Renovation of computer equipment in six computer labs and their
       corresponding integration with a system of smart boards and interactive
       video bean. Three labs were adapted at the Tunja Campus, one at the
       Sogamoso Campus, one at the Duitama Campus, and one at the Bogotá
       Campus.
    • Acquisition of 145 licenses for Virtual Physical Science version 3 (VPS
       Lab)
    • Acquisition of a server for managing the virtual laboratories.
    • Integration of remote labs using TeamViewer into educational activities, as
       well as the integration of simulators into the university’s Virtual Classroom.
       After identifying both open-source and proprietary software that simulates
laboratory services, it was determined that open-source resources would be used
to design pre-class and reinforcement activities for students outside the
classroom, thanks to the availability of these resources on the Internet and their
ease of distribution via the web.
        Meanwhile, the software that was selected for purchase following analysis
and review—namely, Virtual Physical Science—was installed and configured in
the university’s laboratory centers.


4.1 CONFIGURATION OF THE VIRTUAL LABORATORY SYSTEM


       Taking advantage of VPS’s network features, it can be installed in Web
mode, Local Network mode, or User mode. This depends on the organization’s
capabilities.
       At the university, the initial pilot involved installing the licenses on every
computer in the computer labs and managing them locally with one user account
per student, previously created on the local server to ensure authentication and
control over each student’s activities.



                                                                                 242

       An initial phase of basic training in the use of VPS Lab was conducted,
utilizing the system’s Virtual Book of Pre-designed Labs. By clicking on a lab,
users can access the instructions, objectives, and other details of the exercise.
This option offers a printed book translated into Spanish that contains the 48 lab
guides.
       These guides are not the only labs available, as professors with expertise
in the field can create their own labs and guides and implement simulated
practical exercises.
       For web-based configuration, the web server must be set up with Tomcat
Web Services to serve as the servlet engine. This phase is currently being tested
at the university.

5. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK


5.1 CONCLUSIONS


      This study aimed to identify and document educational software projects,
a process that revealed the wide range of developments available in both open-
source and proprietary software.
      It should be noted that the results from this stage of the project are
satisfactory in terms of quantity; approximately 2,000 software solutions were
identified, each documented and organized according to its area of application.
      This study concludes that educational software that is 100% free is scarce,
accounting for just 42.4% of the identified projects and 11.4% of the total number
of simulators.
      With the implementation of laboratories through Virtual Physical Science,
an organizational framework has been created for the development of simulated
laboratory practices , a service that has improved students’ ability to understand
the various topics across different subjects. It has also reduced damage to real
laboratory equipment and materials, as both teachers and students can conduct
simulated experiments before working with actual equipment, particularly with
complex, costly, or high-risk laboratory equipment.
      There is a need to lead this type of project in a more organized manner,
applying quality criteria for educational software and system dynamics, so that
the implementation of simulators as a teaching-learning tool can be consolidated
within the educational community. A strength of this work is that it identified not



                                                                               244

only proprietary-licensed simulators but also simulators under free software
licenses, making these types of solutions accessible to everyone.
       From an educational standpoint, several projects were identified that are
methodologically and pedagogically very sound and could serve as models for
consolidating the educational use of simulators within society.
       The University has identified its methodology, which is adapted from the
Modellus project, and the teaching team has been developing laboratory guides,
using the simulators for practical exercises.


5.2 FUTURE WORK


       With more than 2,000 simulators identified, a very important future task
would be the educational validation of these resources based on educational
software quality criteria. Such research would provide educational organizations
and teachers with better tools for utilizing these open-source resources.
       Furthermore, given the existence of integrated open-source software
development environments, an analysis and study must be conducted to define
the methodology for developing open-source simulators using these systems,
along with their respective validation processes from the perspectives of
pedagogy, instructional design, and the learning theories that underpin the quality
of these systems, as proposed by Rodríguez Abril, Rodríguez-Hernández &
Avella-Forero (2021).
       Work is currently underway on the web implementation of VPS Lab, and
the results will be shared in future projects.
       A subsequent project should take these simulators and validate them
using criteria that measure learning and its impact on knowledge development
processes at a more pedagogical and didactic level.
