CHAPTER 15
 MOBILE PLANETARIUMS AS A
 SCIENTIFIC LITERACY TOOL FOR
 PEOPLE WITH VISUAL
 IMPAIRMENTS


Thiago de Oliveira Borges
PhD candidate in Education
Universidade Estadual de Mato Grosso do Sul (UEMS)

Celi Corrêa Neres
Doctor of Education

Edmilson de Souza
Doctor in Mechanical Engineering
Universidade Estadual de Mato Grosso do Sul (UEMS)
E-mail: edmilson@uems.br


ABSTRACT: This article analyzes the possibilities of scientific inclusion of people
with visual impairments in mobile planetariums, taking as a reference the
experience of the Itinerant Planetarium of the State University of Mato Grosso do
Sul (UEMS). Based on a historical-materialist perspective and drawing on
authors such as Marx, Engels, Gramsci, and Freire, the study discusses the
pedagogical, epistemological, and social barriers that limit access to astronomical
knowledge for this audience. The methodology was based on a critical literature
review and documentary analysis of public accessibility policies in science
spaces. Research on inclusion in museums and planetariums was examined, as
well as reports of concrete experiences with accessible scientific mediation. The
results show that the exclusion of blind and visually impaired people stems not
only from a lack of technical resources, but also from an educational structure
that reproduces cultural hegemony, privileging vision as the central sense in
astronomical learning. The study suggests ways to overcome these barriers,
such as the use of tactile models, audio description, and the training of mediators
sensitive to the specific sensory needs of the public. It concludes that inclusion in
mobile planetariums requires more than specific adaptations: it demands an
epistemological and pedagogical transformation that recognizes people with
visual impairments as active subjects in the construction of knowledge.
Democratizing access to astronomy, therefore, is not just a technical issue, but a
political commitment to equity and human emancipation.




                                                                                 247

KEYWORDS: accessibility, scientific literacy, social inclusion, visual impairment,
scientific dissemination.

RESUMO: Este artigo analisa as possibilidades de inclusão científica de pessoas
com deficiência visual em planetários móveis, tomando como referência a

do Sul (UEMS). Fundamentado na perspectiva histórico-materialista e

com mediação científica acessível. Os resultados evidenciam que a exclusão de
pessoas cegas e com baixa visão não decorre apenas de ausência de recursos
técnicos, mas de uma estrutura educativa que reproduz a hegemonia cultural,

1. INTRODUCTION


       The exclusion of people with disabilities from spaces of science
communication constitutes a structural problem that demands critical analysis
grounded in the relationships between knowledge, power, and human emancipation.
Marx and Engels (2007) had already demonstrated how the unequal appropriation
of the means of cultural production reproduces the asymmetries of capitalism,
turning science into an instrument for maintaining privileges rather than collective
liberation. In the case of students with visual impairments, this perspective reveals
that science venues, such as planetariums, from the standpoint of accessibility for
blind or low-vision individuals, may not be a mere technical failure, but a concrete
manifestation of what Gramsci (1999) termed “cultural hegemony”—a process by
which certain social groups determine which bodies and minds are considered
legitimate to participate in the scientific universe.
       In the Brazilian context, where disability is still frequently associated with
incapacity, the barrier to scientific literacy takes on even more perverse contours.
This stigmatizing association not only limits expectations regarding the cognitive
potential of students with intellectual disabilities but also restricts pedagogical
practices that could promote their full participation in knowledge-building processes.
       Dias and Oliveira (2013), focusing on students with intellectual disabilities,
offer a critical analysis of traditional conceptions that frequently associate this
condition with stagnation in cognitive development, perpetuating the idea of an
“eternal childhood.” From a historical-cultural perspective, the authors argue that
human development is a continuous process influenced by social and cultural
interactions. This approach highlights the importance of the environment and
social relationships in fostering the capabilities of people with intellectual
disabilities, suggesting that, with adequate support, it is possible to achieve
significant levels of autonomy and social participation.
       This view challenges traditional medical models that tend to focus on
individual limitations, proposing instead a more dynamic and contextualized
understanding of disability. This approach is fundamental to promoting a more
equitable society, where all individuals have real opportunities for development
and full participation. (Dias and Oliveira; 2013)



                                                                                  249

       Another relevant aspect to bring to the discussion is the lack of adequate
resources in science venues, such as planetariums, which reflects what is
identified as the “pedagogy of exclusion”: a set of educational practices that, even
without explicit intent, normalize segregation by failing to question their
discriminatory assumptions against people with disabilities. According to Abreu
et al. (2019), upon analyzing accessibility in 15 planetariums and observatories
in Brazil, they conclude that, although there have been advances in physical
accessibility, the communicational and attitudinal dimensions remain largely
unexplored. The lack of institutional policies aimed at the inclusion of people with
disabilities in these spaces highlights educational practices that, even without
explicit intent, perpetuate segregation by failing to challenge discriminatory
assumptions. The authors argue that it is necessary to adopt strategies to
overcome these barriers and invest in funding to promote full accessibility in these
scientific environments. (Abreu et al., 2019).
       According to Costa et al. (2021), it is evident that accessibility in science
museums (the same applies to planetariums) still faces significant challenges.
The research reveals that many of these spaces lack adapted resources that
meet the specific needs of people with disabilities, which limits their full
participation in the activities offered. Furthermore, the importance of
understanding the profile and opinions of spontaneous visitors with disabilities is
highlighted, in order to promote practices that are more inclusive and sensitive to
the diversity present in the audience of these museums. This approach reinforces
the need to rethink inclusion strategies in these environments, ensuring that all
visitors have equitable access to the knowledge and experiences provided by
scientific institutions.
       Neres and Corrêa (2008); Costa, Neres, and Moisés (2023) complement
this analysis by demonstrating how the lack of accessibility in formal and non-
formal educational spaces reinforces social marginalization, creating a vicious
cycle where the inability to access knowledge limits opportunities for civic
participation. In their studies, the aforementioned authors highlight, within the
educational trajectory of people with visual impairments, instances of exclusion
that can only be overcome through access to education in diverse settings and
contexts.



                                                                                250

       Given this situation, and seeking to contribute to the advancement of
inclusion in science settings, it becomes imperative to investigate how to
transform a traveling mobile planetarium into an effective tool for scientific
inclusion for the blind and low-vision public. To this end, this article adopts a
methodological approach that combines a theoretical analysis of the Marxist and
Gramscian foundations of education with the study of concrete experiences of
accessible mediation in science settings, such as science museums and
planetariums. The documentary investigation of Brazilian legislation on
accessibility engages with blind users who have experienced exclusion in science
outreach activities, allowing us to identify not only material and e y barriers, but
primarily the epistemological obstacles that need to be overcome.
       The development of the argument stems from the observation that the
mere technical adaptation of the space will not be sufficient to ensure effective
inclusion. As Freire (1987) demonstrates in his critique of banking education, it is
necessary to reinvent the entire process of scientific mediation, replacing the
unidirectional model of knowledge transmission with a dialogical practice that
recognizes people with visual impairments as active agents in the construction of
astronomical knowledge. This transformation requires rethinking the very notion
of scientific literacy, understanding it not as the passive assimilation of content,
but as a process of empowerment capable of unveiling the structures of
oppression that limit full human development.
       The relevance of this discussion extends beyond the walls of the
university, emerging as a central issue for the construction of a truly democratic
society. When the right to scientific knowledge is denied to people with visual
impairments, one is not only depriving individuals of information about the
cosmos, but also preventing them from developing critical tools to understand
and transform their social reality, which, in the words of Marx and Engels (2007),
means denying them the very status of historical subjects. Thus, fixed or mobile
planetariums, as public facilities for scientific dissemination, have the potential to
become either a space for reproducing inequalities or a laboratory for
revolutionary educational practices, depending on the political and pedagogical
choices that are made.
       By linking the categories of historical materialism with contemporary
debates on inclusive education, this article aims to contribute to the reflection on


                                                                                  251

the need to overcome the dichotomy between theory and practice in the field of
accessibility to science spaces that have notably specialized in science
education. By specifically analyzing the space for scientific outreach provided by
mobile planetariums, it becomes clear that the inclusion of people with visual
impairments is not a secondary or merely technical issue, but a central challenge
for any project that aims to make science a y instrument of liberation, rather than
domination. In the words of Gramsci (1999), “every man is an intellectual,” and
ensuring full access to astronomical knowledge means affirming the inalienable
right of all bodies—including those who perceive the world in other ways—to
actively participate in the construction of human knowledge about the universe.
       The construction of a truly egalitarian society necessarily involves the
democratization of scientific knowledge, understood not as the patrimony of an
intellectual caste, but as a tool for collective liberation. Marx and Engels (2007)
lay the groundwork for this understanding by demonstrating how, under the
capitalist mode of production, science becomes a productive force appropriated
by the ruling classes, transforming into an instrument of domination rather than
emancipation. This analysis reveals that the exclusion of people with visual
impairments from spaces of scientific dissemination is not accidental but
structural—a particular manifestation of the broader process of alienation that
separates workers from the fruits of their intellectual activity. Gramsci (1999)
expands on this reflection by showing how cultural hegemony operates through
control of the means of production and dissemination of knowledge, defining
which social groups have the right to full access to scientific culture.
       The concept of accessibility that emerges from this theoretical analysis
goes far beyond the simple physical adaptation of spaces. As Neres and CorrÊa
(2008) demonstrate, true inclusion requires a radical transformation of the
pedagogical structures that traditionally organize educational spaces. Although
the mobile planetarium already presents itself as an immersive space for science
education that offers sensory experiences, it does not do so in a way that is
accessible to all audiences, particularly the visually impaired, who are practically
excluded from basic processes such as audio description, which are generally
nonexistent. It must be clarified that in these spaces, interaction with the public is
intense, but the narration—whether recorded or led by a planetarium guide—
does not focus on providing abundant detail about the setting, which is partially


                                                                                  252

supplemented in terms of content by the projected visual elements. Specifically,
one can illustrate the experience with celestial bodies , which could not only be
described in terms of their characteristics but also allow visitors to feel them
through tactile models that reproduce their textures and scales, accompanied by
audio narratives enriched with more precise descriptions of the displayed images
linked to the tactile models. Without this profound restructuring to serve the
visually impaired public, even the best technical resources will remain mere
formal concessions, incapable of guaranteeing what she calls “epistemological
accessibility”—the right to understand and not merely to be present.
       The concept of scientific literacy takes on specific contours when applied to
people with visual impairments. Freire (1987) provides the foundations for
overcoming the “banking” view of scientific education, proposing instead a dialogical
pedagogical practice that recognizes these individuals’ prior knowledge and their
particular ways of interacting with the world. It is not simply a matter of adapting
content, but of reinventing the entire process of constructing astronomical
knowledge—in the case of the planetarium—allowing blind or low-vision individuals
to develop their own mental representations of the cosmos through meaningful
experiences. Access to knowledge is a fundamental condition for the full exercise of
citizenship, allowing these individuals to transition from being objects of welfare
policies to active agents in cultural and scientific production.
       The articulation between these different theoretical perspectives reveals
that inclusion in the mobile planetarium cannot be reduced to a technical or
methodological issue. Rather, it is a political-epistemological challenge that
requires confronting the exclusionary structures that have historically organized
the production and dissemination of scientific knowledge. Overcoming these
barriers, as Marx and Engels (2007) argue, will not occur through the mere
natural evolution of institutions, but through the creation of mechanisms for the
production of and access to a truly popular science—a process in which people
with visual impairments must be protagonists, not merely participants or
beneficiaries. In this sense, the accessible planetarium is not an end in itself, but
a necessary step in the construction of a new, e y relationship between science
and society, where astronomical knowledge is effectively appropriated by all
bodies and minds, in their rich sensory and cognitive diversity.



                                                                                 253

2. SCIENCE, INCLUSION, AND HUMAN EMANCIPATION


       The intrinsic relationship between scientific production and social
transformation constitutes the central axis for understanding the challenges of
accessibility in scientific spaces such as mobile planetariums. Marx and Engels
(2007) ground this analysis by demonstrating how the development of productive
forces in capitalist society creates an essential contradiction: while science could
be an instrument of collective liberation, its private appropriation turns it into a
mechanism of domination. This dialectic manifests itself concretely in the
exclusion of people with visual impairments from spaces of scientific
dissemination, which does not represent mere negligence, but a particular
expression of the exclusionary logic inherent in the prevailing system.
       Gramsci (1999) contributes significantly to this reflection by examining how
cultural hegemony is consolidated through control of educational and cultural
apparatuses. The concept of the “organic intellectual,” proposed by the author,
reveals the transformative potential that educators and scientific mediators can
play in transforming the planetarium into a counter-hegemonic space. From this
perspective, the accessible mediation of astronomy ceases to be a merely
technical activity, taking on a political character—an act of resistance to the
intellectual marginalization historically imposed on people with disabilities.
       In the case of planetariums, from the perspective of inclusive education
and considering curricular and pedagogical accessibility, studies highlight the
need for structural transformations across multiple dimensions. First, an
epistemological transformation is necessary, one that challenges the geocentric
paradigms traditionally used in the organization of astronomical knowledge.
Second, a methodological revolution is required, centered on the creation of
pedagogical approaches that value the potentialities—and not merely the
sensory limitations—of individuals. Finally, a political restructuring is required, in
which accessibility is understood as a fundamental right, and not as a benevolent
concession.
       Freire (1987) offers essential contributions to the implementation of a
transformative educational practice, especially through his critique of the banking
model of education. In the context of planetariums, his dialogical pedagogy
proposes a break with the top-down transmission of concepts, advocating instead


                                                                                  254

for collaborative processes of knowledge construction. This approach values
active listening and the participation of individuals in the educational process,
placing the concrete experiences of learners at the center. For visitors with visual
impairments, this implies recognizing their everyday experiences as a legitimate
starting point for scientific understanding, breaking with the traditional logic that
positions them as passive recipients of knowledge. Furthermore, mediation, in
this scenario, must serve as a space for critical examination of the very conditions
of exclusion, promoting reflection on the epistemological and social barriers that
have historically kept them at a distance from the scientific field.
       In a specific case such as the Traveling Planetarium of the State University
of Mato Grosso do Sul (UEMS), the exchange of information based on dialogicity
takes place, and concerns regarding the treatment of content in a critical and
problematizing manner have also been addressed—aspects that required
extensive research involving an audience of over 100,000 visitors. However,
similar to other Brazilian experiences that use planetariums as tools for scientific
literacy, these necessary and desirable advances did not incorporate technically
inclusive methodologies or deeper reflections on political relations, which would
have resulted in solutions addressing accessibility for the visually impaired public
(Borges; Souza, 2022; Junglos et al., 2022).
       According to Chalhub and Gomes (2019), science spaces (in their specific
case, museums) can be inclusive educational spaces, especially for deaf
students, highlighting the importance of communicati y accessibility and scientific
literacy in teacher training. The authors present pedagogical activities developed
in the context of deaf education, related to inclusion and accessibility in
museums, emphasizing strategies such as video captions, animations, and
videos in Brazilian Sign Language (Libras). The study highlights the need for
inclusive policies in museums to cater to the diversity of the public and promote
scientific literacy in an accessible manner. Thus, scientific literacy not only
promotes access to information but also empowers these individuals for a more
conscious and transformative intervention in the social fabric.
       Silva and Elias (2022) discuss the training of agents who mediate in
science spaces, in daily life, or even in schools. For them, both families and
teachers face numerous structural and training challenges in ensuring quality
inclusive education. The research shows that, often, a lack of teacher preparation


                                                                                 255

and a shortage of specific resources exacerbate the process of exclusion,
reinforcing limited views about these students’ capabilities. Thus, breaking with
the social stereotype that associates disability with intellectual incapacity is
essential to making scientific literacy a right for all, regardless of their cognitive
abilities.
        Another study revealed concerning findings regarding the preparedness of
school staff in rural areas. Oliveira and Souza (2011) investigated the
implementation of public inclusion policies at a state school in Belo Horizonte
during 2007 and 2008. Using a qualitative-quantitative approach, the authors
administered questionnaires to 25 teachers and conducted interviews with 10
teachers, the school principal, and the manager of the Special Education
Directorate (DEEP). The results revealed that, although all teachers were in favor
of inclusive education, none had specific training to work with students with
special educational needs, and only two had some knowledge of the relevant
legislation. Furthermore, all reported difficulties in dealing with these students and
observed significant school dropout rates among them.
        Weaknesses in teacher training, the lack of adequate infrastructure, and
insufficient support undermine the effectiveness of inclusion policies. In the
findings of Oliveira and Souza (2011), the teachers interviewed expressed the
need for specific training and better working conditions to meet the demands of
inclusive education. The study concludes that, for inclusion to be effective, it is
essential to invest in the continuing education of teachers, adapt the physical
structures of schools, and ensure the necessary support from educational
authorities.
        The synthesis of these studies points to a radical understanding of
accessibility in the mobile planetarium: not as a peripheral adaptation, but as a
global restructuring of the process of scientific dissemination. This approach
requires overcoming the dichotomy between inclusion and academic excellence,
demonstrating that the development of accessible methodologies does not
represent a “downgrading” of content, but rather its enrichment through dialogue
with new forms of perception and understanding of the cosmos.




                                                                                  256

3. TOWARD A DIALECTICAL AND INCLUSIVE SCIENCE


       An analysis of the relationship between scientific knowledge and human
emancipation reveals a fundamental contradiction: while science possesses
liberating potential, its unequal distribution in class society turns it into an
instrument of domination. Marx and Engels (2007) demonstrate how the
development of productive forces under capitalism creates a rift between
producers and knowledge, alienating the majority from the knowledge they
produce. This analysis offers a privileged lens for understanding the exclusion of
people with visual impairments from scientific spaces not as an accident, but as
a particular manifestation of a system that naturalizes cognitive hierarchies.
       Gramsci    (1999)   expands    this   understanding   by   examining      the
mechanisms of cultural hegemony. His studies on the private apparatuses of
hegemony shed light on how museums and science centers, seemingly neutral,
reproduce dominant worldviews. In the specific case of planetariums and mobi ,
the lack of accessibility reveals what the author termed “organic censorship”—a
process by which certain groups are systematically excluded from cultural
production and enjoyment without the need for explicit prohibitions.
       In analyzing the history of education for people with visual impairments,
using work as a category of analysis, Neres and Corrêa (2008) draw attention to
the persistence of barriers regarding access to knowledge and, consequently, to
scientific participation. Through their studies, it is possible to infer that: a)
Disability is a social construct: the limitations experienced stem less from
biological conditions than from exclusionary social arrangements; b) Inclusion is
a political project: it demands a conscious confrontation with the power relations
that marginalize certain bodies and minds.
       Along these lines, drawing on the studies of Freire (1987), one can derive
methodological tools to operationalize this transformation. His pedagogy of the
oppressed suggests three axes for reinventing scientific mediation: a)
Dialogicity: replacing the academic monologue with collaborative processes of
knowledge construction; b) Problematization: a critical approach to the very
conditions of exclusion as part of scientific content; c) Conscientization: the
articulation between astronomical knowledge and the social experience of
disability.


                                                                                 257

       This theoretical perspective establishes an intrinsic relationship between
scientific literacy and integral human development. In his analysis, the
appropriation of scientific knowledge reveals itself as a pathway to expanding the
horizons of existential possibility for people with disabilities. By accessing this
field of knowledge, these individuals come to perceive themselves not merely as
recipients of science, but as active participants in its construction, which
strengthens their self-image as historical subjects, conscious of their trajectory
and their role in social transformation. Furthermore, mastery of this knowledge
acts as an instrument of critical intervention in reality, by providing elements for
a more complex reading of the world and for the full exercise of citizenship.
       In this way, scientific literacy transcends its informative function, taking on
a profoundly formative and emancipatory dimension. This rationale converges
toward a radical understanding of the accessible planetary: not as a peripheral
adaptation, but as a global reconstruction of scientific practice based on the
recognition of human diversity. The challenge at hand is to transcend the logic of
inclusion as assimilation, proposing instead a model of active coexistence of
differences in the production of knowledge. As the authors analyzed
demonstrate, only this dialectical approach can transform the mobile planetarium
into a true instrument of collective liberation.


4. INCLUSION AS A PRINCIPLE: PROPOSALS FOR ACCESSIBILITY IN
ASTRONOMY EDUCATION


       Building a truly inclusive society requires that the right to knowledge be
guaranteed to all, without exception. In the field of science education, particularly
in astronomy, the barriers faced by people with visual impairments remain
evident. Given this scenario, it is essential to implement concrete proposals that
guarantee equitable access to astronomical content. Adapting teaching
materials, training mediators, and collaborating with specialized teachers are
effective strategies that not only expand access but also promote a cultural
transformation in education.
       First and foremost, the adaptation of materials stands as one of the primary
tools for the democratization of knowledge. Tactile models, such as spheres with
distinct textures to represent planets, enable astronomical content to be grasped


                                                                                  258

through touch—a fundamental sense for blind people. Additionally, the use of audio
description and 3D audio resources to simulate celestial movements enriches the
sensory experience, allowing for a deeper understanding of phenomena. Such
resources not only facilitate learning but also highlight alternative forms of perception
that are often overlooked in traditional educational settings.
       Furthermore, it is essential that professionals involved in the educational
process be prepared to act in an inclusive manner. The training of mediators and
educators provides theoretical and practical support so that knowledge mediation is
sensitive to the needs of different audiences. Courses focused on description
techniques, accessible communication, and welcoming practices thus become key
elements for the effectiveness of inclusive actions, as they broaden the scope of
pedagogical practices and foster an ethical and empathetic attitude among
educators.
       Finally, the importance of institutional partnerships is highlighted.
Collaboration with institutes and organizations of people with disabilities allows
not only for the validation of proposed methodologies but also for the constant
improvement of educational practices. These partnerships ensure that the
solutions developed are aligned with the real demands of the target audience,
avoiding superficial or merely symbolic actions. The dialogue between
institutional knowledge and personal experiences strengthens the legitimacy of
these actions and ensures greater social impact.
       Thus, inclusion in astronomy education goes beyond a technical issue: it
is an ethical and social commitment to equity. The proposals discussed here
demonstrate that, with creativity, dialogue, and commitment, it is possible to
break down the barriers of ableism and offer everyone a truly transformative
educational experience. Investing in inclusion is not just a pedagogical choice—
it is a social duty.


5. PUBLIC POLICIES AND ACCESS TO SCIENCE: PATHWAYS TO SOCIAL
EMANCIPATION


       Universal access to scientific knowledge is a fundamental right that must
be guaranteed by effective public policies. In a country marked by deep
inequalities, viewing scientific inclusion as part of civic education is more than an


                                                                                     259

ideal: it is a social imperative. Among the most urgent proposals are the
integration of accessible science into school curricula, the creation of national
guidelines for non-formal educational spaces, the strengthening of investments
in assistive technologies, and the mandatory accessibility of scientific outreach
equipment.
      The inclusion of accessible science programs in school curricula is a
fundamental step toward ensuring that all students, regardless of their physical,
sensory, or social conditions, have access to scientific knowledge from an early
age. Schools, as spaces for holistic education, must assume the role of
democratizing agents of knowledge, promoting inclusive, interactive, and
culturally contextualized activities. The absence of this perspective in curricula
contributes to the perpetuation of an exclusionary system, in which access to
science remains a privilege of the few.
      Another essential aspect is the creation of national guidelines for inclusion
in non-formal educational spaces, such as museums, planetariums, science fairs,
and science centers. These environments, often neglected by educational
policies, have great potential for engagement and wonder, especially for young
audiences. Establishing accessibility standards and goals in these locations
ensures that the experience with science is not limited to the school walls and
that it reaches diverse audiences, including those historically marginalized.
      Increasing public funding for assistive technologies is also an
indispensable measure. Devices such as screen readers, Braille printers, tactile
materials, and audio description systems enable people with disabilities to
participate independently in scientific activities. However, the scarcity of
resources allocated to the research and production of these materials limits their
availability and makes access more expensive. By prioritizing investment in this
area, the state assumes its rightful role in promoting equity.
      All these proposals converge on a central issue: scientific literacy as an
instrument of social emancipation. In a world increasingly shaped by science and
technology, understanding the scientific foundations of reality becomes essential
for full civil. Science must be recognized as a common good, capable of
transforming lives and communities. Promoting access to science is, therefore, a
concrete way to combat marginalization and expand horizons of autonomy and
agency.


                                                                                260

      The state and public universities play a strategic role in this process. It is
their responsibility to produce knowledge in a socially committed manner, build
bridges between research and the population, and formulate policies that not only
acknowledge historical inequalities but also act directly to overcome them.
      In short, ensuring democratic access to science through structural public
policies is a commitment to a more just, critical, and participatory society.
Scientific inclusion should not be viewed as a favor, but as a collective
responsibility and an indispensable step toward full citizenship.


6. FINAL CONSIDERATIONS


      The analysis presented in this article demonstrates that the inclusion of
people with visual impairments in science outreach settings, such as mobile
planetariums—notably the UEMS Traveling Planetarium—where the author’s
experience in university extension projects during his undergraduate studies,
and, subsequently, the development of research in this same scientific field at the
master’s level, has provided him with a broad empirical perspective on its
pedagogical dynamics. This article brings together analyses grounded in
historical-materialist frameworks to provide a foundation for continuing the
research previously initiated—which was still viewed solely from a technical
perspective, albeit critical of pedagogical issues, yet at the same time entirely
disconnected from accessibility issues for people with visual impairments. Thus,
the reflections presented point to tangible results: the need for implementations
and changes within the science space of the on-screen planetarium that
transcend    specific   technical   adaptations    and    demand      a   profound
epistemological, pedagogical, and political restructuring. It is not merely a matter
of ensuring physical presence, but of guaranteeing the right to active participation
in the construction and appropriation of scientific knowledge, in accordance with
the principles of emancipatory education.
      By articulating the theoretical frameworks of historical-dialectical
materialism with the proposals of an inclusive and dialogical pedagogy, it has
been demonstrated that the scientific literacy of people with visual impairments
must be understood as a process of empowerment and political subjectivation,



                                                                                261

breaking with the welfare-oriented logic that has historically marked educational
practices aimed at this audience.
      In this sense, the planetarium can (and should) be redefined as a space of
resistance and transformation, where science is liberated from its traditional role
as an instrument of exclusion and assumes its potential as a tool for the
democratization of knowledge. To achieve this, universities, public officials,
educators, and the scientific community itself must recognize that accessibility is
not a favor but a right—and that its realization depends on political choices that
place human dignity at the center of the educational project.
      Therefore, making the UEMS mobile planetarium a space of real inclusion
implies recognizing people with visual impairments as legitimate epistemic
subjects, capable of producing and reframing astronomical knowledge based on
their experiences and sensory perceptions. Only in this way can we move toward
a science that is truly popular, critical, and liberating—accessible to all bodies,
perspectives, and ways of existing in the world.

ABSTRACT: The relationship between literature and literacy constitutes a relevant
field of in-vestigation for understanding the processes involved in the formation of
student readers in the Brazilian educational context. Historically, children's literature
and reading practices have been incorporated into literacy processes as pedagogical
tools capable of expanding the cultural dimension of written language learning.
However, different conceptions of teaching and reading have marked this trajectory,
revealing tensions between more instrumental approaches to literacy and
perspectives that value literature as an aesthetic and formative experience. In this
context, this article aims to analyze the historical and pedagogical trajectories of the
relationship between literature and literacy in Brazil, seeking to understand how this
articulation has contributed to the development of practices aimed at the formation of
student readers. Methodologically, this study adopts a qualitative approach,
developed through bibliographic review and documentary analysis of academic
studies that discuss the incorporation of literature into reading and writing teaching
processes. The results indicate that the presence of literature in lit-eracy processes
plays a fundamental role in expanding reading practices in schools, promoting the
development of aesthetic sensitivity, imagination, and in-terpretative competence
among students. It is concluded that the integration be-tween literature and literacy
constitutes a central element in the formation of crit-ical readers, highlighting the need
for pedagogical practices that value literary reading from the early years of schooling.

KEYWORDS: children's literature, literacy, reader formation, literary reading,
history of education.

RESUMO: A relação entre literatura e alfabetização constitui um campo de
investigação re-levante para compreender os processos de formação do aluno leitor
no contexto educacional brasileiro. Historicamente, a literatura infantil e as práticas
de leitura foram incorporadas ao processo de alfabetização como instrumentos
pedagógi-cos capazes de ampliar a dimensão cultural da aprendizagem da
linguagem es-crita. No entanto, diferentes concepções de ensino e de leitura
marcaram essa trajetória, evidenciando tensões entre abordagens mais
instrumentais da alfabe-tização e perspectivas que valorizam a literatura como
experiência estética e formativa. Diante desse cenário, o presente artigo tem como
objetivo analisar as trajetórias históricas e pedagógicas da relação entre literatura e
alfabetização no Brasil, buscando compreender como essa articulação contribuiu
para a consti-tuição de práticas voltadas à formação do aluno leitor.
Metodologicamente, trata-se de uma pesquisa de natureza qualitativa, desenvolvida
por meio de revisão bibliográfica e análise documental de estudos e produções
acadêmicas que dis-cutem a inserção da literatura no ensino da leitura e da escrita.
Os resultados indicam que a presença da literatura nos processos de alfabetização
tem desem-penhado papel fundamental na ampliação das práticas de leitura na
escola, fa-vorecendo o desenvolvimento da sensibilidade estética, da imaginação e
da competência interpretativa dos estudantes. Conclui-se que a integração entre
literatura e alfabetização constitui elemento central para a formação de leitores
críticos, evidenciando a necessidade de práticas pedagógicas que valorizem a
leitura literária desde os primeiros anos da escolarização.

literária, história da educação.

1. INTRODUCTION


       The relationship between literature and literacy in Brazil is an important
field of research for understanding the historical and pedagogical processes that
have shaped the development of the student as a reader. Reading, as a cultural
and educational practice, did not develop in a linear fashion in the country, but
was shaped by different conceptions of teaching, literacy methods, and societal
projects that influenced the organization of schools and pedagogical practices
over time (Silva, 2015; Mortatti, 2006).
       Historically, the first systematic records of reading and writing instruction
in Brazil date back to the colonial period, with the work of Jesuit missionaries
beginning in the 16th century. The education promoted by the Jesuits had a
strong religious and disciplinary character, guided by the Ratio Studiorum, a set
of norms regulating the operation of the Society of Jesus’ educational institutions.
As Saviani (2013) highlights, this method was structured by detailed rules that
organized everything from administrative functions to pedagogical practices
developed in the classroom:


                       [...] by a set of rules covering all activities of those directly involved in
                       teaching. It began with the rules of the provincial, continued with those
                       of the rector, the prefect of studies, the teachers in general, and those
                       for each subject taught... (Saviani, 2013, p. 55).


       Although this model was associated with a process of catechization and
cultural imposition on indigenous peoples, it also represented one of the first
attempts at the systematic organization of education in the colonial territory. In
this context, according to Saviani (2013), the teaching of reading and writing was
strongly linked to memorization and the mastery of linguistic codes, with little
emphasis on comprehension or the development of independent readers.
       Throughout the 19th century, with the establishment of the Brazilian nation-
state, literacy began to take on greater relevance in educational policies. As Mortatti
(2006) analyzes, the schooling process during this period was still marked by
structural precariousness, a lack of pedagogical organization, and a scarcity of
teaching resources. Many schools operated in makeshift spaces, bringing together




                                                                                               266

students of different learning levels under the responsibility of a single teacher, which
hindered the systematization of reading and writing instruction.
       In this context, teaching practices based on the phonics method and the
use of primers became established, characterized by syllabic approaches and
the rote memorization of words (Soares, 2004). According to Mortatti (2006),
these methodologies prioritized the decoding of written language, without
necessarily promoting the development of reading comprehension or the
formation of critical readers. This perspective contributed to the persistence of
conceptions of literacy centered on the technical mastery of reading, dissociated
from the cultural and interpretive dimensions of the text.
       From the 20th century onward, especially with the advancement of
linguistic and pedagogical studies, new reflections emerged on the literacy
process and the role of reading in the formation of individuals. In this context,
authors such as Magda Soares highlight the need to understand literacy beyond
the simple learning of the writing system, linking it to the concept of literacy,
understood as the individual’s integration into social practices of reading and
writing. For Soares (2004, p.78), “literacy involves teaching reading and writing,
but also enabling the individual to participate in social practices mediated by
written language.”
       Parallel to this movement, literature has come to be recognized as a
fundamental element in the reader’s development. Researchers such as Regina
Zilberman highlight that children’s literature plays a central role in shaping
children’s imagination and aesthetic sensibility, “contributing “for the development
of reading as a cultural experience and not merely as a technical skill” (Zilberman,
2003, p. 45). Similarly, Teresa Colomer argues that “the presence of literature in
schools broadens the possibilities for interpretation and fosters the construction
of meaningful connections between students and texts” (Colomer, 2007, p. 32).
       Within this same theoretical framework, Rildo Cosson proposes the
concept of “literary literacy,” understood as “a pedagogical process that enables
students to develop interpretive and aesthetic competencies through the reading
of literary works” (Cosson, 2014, p. 17). For Cosson (2014), literature in schools
must go beyond instrumental use and assume a formative role, contributing to
the development of readers who are critical and sensitive to the multiple
dimensions of the literary text.


                                                                                     267

       Thus, despite the theoretical advances and pedagogical transformations
that have occurred in recent decades, the Brazilian educational system still faces
significant challenges in the formation of readers. Literacy practices that are
excessively focused on the decoding of written language persist, often
disconnected from literary reading and the social practices of reading. This
scenario highlights the need to revisit the historical trajectory of literacy in Brazil,
analyzing how different conceptions of teaching have influenced the relationship
between literature and the formation of the reader.
       In this context, this article aims to analyze the historical and pedagogical
trajectories of the relationship between literature and literacy in Brazil, seeking to
understand how this connection has contributed to the development of the
student reader within the Brazilian educational context. By discussing the
different historical moments and the transformations in conceptions of reading
and literacy, the aim is to highlight the importance of literature as a central
element in the construction of pedagogical practices aimed at the formation of
critical and culturally situated readers.


2. METHODOLOGY


       According to (Minayo, 2009), research methodology can be understood as
the most important theoretical and practical approach adopted by the researcher
in the process of knowledge production. Thus, this study is characterized as
qualitative research of a bibliographic and documentary nature. The choice of this
research methodology is based on the understanding that the subject under
investigation requires a systematic analysis of works, documents, and academic
productions regarding the history of education in Brazil. Thus, the research
methodology, according to Minayo (2009, p. 14), is characterized as,


                       [...] a process that integrates the method—understood as the theory
                       guiding the investigative approach—the operational instruments that
                       enable data collection and analysis (the techniques), as well as the
                       researcher’s creativity, experience, and sensitivity.


       Considering this, the author asserts that methodology is not merely a set
of technical procedures, but incorporates subjective and epistemological



                                                                                       268

dimensions that shape the way reality is interpreted. Thus, in agreement with
Severino (2016), bibliographic and documentary research allows for the
examination of the subject from different contexts, enabling the critical
reconstruction of historical processes. In this vein, in the present study, this
approach was employed to highlight, within the trajectory of Brazilian education,
perspectives that value literature as an aesthetic and formative experience.


3. LITERACY IN BRAZIL: A BRIEF OVERVIEW


       Understanding the relationship between literature and literacy in the
Brazilian educational context requires, first and foremost, a historical analysis of
the processes of teaching reading and writing in the country. As discussed in the
introduction, literacy in Brazil has its roots in the colonial period, when the first
systematic teaching initiatives were carried out by Jesuit missionaries beginning
in the 16th century. According to Saviani (2013, p. 55),


                      [...] Jesuit education was structured around the Ratio Studiorum, a
                      document that organized the functioning of the educational institutions
                      of the Society of Jesus. This model established strict norms for the
                      pedagogical and disciplinary organization of school activities.


       Although this system was linked to catechization and the imposition of
European culture, it represented one of the first forms of institutionalization of
education in Brazilian territory. However, literacy during this period was
restricted to specific groups, mainly members of the colonial elite and the
clergy (Soares, 2004).
       Throughout the 19th century, as the Brazilian nation-state took shape,
literacy came to play a more prominent role in educational policies. However, as
Mortatti (2006) points out, the teaching of reading and writing was still marked by
significant structural and pedagogical shortcomings. Schools often operated
under makeshift conditions and brought together students of varying learning
levels under the supervision of a single teacher. In this context, methodologies
based on primers and synthetic methods became established, particularly the
phonetic and syllabic methods (Soares, 2004). These approaches prioritized the
memorization of syllables and words, emphasizing the decoding of written



                                                                                         269

language at the expense of textual comprehension. According to Mortatti (2006),
such practices contributed to the consolidation of a pedagogical tradition
centered on the mechanical learning of reading.
       This historical perspective helps us understand that, for long periods,
literacy in Brazil was conceived predominantly as technical mastery of the written
code, without necessarily fostering the development of readers capable of
critically interpreting texts.
       Starting in the second half of the 20th century, studies on literacy underwent
significant theoretical transformations, particularly with the incorporation of
contributions from linguistics, cognitive psychology, and the educational sciences. In
this context, the contribution of Magda Soares stands out, as she introduced the
concept of “literacy” into the Brazilian educational debate.
       For Soares (2004), literacy and literacy are distinct yet interdependent
processes. Literacy refers to the learning of the system alphabetic writing,
whereas literacy refers to an individual’s participation in social practices of
reading and writing. In this sense, the author argues that: “Teaching literacy and
fostering literacy are two distinct but inseparable actions: the ideal would be to
teach literacy by fostering literacy, that is, to teach reading and writing within the
context of the social practices of reading and writing” (Soares, 2004, p. 14).
       This perspective broadens the understanding of the reading learning
process, shifting the focus from the simple decoding of text to the subject’s
insertion into social contexts of the production and circulation of written language.
By considering reading as a social practice, the concept of literacy contributes to
rethinking the role of the school in the formation of readers. Learning to read
comes to involve not only technical mastery of the linguistic code, but also the
development of interpretive and critical skills.
       In this sense, for Soares (2004), literacy is no longer understood as an
isolated stage of the educational process but is integrated into broader cultural
practices, among which literary reading stands out.




                                                                                  270

4.   LITERATURE        AS   A    STRATEGY       FOR     LITERACY       AND     THE
DEVELOPMENT OF READERS


       As Zilberman (2003) points out, literature plays a central role in the
development of readers, especially in the context of elementary education.
Several studies indicate that exposure to literary texts from childhood onward
contributes to the development of students’ imagination, aesthetic sensitivity, and
interpretive skills.
       According to Zilberman (2003), children’s literature also plays a
fundamental role in children’s cultural development, enabling reading
experiences that go beyond the instrumental nature often attributed to reading
instruction in school. For the author, “literature should be understood as a form
of artistic expression that broadens the possibilities for interpreting the world”
(Zilberman, 2003, p.25).
       In the same vein, Colomer (2007), in his studies on “literary reading,”
argues that the presence of literature in the school environment allows
students to develop meaningful connections with texts and broaden their
reading experience. According to Colomer (2007, p.33), literary reading
“enables the construction of multiple meanings and fosters the development
of autonomous readers.”
       Thus, we believe that literature helps transform reading and the literacy
process into a cultural and aesthetic experience, moving beyond pedagogical
practices focused exclusively on the mechanical learning of written language. By
exposing students to different narratives, genres, and symbolic worlds, literature
broadens their cultural repertoire and strengthens their relationship with reading.
       In this vein, the relationship between literature and reader development
has been explored in greater depth by studies that emphasize the importance of
“literary literacy” in the school context. Among the leading authors discussing this
topic, Cosson (2014) stands out; for him, the teaching of literature in schools must
go beyond fragmented or merely informative approaches to works and authors.
The author proposes that literature be approached as a literacy practice, allowing
students to develop interpretive and aesthetic skills through direct engagement
with literary texts.



                                                                                271

       According to Cosson (2014), literary literacy consists of a pedagogical
process that enables readers to understand, interpret, and engage with literary
texts at different levels of meaning. This process involves not only individual
reading but also the teacher’s pedagogical guidance and the collective
construction of meaning within the school environment.
       In this context, the teaching of literature plays a fundamental role in the
development of critical readers, capable of interpreting texts in a reflective and
contextualized manner. By integrating literary reading practices into the literacy
process, the school contributes to broadening students’ reading experiences and
strengthening their relationship with written language.
       Thus, we can understand that historically, the connection between literacy,
literacy education, and literature has been a central element in the development
of the student as a reader and an important tool in the literacy process. By
considering the historical, pedagogical, and cultural dimensions of reading, it
becomes possible to understand the challenges and potential of teaching reading
in the Brazilian educational context.


5. CONCLUSION


       The analysis presented in this article has shown that the relationship
between literature and literacy in Brazil is the result of a complex historical
process, marked by different pedagogical approaches and social transformations
that have shaped the development of the student reader. From the colonial
period, with the Jesuits’ organization of education, to contemporary debates on
literacy and the formation of readers, it is evident that the learning of reading and
writing has often been associated with pedagogical models that prioritized
technical mastery of the linguistic code, to the detriment of critical comprehension
and the aesthetic experience of reading.
       Within this theoretical framework, the contributions of various authors
underscore the importance of integrating literature into reading pedagogy through
the concept of literary literacy. For the author, literary reading should be understood
as a formative practice that allows students to interpret, engage in dialogue, and
construct meaning from texts, contributing to the development of critical and
reflective readers (Zilberman, 2003; Soares, 2004; Mortatti, 2006; Colomer, 2007).


                                                                                   272

       Based on the discussions in this study, it becomes evident that the
development of the student reader depends on the interplay between literacy,
literacy education, and literature. When schools restrict reading instruction to the
decoding of the writing system, they limit the possibilities for developing reading
competence and reduce the reading experience to a merely technical activity. On
the other hand, when literature is integrated into the literacy process, reading
takes on cultural, aesthetic, and critical dimensions, expanding students’ learning
and educational opportunities.
       Thus, it can be concluded that the integration of literature and literacy is a
fundamental element in the development of teaching practices that foster the
development of independent and critical readers. The school, in this context,
plays a central role in providing meaningful reading experiences that enable
students to understand, interpret, and engage with different texts and discourses.
       Finally, it is emphasized that reflection on the historical trajectories of
literacy and literature in Brazil contributes to understanding the contemporary
challenges of basic education, especially regarding the formation of readers in a
society marked by the intense circulation of information and the diversity of
languages. In this sense, it is essential to strengthen educational policies and
pedagogical practices that value literature as a formative tool, recognizing its
potential to broaden cultural horizons, develop aesthetic sensitivity, and foster the
development of critical and socially engaged readers.

CHAPTER 17
 ETHOS OF SCHOOL MANAGEMENT IN
 CIEJAs IN SÃO PAULO: A POLYPHONIC
 ANALYSIS OF POLITICAL-PEDAGOGICAL
 PROJECTS


Renato Melo Ribeiro
Doctor in Education
Faculdade de Educação, Universidade de São Paulo (FEUSP)
E-mail: renatoribeiro@usp.br


ABSTRACT: This study analyzed the Political-Pedagogical Projects [PPPs] of
the Integrated Centers for Youth and Adult Education [CIEJAs] of the Municipal
Education Secretariat of São Paulo – SME/SP, with the objective of
understanding the ethos of school management projected by the polyphonic
configuration of these documents. The empirical-textual exploration used as its
corpus the PPPs of the 15 (fifteen) CIEJAs of the SME/SP, to analyze educational
polyphony through descriptors derived from key notions of discourse studies.
This work sought to demonstrate that there is a relative political-pedagogical unity
among CIEJAs (Integrated Centers for Youth and Adult Education), anchored in
a shared institutional ethos, which projects the image of a school management
that knows and follows educational legislation, values democratic management
and collective work, understands the diversity of the public and the specific
challenges of the EJA (Youth and Adult Education) modality, while ideologically
adhering to the critical discourse of popular and emancipatory education, under
the auspices of the educator Paulo Freire and the spectrum of voices that are
inspired by his legacy. Finally, the work highlighted the alignment of this
institutional ethos with the management practices of CIEJAs, as evidenced by
academic and institutional literature that has taken these school units as an object
or source.

KEYWORDS: educational management, youth and adult education, pedagogical
discourse, CIEJA.

RESUMO: Este estudio analizó los Proyectos Político-Pedagógicos [PPP] de los
Centros Integrados de Educación de Jóvenes y Adultos [CIEJAs] de la Secretaría
Municipal de Educación de São Paulo – SME/SP, con el objetivo de comprender
el ethos de la gestión escolar proyectado por la configuración polifónica de estos
documentos. La exploración empírica-textual utilizó como corpus los PPP de los
15 (quince) CIEJAs de la SME/SP para analizar la polifonía educativa mediante
descriptores derivados de nociones clave de los estudios del discurso. Este
trabajo buscó demostrar que existe una relativa unidad político-pedagógica entre
los CIEJA (Centros Integrados de Educación de Personas Jóvenes y Adultas),
anclada en un ethos institucional compartido, que proyecta la imagen de una


                                                                                275

gestión escolar que conoce y cumple la legislación educativa, valora la gestión
democrática y el trabajo colectivo, comprende la diversidad del público y los
desafíos específicos de la modalidad EJA (Educación de Personas Jóvenes y
Adultas), a la vez que se adhiere ideológicamente al discurso crítico de la
educación popular y emancipadora, bajo los auspicios del educador Paulo Freire
y el espectro de voces que se inspiran en su legado. Finalmente, el trabajo
destacó la alineación de este ethos institucional con las prácticas de gestión de
los CIEJA, como lo evidencia la literatura académica e institucional que ha
tomado estas unidades escolares como objeto o fuente.

PALAVRAS-CHAVE: gestão educacional, educação de jovens e adultos,
discurso pedagógico, CIEJA.




                                                                             276

1. INTRODUCTION


       In the field of Discourse Studies, the concept of “ethos” refers to the image
(positive or negative) of the speaker projected by the utterance, which lends
credibility to the spoken text, reinforcing the logical-figurative argumentation that
underpins its thesis or point of view (Charaudeau; Maingueneau, 2016). Regarding
the ethos of school management, its theoretical relevance is justified by its impact
on management practices, which update or reconfigure the projected image, while
at the same time being demanded and evaluated based on the representations
constructed through the interaction between actions and discourses.
       In a country with approximately 11.3 million illiterate people over the age
of 15, Youth and Adult Education [EJA] emerges as a modality provided for by
the Federal Constitution and the Law on Guidelines and Bases for National
Education, with the social mission of bringing marginalized segments of society
into schools, as a public policy aimed at promoting citizenship and social justice
(Arroyo, 2011; Beisiegel, 1997; Brazil, 1988, 1996; Haddad, 2007; Haddad; Di
Pierro, 2000, 2006; Santos; Almeida, 2020; São Paulo [Capital], 2020).
       Created at the beginning of Mayor Marta Suplicy’s administration (2001–
2004), following the restructuring of the former Municipal Centers for
Supplementary Education [CEMES], the CIEJAs were established by Decree No.
43,052, dated April 4, 2003, to complement the Adult and Youth Education (EJA)
offered by regular schools and the literacy initiatives of the São Paulo Literacy
Movement [MOVA]. The operational guidelines for CIEJAs were regulated with
the publication of Law No. 15,648, dated November 14, 2012, emphasizing
students’ prior knowledge, the development of competencies and skills
necessary for the professional context, and active citizenship as a pillar of a
democratic and just society (Faria, 2014; Santos; Almeida, 2020).
       Located in the city’s outskirts, these schools serve youth, adults, and
seniors from Monday through Friday, during morning, afternoon, and evening
sessions, offering flexible schedules and curriculum paths, daily study sessions
of 2 hours and 15 minutes, school meals, academic guidance, make-up classes,
among other measures aimed at ensuring access, retention, and academic
success for a socially vulnerable student population (Santos; Almeida, 2020; São
Paulo [Capital], 2020).


                                                                                 277

       CIEJA managers and professionals join the network through a public
competitive exam but must undergo an internal selection process to be
assigned to these units. This selection process aims to recruit professionals
who possess knowledge of and an interest in the specific pedagogical work of
the EJA modality. In the case of CIEJA, all professionals undergo full-time
training, which ensures group sessions to discuss problems and actions, in
addition to the development of in-service continuing education (Faria, 2014;
Santos; Almeida, 2020).
       However, despite some favorable conditions, CIEJA professionals must
face on a daily basis the challenges and complexities inherent to the EJA modality
in contemporary times, including: 1) the lack of specific training for educators in
this modality; 2) the increase in the number of young people in EJA and the
resulting intergenerational tensions; 3) the increased presence of students with
intellectual disabilities, which requires inclusion initiatives combined with
specialized support at the school; 4) the social vulnerability of students and the
need to establish a support network with other public institutions and local
stakeholders; 5) the difficulties graduates face in continuing their studies in high
school—due to a shortage of spots in the EJA program or a lack of flexibility
similar to that found in CIEJAs; 6) the lack of coordination between EJA and
vocational training, in order to facilitate entry into the labor market and improve
students’ income (Corte; Roggero, 2016; Haddad, 1993, 2002, 2007; Haddad; Di
Pierro, 2000, 2005; Paiva, 1987, 2003; Toledo, 2017).
       Considering these institutional challenges, the Pedagogical Policy Plan
[PPP] plays a central role as a school management tool, especially regarding
institutional evaluation and planning. Furthermore, the PPP is an element in the
construction of the school’s institutional identity, primarily through the articulation
of educational and pedagogical concepts and guidelines shared by the school
community. Especially in the case of CIEJAs, the efforts of management teams
in the process of periodically updating the PPPs and widely publicizing them,
including via the internet, are evident (Carvalho; Gueudeville, 2021; Laurindo,
2017; Silva; Gallego, 2019; Vasconcellos, 1991; Veiga, 1995, 2001).
       In terms of the genre of discourse (Bakhtin, 2003) specific to the school
sphere, the PPPs can be considered a polyphonic institutional text that articulates
the educational discourses valued and legitimized by internal actors and/or


                                                                                   278

        educational management bodies, while simultaneously contrasting (either explicitly
        or tacitly) with other social discourses upheld by other discursive communities.
                In this sense, this study analyzes the Political-Pedagogical Projects [PPPs]
        of the Integrated Centers for Youth and Adult Education [CIEJAs] of the Municipal
        Department of Education of São Paulo – SME/SP, with the aim of understanding
        the ethos of school management projected by the polyphonic configuration of
        these documents.


        2. MATERIALS AND METHODS


                The empirical-textual analysis uses as its corpus the PPPs of the 15
        (fifteen) CIEJAs of the SME/SP (Table 1), made available on the SME-SP’s
        official website or on the units’ webpages, pertaining to the year 2015—a period
        during which there was an institutional effort to update and publicize the
        pedagogical proposals of the school units within the municipal network of the city
        of São Paulo.

        The analysis of educational polyphony draws on descriptors derived from
key concepts in discourse studies (Bakhtin, 2005, 2014; Charaudeau;
Maingueneau, 2016; Maingueneau, 2003), adapting and expanding methods
from the system of polyphonic text decomposition developed in previous research
(Ribeiro, 2018, 2023).
        Within the scope of this research, the following key concepts are
prominent: enunciator, utterance, and discourse. The term “speaker” will be used
to designate the representations of voices embedded in the texts, whether as a
narrating/quoting voice or a narrated/quoted voice, through an intertextual
relationship between them. The term “utterance” refers to the complete
manifestation of a given speaker (author or source) within the text. In turn,
discourse refers to circulating social discourses that share ideological values,
common rhetorics, core content, or recurring expressions, constituting discursive
communities that establish relationships of alliance, coexistence, or opposition
within a given socio-institutional sphere (Bakhtin, 2003, 2005, 2014;
Maingueneau, 2003).
        To operationalize the analysis of the polyphony of PPPs, a system of
polyphonic decomposition analysis of PPPs is used, based on the levels and
descriptors specified in Table 2.


  Table 2. Specification of the levels of analysis and the textual-discursive descriptors for the

                                                                                               280

       Through the levels of analysis, a decomposition of the voices present in
the texts is carried out, such as the enunciator-author (narrating voice, citing
voice) and the enunciator-source (narrated voice, cited voice), with a view to
describing textual and discursive evidence (theme, discourse, argument) that
supports and allows for the inference of the management ethos projected by the
statements (effects of meaning). Each descriptor is a textual or discursive
variable (unit of record) that aids in describing the voices present in the textuality
of the PPPs.
       Based on these levels and their descriptors, an online form (using Google
Forms) was developed to convert the “document corpus” into a “spreadsheet
corpus,” which will organize the categories, linguistic evidence, and analytical
comments in a matrix format. The creation of this single textual-discursive
database allows us to: 1) quantify the occurrences of descriptors in the analyzed
textual material; 2) qualitatively assess the utterance(s) of a given descriptor
across the corpus.
       To infer the ethos of school management projected by the textual-
discursive configuration of the CIEJAs’ PPPs in the city of São Paulo, the
polyphonic analysis followed these steps:
    1. analysis of voices—the individual and institutional subjects who appear as
       enunciator-authors (citing parties) and enunciator-sources (cited parties)
       and the delimitation of their utterances;
    2. analysis of central themes – which are the “objects” with disputed
       meanings in the educational arena;
    3. analysis of discourses—which are the ideological-rhetorical formations
       circulating in the socio-institutional sphere of education.
       This study seeks to demonstrate that the relative political and pedagogical
unity of the CIEJAS points to a shared institutional ethos, projecting the image of
a school administration that understands and adheres to educational legislation,
values democratic management and collective work, and recognizes the diversity
of its student body and the specific challenges of adult education, while at the
same time ideologically adhering to the critical discourse of popular and
emancipatory education, under the influence of educator Paulo Freire and the
spectrum of voices inspired by his legacy.



                                                                                  281

3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION


       The preliminary results of the research, derived from the analysis of the
PPPs of the 15 (fifteen) CIEJAS in the city of São Paulo, prepared in 2015, are
presented below. To infer the descriptive features that make up the ethos of
school management shared by the SME-SP CIEJA network, the thematic,
discursive, and argumentative descriptors that appeared across the PPPs are
systematized. Finally, the descriptors of the intertextual relationships between
enunciator-authors (CIEJA Unit/DRE) and source-enunciators (voices cited,
directly or indirectly) are listed and exemplified, highlighting their impact on the
projection of this institutional ethos.
       Notwithstanding the unique characteristics of each document, the CIEJAs’
PPPs share a compositional structure anchored in ten (10) key themes: T01 –
Pedagogical Policy Project; T02 – Educational Legislation; T03 – Problem-Based
Education; T04 – Pedagogical Approach; T05 – Special Education; T06 - Student
Profile; T07 - Democratic Management; T08 - Social Function of the School; T09
- Vocational Education; and T10 – Learning Assessment.
       These key themes provide the subject matter (subthemes; topics; events)
for a set of 4 (four) ‘educational discourses’ that inhabit the zone of discursive
intersection of the analyzed PPPs: D01 – “legal discourse on the right to
education”; D02 – “critical discourse”; D03 – “discourse of pedagogical
movements”; D04 – “discourse of equity and inclusion.”
       Within the scope of this study, the category ‘educational discourse’ refers
to a social discourse circulating in the educational sphere, which mobilizes
ideological values, thematic nuclei, and specific argumentative content,
distinguishing itself from other social discourses with which it establishes
conjunctive (coalition) or disjunctive (controversial) relationships.
       In general, the “legal discourse on the right to education” addresses topics
related to educational legislation and the pedagogical policy project through
statements whose argumentative content asserts that the CIEJAs and their PPPs
are in compliance with the legally established right to education (1988 Federal
Constitution; Law on Guidelines and Bases for National Education—Law 9394/96),
including the existence of pedagogical work with objectives, curricular organization,
and planning explicitly outlined in the school’s own PPP, as required by law.


                                                                                 282

        The “critical discourse,” on the other hand, addresses themes such as
problem-posing education, democratic management, and the social function of
the school, through argumentative content that values the educational principles
proposed by Paulo Freire, the participation of the internal and external community
in school management, and the importance of the school for the democratization
of systematized knowledge and the transformation of society.
        In turn, the “discourse of pedagogical movements” addresses topics
related to teaching approaches and learning assessment, distinguishing itself
from the discourse of traditional pedagogy and technical school assessment,
while proposing the use in EJA of methods from differentiated, constructivist, and
socio-interactionist pedagogy, as well as the process-oriented and formative
assessment of its students.
        The “discourse of equity and inclusion,” meanwhile, addresses topics
related to Special Education, the profile of EJA learners, and vocational
education, through arguments that highlight the school inclusion of students with
disabilities in CIEJA, the meeting of the educational and specifi al needs of
population segments in peripheral neighborhoods and vulnerable social groups
(Black people, women, the elderly, the unemployed, youth who have dropped out
of regular school, etc.), linking basic education and vocational training from a
perspective of including these learners in the labor market.
        Table 3 lists the argumentative, discursive, and thematic descriptors,
accompanied by statements that exemplify their textual manifestation in the
research corpus. As the meaning of each statement, the descriptive trait that
constitutes the ethos of school management in the CIEJAs of the City of São
Paulo is presented.

          Thus, the educational discourses circulating in the PPPs analyzed
manifest themselves in concrete statements that project an institutional image of
the CIEJAs of the SME-SP, or rather, a school management ethos characterized
by the following features: a commitment to institutional work grounded in the
Pedagogical Policy Project and in compliance with legislation on the right to
education; alignment with the problem-posing pedagogy proposed by Paulo
Freire;     use   of    didactic-methodological          approaches        from    differentiated,
constructivist, and socio-interactionist pedagogy, as well as procedures for
continuous, formative, and qualitative assessment in Adult and Youth Education
(EJA); support for and inclusion of socially vulnerable students and those in
Special Education; integration of general education and vocational training from
an inclusive perspective; democratic management of CIEJAs and the
development of an emancipatory education committed to social transformation.
          This ethos of school management is constructed within the polyphonic
“concerto” established between the enunciator-author (the CIEJA) and the source
enunciators, in the form of epigraphs and quotations (direct or indirect) within the
paragraphs, to confer authority and legitimacy on the political-pedagogical
discourse of the CIEJAs. Table 4 specifies and exemplifies the most recurrent
descriptors of intertextuality in the research’s textual material.
