       In this sense, one’s own statements and those of others (from intellectuals,
legal texts, institutional documents, and school stakeholders) create an
intertextual fabric that produces, as the meaning-making effect of the CIEJA
network’s political-pedagogical texts, a public and shared image of school
management committed to inclusive, critical, democratic, and emancipatory
youth and adult education.
       Finally, it is worth noting that this institutional ethos aligns with the school
management practices of the CIEJAs that have been highlighted in academic and
institutional literature (Faria, 2014; Santos and Almeida, 2020; São Paulo
[Capital], 2020), that is, with a social commitment to young, adult, and elderly


                                                                                               288

learners in peripheral neighborhoods, materializing in management mechanisms
that aim to ensure retention, academic success, and inclusion for this student
segment, which has historically been marginalized in our country and neglected
by educational policies.


4. CONCLUSION


      The textual evidence analyzed indicates that there is a relative political-
pedagogical unity among the CIEJAS, anchored in a shared institutional ethos,
which projects the image of a school administration that understands and follows
educational legislation, values democratic management and collective work, and
comprehends the diversity of the student body and the specific challenges of the
EJA modality, while at the same time ideologically adhering to the critical
discourse of popular and emancipatory education, under the banner of educator
Paulo Freire and the spectrum of voices inspired by his legacy.
      This ethos of school management is constructed amid the polyphonic
“concerto” established between the enunciator-author (the CIEJA) and the source
enunciators, in an intertextual fabric that articulates its own statements and those
of others to confer authority and legitimacy on the CIEJAs’ political-pedagogical
discourse, or rather, a public image committed to critical, democratic, and
emancipatory education.
      Finally, the study highlighted the alignment of this institutional ethos with
CIEJA management practices highlighted in the academic and institutional
literature that focused on these schools as their subject or source.

ABSTRACT: Introduction: Evidence-Based Medicine (EBM) is a cornerstone of
modern clinical practice, representing a competency fundamentally grounded in
biostatistics. However, the instruction of this discipline in Brazilian undergraduate
medical education faces historical obstacles, most notably "statophobia" (Lemos,
2022). METHOD: A narrative review with a qualitative approach was conducted
to analyze the gap between traditional biostatistics teaching and the new
competencies required by the National Curricular Guidelines (DCNs) published
in 2025. The search was performed across indexed databases: LILACS,
MEDLINE/PubMed, SciELO, and Google Scholar, including full-text studies in
Portuguese and English (2020 to 2025). RESULTS AND DISCUSSION: The
literature indicates that the pedagogical model isolating biostatistics within the
basic sciences phase is ineffective, leading to low retention and high levels of
anxiety (Souza, 2020; Lemos, 2022). This model creates gaps in the explicit
competencies mandated by the new DCNs, such as the ability to "critically
interpret the literature" (Brasil, 2025b, Art. 8, Item X). This deficiency negatively
impacts both undergraduate research (Santos et al., 2023) and future clinical
practice, leaving professionals vulnerable to flawed scientific interpretations.
CONCLUSION: The reform of biostatistics education is not merely a curricular
update or academic pedantry; it is a fundamental and urgent pillar for the
development of an autonomous, critical, and reflective physician. Such training is
essential for practicing 21st-century medicine, ensuring patient safety and quality
of care through the practical and critical application of the best available scientific
evidence.

KEYWORDS: biostatistics, evidence-based medicine, medical education,
curriculum, National Curricular Guidelines.

RESUMO: Introdução: A Medicina Baseada em Evidências (MBE) é um pilar da
prática clínica moderna, uma competência fundamentada na bioestatística.
Contudo, o ensino desta disciplina na graduação médica brasileira enfrenta
obstáculos históricos, notadamente a "estatofobia" (Lemos, 2022). MÉTODO:
Revisão narrativa com abordagem qualitativa com o objetivo de analisar o hiato
entre o ensino tradicional da bioestatística e as novas competências exigidas
pelas Diretrizes Curriculares Nacionais (DCNs) publicadas no ano de 2025. A
busca foi realizada nas bases de dados indexadas: LILACS, MEDLINE/PubMed,
Biblioteca SciELO e Google Scholar com estudos na íntegra em português e
inglês (2020 a 2025). RESULTADOS E DISCUSSÃO: A literatura demonstra que
o modelo pedagógico que isola a bioestatística no ciclo básico é ineficaz,
gerando baixa retenção e alta ansiedade (Souza, 2020; Lemos, 2022). O modelo
cria lacunas nas competências explícitas exigidas pela nova DCN, como a
capacidade de "interpretar criticamente a literatura" (Brasil, 2025b, Art. 8º, Inciso
X). Essa deficiência impacta negativamente tanto na iniciação científica (Santos
et al., 2023) quanto na futura prática clínica, tornando o profissional vulnerável a
interpretações científicas inadequadas. CONCLUSÃO: A reforma do ensino da
bioestatística não é mera atualização curricular ou preciosismo acadêmico, é
pilar fundamental e urgente para a construção de um médico autônomo, crítico
e reflexivo, capaz de praticar a medicina do século XXI, garantindo a segurança
do paciente e a qualidade do cuidado através da aplicação real e crítica da
melhor evidência científica disponível.



                                                                                   294

PALAVRAS-CHAVE: bioestatística, medicina baseada em              evidências,
educação médica, currículo, Diretrizes Curriculares Nacionais.




                                                                        295

1. INTRODUCTION


       Throughout its long history, the practice of medicine has undergone
profound transformations in its pillars of authority and knowledge. For centuries,
the dominant paradigm was grounded in the authority of masters, oral tradition,
and pathophysiological inference, where individual clinical experience and
deductive reasoning—though essential—often prevailed without rigorous
external validation. The late 20th century, however, saw the consolidation of a
paradigm shift that redefined the foundations of healthcare decision-making:
Evidence-Based Medicine (EBM). Formalized by Sackett et al. (1996), EBM
proposes that modern clinical practice be the explicit, diligent, and judicious
integration of the best available scientific evidence with individual clinical
expertise and the patient’s values and preferences.
       This new paradigm, now widely accepted as the gold standard of practice,
has shifted the center of gravity of medical knowledge. The “best available
evidence” has become a non-negotiable component of good practice. However,
the effective implementation of EBM in daily clinical practice remains a global
challenge, and particularly so in Brazil. As a recent analysis of the national
landscape points out, “we are far from the practice of evidence-based medicine
in Brazil” (Faria, 2021). The challenge no longer lies in a scarcity of information,
as in past eras, but paradoxically in its overabundance. The contemporary
healthcare professional is immersed in an exponential volume of scientific
publications, a veritable “infodemic” where high-quality studies are mixed with
research featuring questionable methodologies, conflicting results, or subtle
biases—often sponsored.
       Given this scenario, the most crucial skill for the 21st-century physician is
no longer the memorization of facts, but rather the ability to critically evaluate (the
“appraisal”). This is the ability to navigate the ocean of information,
methodologically dissect a scientific article, identify its biases, assess the internal
validity of its findings, and, finally, judge the impact and applicability of these
results for the individual patient. This ability to filter out the noise and extract the
signal is what truly enables the professional to stay up to date and provide the
best care.



                                                                                    296

      It is precisely at this stage of “appraisal” that Brazilian medical education
encounters its greatest and most persistent bottleneck.
      Current legislation leaves no room for doubt: “critically interpreting the
literature” and “grounding decisions in evidence” are no longer desirable skills;
they are mandatory competencies. The curriculum model that isolates
biostatistics in the basic cycle and generates “statophobia” (Lemos, 2022; Souza,
2020) has thus become anachronistic and legally insufficient, as it fails to produce
the professionals that the new DCNs require.
      The central objective of this narrative review article is to analyze the
inseparable relationship between Evidence-Based Medicine and the field of
biostatistics, in light of the new regulatory requirements of the 2025 DCNs. It is
argued that overcoming this historical gap requires a structural curricular reform,
abandoning the isolated disciplinary model in favor of the longitudinal integration
of biostatistics and clinical epidemiology, contextualized by active methodologies
(Pereira et al., 2024) and linked to the real-world problems of medical practice,
as    already    explored    by      some    institutions   (DEPARTMENT         OF
GYNECOLOGY/DGO-FMRP-USP, 2022). Only in this way will it be possible to
train physicians who are critical consumers, rather than mere spectators, of the
science that guides their actions.


2. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK


      In analyzing the critical intersection between medical education, the
practice of Evidence-Based Medicine (EBM), and the discipline of biostatistics, it
is argued that the current pedagogical structure of many medical schools in Brazil
is insufficient to develop the required critical evaluation skills, creating a gap
between the trained physician and the professional demanded by the new
National Curriculum Guidelines (DCNs) of 2025.


2.1 BIOSTATISTICS AS THE LANGUAGE OF EVIDENCE-BASED MEDICINE


      The practice of Evidence-Based Medicine (EBM) represents one of the
most significant paradigm shifts in the history of healthcare. It has shifted the
focus of clinical decision-making, moving it away from tradition, the authority of


                                                                                297

specialists, and pure pathophysiological inference toward a model that requires
the explicit and judicious integration of the best available scientific evidence with
clinical expertise and the patient’s values. This process is often summarized in
the “Five As”: “Ask,” “Acquire,” “Appraise,” “Apply,” and “Assess” (Straus et al.,
2009).
         While modern medical curricula have strived to teach students to formulate
clinical questions (the PICO) and search for articles in databases, the real
bottleneck—the gap in training—lies in the third step: “Appraise.” Critical
appraisal is the ability to dissect a scientific study to judge its internal validity (is
the study free of bias?), its impact (is the effect size clinically relevant?), and its
applicability (do the results apply to my patient?).
         This is where biostatistics comes into play. The practice of EBM requires
that healthcare professionals be, fundamentally, critical consumers of science.
However, as Chaoubah (2021) points out, biostatistics is often perceived as “a
field with a rather controversial image among healthcare professionals.” This
controversy is not merely academic; it is rooted in a generalized anxiety about
mathematics and in students’ perception that the discipline is an abstract
mathematical barrier, divorced from the human reality of medical practice.
         The problem is that this perceived difficulty is not trivial, and its
consequences are serious. Misinterpretation of fundamental statistical concepts
is endemic in the literature on medical education. Concepts such as the p-value,
for example, are routinely misinterpreted—not as the probability of observing the
data (or more extreme data) if the null hypothesis is true, but erroneously as “the
probability that the null hypothesis is true.” Similarly, Confidence Intervals (CI)
are often viewed merely as a test of significance (if the 95% CI crosses 1.0 in
Relative Risk, it is not “significant”), ignoring their primary function: to
demonstrate the precision of the effect estimate.
         This statistical illiteracy leads directly to two dangerous clinical
consequences. The first is the adoption of ineffective or harmful practices. A
physician     lacking   statistical   fluency   can   easily   be   persuaded     by    a
methodologically flawed study (e.g., high risk of selection bias, lack of blinding)
that, by chance, presents a “p < 0.05.” He may adopt a new, expensive drug- ,
believing it to be superior, without realizing that the effect size was statistically



                                                                                       298

significant but clinically irrelevant (e.g., a new drug for hypertension that reduces
systolic blood pressure by only 2 mmHg more than the placebo).
       The second consequence, equally dangerous, is the rejection of effective
practices. A high-quality study with a small sample size (undersized) may fail to
achieve statistical significance (e.g., p = 0.07), even though it shows a strong
trend toward benefit. A professional illiterate in statistics dismisses this study as
“negative,” failing to recognize that the lack of statistical significance is not
evidence of the absence of an effect, but rather the absence of evidence (due to
the study’s low statistical power).
       Therefore, biostatistics is not an auxiliary discipline; it is, literally, the
language in which scientific evidence is written, debated, and validated (MELO
et al., 2023). Without functional mastery of this language, the physician regresses
from an EBM practitioner to a protocol executor. They become passive readers,
dependent on the interpretations of third parties, whether they are the authors of
the article (who may have their own biases), representatives of the
pharmaceutical industry (who will present the data from the most favorable
perspective), or so-called “opinion leaders” (who may themselves be out of date).
       This scenario of intellectual dependence runs counter to the very essence
of EBM, which, as Faria (2021) points out, aims to shift medical practice from
authority to evidence. A physician who does not understand biostatistics cannot
evaluate the evidence; they are forced to rely on the authority of those who
interpret it for them, returning to the paradigmatic model that EBM sought to
overcome. “Statistical literacy” ceases to be an academic distinction and
becomes a core clinical competency for patient safety.


2.2 THE LANDSCAPE OF EDUCATION AND THE NEW NATIONAL
CURRICULUM GUIDELINES (2025)


       Despite the central role of biostatistics in modern medical practice, the
predominant pedagogical model in medical schools in Brazil appears to be
structurally prone to inaccuracies. Historically, the vast majority of medical
schools have scheduled biostatistics courses (often combined with basic
epidemiology) during the first semesters of the program, within the so-called
“basic cycle.” During these early stages, students are focused on acquiring


                                                                                 299

fundamental knowledge such as anatomy, biochemistry, and physiology, and
have little or no exposure to clinical practice or the reading of complex scientific
literature; such an approach presents chronic and systemic problems.
       The first is absolute decontextualization. A first- or second-year student
cannot understand the relevance of a chi-square test or a logistic regression
analysis when they have never encountered a real clinical problem requiring the
reading of a clinical trial. The subject is perceived as an abstract mathematical
obstacle, a curricular requirement to be overcome, rather than a clinical tool to be
mastered. In a study conducted at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro
(UFRJ), Souza (2020) describes exactly this scenario: the traditional, lecture-
based, and decontextualized teaching of biostatistics in the basic medical
curriculum led to high rates of dissatisfaction and failure, necessitating profound
pedagogical reforms.
       The second problem, a direct consequence of the first, is the development
of “Statophobia.” The term, coined by Lemos (2022) to describe the reality of
Brazilian medical education, defines the aversion, fear, and anxiety that students
develop toward statistics. This “phobia” is not mere disinterest; it is a
psychological and cognitive barrier that blocks learning. The student not only fails
to learn but also begins to actively avoid any contact with the subject.
       The third problem is the forgetting curve. Knowledge, even if acquired
momentarily to pass a test in the basic cycle, is quickly lost. Because it is “inert”
knowledge (unapplied, uncontextualized, and unrevised), it is not transferred to
long-term memory. When this student, now in residency (four or five years later),
finally needs to read a scientific article to discuss a clinical approach, the
statistical foundation has already completely dissipated. The result is frustration
and the reinforcement of “statophobia” (Lemos, 2022).
       This flawed pedagogical model, which for decades produced physicians
with chronic difficulties in scientific interpretation, has become not only
anachronistic but now legally insufficient. The new CNE/CES Resolution No. 3,
dated September 30, 2025 ( , 2025b), which establishes the current DCNs and
revokes the previous 2014 resolution, makes the case for curricular reform a
regulatory imperative.
       The 2025 DCNs are explicit and incisive in outlining the graduate’s
competency profile, requiring skills that are impossible to achieve without a


                                                                                 300

functional mastery of biostatistics and clinical epidemiology. An analysis of Article
8 of the resolution reveals the centrality of this competency:


                      Subsection X (Practice of EBM): The guideline requires that physicians
                      be capable of “carrying out actions responsibly, with safe, effective
                      practices grounded in the best available scientific evidence, and being
                      able to critically interpret the literature, [...] through evidence-based
                      medicine” (Brazil, 2025b). “Critical interpretation” is at the heart of
                      appraisal, an action that depends entirely on statistics.
                      Subsection XXI (Integration of Knowledge): The standard stipulates
                      that graduates must “utilize, in an integrated, critical, and contextualized
                      manner, knowledge from the biomedical, clinical, epidemiological, and
                      social sciences to inform clinical decision-making, [...] always grounded
                      in the best available scientific evidence” (Brazil, 2025b). Clinical
                      epidemiology is the direct application of biostatistics at the bedside.
                      Subsection XXV (Critical Evaluation of Technologies): The DCN goes
                      further and requires that physicians be capable of “guiding themselves
                      through the critical evaluation of technologies, interventions, and
                      clinical practices based on cost-effectiveness criteria, [...] grounding
                      decisions in scientific evidence” (Brazil, 2025b). This competency
                      requires the ability to read not only clinical trials but also
                      pharmacoeconomic studies, which rely on even more complex
                      statistical models.


       It is absolutely clear that the intention of the new DCNs is to train
physicians to be scientists of practice, critical evaluators of science. The
educational model that isolates biostatistics in the basic cycle and, as a
consequence, generates “statophobia” (Lemos, 2022), fails miserably in
producing the professional described in this resolution. There is, therefore, a
profound dissonance between the pedagogy practiced and the current
regulations.


2.3 THE IMPACT ON UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH AND FUTURE
PRACTICE


       The consequences of this educational gap unfold on two main fronts, both
with long-term impacts: the failure to support scientific initiation during
undergraduate studies and the inability to maintain an up-to-date clinical practice
after graduation.
       First, the 2025 DCNs not only require physicians to be scientifically literate
but also reinforce the university’s role in training new researchers. Article 16
clearly states that training “must integrate, in an inseparable manner, the activities
of teaching, research, and extension, promoting scientific initiation” (Brazil,


                                                                                             301

2025b). The intention is not necessarily for every physician to become a
laboratory researcher, but for every physician to understand the scientific method
from the inside, as a way to enhance their “scientific thinking.”
       However, for students involved in research, a lack of proficiency in
biostatistics is severely limiting. A 2023 Brazilian study, which analyzed medical
students’ involvement in scientific research, revealed a disheartening paradox:
although a majority (66.1%) feel motivated to produce scientific work, an even
more overwhelming majority (80.9%) identified difficulties in doing so (Santos et
al., 2023). The study indicates that among the main obstacles perceived by
students are “inadequate guidance” and “lack of knowledge about the scientific
process.” Students have the desire to conduct research, but educational
institutions fail to provide the methodological tools.
       A 2022 systematic review, focused on research programs for medical
undergraduates in Brazil, corroborates this view in an even more specific way.
The review identified that “lack of familiarity with statistics” is one of the significant
barriers most frequently cited by students for engaging in scientific research
(Souza; Zuniga, 2022). In practice, what happens is that students with “statofobia”
(Lemos, 2022) end up, at best, conducting narrative literature reviews or case
reports, which contribute little to their methodological training. They are unable to
design an analytical study, calculate a sample size, or analyze their own data,
becoming mere data collectors for their advisor or dependent on a professional
statistician, without being able to critically discuss the methods employed. The
DCN’s goal of promoting scientific research (Brazil, 2025b, Art. 16) remains
unfulfilled.
       Second, and even more seriously, the impact extends to the graduate’s
future practice. A physician who graduates without mastery of statistical
interpretation cannot meet the core competencies outlined in Items X, XXI, and
XXV of Article 8 of the DCNs (Brazil, 2025b). Medicine is a rapidly evolving
science; what is considered the gold standard today may be obsolete or proven
ineffective in five years. The only tool that guarantees professional longevity and
patient safety is the capacity for self-learning and continuous updating.
       The professional who carries the “state phobia” from undergraduate
studies (Lemos, 2022) tends not to read scientific articles after graduation. Their
clinical practice becomes rigid, held hostage by the protocols they learned during


                                                                                      302

residency. They become unable to critically incorporate new therapies or, equally
important, to avoid prescribing practices that science has already shown to be
futile or harmful.
       This professional becomes vulnerable. Without the ability to “critically
interpret the literature” (Brazil, 2025b, Art. 8, Item X), they are easy prey for
pharmaceutical industry marketing. A representative may present a study with a
flawed design (e.g., a “non-inferiority” trial with inadequate margins, or a study
using a “surrogate endpoint”) and promote it as evidence of superiority. The
physician, unable to identify the methodological fallacy, adopts a new drug—often
more expensive and without real benefit—burdening the healthcare system and
potentially exposing the patient to unnecessary risks. The pedagogical lapse in
biostatistics transcends the academic realm and becomes a problem of public
health and the sustainability of the system.


2.4 PROPOSALS FOR CURRICULAR ADJUSTMENT


       Given the diagnosis—a teaching model that generates phobia (Lemos,
2022), fails to retain knowledge (Souza, 2020), and does not meet the new
National Curriculum Guidelines (Brazil, 2025b)—the solution cannot be
superficial. The simplest—and also the most misguided—response would be to
simply increase the course load for biostatistics in the basic cycle. This, in fact,
would tend to exacerbate the problem, intensifying “statophobia” and the
perception that the discipline is irrelevant.
       The literature on medical education in Brazil and worldwide suggests that
the change must be structural, focusing on two main axes: longitudinal integration
and contextualization through active methodologies.
       The first axis is Longitudinal Teaching. Instead of a course concentrated
in a single semester at the beginning of the program, biostatistics—ideally
integrated with Clinical Epidemiology and MBE—should permeate the entire
medical curriculum. Knowledge should be built through “scaffolding,” where
complexity increases as the student progresses.
       In this model, elementary school students can learn descriptive statistics
(means, medians, standard deviations). Later, in the clinical cycle, while taking
the Cardiology module, they will learn about randomized clinical trials (RCTs) by


                                                                                303

reading, in practice, a seminal study on a new antihypertensive drug, calculating
and interpreting the Relative Risk (RR) and the Number Needed to Treat (NNT).
When moving on to Radiology, they will learn about diagnostic tests, interpreting
sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and ROC curves. Innovative curriculum
models in Brazil are already beginning to apply this philosophy. The FMRP-USP
curriculum, for example, has implemented longitudinal tracks that run parallel to
the clinical modules, including a specific track on “Scientific Thinking,” which
accompanies the student throughout their training (DEPARTMENT OF
GYNECOLOGY/DGO-FMRP-USP, 2022); this approach ensures that statistical
knowledge is applied at the moment it becomes relevant, facilitating retention and
understanding.
       The second axis is Active and Contextualized Learning. It is essential to
move beyond the traditional lecture-based model, focused on theoretical classes
and formulas, which has proven ineffective (Souza, 2020). A 2024 review on the
use of active methodologies in medical education in Brazil highlights the success
of approaches such as Problem-Based Learning (PBL) and Team-Based
Learning (TBL) in engaging students (Pereira et al., 2024).
       In the context of biostatistics, the most powerful active learning tool is the
“Journal Club,” provided it is restructured. Traditionally, many journal clubs focus
on presenting the article’s conclusions. The ideal model, aligned with the 2025
National Curriculum Guidelines (CBNs), is the methodology-focused “Journal
Club.” The discussion, facilitated by a faculty member, should start from a real
clinical problem and guide students to dissect the article, focusing on its design,
biases, statistical analysis, and validity. The central question shifts from “What
did the article conclude?” to “Should I believe this conclusion? And does it change
my practice?”
       Implementing this change, however, faces its own challenges, notably the
need for faculty training (Pereira et al., 2024). Many clinical faculty members are
excellent physicians, but they may also carry the “statophobia” from their own
training, feeling insecure about mediating methodological discussions. Therefore,
curriculum reform must be accompanied by a robust faculty development
program.
       The solution to the biostatistics gap in medicine is not “more statistics,” but
“better statistics”—statistics taught in the right place, at the right time, and in the


                                                                                   304

right way. The ultimate goal is to transform the perception of the discipline: from
a feared mathematical barrier (Lemos, 2022) to an indispensable clinical tool, the
true language of modern medicine, empowering physicians to fulfill what the 2025
National Clinical Guidelines (DCNs) and society demand of them: the practice of
safe, effective, and truly evidence-based medicine.


3. METHODOLOGY


       To construct this narrative review, methodological procedures were
adopted to define the type of study, data sources, literature selection criteria, and
processes for analyzing and synthesizing the information.
       The choice of a narrative literature review as the methodological approach
is justified by the nature of the subject matter, which is ideal for describing,
analyzing, and discussing the “state of the art” of a topic, especially when the
objective is to construct a theoretical and contextual argument (Rother, 2007;
Page et al., 2021).
       The purpose of this article is not to quantify the effectiveness of a teaching
intervention, but rather to critically analyze the gap between current pedagogical
practice in the teaching of biostatistics, the difficulties documented in the literature
(e.g., “statophobia”), and the new regulatory requirement imposed by the 2025
National Curriculum Guidelines (Brazil, 2025b). The narrative review allows for
interpretive synthesis and the construction of a cohesive argument based on
heterogeneous sources, including opinion pieces, essays, observational studies
on teaching, and official documents.
       To collect the bibliographic material, a non-systematic but comprehensive
survey was conducted in the main health sciences databases, with particular
emphasis on Brazilian scientific output, in line with the geographical scope of the
problem.
       The databases consulted were:
    a) SciELO (Scientific Electronic Library Online): Selected as the primary
       indexer of scientific literature published in Brazil and Latin America,
       ensuring direct access to the epicenter of the national discussion on
       medical education.



                                                                                    305

    b) LILACS (Latin American and Caribbean Health Sciences Literature): Used
       to complement the search in the regional context, capturing publications
       that might not have been indexed in SciELO.
    c) PubMed/MEDLINE (National Library of Medicine): Consulted to identify
       high-impact international studies on the teaching of biostatistics and EBM,
       allowing for a global contextualization of the issue, although the focus of
       the analysis remained on the national literature.
    d) Google Scholar: Used to search for so-called “gray literature,” such as
       theses, dissertations, and, crucially, to locate official documents and
       publications from educational institutions (e.g., pedagogical projects or
       experience reports, such as the one cited from FMRP-USP).
       The search process was intentional and iterative, starting with key
descriptors and expanding through the analysis of references from the articles
found (“snowballing” or “cascading search”).
       Search terms in Portuguese and their English equivalents were defined,
which were cross-referenced and combined using Boolean operators (AND, OR)
in a manner adapted to each database. The main search terms used were:
    • (Biostatistics) AND (Medical Education OR Medical Teaching);
    • (Evidence-Based Medicine OR "Evidence-Based Medicine") AND
       (Curriculum OR "Curriculum");
    • (Statistical Literacy OR "Statistical Literacy") AND (Medicine OR Health);
    • (Statophobia) AND (Health OR Medicine);
    • (Scientific Initiation) AND (Medicine OR Student);
    • (National Curriculum Guidelines) AND (Medicine 2025).
       A preferred time frame was established for publications from the last five
years (January 2020 to October 2025). This time frame is justified by the need to
capture the most recent landscape of medical education and the pedagogical
discussions that preceded and followed the publication of the new National
Curriculum Guidelines. Exceptions to this timeframe were deliberately made to
include: (a) key official documents (BRASIL, 2025b); and (b) seminal articles or
classic references on EBM and review methodologies (e.g., ROTHER, 2007),
essential for the theoretical foundation.




                                                                              306

       The inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied in two phases: first, by
reading titles and abstracts, and second, by reading the full texts of the
preselected articles.
Inclusion Criteria:
    1. Articles (original articles, reviews, editorials, essays) that discuss the
       teaching and learning of biostatistics, epidemiology, or EBM in
       undergraduate medical programs or health-related courses in the Brazilian
       context.
    2. Studies addressing the difficulties, perceptions, or anxiety (“statophobia”)
       of students and health professionals regarding statistics.
    3. Articles that propose or report experiences with curricular innovation in the
       teaching of these disciplines (e.g., active methodologies, longitudinal
       teaching).
    4. Literature on the promotion of scientific research in medical undergraduate
       programs in Brazil.
    5. Official documents from the Ministry of Education (MEC) and the National
       Education Council (CNE) relevant to the topic.
    6. Publications in Portuguese, English, or Spanish.
    Exclusion Criteria:
    1. Articles that use biostatistics as a tool to analyze clinical data (e.g., clinical
       trials, cohort studies) but do not discuss the process of teaching or learning
       biostatistics.
    2. Studies focused exclusively on the teaching of statistics in courses outside
       the health field (e.g., Engineering, Exact Sciences).
    3. Conference abstracts, due to their concise nature, which would not allow
       for an in-depth analysis.
       After the final selection, the articles were read in their entirety and
subjected to a qualitative content analysis. This process was not aimed at
quantitative data extraction, but rather at identifying themes, central arguments,
gaps, and areas of consensus in the literature.
       The analysis and synthesis process followed three stages:
    1. Reading and Indexing: Each article was indexed to extract its main theses,
       methodologies employed (in the case of experience reports), and
       conclusions.


                                                                                     307

    2. Thematic Categorization: The extracted information was grouped into
       thematic categories that emerged from the literature itself, aligned with the
       objectives of this study. These categories formed the structure of section
       “3. Development and Discussion,” namely: (a) Biostatistics as the
       language of EBM; (b) The landscape of education and the 2025 National
       Curriculum Guidelines; (c) The impact on clinical practice and future
       practice; and (d) Proposals for curricular adaptation.
    3. Critical Narrative Synthesis: Finally, the review was drafted, connecting the
       literature findings in a cohesive manner. This synthesis did not limit itself
       to summarizing the articles, but sought to interpret them critically, placing
       them in dialogue and contrasting them with the central document of the
       analysis: the new 2025 DCNs (Brazil, 2025b). The objective was to
       construct an analytical narrative that highlights the pedagogical gap and
       justifies the urgency of the curricular reform proposed in the title of this
       work.


4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION


       In the context of scientific initiation (SI), the consequences of this
educational gap are twofold and directly impact the two pillars of the medical
career: research and patient care. As the central objective of this review, the
difficulty is evident. A 2023 Brazilian study that analyzed medical students’
involvement in scientific research revealed a paradox: although 66.1% of
students feel motivated to conduct research, an overwhelming majority of 80.9%
identified difficulties in producing scientific work (Santos et al., 2023). Among the
main obstacles identified are “lack of knowledge about the scientific process” and
“inadequate guidance.” Corroborating this finding, a 2022 systematic review of
undergraduate medical research programs in Brazil identified “lack of familiarity
with statistics” as one of the most significant barriers perceived by students to
engaging in research (Souza; Zuniga, 2022). Students may even want to conduct
research, but the university ultimately fails to provide the most basic
methodological tools for doing so.
       In the context of clinical practice, the consequence is even more serious.
The physician who graduates with “statophobia” (Lemos, 2022) tends not to read


                                                                                 308

scientific articles after graduation. Their practice becomes rigid, held hostage by
the protocols they learned during residency, unable to incorporate new therapies
or abandon practices that science has already proven to be ineffective or harmful.
They   become     incapable     of   self-criticism     and     continuous       professional
development, pillars of good medicine.
       What was once a pedagogical shortcoming lamented by educators
became, as of 2025, an unavoidable regulatory imperative. The new National
Curriculum Guidelines (DCNs) for the Undergraduate Medical Program (Brazil,
2025b), which repealed the previous 2014 resolution, are emphatic and explicitly
in requiring graduates to possess competencies that are, in essence, dependent
on biostatistics and epidemiology. The new standard requires, among other
things, that physicians be capable of:


                      "develop actions [...] grounded in the best available scientific evidence,
                      being able to critically interpret the literature, [...] in accordance with
                      evidence-based medicine" (Brazil, 2025b, Art. 8, Item X).
                      "utilize, in an integrated, critical, and contextualized manner, knowledge
                      from the [...] epidemiological and social sciences to inform clinical
                      decision-making, [...] always grounded in the best available scientific
                      evidence" (Brazil, 2025b, Art. 8, Subparagraph XXI).
                      "be guided by the critical evaluation of technologies, interventions, and
                      clinical practices [...] basing decisions on scientific evidence" (Brazil,
                      2025b, Art. 8, Item XXV).


       The critical evaluation of scientific literature is a task that cannot be
performed without a functional mastery of biostatistics. Concepts such as p-
value, confidence interval, relative risk (RR), odds ratio (OR), number needed to
treat (NNT), survival analysis, and logistic regression are not mere academic
jargon or tools exclusive to researchers; they are the lingua franca in which
scientific evidence is written, validated, and communicated (Chaoubah, 2021).
Without fluency in this language, the physician, no matter how brilliant in clinical
presentation or pathophysiology, becomes a passive consumer of science,
forced to accept the conclusions presented in abstracts or, even more
dangerously, to rely on the interpretations of third parties, whether from outdated
institutional protocols or representatives of the pharmaceutical industry.
       The problem is that, historically, the teaching of biostatistics in medical
schools has been treated not as an essential clinical competency, but as a
peripheral mathematical discipline. Commonly placed in the foundational years,



                                                                                             309

far from the clinical practice where its relevance would be evident, the subject is
often taught in an abstract manner, focused on formulas and calculations, and
disconnected from the real-world problems of the ward or outpatient clinic. This
flawed pedagogical approach has a documented and deeply harmful outcome:
“statophobia.” This term, coined by Lemos (2022), describes the aversion, fear,
and anxiety that health students develop toward statistics, creating a
psychological block that persists throughout their professional lives and becomes
an active obstacle to the practice of EBM.
       Recent national literature corroborates this diagnosis. In a reflection on his
teaching practice at UFRJ, Souza (2020) describes the traditional teaching of
biostatistics as expository and decontextualized, generating high rates of
dissatisfaction and failure, which required a complete overhaul of the course.
Melo et al. (2023) reinforce this view, describing biostatistics as a “challenge for
students and health professionals,” highlighting the subject’s “bad reputation” and
the widespread difficulty in its application.
       The discussion demonstrated that, although biostatistics is the lingua
franca in which scientific evidence is validated and communicated (Chaoubah,
2021), its teaching in medical schools is often relegated to an isolated component
of the basic curriculum. This approach, decontextualized from clinical practice,
fails to demonstrate the discipline’s immediate relevance. The result, widely
documented in the literature, is the creation of a significant psychological and
cognitive barrier: “statophobia” (Lemos, 2022). This phenomenon transforms a
tool that should be one of intellectual empowerment into an obstacle, generating
aversion and anxiety that persist throughout the physician’s professional life.
       The turning point of this analysis is the enactment of the 2025 DCNs. The
new resolution leaves no room for ambiguity: it solidifies, at the regulatory level,
the requirement for competencies that are entirely dependent on statistical and
epidemiological literacy. By stipulating that graduates must be able to “critically
interpret the literature,” utilize “epidemiological knowledge,” and “be guided by
critical evaluation [...] basing decisions on scientific evidence,” the legislation
renders the pedagogical model that generates “statophobia” legally obsolete. It
follows that educational institutions that maintain the traditional model of teaching
biostatistics will, in fact, be at odds with the core competencies required by the
new guideline.


                                                                                  310

5. CONCLUSION


       This narrative review sought to analyze the critical intersection between
the practice of Evidence-Based Medicine (EBM), medical education in Brazil, and
the fundamental—and often neglected—role of biostatistics. An analysis of recent
national literature, in light of the new National Curriculum Guidelines (DCNs) for
the Undergraduate Medical Program (Brazil, 2025b), leads to the conclusion that
the pedagogical model traditionally employed for teaching this discipline is not
only anachronistic, but structurally insufficient to train the healthcare
professionals that contemporary society and new regulations demand.
       The dual impact of this educational gap was also evident. First, it
undermines the DCNs’ own goal of fostering scientific initiation, as demonstrated
by studies pointing to the “lack of familiarity with statistics” (Souza; Zuniga, 2022)
and “lack of knowledge about the scientific process” (Santos et al., 2023) as
central barriers perceived by students, despite their expressed interest. Second,
and more seriously, there is a projected direct impact on future clinical practice:
physicians graduating from this model become vulnerable professionals, unable
to keep up with the continuous updating that modern medicine demands. Without
the ability to critically evaluate new studies, the professional becomes hostage to
outdated protocols or, worse, susceptible to the biased interpretations of
pharmaceutical industry marketing, compromising patient safety and the
sustainability of the healthcare system.
       This study corroborates the conclusions of recent literature (Souza, 2020;
Pereira et al., 2024) that the solution to this gap does not lie in a simple increase
in the course load for the subject in the basic cycle, a measure that could even
exacerbate “statophobia” (Lemos, 2022). The solution requires a structural
curriculum reform, based on the longitudinal integration of biostatistics and
clinical epidemiology throughout the entire course, from the basic cycle through
to the internship. Statistical knowledge must be built incrementally, applied, and
revisited in the context of the real clinical problems of each module
(DEPARTMENT OF GYNECOLOGY/DGO-FMRP-USP, 2022). This approach,
combined with the use of active methodologies that transform the student from a
passive recipient into an active participant in scientific discourse, is the path to
redefining the discipline: from a mathematical barrier to an essential clinical tool.


                                                                                  311

      One limitation of this narrative review is that it did not aim to provide a
comprehensive overview of the literature, but rather to develop a thesis grounded
in the current landscape of Brazilian medical education.
      In light of the above, it is recommended that the Core Teaching Units
(NDEs) of medical schools immediately begin a review of their Course
Pedagogical Projects (PPCs). This review should explicitly focus on aligning with
the competencies outlined in items X, XXI, and XXV of Article 8 of the DCNs
2025, planning the transition from an isolated disciplinary model to a longitudinal
framework of “scientific thinking” or “evidence-based medicine.” It is also
suggested, as an agenda for future research, that comparative studies be
conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of these new longitudinal models versus
traditional ones, measuring not only the acquisition of knowledge but also the
reduction of “exam anxiety” and actual proficiency in critical evaluation by the end
of the course.
      Finally, the reform of biostatistics education is not merely a curricular
update or an academic nicety. It is a fundamental and urgent pillar for the
development of an autonomous, critical, and reflective physician, capable of
practicing 21st-century medicine, ensuring patient safety and the quality of care
through the practical and critical application of the best available scientific
evidence.

CHAPTER 19
 THE FOCUS GROUP AS A SPACE
 FOR TEACHER TRAINING TO
 DEVELOP CRITICAL TRINKING


Ruth Cristina Soares Gomes Araújo
Doctor in Education
Universidade Estadual do Amazonas (UEA)

Evandro Ghedin

Clodoaldo Pires Araújo

ABSTRACT: This text discusses the construction of critical thinking in the
teaching and learning process in Basic Education. It arose in the context of
research con-ducted during a doctoral degree in education. Among the various
research questions, we highlight: What do teachers think about the construction
of criti-cal thinking in the teaching-learning process? Critical thinking is a higher
cog-nitive process that is not innate; it needs to be intentionally and systematically
constructed. Thus, we aim to analyze the perception of Basic Education teach-
ers regarding the construction of critical thinking in the teaching and learning
process. The research is qualitative, focusing on historical-dialectical material-
ism and using the focus group technique. The results show that teachers rec-
ognize the need to develop thinking in a more systematic way, as it is still pos-
sible to see a pedagogy of passivity and "domestication" in schools, where praxis
needs to be better understood among the teaching staff.

KEYWORDS: reflection, critical thinking, teaching, teacher training.

RESUMO: Este texto discute sobre a construção do pensamento crítico no
processo ensi-no e aprendizagem na Educação Básica. Surgiu no contexto da
pesquisa rea-lizada durante o doutorado em educação. Dentre os vários
questionamentos da pesquisa, destacamos: O que os professores pensam sobre
a construção do pensamento crítico no processo ensino-aprendizagem? O
pensamento crí-tico é um processo cognitivo superior que não é inato, precisa
ser construído de maneira intencional e sistemática. Desse modo, objetivamos


                                                                                  315

analisar a per-cepção dos professores da Educação Básica sobre a construção
do pensa-mento crítico no processo ensino e aprendizagem. A pesquisa
configura-se como qualitativa, com enfoque no materialismo histórico-dialético e
com a téc-nica do grupo focal formativo. Os resultados evidenciam que os
professores reconhecem a necessidade de desenvolver o pensamento de
maneira mais sistemática, pois ainda é possível visualizar uma pedagogia de
passividade e “domesticação” nas escolas, onde a práxis precisa ser melhor
compreendida entre o corpo docente.

PALAVRAS-CHAVE: reflexão, pensamento crítico, ensino, formação de profes-
sores.




                                                                            316

1. INTRODUCTION


       This text is the result of research conducted in the municipality of Parintins
in the state of Amazonas during the doctoral program in Education at
PPGE/UFAM. The thesis was developed based on numerous questions and a
continuous process of reflection on the construction of critical thinking in
pedagogical mediations. Among the questions, we highlight: What do teachers
think about the development of critical thinking in the teaching-learning process?
This is because critical thinking is a skill that must be developed as early as in
basic education. To this end, teachers must be aware of its true meaning and
provide students with the necessary conditions to move beyond the repetition and
memorization of content, enabling them to achieve critical thinking through a
reflective process. Given this, we aim to analyze what teachers think about the
development of critical thinking in the teaching-learning process in Basic
Education. We opted for the focus group technique, grounded in the dialectical
materialism method, thereby creating a training space for discussions and in-
depth exploration of the development of critical thinking through reflection. This
constituted a training space for teachers, taking on the dimension of a Formative
Focus Group. Six (6) elementary school teachers from different schools
participated in the research. There were four (4) meetings discussing issues
related to reflective-critical training based on a previously organized script.
       The Training Focus Group technique was chosen because it allows Basic
Education teachers to share their experiences and perceptions regarding the
development of critical thinking in the teaching-learning process. We intentionally
chose to address the theme of the reflective-critical teacher using previously
selected texts, sparking discussions among participants so that we could create
a training space where they could understand what reflective-critical training
entails.
       We use the term “reflective-critical” because without reflection there is no
criticism; there is no possibility of analyzing the real circumstances of social
problems. Thinking critically implies having the creativity to do things differently,
to innovate, to create something new from something simple. It means having the
courage and boldness to challenge what is not common, transforming it into



                                                                                  317

something new. Creativity is essential in the learning process, since the brain is
activated more and better by what it does not yet know and is curious to learn.
        It must become a mental habit that can break away from the mere
reproduction of knowledge. To experience a better society, the teaching-learning
process must intentionally and systematically foster the development of more
sophisticated thinking. However, during the meetings of the Formative Focus
Group, we observed that teachers face difficulties in developing critical thinking
in students due to various factors, such as: a lack of understanding of the
inseparability of theory and practice, the school’s lack of commitment to the
critical education of students, and teachers’ weakness in pedagogical
interventions that foster the development of reflection and critical thinking.


2. WHAT IS CRITICAL THINKING?


        Human beings are superior to every other species. This superiority stems
from a capacity that is uniquely their own: thinking. Thinking is inherent to human
beings; they are born to think; they are human because they think. However, what
we will address in this text is not mere thinking, something that everyone
possesses. Rather, it is a form of thinking that overcomes the processes of
alienation1 and that humans themselves have created. We are talking about a
form of thinking that can change the way we perceive and interpret reality. Critical
thinking transcends this innate human capacity for thought. Critical thinking is not
innate; it must be cultivated. To this end, we propose teacher training programs
as an appropriate setting for its development.
        According to Cohen (2017), critical thinking consists of a set of transferable
skills; that is, once something is learned, it can be equally applied to other
contexts, permeating the entire range of academic disciplines and applying to all
spheres of human activity. This justifies the relevance of developing critical
thinking in teacher training, as this higher-order thinking skill extends beyond the
classroom.


1 In other words, alienation occurs not only as a relationship between subject and object, but also

as a relationship between the worker and other people—that is, alienation exists only between
human beings. Labor not only produces objects in which people do not recognize themselves,
but also a peculiar type of relationship among people, in which they stand in opposition to one
another due to their conflicting roles in the production process (Vazquez, 2011).


                                                                                               318

       Thinking critically means possessing greater skills to solve everyday
problems in a dynamic and intelligent way. It is a form of thinking that does not
operate in isolation; rather, due to its complexity, it requires the mobilization of
other mental processes, such as language and emotion, as highlighted by the
author.
       Developing critical thinking is laborious, as it requires teachers to aim to
engage more complex areas of the brain; to do so, they must devise strategies
that challenge students’ comfortable ways of thinking, creating cognitive conflicts
that destabilize existing knowledge so it can be reorganized in a different way. To
this end, more cognitive processes are mobilized, in addition to those we typically
use for routine tasks. Pedagogical interventions should provide students with
situations that engage cognition in a more complex manner. This involves
challenging the brain to mobilize more cognitive processes during activities based
on the studied content. The sooner the brain is mobilized to think critically, the
greater our chances of shaping conscious and responsible citizens in the
construction of a fairer and better society for all.


2.1 FOCUS GROUP: CONCEPT AND CHARACTERIZATION


       For Lervolino and Pelicioni (2001), the essence of the focus group lies
primarily in the interaction between participants and the researcher, whose
objective is to obtain data through discussion on specific topics, hence the name
“focus group.” The focus group is a data collection technique that occurs through
group interaction with the aim of fostering a critical examination of a specific topic
under discussion. We chose this technique to create a training space for in-depth
exploration of the development of critical thinking in the teaching-learning
process, hence the name Formative Focus Group. A striking feature of this
technique is the group- y interview, where interaction is an integral part of the
method (Baches, 2011).
       It is through this interaction that the topic in question is addressed in a way
that promotes group discussion, allowing participants to hear divergent opinions
and form new ones through reflection. Critical thinking was the central theme of
the focus group discussions, as the main contribution of this technique to this
research is its ability to facilitate discussions and comparisons among


                                                                                  319

participants’ opinions. To this end, it consists of the participants, who must share
a common characteristic; and the moderator or facilitator, who may be the
researcher themselves, whose role is to “facilitate all phases of the process, such
as defining a topic guide—which consists of a summary of the issues to be
addressed—as well as a framework to guide the meeting” (Backes, 2011, p. 3).
Gatti (2005) also highlights the role of the moderator and its relevance to the
focus group, specifying its main characteristics: the moderator must be
experienced, skilled, articulate, sensitive, flexible, and capable of leading the
group confidently, competently handling the relationships and interactions that
develop and the situations that arise within the group. In addition to the
moderator, the assistance of a note-taker is recommended. However, the note-
taker does not interfere with the group (Gatti, 2005), but takes cursive notes on
what is happening and what is being said. Their presence is important in order to
record in the field notebook something that might go unnoticed by the moderator.


2.2 SELECTION OF PARTICIPANTS


          According to Gatti (2005), the focus group should be composed based on
certain criteria associated with the research objectives, with a composition
grounded in the participants’ common characteristics, yet allowing for some
variation among them so that different or divergent opinions may emerge. It is
necessary to consider what is known about the target social group, since some
common trait among the participants must exist, as this forms the basis of the
focus group work (Gatti, 2005).
          Following these guidelines, participants were selected based on several
criteria. First, they had to be graduates of the Parintins Center for Higher Studies
from the 2013/2 to 2017/2 academic years, which reflects a formative process;
second, they should have completed a course whose documentary analysis
indicated a reflective-critical education, that is, courses in Education, Language
Arts, History, Geography, Biological Sciences, Chemistry, and Physics; and third,
they should be working in Basic Education. To identify these individuals, we
initially requested a list of graduates for the desired period from the CESP/UEA
office.



                                                                                320

       Upon contacting the first participant, we were able to locate other
graduates who met the research criteria. This was not a simple task, as many of
those trained by the institution work in rural schools in the municipality of
Parintins, while others returned to their municipalities of origin. We visited several
schools and spoke with various teachers; however, most did not meet the study’s
criteria. This required great patience and persistence on the part of the
researcher, who had to rely on the support of former students to find participants
for the study group. Once the participants were selected—some in person at their
workplace, others via phone calls—invitations were sent out formalizing the date
and time of the in-person meeting.


2.3 FIRST MEETING: REFLECTING ON INITIAL TRAINING


       Although 15 (fifteen) invitations were distributed, the attendance of 9 (nine)
participants was confirmed via message the day before; however, only 6 (six)
showed up. We decided to proceed with the six participants, since a focus group
should not be too large, nor should it be excessively small; its ideal size is
between six and twelve people (Gatti, 2005). The environment was carefully
prepared, as Gatti (2005) emphasizes, noting the importance of participants
sitting face-to-face to ensure direct interaction. We provided a large table that
allowed for good visibility among participants, as the author states; comfortable
chairs; a recorder; a microphone to assist with recordings; and a table with snacks
and water. It was held in a room at the Center for Higher Studies of Parintins –
CESP/UEA.
       The researcher herself served as the group’s moderator, and we were able
to count on a rapporteur selected based on their prior knowledge of the research
process and their enrollment in a doctoral program in education, thereby
contributing the discretion, ethics, and reliability inherent to this research
technique. After welcoming the participants, the purpose of forming the formative
focus group and the rationale for selecting the participants were explained.
Everyone seemed quite at ease, as some already knew each other and the
location was part of their educational background. Next, the participants received
the Informed Consent Form so they could formally decide whether they wished
to participate in the focus group. Of the six present, all signed the form.


                                                                                  321

            We gave a brief presentation on the research objective and then provided
   an opportunity for participants to introduce themselves and describe their training
   experience at the Parintins Center for Higher Studies. We adhered to Gatti’s
   (2005) recommendation that the confidentiality of participants’ records and
   names must be ensured. As for the participants’ names, they had the opportunity
   to choose a pseudonym to be used in the study. The table below presents the
   data obtained from a semi-structured questionnaire administered after the
   participants’ introductions.
