                                                                                                        322

       The purpose of the questionnaire was not merely to outline a profile of
each participant—since this is already evident in their statements—but above all,
to understand what each person means by reflective-critical training. We chose
to conduct this inquiry in writing so that, for the time being, no one would be
influenced by others’ opinions, which is natural in the focus group technique.
Understanding what participants think about critical training during the first
meeting allows us to get a superficial glimpse of their training process and even
to sense what their work in Basic Education has been like. In this sense,
Professor Val states that “reflective-critical training is where a person has the
opportunity to express their thoughts free from oppression.” In other words, it is
when we can speak, question, and ask without being punished for it.
       Professor Mere, on the other hand, asserts that “reflective-critical training
is a process of formation that always requires an observation, a reflection, a
thought...”. A critical stance is capable not only of seeing re ity—the contradictions
and conflicts inherent in it—but also of acting to change it.
       “The training of the reflective-critical teacher is based on creating
conditions for improvements in education...” (Professor Derson). To foster critical
thinking in students, adequate conditions are indeed necessary, such as good
schools and quality teaching materials; however, teacher training is an essential
part of this process.
       According to Professor Paty, reflective-critical training concerns “the
capacity that the individuals involved in the teaching-learning process—that is,
teachers and students—have, or are able to develop, to perceive the reality they
live in.” Perceiving reality and changing it is emphasized in this teacher’s remarks.
This means that critical thinking enables changes in people’s behavior, changes
that occur first in their thinking. One cannot make significant changes to reality
without first seeing it as it truly is.
       Teacher Su, who holds a degree in Physics and has the longest
experience in Basic Education, states that critical education is “when one
develops the behavior of being a thinking being...” Thinking is inherent to human
beings; it is, in a way, innate, the result of a social process, according to Ghedin
(2003).
       When asked about this, Teacher Sol says that “having a reflective-critical
education is a way of thinking about how one is acting—that is, one’s actions in


                                                                                  323

moments that demand greater participation, such as in a school setting—and
reflecting on how I am acting...” It is not just any kind of thinking, but rather a form
of thinking that enables transformation.


2.4 SECOND MEETING: THE FORMATION OF THE REFLECTIVE-CRITICAL
TEACHER


       The objective of this second meeting was to initiate a discussion with the
group on critical training based on the text: Philosophy and the Formation of
Reflective-Critical Thinking (Ghedin, 2003). The text was distributed to
participants at the first meeting as a suggested reading. However, we noticed
during the discussions a lack of familiarity with the concepts discussed in the text,
as only four of the six participants attended, and of these, two admitted they had
not read it. This caused certain difficulties in the discussions, requiring more
frequent mediation by the moderator through questioning to keep the discussion
on track, as the dialogues often veered off in other directions. Thus, the question
under debate was: What does it mean to be reflective and critical?
       It is necessary to establish a pedagogy of transgression and thus teach
how to think in order to reflect (Ghedin, 2003). However, the participants claim
that the school lacks the space and time to develop this type of thinking; let us
look at an excerpt from the dialogue:


                       “...the course load is very heavy, and we end up not covering the topics
                       that actually foster reflective students (Teacher Paty).”
                       “The system is increasingly focused on meeting government goals...
                       (Teacher Val).”
                       “...this teaching approach is wonderful, but the reality at school is quite
                       different. The lab was fully equipped; I tried to make the most of the
                       space and focus on hands-on practice, but then they need grades, and
                       the teacher is caught between a rock and a hard place—either they do
                       things differently or they go along with the school’s pace... I teach
                       physics and end up neglecting the reflective aspect... the system
                       demands grades... (Teacher Su).”


       As explained, school has been a place for domestication. The participants
emphasize that fostering critical thinkers is not the government’s goal. This is
because, as the discussions reveal, the heavy workload and the overemphasis
on grades and metrics dominate every aspect of school life. In this sense, the



                                                                                             324

school, as an agent of the government, does not create opportunities for the
development of individuals who think critically.
       This justifies the need for critical thinking to be developed through
pedagogical interventions when working with curricular content, where the
teacher, by selecting this content, can encourage questioning and doubt,
stimulating curiosity and creativity through well-planned pedagogical strategies.


                       “Silent students, eyes fixed on the teacher...” (Teacher Paty).
                       “He is the expert; there is no debate! There is no teacher-student
                       interaction” (Teacher Su).
                       “It’s the taming of the body.” (Teacher Paty).


       In fact, what is sought is the taming of the mind. We were taught that we
only learn when we are seated, copying, and silent; it is a school tradition that
has stood the test of time. An education that does not work toward
problematization, doubt, and questioning has only one path: to reproduce the
teaching-learning process of traditional pedagogy (Ghedin, 2003). This pedagogy
is evident in the voices of the participants, as well as in the reality they experience.
There is a discourse that traditional education is a thing of the past; however, it
is very much present through the “banking” model of education so often
discussed by Paulo Freire, in which the teacher deposits all the information into
the student, and the student receives, stores, and then returns it exactly as
received. Such information cannot be transformed into knowledge. This is not
permitted.
       The reproduction and mechanization of teaching have been disguised by
a discourse of “education for all,” “quality education,” and “inclusion and
accessibility.” Ultimately, what has been done is to deny the individual the full
development of their cognitive, affective, and social capacities.


                       “In preschool, they learn by playing, doing this, doing that, playing with
                       playdough... so parents have this idea: ‘Oh, my child is going to school.’
                       He has to learn right away how to hold a pencil. It’s not like that! ‘When
                       will my child bring homework home?’ They have this view that school is
                       all about testing… that to learn, you have to be in the classroom… if
                       you leave… if you’re playing… you’re not learning (Teacher Val).”
                       “We’re already so immersed in this pattern that breaking free from it is
                       very complicated (Teacher Paty).”




                                                                                             325

       Breaking free from this educational model and building a more
sophisticated way of thinking capable of perceiving and analyzing the
contradictions present in reality is neither an easy task nor a quick process. It
takes time to change ways of thinking rooted in theories that increasingly oppress
and alienate the individual. It is from this perspective that we cannot miss the
opportunity to develop in early childhood education students neural connections
that direct their thinking toward critical thinking, creativity, and curiosity. It is in
this sense that language plays a fundamental role, when the teacher chooses
activities that dynamically engage students’ cognitive processes—distinctive
activities that better stimulate attention, memory, and perception, leading to
cognitive development that goes beyond the mere accumulation of information.
       The discussion about how schools are organized to meet government
requirements led, at various points in the discussion, to a shift away from the
meeting’s objective, thus veering into other topics. To this end, the moderator,
aiming to bring the group back to the topic at hand, asked the participants: Has
our training enabled the development of critical thinking? How do we deal with
the relationships already established in the school? How do we perceive these
relationships? How does the school seek to alienate? The text used for reading
addresses these questions.


                       Education must make a leap from tradition to transgression. It
                       constitutes itself as transgression; that is, in order for it to assume its
                       proper role, it must foster transgression as a pedagogical space for
                       freedom and the expression of the most varied forms of creativity—not
                       merely the Cartesian rational model, characteristic of modern
                       conceptions of knowledge, but one that does not correspond to the
                       human demands of our time (Ghedin, 2003, pp. 38–39).


       In this regard, Teacher Paty states that, from this perspective, the student
“will be a mere reproducer, doing everything as told.” This is because their
capacity to question and doubt has not been developed within the teaching-
learning process; it is the Cartesian model, where there is no room for questions.
However, Teacher Sol points out that: “I like it when they discuss their opinions,
especially when we talk about politics. Some have formed opinions. Our school
has no projects; it’s just class, class, class, test, class” (Teacher Sol). With this,
we understand that there is no space in school to develop critical reflection since
the “class” is a set of exercises that must be answered in writing by the students.


                                                                                              326

Thus, the participants were asked again: Is it possible to develop critical thinking
in students?


                       “I believe students already have this way of thinking, but many of them
                       don’t try to assert themselves, and when they do, there are a lot of
                       people who stand in their way. When I try to assert myself... I can’t give
                       an opinion, and then 10 people are already against me (Teacher Sol).”


       The school has denied students the full development of their cognitive abil-
ities. This occurs when it prevents them from expressing their opinions in order
to compare them with others’ ideas. For critical thinking to develop, it needs en-
vironments that stimulate creativity, problem-solving, and responsible decision-
making regarding the problems of reality. This is because, although all human
beings are capable of thinking, the school, as a space for education, must enable
the development of higher cognitive processes.


2.5 THIRD MEETING: THE UNITY OF THEORY AND PRACTICE IN THE
REFLECTIVE-CRITICAL TRAINING OF TEACHERS


       The text Philosophy and Praxis (Ghedin, 2003) was distributed at the previous
meeting to aid discussions and provide participants with a theoretical foundation on
the topic at hand. Since some participants had not read the previous text, we set aside
time (fifteen minutes) at the beginning of the meeting for them to read it before starting
the discussions. After this, we returned to the question: what does it mean to be
critical? Emphasizing that such a stance does not imply a practice detached from
theoretical knowledge that explains reality in a dialectical, dynamic, and contradictory
manner. To this end, we highlighted an excerpt from the text:


                       While practical activity presupposes effective action on the world that
                       results in its real transformation, theoretical activity merely transforms
                       our consciousness of facts, our ideas about things, but not the things
                       themselves. However, we believe that this transformation of
                       consciousness regarding things is a necessary prerequisite for a
                       practical process to operate at the theoretical level (Ghedin, 2003,
                       p.41).


       In fact, no education takes place without theory, not even traditional
education. Nevertheless, the educational perspective discussed throughout this
work prioritizes a consistent theoretical framework grounded in a dialectical


                                                                                             327

perspective. This is because, in our view, only a dialectical approach is capable
of analyzing and explaining reality as it is, and thus enabling significant changes
in the teaching-learning process, which will be reflected in society. Thus,
immediately after the question was posed, Professor Paty responded with great
conviction:
       “It was by thinking about this reflective training and seeking to observe the
critique within it. It was a critical-reflective process (Professor Paty).”
       Always speaking with confidence, emphasis, and a questioning tone,
Professor Paty indeed reflects a critical education. This is evident through her
language, her discourse, and the way she relates the facts. A history graduate,
she highlighted on several occasions her satisfaction with the program and how
it provided her with a civic education. Professor Val also demonstrated great
conviction in answering the question. In addition to affirming that she underwent
a formative process from a critical perspective, she highlights Professors Ramos
and Bartoli as mediators of that process.


                       “I remember Professor Ramos very well; he always used to say to us:
                       ‘Today, in class… we’re going to put this theory into practice; we’re
                       going to act as if we were actually teaching out there in the countryside.’
                       How would you convey this theory to your student who is out in the
                       countryside? How would you go about it? He always tried to do that—
                       most of them did—and Professor Bartoli always did that a lot too
                       (Professor Val).”


       Professor Val also played a very effective role in the meetings. She always
took a strong stance, even if at times her speech overemphasized practice, but
as she read the texts, her discourse gradually shifted; the texts began to influence
her way of thinking and broaden her perspective on the subject.


                       “...Professor Tati, Professor Bartoli—he would push us, prod us,
                       question us, stir us up. I mean, he really messed with our heads! ‘You
                       guys are so stagnant!’ He wanted us, one way or another, to be critical,
                       to wake up, to face reality (Professor Val).”


       Professor Val is very firm in stating that her undergraduate education
fostered a reflective-critical mindset. She mentions some professors, even
without being prompted in the questioning, and this assertion is repeated in the
final session. Questioning the way we think about reality allows for the
construction of a new reality in thought and action.


                                                                                             328

       The text discussed in this session allowed participants to consider reality
from a dialectical perspective, imbued with the inseparable relationship between
theory and practice—something that did not occur in previous sessions, where
practice was overemphasized on several occasions. The text addresses the unity
between theory and practice, as well as reflection-action, viewed as elements
that act reciprocally and concurrently in a teacher training process. In this sense,
it is evident that reading the text prompted a rethinking of the role of theory and
how it relates to reflective-critical training, as the testimonials show.


                       “He addresses the issue of working solely on theory without relating it
                       to practice—and vice versa—within the teaching-learning process; the
                       issue becomes mechanical, so it is a mechanization of teaching”
                       (Professor Paty).
                       “The separation of theory and practice is a negation of identity... He
                       says here that dichotomizing theory and practice is simultaneously
                       separating reflection and action” (Professor Val).


       Thinking critically means thinking from a theoretical foundation that
enables a practice capable of developing in the student sufficient cognitive
abilities to modify their environment through more complex thinking. Separating
theory and practice risks losing the possibility of reflection and understanding,
denying human identity (Ghedin, 2003). We have no doubt that this was made
very clear to the participants, as they were able to see the relevance of theoretical
study in educational work, unlike in the first meeting.


                       “I agree when the text says that this relationship between theory and
                       practice builds teaching knowledge. But it only builds it when you’re
                       actually there. Unfortunately, I disagree that, in university, teaching
                       knowledge isn’t built yet. Because you haven’t had the practice yet.
                       Even if you go into the field, in a teaching situation, in a classroom
                       setting, or on an internship, you’ ’t actually the teacher. You’re just there
                       observing; you’re just imagining they’re your students, but they aren’t
                       your students” (Professor Derson).


       Teaching knowledge, according to Ghedin (2003), is the result of a long
historical process of organization and elaboration by society of various forms of
knowledge, for which the teacher is responsible for transmitting. Since it is a long
historical process, the university cannot be solely responsible for the construction
of this knowledge. It is necessary for the teacher, through their experiences, to
construct new knowledge based on research and reflection on their own practice



                                                                                               329

in an intentional and systematic process; however, it is within the undergraduate
program that one learns how to do this, as it is during this period that one learns
to systematize information and transform it into knowledge—a crucial step in the
construction of teaching knowledge.
       The internship, for example, imbued with research (Pimenta; Lima, 2012),
is a strategy, an opportunity to train the intern as a future teacher, where they can
develop the mindset and skills of a researcher based on internship situations,
designing projects that allow them to understand and critically analyze the
situations they observe.


2.6 FOURTH MEETING: HIGHER EDUCATION FACULTY WHO FOSTER
CRITICAL THINKING


       Given that in the previous meeting some participants did not make it clear
whether their undergraduate training was from a critical perspective or not, we
began the final meeting by revisiting this question. However, in addition to this,
for those who stated they had participated in a critical education, we also asked:
Which faculty members do you consider to have most fostered critical thinking
during your undergraduate studies? Our objective with this question was, after
identifying these faculty members, to delve deeper into certain issues using the
open-ended structured interview to learn from them how they work and how they
foster critical thinking in pedagogical interventions during the teacher training
process.
       In addition to this question, we also asked the participants: What did the
experience of reflecting on your training in this group mean to you? The answer
to this question is very significant, given that the focus group had to be relevant
not only to the researcher but also to the participants. Participation would have
to, in addition to achieving the research objectives, also enable the construction
of some knowledge based on the experience with the group, allowing for
moments of reflection on the training received during undergraduate studies, as
well as the work they carry out in Basic Education.


                      “Professor Ramos was very critical. He worked in a very clear way on
                      how to approach critical thinking, how to integrate theory and practice...
                      How to address a specific subject, given that the rural context is totally


                                                                                            330

                      different from the city. Professor Bartoli was also very critical... In the
                      classroom, he would divide us into groups. Each group would defend a
                      position, and one group would challenge the other.” (Teacher Val).


       As expressed in this teacher’s statement, the educators mentioned work
through theory and practice, using groups that engage in mutual questioning,
always emphasizing the realities they would encounter as teachers, guiding
students to reflect on what their teaching would be like amidst the various realities
they would face.


                      “I remember Professor Souza with his political pedagogy. He made me
                      question so many times the politics I hated so much... Professor Leal,
                      that gentle side of hers, but always questioning, seeking to understand
                      the child. Professor Dutra, at first it was through sociology” (Professor
                      Sol).


       During the four meetings, we noticed that their discourse focused more on
the daily school life experienced in rural schools than on the issues raised
themselves. It became evident how difficult it was for the teacher to discuss the
topic, even though she made an effort to participate in the meetings. This analysis
is based on the group discussions, where she participated little in the dialogues.
Her language reveals a lack of critical thinking.


                      “When I mentioned at the last meeting that for me, my undergraduate
                      program wasn’t 100% about practice and theory, because unfortunately
                      I had some professors who stayed only in the classroom, only in theory,
                      and didn’t take us out to do something different... One time we went out
                      into the field to carry out projects. One of them was with Professor
                      Maia, who runs the Leleco project, which is now quite well-known at the
                      University, a reading project... So Professor Maia had a significant
                      impact on my undergraduate experience, not only because of the
                      project, but also because she created the vocabulary lists for us to work
                      on the Portuguese language. And so I am trying to foster critical-
                      reflective thinking with my students.” (Professor Derson).


       Stating that he felt a lack of unity between theory and practice during his
undergraduate studies, Professor Derson highlights Professor Maia for her work
on the reading project called Leleco. Through this project, it was possible to
integrate theory and practice, which was very meaningful to him. A teaching-
learning process that prioritizes powerful and creative pedagogical practice must
be integrated with pedagogical projects conceived and designed beyond the
narrow confines of disciplinary boundaries.



                                                                                             331

       Critical thinking is developed through activities that mobilize various
cognitive processes in a dynamic and concurrent manner. Project-based work,
initiated from a problem, can spark students’ curiosity to the extent that they
participate as active and creative agents in the planning and execution of
activities.
       Diverse activities provide opportunities for students to view specific
content or reality in a different way. This is important because as we engage in
different activities, we establish new neural connections, forge new pathways in
the brain, and thereby enable the mobilization of more cognitive processes—
which is essential for the development of more complex thinking. The new always
generates conflict and discomfort. Situations like these mobilize thought and
reasoning and stimulate intelligent actions.


                       “The projects we worked on were usually group projects, and whenever
                       there was a presentation, seminar, or similar event, each group giving
                       a presentation had to be questioned by the other groups. And there
                       were situations—and Professor Marinho did this a lot—where, in
                       addition to one group being questioned, the other had to take a stance
                       in favor, always sparking a debate... We could use theater,
                       documentaries, or produce short films, as long as we also incorporated
                       into the dialogue with the subjects we were working with.” (Professor
                       Paty).


       As we have seen throughout this study, questioning fosters reflective-
critical thinking (Ghedin, 2003). Working in groups, challenging them, and
promoting discussions is highly relevant when seeking a distinctive form of
education—one that goes beyond the accumulation of information but considers
reality as subject to changes brought about by the individual themselves.


                       “Professor Dantas would sometimes hand out handouts to us. And right
                       on the first day of class, he said: ‘You’re going to face many struggles.’
                       Another teacher was Figueiredo. He would bring the concept map to
                       our classroom. He would have the group there question one another,
                       ask questions. He would have us construct that map based on the text
                       he gave us... It made me a critical thinker, and I’m still striving to be
                       one” (Professor Mere).


       Concept maps are a resource developed by Novak, serving to promote
meaningful learning based on David Ausubel’s theory, where new ideas and
information are internalized and anchored in the subject’s cognitive structure,
modifying it (Razera, et al., 2009). It is a relevant activity in that it allows students


                                                                                             332

to extract concepts from texts and construct the map according to the hierarchy
of those concepts.


                      “Our main interest is to eliminate from that period the subjects that get
                      in the way of the others, which allows us to focus on the others. So, our
                      main concern was to streamline, eliminate the lists, and not get bogged
                      down in assessments” (Teacher Su).


       Pimenta and Lima (2012) concur with this statement, as they clarify that
when teaching specific content, teachers often focus solely on cognitive
knowledge, where the most important aspect is knowledge of that subject area,
centering on content distant from students’ reality and focusing only on the
material being covered.


3. CONCLUSION


       The concept of the reflective-critical teacher was gradually developed
throughout the activities. And this goes beyond the research objectives, since the
knowledge built with the group will be reflected in the practices they carry out in
the classroom. The discussions held during the meetings also revealed
indignation regarding the way the system or “government” works to perpetuate
mechanistic pedagogy, where the interest lies not in forming thinking individuals,
but in achieving high scores without demonstrating any quality. In this sense, the
participants recognize the need for a pedagogy of transgression, where one can
break away from domestication and establish an education that teaches critical
thinking. However, they emphasize that this is not an easy process to carry out,
since what the school wants is “silent students” and the teacher is already
immersed in “this pattern, so escaping it is very complicated.” It is the
domestication of thought, which first affects the teacher, then the student,
undermining the whole of society. This is because education advances when
actors acquire the cognitive capacity to reflect on how they think and how they
act. And not only that. When they decide to modify their practices in order to
improve them, thereby encouraging individuals to seek new ways of being, doing,
and living. This means building a fairer and better society, where everyone can
live with dignity.

CHAPTER 20
 THE ORAL POETRY OF MARACATU
 DE BAQUE SOLTO: STRATEGY
 FOR EXPANDING THE LITERARY
 LITERACY OF STUDENTS IN THE
 4TH PHASE OF EJA

Joseane do Nascimento Rocha
Master of Arts in Literature
Universidade de Pernambuco (UPE)
E-mail: joseanerocha3112@gmail.com

Josivaldo Custódio da Silva
Doctor in Literature and Culture
Universidade de Pernambuco (UPE)
E-mail: josivaldo.silva@upe.br

Maria do Rosário da Silva Albuquerque Barbosa
Doctor in Applied Linguistics and Language Studies
Universidade de Pernambuco (UPE)
E-mail: rosario.silvabarbosa@upe.br


ABSTRAC: This article aims to expand the literary literacy of students in the IV
phase of EJA – Youth and Adult Education, based on reading and interpretation
of the loas of Maracatu de Baque Solto or Rural. Starting from the student's
reading experience, and through the approaches of Reception Aesthetics
(JAUSS, 1994), the Reception Method (AGUIAR and BORDINI, 1988) and
Literary Literacy (COSSON, 2011), we developed a proposal for students from
the municipality of Lagoa do Carro-PE, enrolled at the Dagoberto Lobo municipal
school. This research is characterized by a qualitative approach, of an applied
nature and an action research procedure. The proposal presented here uses,
based on stages of the Reception Method, stages of the basic sequence –
motivation, introduction, reading and interpretation – and contextualizations of the
expanded sequence of Literary Literacy and theses of Reception Aesthetics.
Difficulties in interpretation were analyzed based on the participants' written
productions, originating from texts read and prepared during each workshop
developed within the applied stages. The results provided us with a qualitative
analysis of the occurrences of each index of contextualizations and theses
identified in the written productions. Throughout the research, we identified
negative issues and positive advances until we reached the conclusion with the
final product: the presentations of the TCEF – Elementary School Completion
Works – whose themes were developed relating to maracatu de baque vento.
Therefore, the expansion of the literary literacy of the research participants is


                                                                                335

visible, especially in the creative writing part in the last workshop, even if they
present problems with interpretation, spelling, in short, deviations from the
standard norm.

KEYWORDS: oral poetry, maracatu de baque solto, literary literacy, reception
aesthetics, reception method.

RESUMO: Esse artigo possui como objetivo ampliar o letramento literário de
estudantes da IV fase da EJA – Educação de Jovens e Adultos, a partir de leitura
e interpretação das loas de Maracatu de Baque Solto ou Rural. Partindo da
experiência leitora do estudante, e através das abordagens da Estética da
Recepção (JAUSS, 1994), do Método Recepcional (AGUIAR e BORDINI, 1988)
e do Letramento Literário (COSSON, 2011), desenvolvemos uma proposta para
estudantes do município de Lagoa do Carro-PE, matriculados(as) na escola
municipal Dagoberto Lobo. Esta pesquisa caracteriza-se por uma abordagem
qualitativa, de natureza aplicada e procedimento de pesquisa-ação. A proposta
aqui apresentada utiliza, a partir de etapas do Método Recepcional, etapas da
sequência básica – motivação, introdução, leitura e interpretação – e
contextualizações da sequência expandida do Letramento Literário e teses da
Estética da Recepção. As dificuldades de interpretação foram analisadas com
base nas produções escritas dos(as) participantes, oriundas de textos lidos e
elaboradas no decorrer de cada oficina desenvolvida dentro das etapas
aplicadas. Os resultados nos proporcionaram uma análise qualitativa das
ocorrências de cada índice de contextualizações e teses identificadas nas
produções escritas. Ao longo da pesquisa, identificamos questões negativas e
avanços positivos até chegarmos à conclusão com o produto final: as
apresentações dos TCEF – Trabalhos de Conclusão do Ensino Fundamental –
cujas temáticas se desenvolveram referentes ao maracatu de baque solto.
Portanto, é vísivel a ampliação do letramento literário dos(as) participantes da
pesquisa, principalmente na parte de escrita criativa na última oficina, mesmo
que apresentem problemas de interpretação, de grafia, enfim, de desvios da
norma padrão.

PALAVRAS-CHAVE: poesia oral, maracatu de baque solto, letramento literário,
estética da recepção, método recepcional.

1. INTRODUCTION


       The Adult and Youth Education (EJA) program is designed for those who
did not have access to or were unable to continue their elementary and secondary
education at the appropriate age and will now be guaranteed such opportunities,
in accordance with LDB 9.394/96 and Normative Instructions/PE 02/2004,
15/2008, and 02/2011, access to school with a language specific to this audience.
       Maracatu de Baque Solto, or Rural Maracatu, also known as Maracatu de
Orquestra, according to Moura (2016, p. 90), “[...] originated in the sugarcane
mills; most of its performers still make their living today from planting and cutting
sugarcane.” It features several characters, among them the caboclo de lança,
who is the most emblematic symbol of this folkloric tradition. The northern forest
region of Pernambuco is the birthplace and setting for the tradition of this folk
dance, and to this day, it has been passing on its mysteries and charms from
generation to generation, preserving its religious elements, sacred aspects, and
oral tradition. The latter, which is of interest to us, will become the subject of study
and a tool for action in the pedagogical work proposed here. It is worth noting that
Rural Maracatu differs from Maracatu Nação or Baque Virado, which were not
used in this research.
       The loas of Maracatu de Baque Solto2 , in a certain sense, are part of the
playful, carnivalesque, artistic, cultural, and social universe of the community in
the municipality of Lagoa do Carro, in the Zona da Mata Norte region of
Pernambuco. For this reason, we proposed that the students—referred to here
as participants—delve into the verses of the loas of Maracatu de Baque Solto or
Rural, so that they might expand their knowledge of the poetic and imaginative
universe of the Maracatu masters. In this way, we promoted literary literacy
through the improvised verses of this popular artistic expression; that is, we used
texts drawn from the sambadas and performances of the revelers.
       Sambadas are gatherings of two maracatu de baque solto groups,
practices known in various cities in the Mata Norte region of Pernambuco, with
the city of Nazaré da Mata as the main representative of this expression of
popular culture. In the “sambada de pé de parede,” for example, two masters


2 From now on, we will use only the term “Maracatu de Baque Solto.”




                                                                                    337

engage in a poetic duel, each with their own performers creating choreography
and playing in support of their master. In this way, we understand that this genre
is already part of the students’ sonic and poetic universe, not just during Carnival,
but all year round.
         In light of this, the general objective of this study was to analyze the
interpretation of literary texts by students in the fourth phase of the Adult and
Youth Education (EJA) program, using the popular literature of maracatu de
baque solto loas as a means of introducing them to the world of reading and
expanding their literary horizons. Our specific objectives were to introduce
students to the loa genre as an aesthetic and literary experience; analyze
contextualizations and possible theses of Reception Aesthetics in students’
written work; conduct oral and interpretive readings of literary texts in the
classroom; and assess students’ comprehension and interpretation of literary
texts.


2. THEORETICAL AND CRITICAL ASSUMPTIONS


         According to Frantz (2011, p. 35), we understand that a poetic and/or
literary text “[…] can be identified through its polysemy and the connotative nature
of its language. In literature, therefore, it is defined by the special use made of
language.” This observation leads us to believe that literary texts treat language
in a special way and imply a particular quality in linguistic treatment. Literature
plays an important role in the humanistic development of individuals (Candido,
2011). Through reading these texts, it is possible to adopt new perspectives,
understand new cultures, and acquire new knowledge.
         The various possibilities for perspectives and alternatives—whether real
or imagined—offered by literary language do not depend solely on the polysemic
nature of language, but above all on the reader’s cultural background and the
historical and social context in which such readings take place. The work
becomes a “social object [...]. It is, therefore, in the process of interaction that the
meaning(s) of the text are constituted, making the reader’s participation
fundamental.” (Frantz, 2011, p. 37).
         The characteristics of the poem genre include versification, the
organization of verses into stanzas, the possibility of rhymes, and the aesthetics


                                                                                    338

of different forms and rhythms. The poem refines the word with musicality, making
use of devices such as polysemy, wordplay, and various possibilities for
interpretation. This genre allows us to reflect on daily life and the imagination and
makes us more sensitive to realities, broadening linguistic perception and
enriching vocabulary, ideas, and diverse thoughts.
       The liberating nature of literary art stems from the fact that, according to
Zilberman (1989, p. 54), “The eminently liberating nature of art, which merges the
transgressive and communicative roles, is made explicit through the aesthetic
experience, which consists of three simultaneous and complementary activities—
poiesis, aisthesis, and catharsis.” Poiesis corresponds to the foreground and
“corresponds to the pleasure of feeling like a co-author of the work” (Zilberman,
1989, p. 55).
       More closely related to the aesthetic experience itself, the second level,
aisthesis, refers “to the effect, brought about by the work of art, of renewing the
perception of the surrounding world” (Zilberman, 1989, p. 55). As for katharsis,
Jauss defines it as “the realization of a process of identification that leads the
viewer to adopt new norms of social behavior, in a return to ideas previously
expressed,” as Zilberman notes (1989, p. 57); that is, “the viewer not only feels
pleasure but is also motivated to act” (Zilberman, 1989, p. 57).
       Jauss (1994), in addition to his discussion of the aesthetic experience, also
seeks to scientifically establish the method of literary hermeneutics, going beyond
regional, theological, or legal hermeneutics that focus on interpreting historical
texts from the past, as noted by Zilberman (1989) and Figurelli (1988),
respectively.
       Following Jauss’s premises, only the process of Reception Aesthetics “[...]
can lead the viewer to abandon the attitude of passive contemplation and, thanks
to a reformulation of poiesis, to actively participate in the experience of creating
the work of art,” comments Figurelli (1988, pp. 269–270). Delight, enjoyment, and
experience are defended by Jauss as moments of the experience of the first
stage of aesthetic perception.
       Jauss, in turn, presented proposals for approaching the study of literature
through his so-called seven theses (JAUSS, 1994), in which he contextualizes
and analyzes different approaches to literary study based on these seven theses:
1st thesis: the historicity of literature does not arise from chronology or year of


                                                                                 339

publication, but from the dynamic dialogue between the reader and the literary
work; 2nd thesis: the reader’s literary experience presupposes “prior
knowledge”—pointing to their expectations and interests; 3rd thesis: concerns
aesthetic distance—the gap or non-coincidence between the reader’s horizon of
expectations and the horizon of expectations evoked by a work; 4th thesis: the
meanings of a literary text are constructed through readers’ interpretations of the
work throughout history; therefore, the reader’s historical context is decisive in
the construction of the literary work’s meanings. Here lies the path of literary
hermeneutics: comprehension, interpretation, and application.; 5th thesis: The
significance of a literary work is determined not only by the initial moment of
reception and reading in history, but by the diachronic aspect, that is, by the
countless subsequent readings that modify and expand the work’s meaning over
time; 6th thesis: Here we have the synchronic perspective, that is, the reading of
the work at a given historical moment, including the moment of its production,
although it also engages with the diachronic aspect; in other words, the diachronic
and synchronic aspects go hand in hand in the construction of the work’s
meanings; 7th thesis: it engages with the diachronic and synchronic aspects, as
well as exploring the reader’s experience through the relationship between
literature and practical life.
       The reader’s role is fundamental to the very definition of the aesthetic
object, and from this perspective, reception theory developed from the studies of
the Polish philosopher Ingarden in the 1930s and the Czech scholar Felix Vodicka
in the 1940s. The sum of these studies gave shape to the so-called Receptionist
Method based on the possible transformations of the creator’s artistic work into
an aesthetic object for the reader (Aguiar; Bordini, 1988, pp. 81–82).
       According to Zilberman (1982, p. 103), the author and the reader interpret
the work based on the following aspects: intellectual, ideological, linguistic, and
literary. In addition to the affective aspects that will function as determinants for
the acceptance or rejection of the other aspects.
       The Receptional Method consists of five stages: determination of the
horizon of expectations, fulfillment of the horizon of expectations, rupture of the
horizon of expectations, questioning of the horizon of expectations, and
expansion of the horizon of expectations, according to Aguiar and Bordini (1988).



                                                                                 340

       Regarding literary literacy, based on reading, we have the concepts of
comprehension and interpretation of literary texts. Cosson (2011) developed a
methodology he termed the “basic sequence,” which consists of four steps:
motivation, introduction, reading, and interpretation. The basic sequence is a
methodological approach for developing the practice of reading literary texts in
school. This approach aims to foster a perspective of literacy- d on reading and
teaching literature. The motivation and introduction strategies should highlight the
literary text being studied, giving it the necessary importance to keep readers
interested and motivated to read. The stages of reading and interpreting the text,
on the other hand, represent the “high point” of the text in the experience of
literary literacy. As a methodology, the basic sequence presents a proposal for
accessibility that makes the text available not only for reading appreciation but,
above all, for meaningful interpretation.
       The basic sequence presented by Cosson (2011, p. 51) highlights the
importance of systematic work for the objective construction of a consistent
methodology for teaching literature.
       However, it was necessary to add something to the studies already
conducted and to the application of the methodology already presented, which
he called the expanded sequence. Through this, the author adds two further
lessons from the literature within the steps initiated in the basic sequence. “The
expanded sequence makes the connections we propose between literary
experience, knowledge, and education—embedded within the scope of this
literacy in school—more evident.” (Cosson, 2011, p. 76).
       The expanded sequence allows for further levels of interpretation, divided
into two stages, each of which is subdivided. In the first interpretation, the reader
is guided through different forms of contextualization, such as: theoretical
contextualization, historical contextualization, stylistic contextualization, poetic
contextualization, critical contextualization, presentational contextualization, and
thematic contextualization. In the second form of interpretation, there is a deeper
exploration of one or more of the previous contextualizations. It is a deeper dive
into the aspect chosen and/or guided by the teacher and/or the reader.
       Regarding the poetics of oral literature and popular culture, Zumthor
(2010, p. 8) unravels the mysteries of oral poetics: “The primordial symbolism
integrated into the phonetic exercise manifests itself eminently in the use of


                                                                                 341

language, and it is there that all poetry takes root.” For the author, the distinction
between voice and language implies a conceptual distance that allows for distinct
discussion and study of the “ .” Every act of speech is uttered by those who hold
the right to speak and establishes a unique act of authority. This act names the
act itself by speaking it. In this research, the acts of orality in the loas of the
maracatu de baque solto become objects of study through the lens of reception
aesthetics, stages of the reception method, and sequences of Literary Literacy.
       Understanding sambadas and loas: The spectacle takes place not only
during Carnival performances—which occur only annually—but also in the
terreiros of the peripheries, rural homesteads, and communities, when the
festivities, called sambadas, take place. These have various purposes: to
rehearse, socialize, celebrate, worship, and keep the tradition alive, which is
typically familial.


                      [...] ‘sambadas’—where two masters take on the challenge of
                      improvisation. These can be ‘short’ (samba de 6 or 4) or ‘long’ (samba
                      de 10), but this difference arises only in the realm of the poetry
                      expressed in the loas/toadas, since the rhythm remains the same [...]
                      And finally, we have the galope, considered by the performers a
                      moment of ‘farewell,’ as it is known that, after its performance, a
                      ‘farewell march’ will follow, usually thanking those involved for their
                      participation. (Brasil, 2013, pp. 115–116, emphasis added).


       The duels of yesteryear are represented today by the songs of the
maracatu masters, for they are the great leaders of their nations. It is the master
who defines the rhythmic characteristics of each group. He is considered the
poet, for it is he who must create and recite the poems composed on the spot
and performed in a spectacle called sambada.


3. METHODOLOGY


       We used qualitative research with an interpretive approach, which, in turn,
“is conducted in areas where there is little accumulated and systematized
knowledge. Due to its exploratory nature, it does not involve hypotheses, which,
however, may arise during or at the end of the research” (Vergara, 2009, p. 42).
       In this research model, the researcher can reflect on their own attitudes
and observations in the field, considering the participants’ interventions and



                                                                                         342

reactions. Indeed, this subjectivity in handling the process— d with different
approaches—is part of the characteristics of qualitative research, bringing a
diversity of possibilities and theoretical approaches as participants in the process.
       Regarding qualitative procedures, according to Creswell (2007, pp. 184–
188), “they are based on text and image data, have unique steps in data
analysis, and use diverse research strategies.” The researcher is permitted to
engage in participants’ experiences in an active and interactive manner.
       One of the approaches in qualitative research is theoretically grounded in
ethnomethodology and constructionism, focusing on daily routines and the
production of social reality, with the aim of “describing the processes involved in
the production of situations and environments [...], as well as existing social
order.” (Flick, 2009, p. 29).


                       From this perspective, data are collected through focus groups,
                       ethnography, or (participant) observation, as well as audiovisual
                       recordings. These data are then analyzed using discourse or
                       conversation analysis (Flick, 2009, p. 29).


       The project was carried out at a public school in the municipality of Lagoa
do Carro, Pernambuco, in a fourth-level Adult and Youth Education (EJA) class
held in the evening. The class consisted of 15 students. All students were eligible
to participate in the study, but only 10 were included in the sample. The selection
criteria were attendance and punctuality in submitting assignments. If all
participants had actively participated in the research activities, the selection
would have been made by drawing roll call numbers from their student IDs.
       To establish the students’ expectations, we administered a questionnaire
to identify their thematic and aesthetic interests and what would be most
appealing to them within the diverse reading universe. Next, we conducted four
workshops, the objective of which was to analyze the interpretive reading of
literary texts by the participating students, using the strategy of employing rural
maracatu chants as a means of introducing them to the world of reading.
       The workshops were preceded by the administration of a diagnostic
questionnaire to analytically establish the students’ initial profile. The instructional
sequence     was    implemented     immediately after       the   questionnaire    was
administered, with an emphasis on Aguiar and Bordini’s Receptive Method and



                                                                                    343

monitoring of the proposed activities to ensure the participation of all involved and
the effectiveness of the activities.
       The questionnaire was administered during a single 40-minute class, and
the workshops consisted of a total of four sessions, each comprising two 40-
minute classes, bringing the complete sequence to nine classes. All sessions
were documented through descriptive analyses of the questionnaire and the texts
produced in each workshop.


4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION


       Based on the results obtained from the responses to the administered
questionnaire, we observed that the students reported a concerning relationship
with literature and popular culture, which corresponds to the stage of determining
the students’ expectations. While their relationship with literary texts is clearly
restricted to school settings for the most part, the culture of rural maracatu—even
though it is native to the region where the research was conducted—is unknown
and even disparaged by the students for religious reasons, demonstrating
prejudice and a lack of information.
       The “matuta” or regional colloquial language used by the author draws
students in and captures their attention. The choice of text was a good one and
met the expectations for interaction and participation of the entire class, which
read it, discussed it, and wrote short essays about the memories the text
*Paisagem de Interior* evoked.


4.1 ASSESSMENT TO DETERMINE STUDENTS’ EXPECTATIONS


       Based on the results obtained from the responses to the administered
questionnaire, we observed that students reported a concerning relationship with
literature and popular culture. At the same time, their relationship with literary
texts is clearly restricted to school settings, for the most part. The “ ” culture of
maracatu de baque solto, despite being native to the region where the research
was conducted, is still largely unknown and, for religious reasons, even
disparaged by some students, demonstrating prejudice and a lack of information.



                                                                                 344

       The lack of knowledge and the prejudice mentioned above prompted us to
explore the theme of maracatu de baque solto, given that the context in which
the loas are performed during the sambadas of maracatu is part of the cultural
and artistic landscape of the region where the participants live. The theme of
religiosity is implicit in the culture of maracatu de baque solto; thus, the religious
and cultural prejudice on the part of the participants pointed us toward a
discursive need that provided us with a dynamic of listening, knowledge
production, and a shift away from the perspectives initially presented.
       The shift in methodological strategy occurred with the initial results of the
questionnaire. The introduction of workshops using a prose text was not initially
planned; it was implemented to address the expectations observed in the results
of the expectation horizon assessment. Before the consultation, we assumed that
the loas would be readily accepted as a literary literacy proposal; however, the
assessment phase revealed opposing viewpoints, including the identification of
reasons for non-acceptance.


4.2    APPLICATION         OF      THE      RECEPTIONIST          METHOD        AND
CONTEXTUALIZATIONS OF LITERARY LITERACY


       Workshop I: Meeting the horizon of expectations (2 40-minute classes)
       Response/receptivity – The morning poetry of Jessier Quirino. Text 01:
“Interior Landscape.” The response to the horizon of expectations took the form
of a narrative poem to enhance receptivity.
       Motivation/Introduction: illustrative video about the rural landscape.
       Reading: The text was first read silently, then collectively, with attention
to intonation, rhymes, and verses, guided by the teacher. After the collective
reading, the teacher drew attention to the text’s structure, verses, rhyme,
language and its regional characteristics, and parallelism.
       Interpretation: In this session, the teacher drew attention to the
contextualization that brings the work to life, through the language and settings
depicted in the poem, such as the parallels we believe arose spontaneously, and
the thematic contextualization, through the rural context presented in the text,
though without using those terms, in addition to pointing out elements that
indicate some of Jauss’s theses (1994), particularly the 2nd and 7th.


                                                                                  345

       Based on the written works resulting from the reading and interpretation of
the poem, we observed contextualizations that brought the region’s landscapes
to life and provided thematic context—reflections of the memories of most of the
student informants in this study, drawn from the experiences they lived through
and shared during their childhood. Thus, through reading the poem, the students
engaged in the observation of social reality, production processes, situations, and
environments, as predicted by Flik (2009, p. 29).
       The first workshop was conducted as part of the Receptive Method to meet
the expectations of the research participants, who initially rejected the proposal
for the poems, as indicated by the questionnaire administered; however, the data
showed us that they were receptive to matuta literature and narrative poetry,
pointing to the possibility of good acceptance of the poetic genre. Thus, we used
the matuta poetry of the writer Jessier Quirino. In this way, they already presented
us with elements of the second thesis of Jauss’s theory (1994).
       Following the presentation of the methodology, the application aimed at
the production of written texts, in which we observed contextualizations that
evoke the present ( ) and thematic elements ( ) related to rural landscapes; this
stems from the memories, experiences, and life stories of most of the student
informants in this study.
       The writing activities were conducted in pairs to facilitate better acceptance
of the writing process. The students involved are not accustomed to reading or
writing. Resistance to writing was reduced by the proposal to work in groups.
Each informant was identified by a number ranging from 01 to 10, and for each
group, we identified the numerical associations, along with their individual and/or
collective contributions.
       After the teacher led the activities, the students read the text and even
formed pairs to interpret one of its stanzas. The criterion for analysis was to
identify a memory shared by the participants. This was motivated by their
experiences in the countryside and rural activities, with which most students in
this class easily identify. Hence the contextualizations that brought the text into
the present and the thematic focus, precisely through life experiences, bringing
to light Jauss’s theses (1994), particularly the second (the reader’s aesthetic
experience), third (the aesthetic character of the text), sixth (the synchronic
aspect), and seventh thesis (the relationship between the work and practical life).


                                                                                 346

      Everyone had a story to tell based on the text. They felt engaged and
identified with a passage, if not the entire text. Through reflection on their
memories and analysis of the relationship between the present and the past, they
were encouraged, based on the theme, to construct an interpretation that could
merge two contextualizations.
      Let’s look at some examples of the participants’ interpretations from
Workshop 01:

      The participants made it clear that the memories evoked by Jessier

they presented it orally, they also positively highlighted these memories and the
personal experiences depicted in the text, reflecting the thematic context and the
presenter’s role in conveying the nostalgia for those lived experiences.
      The writing in verse led us to the reproduction of the verses from the
original text. The aesthetic perception became visible through the structure of the
verses, linked the two texts, and presented the authors’ intention to bring their
forms closer together.
      The fact that the text’s narrative predominantly uses the past tense
reinforced the nostalgic atmosphere and the search for positive memories of the
practices and experiences lived in the northeastern countryside. Therefore, the
students here demonstrated an understanding of the revival of childhood

memories and of the activities, work, and landscape that came to mind upon

      The aesthetic reception of the text and Jauss’s (1994) second thesis were
also evident through prior knowledge: “[...] we used to take / Bigu in trucks [...]

enabled a better reception and development of the theme, leading to greater
fluency as well.
      We also examined the relationship between literature and practical life,
which, according to Jauss (1994), forms the basis of his 7th thesis. The students
wrote an essay based on the experiences they had lived through and shared
during their childhood.

       The thematic contextualization was evident, as they did not stray from the

       The relationship between literature and practical life, as in Jauss’s (1994)

       Workshop II: Rupture of the Horizon of Expectations (2 classes of 40 min.)
       At this point, we introduce the loa genre through the samba curto, one of
the styles of Maracatu de Baque Solto. Text 02: “O maracatu”3 .

       Within the context of the loas of maracatu de baque solto, the poem “O

expression and the poet’s satisfaction in sharing his work. It features simple
language, with little complexity but great expressiveness regarding the culture it
represents and the literary language itself.

expressiveness regarding the culture it represents. We examined the texts

      The aesthetic experience involves the appropriation of the aesthetic
object. Thus, it was necessary for the students to understand the modes of

      We observed that, despite significant difficulties with verbal expression,

                      “This maracatu ode
                      Told by a simple
                      Maracatu master, of

       We note that even though the participant focused solely on describing the

poet’s achievement to grace, a gift, a divine blessing. It is a particular way of
bringing the feeling of the poetic self into the present and personal context of the
reader/student.
       We observe, however, the prior knowledge presented in his interpretation
regarding the writing of the source text: “[...] Maracatu master, of humble origins
[...]” which even influences his way of analyzing the social context of the text’s
production conditions. Here, we also observe Jauss’s (1994) second thesis,
which manifests itself through this prior information, contributing to a
contextualization of the discussions on textual production.
       When considering the prior conditions of the text’s oral production, we can
also more easily associate them with the conditions of practical life: “[...] he says
that / After much suffering, he realized a dream / By releasing his CD [...]”. The
pragmatic condition of speech act and situation expressed here is consistent with
Jauss’s (1994) seventh thesis in observing the use of practical experiences
portrayed through the text.
       From a linguistic perspective, some cohesion interventions are necessary;
however, the orthographic and syntactic elements do not hinder the coherent
development of the text.

        Workshop III: Questioning the Horizon of Expectations (2 classes of 40
min.)
        With this activity, the goal was to go beyond previous expectations and
engage in the reading of a literary text that would provoke questions and
discussions regarding the previous texts. We did not use the two sequences from
the Literary Reading Guide—motivation and introduction—but only the reading
and interpretation.
        Text 03: “Morte do sambador” – a samba in 10-syllable lines – in the
“Décima” format, that is, ten lines of seven poetic syllables each with a regular
rhyme scheme of A-B-B-A-A-C-C-D-D-C, from the CD *No Baque Solto* by Siba
and Barachinha (2003). After discussing the text, the students individually
produced analyses of the texts, based on the teacher’s guidance, who provided
information and examples regarding the verses, rhythm, and rhymes of the text.
The activity addressed two questions: 1 – What is the theme of the text? Explain.
and 2 – What type of language is used in the text? Justify.

                       2 – “Cultural”

elements of the verses that highlight the value and mastery of each sambador,

infer an understanding—albeit a simplistic one—of a contextualization that brings
the present to life, of the cultural praxis of rural maracatu, which also points to
Jauss’s (1994) 7th thesis, which applies to questions of practical life, and thus to
the very context of death mentioned above.
      The responses from participants 03 and 05 follow the same pattern of
understanding regarding the sambada “Morte do Sambador.” Let us examine the
response from participant 04:


            Figure 6. Participant 04 – Textual production from the 3rd workshop:




                  Source: Research archive. Transcription follows below:

      From the responses provided, we also observe that the participant

also confused with the title, the fact that the excerpt in parentheses was copied

explanation.
      The answer to the second question contains another error: the
classification of the language as “baque solto” reveals a variation in the maracatu
rhythm that the participant evidently identifies without reflecting on the language
itself as used by the poet, yet which nevertheless demonstrates another
attempt—this time with a view to the poetic contextualization of the text through
the lens of the rhythm used by the loas, the context of the text’s musicality.
However, this answer points to prior knowledge: “baque solto.” In Jauss’s (1994)



                                                                                   354

second thesis, it becomes evident that interpretation may present elements of
experience from the reader’s horizon of expectations, which anticipate the text, and the
third thesis, which addresses the aesthetic experience of the text that contributes
to the interpretation of the work. In this case, the perception of rhythmic and
musical expression is also language, even though this was not the approach
requested in the second question. Let us look at participant 06:

       As we have seen so far, the text’s theme is already contained in the title.
Death is the most general theme, which, however, is specified in the way the
lyrical “I” addresses his own death. Thus, since this is the most general theme,
the response “death of the samba dancer” points to a thematic contextualization,
although the participant could have better articulated the theme. Therefore, it is
unclear whether the participant reproduced the title because they understood that
the title already contains the theme and that they would have the same meaning,
or simply did not bother to reflect on the prompt.
       The absence of a response to the second item allows us to consider the
possibility of a refusal to participate and interact in the activity; this is a possibility
characteristic of this group of students who, often— —for various reasons, do not
interact, do not participate, or simply lead us to believe that they are interacting.




                                                                                       357

            Figure 10. Participant 10 – Textual production from the 3rd workshop:




                   Source: Research archive. Transcription follows below:


                        1 – “What is the topic of the text? It talks about the death of the samba
                        dancer
                        2 – What kind of language is used in the text? It discusses the

       The first answer merges the title with the theme, yet points toward a
specific interpretation of the text. Although most other participants answered
“death,” the text is quite emphatic about a specific death. The entire text deals
with how the speaker deals with their own death—clearly, a deeper insight into
the thematic context.
       The second response is the only one that points to a linguistic
understanding of colloquial language or “Brazilian vernacular,” demonstrating an
awareness of language and linguistic content—topics covered in class—through
which the participant shows linguistic comprehension of the text and the use of
language as an aesthetic element within it, from the perspective of poetic
contextualization.
       Despite providing more mature responses compared to the other
participants, this participant did not explore the text further, limiting themselves to
answering only the questions. In fact, all participants erred in their explanations
and justifications regarding the questions asked.
       The poem presented here is more complex. First, because it depicts a duel
in which the poets interact and compete to the rhythm of the maracatu de baque
solto. Second, because each poet strives to stand out through allegories and
figures of speech that allow the listeners— —to choose one over the other.
Whether through the way words are used or the strangeness that each phrase
may present, while simultaneously expressing an idea in favor of the master
(poet) or the nation he represents. Third, the verses of both poets elevate the
figure of the poet by describing what their deaths would be like, their absences,
and the legacy they leave for the culture of maracatu de baque solto.



                                                                                             358

       The possibility of interpretations and contextualizations based on this
poem goes beyond the text itself, thus reaching the extratext. Our familiarity with
oral language and the theme of death provided us with a wide range of
possibilities for discussion and questioning; after all, the text was chosen to
provide not only a rupture but, above all, questions about the language, culture,
and religiosity present in the poem. The theme addresses a pragmatic aspect of
religious experiences—death—another point of conflict, given that it is a religious
experience.
       Faith is a sensitive and solemn topic; however, the text approaches it in a
carnivalesque manner. For some students, the natural way the topic of “death”
was handled felt comfortable and familiar, even satirical and comical. For others,
pure heresy! Thus, this reading was steeped in religiosity and moralism. Even so,
it was possible to meet the expectations of the workshop’s proposal to “Question
the horizon of expectations” of the students, evident in the oral discourses and
written works that, even while exploring the poem only briefly, enabled the
researcher to raise further questions in the classroom later on.
       We also observed interpretive instances through Jauss’s (1994) 2nd and
7th theses, present in the participants’ texts, which at times engage with
contextualizations, according to Cosson (2011). In reality, in the written work, we
did not identify a satisfactory level of understanding of the poem, and responses
were limited to objective and simplistic answers to the questions. However, in oral
discourse, there were discussions and plausible inferences about the text,
revealing a preference for speech over writing. Those who truly engaged and
interacted managed to develop insights and questions that challenged their
preconceptions, their perspectives, and, at the very least, their attitudes regarding
respect for differences in thought and sociocultural conduct— , particularly
regarding the cultural universe of the maracatu de baque solto master.
       Workshop IV: Broadening the Horizon of Expectations (2 40-minute
sessions)
       In this workshop, the aim was to give participants the opportunity to explore
one of the classics of Brazilian literature and broaden their horizons in terms of
reading and poetic language, enabling a new interpretation based on Jauss’s
theories (1994) and Cosson’s contextualizations of the expanded sequence
(2011). Text 04: “Motivo,” by Cecília Meireles (1994).


                                                                                 359

       At this stage of the research, we examined the texts written by the
participants following the reading and discussion of Cecília Meireles’s “Motivo,”
as well as their own compositions resulting from an attempt at poetic, versified
writing—without concern for rhyme, focusing solely on stylistic and poetic
observations.
       The poem represents a reflection on the act of writing poetry and the
importance of being a poet, the social role of the poet, and their contribution to
the world. After reading the poem, the participants wrote in response to the
guiding question “What does it mean to be a poet?” Despite its potential for
interpretation, the poem uses simple language to explore what it means to be a
poet, addressing feelings, life’s problems, and even the element of death.
       It is evident that the texts we observed in previous workshops use
colloquial language, but now the objective of this stage was to make the student
realize the role of the poet and experiment with poetic, lyrical, and versified
language. Therefore, engaging with Cecília’s poem through the reader’s poetic
creativity, provoking and broadening the horizon of expectations, fostering an
interest in stylistics, figures of speech, standard language, and the “beautiful,” as
we will see below. Let us examine the responses to the provocative question:
What does it mean to be a poet?


                Figure 11. Participant 01 – Text produced in the 4th workshop:




                   Source: Research archive. Transcription follows below:


                        “ To be a poet is to be free
                        to be able to write suddenly;
                        Knowing how to transform everything that is sad
                        into happy moments forever .”


       The concept of poetry presented here is linked to the oral tradition of loas
and the repente of sambadas. We also note that poetry transforms feelings and




                                                                                 360

conveys joy. It is clear that poetry is associated solely with beauty, focusing only
on the positive aspects—a narrow view of poetic “beauty.”
       We also observe the structure of the verses that make up the quatrain with
external rhymes, alternating ABAB: Free/repente/sad/always. The lexical choice
reflects an aesthetic concern, highlighting a poetic contextualization, while also
constructing a concept of freedom through the metaphor “Ser Livre” (To Be Free),
which, with the linguistic emphasis of capital letters, underscores a significance
marked not only by the spelling, but above all by its subjective and conceptual
message of the poetic being, for only he [the poet] knows how to transform all
that is sad.
       In the last line, a hallmark of fairy tales points to a notion of intertextuality,
broadening the horizon of expectations regarding the beginning of the research.
The revival of the expression “happily ever after” refers us not only to the poetic
context, particularly the aesthetic experience, but also to prior knowledge,
highlighting Jauss’s (1994) second thesis, in addition to the context of practical
life, the 7th thesis, by attributing to the poet the function of transforming sadness
into   happiness,      thereby    engaging       in    dialogue      with    the    presentifying
contextualization.
       There is a concern on the part of the participant to maintain the thematic
context, focusing not only on answering the questions presented but, above all,
on doing so in a free and creative manner. Let us consider the following
participant:


               Figure 12. Participant 02 – Text produced during the 4th workshop:




                    Source: Research archive. Transcription follows below:

                         “To be a poet is to run like the wind, to fly with the birds without leaving
                         the spot; it is a rain that doesn’t wet, it is crying until you sob
                         Without any feeling, it is a tear that rolls down, a passion
                         that cannot be forgotten, or a love that, when it doesn’t kill
                         drives you mad”

       Here, there is a response in the form of lyrical and melodic creation;
however, the participant showed some difficulty with organization and
versification. The attempt to personify what it means to be a poet became
“incoherent” due to the absence of punctuation; however, when read slowly, it
exhibits coherence and fulfills the proposal to delve into subjectivity and attempt
to describe this complex being. Thus, we have the expression of both poetic and
stylistic contextualization. It is possible to reorganize the text into verses and see
that the draft presented above conceals a sequence of verses with alternating
external rhymes: ABBA, followed by two other verses with paired external rhymes
CC:

                       To be a poet is to run like the wind
                       to fly with the birds without leaving your spot.
                       It is a rain that does not wet it is crying until sobbing
                       Without any feeling.

                       It is a tear that rolls down a passion that is not forgotten
                       or a love that, when it doesn’t kill, drives you mad [emphasis added].


       The thematic contextualization is also visible, as the verses attempt to
describe “being a poet,” seeking to respond to the proposal in a lyrical manner,
in accordance with the perception of reality. Thus, we observe in the verses
above a contextualization that brings the text into the present, as well as a
concern with the experience and aesthetic distance from the source text, pointing
to Jauss’s (1994) 3rd and 4th theses.


           Figure 13. Participant 04 – Textual production from the 4th workshop:




                  Source: Research archive. Transcription follows below:
