narrative form to describe their dreams, laments, sorrows, and pains.
       The student was more concerned with writing a “poetic essay” rather than
focusing on the prompt and answering the guiding question, which points to a
dynamic of perceiving oneself as a poet. The text is evidence that the participant
felt at ease expressing their feelings, pains, and laments through poetic language.
Even without answering the guiding question “ ” for the creative piece, the
participant demonstrated freedom and affinity with the poetic text.
       We can also observe an attempt at internal rhymes that stand out:
“time/time/lament/within.” Instead of answering what it means to be a poet, the
participant decided to “Be a poet” [emphasis added].

and contradictory in equal measure. In fact, since this is a text about being a poet,

              Figure 16. Participant 07 – Text produced in the 4th workshop:

                       “Being a Poet

       Although rudimentary and with grammatical and spelling errors, the
participant demonstrated logical development of their thinking. They reflected on
what it means to be a poet and expressed it coherently. Furthermore, the
versification issues did not prevent them from clearly expressing their perception
of the poet; their sensitivity reveals a lyrical tone in the exposition of the poetic
process, while simultaneously establishing a poetic and thematic context.
       We also observed the reader’s everyday experience aligning with the
literary text, as stated in Jauss’s (1994) 7th thesis, and a concern with the work’s
aesthetic experience and the meanings of the text for its better perception,
pointing to the 4th and 5th theses of Reception Aesthetics.


           Figure 17. Participant 09 – Textual production from the 4th workshop:




                  Source: Research archive. Transcription follows below:


                       “Being a poet isn’t just about writing.
                       Poetry isn’t. It’s what was
                       Feeling. Being a poet is
                       to lay bare the soul.


                                                                                          365

                        The poet
                        A poet’s verses
                        enchant with every sensation...
                        The poet draws from himself the beating
                        of his soul.”


       The participant seeks a way to express what it means to be a poet. They
offer some statements, such as that being a poet is “[...] to lay bare the soul [...]
The poet draws from within the beating of his soul.” These poetically cohesive
and coherent excerpts stand out for their poetic lyricism; thus, they excel in their
description of the poetic act , for the act of writing poetry is to give a part of oneself
to another. However, a careful observation led us to believe that the passages
are superimposed and do not follow the same linguistic style, as the end of the
text features vocabulary that is unusual for the participant.
       Consequently, we conducted an online search and confirmed that the text
was indeed copied from the website “pensador.com/frase,” as the participant’s
other writings do not exhibit a well-structured poetic style. In a private
conversation, we spoke with the participant, informed them of what had
happened, expressed our disappointment, and asked that this not occur again in
their academic and personal life, as plagiarism is a crime under Article 184 of the
Penal Code. The first part “[...] to bare the soul” was copied from the text by Neusa
Marilda4 and the second part “[...] to pulse from your soul” was taken from the text
“O Poeta” by Mara Hernandes5 , as shown on the website cited above. We
decided to include the text here as a precaution for works of this nature, especially
since the authors are not identified. Participants 03 and 08 did not wish to
participate, so we respected their wishes and rights.

                   Source: Research archive. Transcription follows below:

5 https://www.pensador.com/frase/NzIzMDc2/

                       “I am sensitive to any suffering. I go from sadness
                       to contentment. I feel sad, I feel
                       happy. I am like a river or an empty well
                       and whether I suffer or smile, it is because I am a poet.
                       Being a poet means taking a slap in the face and not always

                       It’s also being silly and writing a bald poem,
                       thinking it’s full-headed.”


       The participant found a lyrical way to express their thoughts on being a
poet. The text features a freer verse form and includes chained rhymes, departing
from the classical aesthetic pattern: suffering/contentment, river/emptiness, and
poet/goofball/bald. They attempted to paraphrase the source text and added
some elements that indicate an effort to meet the prompt’s requirements. They
constructed an imperfect rhyming scheme (assonance/rhyme): “world.../hairy”
and successfully addressed what it means to be a poet, presenting a poetic
contextualization.
       There was a concern with maintaining the theme, as we observed that the
author manages to detach from the source text and express themselves
autonomously, presenting thematic and presentific contextualizations, also
through application in practical life, as in: “Being a poet is putting yourself out
there and not always pleasing everyone...” highlighting Jauss’s (1994) 7th thesis.
       Here we have reached, for now, the conclusion of this phase of our
research. The level of poetic elaboration in Cecília Meireles’s poem aimed to
achieve the objective of breaking with the horizon of expectations, understanding,
and   interpretation    regarding     thematic     contextualization,      presentational
contextualization, poetic and stylistic contextualizations, as well as the
observation of Jauss’s (1994) theses, according to Reception Aesthetics, also
considered in this work, and which, in a certain way, we saw were met by the
participants’ poetic gaze.
       Thematic contextualization, possibly the most basic, came to the fore and
also enabled the presence of presentifying reflections, observed in most of the
texts produced by the students. As for poetic language, we intended for the
participants to construct a text prioritizing literary style, which, in a certain way,
they also did. The reading of the poem “Motivo” highlighted the stylistic distance
from previous poems and the use of standard norms, prompting the participants
to engage in moments of writing and even rewriting their own lyrical texts.



                                                                                     367

      The use of standard language in the poem is evident, with a smooth and
delicate style that facilitates metapoetry—that is, it highlights the poetic moment,
the present moment of life. The subjectivity of the theme was not enough to hinder
a comprehensive understanding, and the participants were able to meet the
expectations of broadening their horizons by breaking away from colloquial and
regional language while reading the literary text. The proposal to broaden the
horizon of expectations arose from the lexical choices and text construction that
present, even if in a basic way, poetic elements through the reading of the poem
“Motivo” by Cecília Meireles. Due to the aesthetic and stylistic approach of the
text, which belongs to the canon of Brazilian literature from the second modernist
phase, the poem challenged the participants, but it did not prevent them from
constructing their own works with poetic elements in a colloquial language
characteristic of their reading experience.


5. FINAL CONSIDERATIONS


      Regarding the workshops conducted, the participants revealed their
personal experiences primarily through contextualizations that brought the
present into focus and thematic explorations. From this perspective, we can
understand that their life experiences and interpretations of the world align with
the narratives of the texts they read. Even with the superficiality of some texts
produced by the participants, revealing great difficulty in developing their
writing—especially in spelling, syntax, and thematic organization—the texts
produced here show us that EJA students can produce texts in which they
express their emotions, values, and desires for a more just and democratic life.
      It is evident from the interpretations presented by the participants that they
faced significant difficulty in organizing their ideas in a cohesive and coherent
manner; however, the vast majority of the texts produced do, to some extent,
address the thematic and presentational contexts and, at times, the poetic
context, as Cosson (2011) explains in the expanded sequence. Thus, from the
perspective of literary development, it was possible to spark a curious interest in
literature and, above all, in the aspects of popular culture found in the loas of
maracatu de baque solto, which resulted in the final production of presentations



                                                                                368

for the TCEF— -Conclusion of Elementary School Projects—whose themes were
developed around the subject of maracatu de baque solto.
       The more erudite language of Cecília Meireles’ text introduced a new
setting and a more canonical language, embodying literary language,
estrangement, lyricism, and poetry for the research participants. The difficulties
in written production point to challenges that need to be overcome. The objective
of the proposal, however, was achieved, as the introduction of literary literacy
occurs through access to the text, by breaking down the barriers of the literary
world, and through the encouragement and promotion of reading and writing that
took place throughout the workshops.
       The greatest challenge, however, does not end here. The continuation of
literary activities, reading practices, and access to popular culture must continue
to encourage adult education students to remain motivated to read literary texts.
Reading develops through practice, dialogue, the exchange of experiences, and
the encouragement that is also the role of the school.
       The findings of this research may help other researchers and teachers to
use the tools proposed here, as well as other sources of popular culture, to
facilitate literary literacy practices.
       The appreciation of local cultures, knowledge, and cultural practices is of
great importance for the restoration of citizenship, empowerment, and a sense of
belonging to the local culture. The search for one’s origins and their significance
helps build a people’s identity. Literature has the social role of documenting these
practices and reflecting customs and cultures in its stories. That is why we often
identify with characters or even with settings presented in texts.
       An educational approach that values popular culture and draws on the
Receptive Method in conjunction with the Literary Literacy methodology offers a
new perspective on a potential methodological path that is relevant to educational
practice, as the development of reading skills requires a structured sequence and
instructional support that facilitate gradual progress.
       Schools must foster an engaging environment, value reading through
human experience, and provide support, guidance, and acceptance of the
interpretations and contextualizations that emerge from this context, particularly
for adult learners. But, of course, this also depends on the student’s willingness.
There must be receptivity and empathy toward the approach and the texts.The


                                                                                369

reader of a literary text must interact with the text, engage with it, discuss it,
devour it, and reflect on it so that both reader and text can build literary literacy—
that is, proficient reading.
       Therefore, one cannot assume that the reader of a literary text is ready or
fully prepared solely through the pedagogical approaches implemented at school;
however, by valuing the student’s potential and believing in the process of literary
literacy, it is possible to expand the reading of literary texts.

 ACTIVE METHODOLOGIES IN

ABSTRACT: The transformation of higher education in health demands
strategies that promote student autonomy and critical thinking, and although
active methodologies are recognized as strategic tools, their application in
complex disciplines such as Epidemiology remains incipient. This study aimed to
map and critically analyze the scientific production between 2020 and 2025 on
active methodologies in undergraduate health education, with a specific focus on
the teaching of Epidemiology. This is an integrative review according to
Whittemore and Knafl, conducted on the CAPES Platform (SciELO, PubMed,
LILACS, ERIC). Of the initial search of 676 records, 97 met the eligibility criteria.
The results revealed a predominance of qualitative research (68.5%) and
experience reports, concentrated in Medicine (37.1%) and Nursing (33%). The
most frequent strategies were Gamification (39.2%), ICTs (30.9%), and
Simulation (18.6%), with recurring methodological combinations. The main
associated results included engagement (Gamification, 84%), critical reasoning
(Clinical Case, 94%), and interactivity (ICTs, 80%). Epidemiology showed the
lowest representation (4.1%), highlighting underutilization of active strategies,
especially gamification. It is concluded that active methodologies demonstrate


                                                                                 372

consistent benefits for health education, but a paradox persists between their
potential and marginal application in the teaching of Epidemiology. This gap
demands urgent investments in research and specific pedagogical development
for this discipline.

KEYWORDS: active methodologies, health education, epidemiology, under-
graduate studies.

RESUMO: A transformação do ensino superior em saúde demanda estratégias
que promovam autonomia e criticidade discente, e embora as metodologias
ativas sejam reconhecidas como ferramentas estratégicas, sua aplicação em
disciplinas complexas como a Epidemiologia permanece incipiente. Este estudo
teve como objetivo mapear e analisar criticamente a produção científica entre
2020 e 2025 sobre metodologias ativas na graduação em saúde, com recorte
específico para o ensino de Epidemiologia. Trata-se de uma revisão integrativa
conforme Whittemore e Knafl, conduzida na Plataforma CAPES (SciELO,
PubMed, LILACS, ERIC). Da busca inicial de 676 registros, 97 atenderam aos
critérios de elegibilidade. Os resultados revelaram predominância de pesquisas
qualitativas (68,5%) e relatos de experiência, concentrados em Medicina (37,1%)
e Enfermagem (33%). As estratégias mais frequentes foram Gamificação
(39,2%), TICs (30,9%) e Simulação (18,6%), com combinações metodológicas
recorrentes. Os principais resultados associados incluíram engajamento
(Gamificação, 84%), raciocínio crítico (Caso Clínico, 94%) e interatividade (TICs,
80%). A Epidemiologia apresentou a menor representatividade (4,1%),
evidenciando subutilização de estratégias ativas, especialmente gamificação.
Conclui-se que as metodologias ativas demonstram benefícios consistentes para
o ensino em saúde, porém persiste um paradoxo entre seu potencial e a
aplicação marginal no ensino de Epidemiologia. Tal lacuna demanda
investimentos urgentes em pesquisa e desenvolvimento pedagógico específico
para esta disciplina

PALAVRAS-CHAVE: metodologias ativas, ensino em saúde, epidemiologia,
graduação.




                                                                              373

1. INTRODUCTION


       Epidemiology involves the study of factors that impact the health-disease
process in individuals and populations, encompassing concepts such as
morbidity, mortality, incidence, and life expectancy (Souza et al., 2010). It is a
field that integrates contributions from statistics, medicine, and public health,
without dissociating itself from the critical understanding provided by the
humanities      (Barata,   1997).   Epidemiology    is   considered    essential    in
undergraduate health programs, as it enables the identification of disease
mechanisms, the development of health profiles, and the guidance of priority
interventions (Souza et al., 2010). When well- , it can be applied to identifying
needs, risks, and priorities in health services, thereby facilitating the optimization
of resources.
       In recent years, epidemiology has gained prominence due to the COVID-
19 pandemic, a context in which much of the scientific evidence underpinning
health recommendations stemmed from epidemiological studies (Netto; Corrêa,
2020). However, the multifaceted nature of the discipline poses challenges to its
teaching, especially given the growing complexity of the content and the need to
formulate cohesive methodologies (Cauduro; Kuchenbecher, 2011). Added to
this is the fact that epidemiology involves mathematical knowledge, an area often
associated with difficulties for undergraduate students (Vilaça et al., 2020). In this
context, using the difficulties in teaching through the traditional method as a
premise, we sought to investigate the advantages associated with the application
of active methodologies, with a focus on the Epidemiology component, through
an integrative literature review.


2. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK


       Higher education institutions play a fundamental role in training
professionals capable of meeting the demands of the labor market, requiring
continuous adjustments to teaching-learning processes (Lacerda; Machado,
2024). In the face of social transformations, traditional teaching approaches have
proven insufficient, making a rethinking of higher education necessary (Leão,
1999). A central aspect is the promotion of student autonomy, linked to the


                                                                                   374

renewal of the student profile in the face of new technologies (Torres; Hilu;
Siqueira, 2015). This connection between learning and autonomous development
highlights that the educational process fulfills a social and political duty by
promoting the exercise of citizenship (Dewey, 2007).
       In this context, active methodologies emerge as spaces that allow students
to develop self-governance, autonomy, and reflective processes (Oliveira, 2019).
The literature legitimizes them as relevant mechanisms for stimulating critical
thinking, problem-solving skills, and the alignment between theory and everyday
reality (Oliveira, 2019).


2.1 THE USE OF ACTIVE METHODOLOGIES IN HEALTH COURSES


       The application of active methodologies in formal education in Brazil
intensified starting in the 2000s with the implementation of the National
Curriculum Guidelines for undergraduate health programs, resulting in initiatives
such as the Aprender SUS Program and the National Policy on Continuing
Education (Prado; Velho, 2012).
       A variety of successful experiences could then be observed. In the
Master’s in Nursing program at UFSC (2012), the Maguerez Arc proved effective
in stimulating curiosity and promoting action-reflection-action (Prado; Velho,
2012). In the Medicine program at Universidade Vila Velha (2015), the
combination of the Maguerez Arc with PBL sparked students’ interest in social
awareness (Dalla; Moura; Bergamaschi, 2015). At UFRJ, 78% of students
perceived themselves as active learners, and 92% felt better prepared to work in
the public health system (Gomes et al., 2010). In the Dentistry classes at UEPB,
the Critical-Reflective Portfolio and ICTs fostered a critical-reflective profile (Reul
et al., 2016). The use of gamification in the Bioethics component, through Kahoot,
increased motivation in dense content (Maranhão; Reis, 2019). These
experiences demonstrate the success of active methodologies in promoting
autonomy, active participation, and critical thinking.




                                                                                   375

2.2 THE TEACHING OF EPIDEMIOLOGY IN UNDERGRADUATE EDUCATION


         The teaching of epidemiology in Brazil began in the 1920s, closely linked
to Public Health, incorporating social sciences and statistical techniques (Barata,
1997). The training was guided by social epidemiology, based on the humanities,
addressing social determinants of the health-disease process (Barata, 1997).
         Currently, the complexity of this component has increased, presenting
challenges to faculty in formulating cohesive methodologies (Cauduro;
Kuchenbecher, 2011). Authors suggest that small-group approaches, using
collaborative platforms, can be valuable for deepening knowledge (Cauduro;
Kuchenbecher, 2011). Playful activities foster the development of critical thinking
skills and teamwork (Silva; Oliveira; Silva, 2018).
         In the face of social transformations, higher education must adapt to
enable students to achieve the expected competencies (Lacerda; Machado,
2024). Active methodologies emerge as strategies that foster the development of
autonomy, critical-social reflection, and student agency (Leão, 1999; Oliveira,
2019).


3. METHODOLOGY


         This is an integrative literature review conducted on the CAPES Journal
Platform (SciELO, PubMed, LILACS, and ERIC databases), following the five
steps outlined by Whittemore and Knafl (2005). The guiding question was
structured based on the PICo framework (Cochrane, 2023): Population –
undergraduate health students; Interest – application of active methodologies;
Context – curricular components in Brazil between 2020 and 2025. The following
Boolean combinations were used: (“Active methodologies”) AND (“Health
undergraduate programs”) and (“Active methodologies”) AND (“Teaching of
epidemiology”), with filters for empirical articles, case studies, and experience
reports in Portuguese, English, and Spanish, with open access.
         Initially, 676 articles were identified; 53 duplicates were removed. During
the screening of titles and abstracts, conducted by two independent reviewers,
354 studies were excluded for being outside the scope. Of the 269 articles
selected for full-text review, the following exclusion criteria were applied: not


                                                                                376

focusing on undergraduate health students (47), being a systematic review or
meta-analysis (43), and restricted access (21). Ultimately, 97 studies comprised
the sample.
       The data were then organized into spreadsheets, from which descriptive
variables (author, year, country, methodological design) and thematic variables
(type of active methodology, curricular component, learning outcomes) were
extracted. The analysis combined quantitative (frequencies and correlations) and
qualitative (categorical synthesis of benefits, challenges, and emerging patterns)
approaches. The results were organized into a PRISMA® flowchart, comparative
tables, and a critical synthesis.

4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION


       The temporal distribution of publications reveals progressive growth
between 2020 and 2025, peaking in 2023–2024. Of the 97 articles analyzed,
97.9% are from Brazil. The qualitative approach predominates (68.5%), followed
by action research (13.7%). Regarding undergraduate fields, Medicine (37.1%)
and Nursing (33%) are the most represented, while Speech-Language Pathology
(4.1%) and Occupational Therapy (3.1%) have the lowest frequencies. In terms
of fields of knowledge, Public Health and Management (14.4%) leads, with a
focus on subfields such as health policies and the SUS, followed by
Morphofunctional Sciences (13.4%) and Nursing Practices (12.4%).

       Among active methodologies, gamification (39.2%) and ICTs (30.9%) are
the most widely used, with frequent combinations: gamification with ICTs (12
instances), ICTs with the flipped classroom (10), clinical case studies with
simulation (9), and problem-solving with the Maguerez Arc (8). Regarding the
associated outcomes, the following stand out: engagement for gamification (84%
of the studies), critical thinking for clinical cases (94%), interactivity for ICTs
(80%), and contextualized reflection for problem-based learning (93%).
Methodologies such as Maguerez’s Arc, conversation circles, and dialogic
classes show a 100% association with their main outcomes.

       The results show a predominance of qualitative research, with a lower
frequency of experimental or longitudinal studies, indicating that most of the
evidence derives from practical applications in real classroom contexts (Ferreira;
Santos, 2021). The scarcity of controlled studies limits the ability to establish
direct causal relationships between methodologies and learning outcomes
(Gomes, 2001). A significant concentration of studies is observed in Medicine and
Nursing, while Speech-Language Pathology and Occupational Therapy are less
represented. Regarding complementary approaches, a frequent combination was
observed between Gamification and ICTs and between Clinical Case and
Simulation, indicating recurring practices of integration between active strategies
(Sandmann et al., 2023).
       Regarding        curricular     components,         Public      Health/SUS         and
Morphofunctional Sciences are the most studied categories, while Epidemiology


                                                                                           380

appears with significantly lower frequency (4.1%). There is a notable absence of
studies specifically testing gamification for epidemiology, although articles on
gamification    report   improved    content    retention—a     relevant   skill   for
epidemiological calculations (Vilaça et al., 2020). The data reveal a contradiction
between the frequency of gamification and its underutilization in epidemiology
education, given its potential for engagement and content retention (Tolomei,
2017).


4.1 MOST COMMON STRATEGIES


4.1.1 Gamification


         The 38 articles analyzed demonstrate that gamification facilitates
knowledge assimilation and makes the educational dynamic more participatory
(Monteiro et al., 2020). This approach connects students’ technological world to
pedagogical objectives, allowing for the exploration of different learning profiles
(Rocha et al., 2021; Silva et al., 2022). It provides fun and relaxation, stimulating
creativity and interaction (Botelho et al., 2023). Diversifying assessment methods
increases motivation and engagement (Oliveira et al., 2023). Playful teaching has
proven effective in understanding and reviewing content (Costa et al., 2020;
Faustino et al., 2020), encouraging teamwork (Lima et al., 2024; Mendes et al.,
2024). In Biochemistry, educational games have improved knowledge acquisition
and made content more accessible (Alcantara et al., 2022; Marinho et al., 2023),
in addition to developing interpersonal skills (Laguna; Marques, 2022).
         The effectiveness of games depends on a design tailored to disciplinary
objectives (Singh et al., 2024) and the quality of gameplay (Silva et al., 2022).
"Serious games" are relevant in healthcare because they allow for the safe
simulation of procedures (Aquino et al., 2022). However, implementation faces
challenges: it is essential to establish clear goals (Marcuzzo et al., 2023); many
faculty members lack adequate training (Monteiro et al., 2020); a lack of
technological resources can be limiting (Godoy et al., 2020); and ensuring
equitable engagement requires pedagogical sensitivity (Lima et al., 2024;
Marinho et al., 2023).



                                                                                   381

4.1.2 Information and Communication Technologies (ICTs)


         The integration of ICTs promotes interactivity, personalized teaching, and
skills development (Silva et al., 2022; Fontana et al., 2020). Proximity to
technological devices enhances technical and scientific skills (Lopes; Lenz,
2023), which is crucial in contexts where practice requires familiarity with digital
tools (Feitosa et al., 2022). New generations find technology to be a natural
language (Mendes et al., 2024). ICTs foster skills in teachers and students
(Ribeiro; Abbade, 2024). Examples include linking content to pop culture
(Mendonça et al., 2023). The National Curriculum Guidelines highlight the
importance of technological integration (Damázio et al., 2022). Modalities such
as synchronous and asynchronous remote learning have tended to remain
(Fleury; Possolli, 2022; Maia et al., 2020).
         Teachers’ technological training is crucial (Marcuzzo et al., 2023).
Audiovisual resources aid in knowledge construction (Almeida et al., 2024;
Cunha et al., 2020). Key challenges include: adapting assessment processes
(Botelho et al., 2023), students’ difficulty in stepping outside their comfort zone
(Cavalcante et al., 2023), and limitations in teacher qualifications (Celeste;
Dourado, 2021). Addressing these challenges depends on the institution’s role in
promoting courses on active methodologies (Silva; Irineu, 2021).


4.1.3 Simulation


         Simulation promotes the integration of theory and practice in a safe
manner (Fernandes et al., 2021), preparing students for ethical dilemmas (Ferraz
et al., 2021). Maestri et al. (2020) warn of a dissonance between innovative
discourse and practice that remains centered on lecture-based classes. When
well-structured, it allows for the practice of clinical reasoning (Ximenes et al.,
2020).
         Simulating cases involving bioethical dilemmas develops skills for
multiprofessional decision-making (Ferraz et al., 2021). Regarding emotional
aspects, it can generate anxiety (Ferraz et al., 2021). The role of the tutor- r is
crucial for creating a safe environment (Godoy et al., 2020), with structured
feedback being an essential step (Santana et al., 2023). It has proven effective


                                                                                382

in developing technical and non-technical skills (Silva et al., 2023). It allows for
practice in Primary Care without exposing patients to risks (Gaspar et al., 2023).
Limitations include: challenges in the teaching transition (Maestri et al., 2020),
difficulty in maintaining interest (Gaspar et al., 2023), low realism of scenarios
(Godoy et al., 2020), and increased planning time (Gaspar et al., 2023).


4.2 EPIDEMIOLOGY AND ACTIVE METHODOLOGIES


      Epidemiology     education    has    incorporated    active   methodologies,
especially during emergency remote learning (Ries et al., 2023). Gamification
emerges as a promising strategy (Silva et al., 2023). Successful experiences
have combined networked technologies and active methodologies, enabling
student-centered learning (Ries et al., 2025), which requires faculty professional
development (Lopes; Lenz, 2023).
      The pandemic has accelerated the adoption of these methodologies,
which draw on real-world problems (Aquino et al., 2022). Group dynamics and
problem-based scenarios help students engage with the realities of the SUS
(Maia et al., 2020). Educational games prove valuable, stimulating interactive
learning (Rodrigues et al., 2020). Gamification allows for the simulation of real-
world situations, facilitating the understanding of complex concepts, provided it is
aligned with pedagogical objectives (Maia et al., 2020; Ries et al., 2023).
Challenges include teachers’ technological fluency (Ries et al., 2023) and striking
a balance between competition and collaboration (Rodrigues et al., 2020). The
integration of active methodologies with epidemiology promotes the acquisition
of theoretical knowledge and the development of practical skills (Cauduro;
Kuchenbecher, 2011).


4.3 PEDAGOGICAL IMPACTS


      Active methodologies promote a paradigm shift, breaking away from the
traditional teacher-centered model and establishing the student as the
protagonist (Cunha et al., 2020). They foster a problem-based construction of
knowledge, developing higher-order cognitive skills (Neto et al., 2022). Group
dynamics develop argumentation and the organization of thought (Laguna;


                                                                                383

Marques, 2022). They prove effective in promoting critical thinking and socio-
emotional skills (Passos et al., 2024), stimulating creativity and collaboration
(Araujo et al., 2024). Democratic collectives are formed (Souza; Duque, 2023).
         In healthcare, they foster a humanistic, critical, and reflective mindset
(Delfino; Caprara, 2020), moving beyond rote memorization. Dialogic practices
are more effective in knowledge retention (Santos; Santos, 2021). Student
agency promotes self-directed learning (Marques, 2023; Leitão et al., 2023).
However, implementation requires curricular changes (Silva et al., 2024) and
faculty adaptation to overcome resistance (Cardoso et al., 2021; Fontana et al.,
2020).


5. CONCLUSION


         This study systematized evidence on the use of active methodologies in
health undergraduate programs, with a focus on the teaching of Epidemiology.
The results show a concentration of studies in Nursing and Medicine, with
gamification, ICTs, and simulation being the most commonly used strategies,
offering multiple benefits for the teaching-learning process. However, few studies
were found describing the use of active methodologies in the teaching of
Epidemiology, especially gamification. The studies point to positive impacts on
student education, and despite the challenges, a growing trend in publications is
observed. The inherent weaknesses of integrative reviews, such as publication
bias and subjectivity in analysis, are acknowledged, and peer review was adopted
to mitigate these limitations.

CHAPTER 22
 VIOLENCE AT SCHOOL: A
 PRELIMINARY STUDY INDICATIVE
 OF PUBLIC POLICIES FOR
 EDUCATING CITIES


Maria Sílvia Bacila
Doctorate in Education from Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Paraná
(PUCPR)
Universidade Tecnológica Federal do Paraná (UTFPR)
E-mail: bacila@utfpr.edu.br


ABSTRACT: Violence at school is a complex and impactful phenomenon, which
encompasses aggressive, threatening and harmful behaviors in the school
environment, such as bullying, physical and verbal aggression, discrimination
and vandalism. This study had the general objective of understanding the nature
of violence at school and the specific objectives of identifying the types of
violence prevalent in educational cities, as well as evaluating managers'
perceptions of its impact on the school environment and student performance.
Carried out through a survey-type research, the target population were
educational managers from educating cities belonging to the Brazilian Network
of Educating Cities (with 9 respondents from atotal of 33 member cities), using
the data collection technique through questionnaires via Google Forms.
Data analysis was qualitative and/or quantitative. Based on authors such as
Abamovay and Rua (2002), Guimarães (1998), Maldonado (2011), Matos and
Gonçalves (2009), Teixeira and Kassouf (2015), the study focused on 9
member cities of the Brazilian network of educating cities, committed with
the promotion of education. The results highlighted the importance of public
policies in educational cities to promote safe and           welcoming school
environments, aiming to prevent violence and improve students' academic
performance. For future studies, it is recommended to further explore the
underlying causes of violence in schools, as well as investigate effective
prevention and intervention strategies. Furthermore, it would be relevant to study
the relationship between school violence and academic performance in the long
term, as well as investigate the role of families and the community in
promoting safe and healthy school environments.

KEYWORDS: public policy, educating cities, violence at school.

RESUMO: A violência na escola é um fenômeno complexo e impactante,
que abrange comportamentos agressivos, ameaçadores e prejudiciais no
ambiente escolar, como bullying, agressões físicas, verbais, discriminação e
vandalismo. Este estudo teve como objetivo geral compreender a natureza da


                                                                              391

violência na escola e como objetivos específicos identificar os tipos de
violência prevalentes em cidades educadoras, bem como avaliar a
percepção dos gestores sobre seu impacto no ambiente escolar e
desempenho dos estudantes. Realizado por meio de uma pesquisa do tipo
levantamento, a população-alvo foram gestores educacionais de cidades
educadoras pertencentes à Rede Brasileira de Cidades Educadoras (sendo 9
respondentes de um total de 33 cidades membro), utilizando a técnica de
coleta de dados por questionários via Google Forms. A análise dos dados foi
qualitativa e/ou quantitativa. Embasado em autores como Abamovay e Rua
(2002), Guimarães (1998), Maldonado (2011), Matos e Gonçalves (2009),
Teixeira e Kassouf (2015), o estudo focou em 9 cidades membros da rede
brasileira de cidades educadoras, comprometidas com a promoção da
educação. Os resultados destacaram a importância das políticas públicas em
cidades educadoras para promover ambientes escolares seguros e acolhedores,
visando à prevenção da violência e ao melhor desempenho acadêmico dos
estudantes. Para estudos futuros, recomenda-se explorar mais a fundo as
causas subjacentes da violência nas escolas, bem como investigar estratégias
eficazes de prevenção e intervenção. Além disso, seria relevante estudar a
relação entre a violência escolar e o desempenho acadêmico a longo prazo,
assim como investigar o papel das famílias e da comunidade na promoção de
ambientes escolares seguros e saudáveis.

PALAVRAS-CHAVE: políticas públicas, cidades educadoras, violência na
escola.




                                                                         392

1. INTRODUCTION


      School violence is a complex and impactful phenomenon that
encompasses a range of aggressive, threatening, or harmful behaviors occurring
in the school environment. These behaviors may include bullying, physical and
verbal aggression, discrimination, harassment, vandalism, among others. School
violence can have various origins, such as family, social, psychological, and
cultural issues, in addition to being influenced by the school environment itself.
      The occurrence of violence in schools can have several serious
consequences, not only for the victims but also for the perpetrators and for the
overall atmosphere of the educational environment. Victims may suffer
emotional, psychological, and physical harm, which affects their academic
performance, mental well-being, and social well-being. Violence can also
contribute to school dropout rates, increased misbehavior, the deterioration of
interpersonal relationships, and student demotivation.
      To address school violence, it is essential that educational administrators,
teachers, students, and families are engaged in strategies to prevent and combat
this problem. The implementation of school coexistence policies, social-
emotional learning programs, and teacher training to identify and intervene in
cases of violence, promoting dialogue and a culture of peace are some of the
measures that can contribute to building a safe, inclusive, and learning-friendly
school environment.
      Addressing violence in schools requires a multidisciplinary approach,
involving not only repressive measures but also the promotion of ethical values,
mutual respect, empathy, and citizenship. It is essential that school systems
remain attentive to the demands and challenges related to school violence in
order to constantly seek to improve their practices and policies to ensure a
healthy and welcoming educational environment for all involved.
      According to Abramovay and Rua (2002) cited in Teixeira and Kassouf
(2015), violence in schools is not a new issue in the modern Western world. Since
the first studies conducted on the subject in the United States in the 1950s,
various facets of this phenomenon have undergone significant changes,
becoming even more concerning. Phenomena such as the emergence of
weapons in schools, the spread of drug use, and the expansion of gangs—often


                                                                                393

associated with drug trafficking—have profoundly impacted the school
environment, requiring increasingly effective responses.
       According to Guimarães (1998), school violence in Brazil has shown an
alarming increase in recent years, characterized, in particular, by the marked
presence of drug trafficking, gangs, and extreme poverty. In a study conducted
in several state capitals across the country, Abramovay and Rua (2002)
concluded that physical violence and property damage are the predominant types
of violence in schools, which have generated significant negative impacts on the
quality of teaching and learning. These effects have considerable repercussions
on the development of the country’s human capital, a crucial element for
economic development.
       The main objective of this study was to understand the origins of violence
in educational institutions. Furthermore, the study sought to identify the different
types of violence frequently observed in school environments in cities focused on
education. Additionally, it aimed to analyze the perceptions of school
administrators regarding the impact of this violence on the school climate and
students’ academic performance.


2. RESEARCH IN EDUCATING CITIES


       In this study, the research was a survey, with the target population being
educational administrators in the Educating Cities belonging to Rebrace, with 9
administrators responding out of a total of 33. The data collection technique used
was through questionnaires in Google Forms format. The analysis of the collected
data was conducted qualitatively and/or quantitatively. It is important to note that
the questionnaires were completed after the participants provided their free and
informed consent, to ensure ethics and transparency in the research process.
       The study is based on nine member cities of the Brazilian network of
Educating Cities and indicates a specific research focus on these locations, which
share a commitment to promoting education as a central pillar of their
administration, in line with the principles of the Charter of Educating Cities.
       This choice suggests that the research seeks to explore how these cities
have addressed the issue of violence in schools, considering education as a



                                                                                  394

fundamental tool for promoting school environments that are safer, more
inclusive, and conducive to student development.
       By focusing on these cities, the study seeks to understand and share best
practices, policies, and strategies that these municipalities have adopted to
prevent and combat violence in schools, in order to promote a culture of peace
and respect, as advocated by the Educating Cities approach. This integrated and
educational approach reflects the importance of considering education a central
pillar for building more just and equitable societies.
       The Charter of Educating Cities highlights the importance of promoting a
safe and inclusive school environment, free from violence. It emphasizes that
member cities commit to ensuring that schools are spaces of a community that
promotes peace, solidarity, and mutual respect, with the aim of protecting the
fundamental rights of all students.
       Furthermore, the charter emphasizes the responsibility of cities to foster
the development of critical and active citizens, capable of contributing to the
construction of a more just and egalitarian society. In this sense, the prevention
of violence in schools is essential to ensure that students can enjoy an
environment conducive to learning, personal development, and the exercise of
citizenship.
       The Charter of Educating Cities highlights the importance of promoting
schools as safe and welcoming spaces, where violence is combated and
replaced by values of respect, dialogue, and cooperation, thereby contributing to
the formation of a more just and democratic society.
       Survey research, also known as a survey, is a widely used method for
collecting information about a specific population, usually through standardized
questionnaires distributed to participants. This type of research seeks to obtain a
general and representative overview of the opinions, attitudes, behaviors, or
characteristics of a given group regarding the topic under investigation.
       By analyzing the data collected through these questionnaires, it is possible
to identify trends, patterns, and correlations that help understand the nature and
extent of the problem of school violence, as well as inform the development of
more effective and targeted prevention and intervention strategies and policies.
Survey-type research allows for a systematic and quantitative approach to



                                                                               395

investigating the issue of school violence and can provide valuable insights for
the development of solutions and preventive measures.
       In the first set of questions in the survey on school violence, the specific
aim was to investigate school administrators’ perceptions regarding three
important aspects: the volume of violence cases, the impact of violence on
student performance, and the adequacy of teacher training for addressing
violence.
       Perceptions regarding the volume of cases in educational institutions can
be fundamental to understanding the severity of the problem and directing efforts
toward the implementation of preventive and corrective measures. About 55.6%
of the 9 respondents consider level 5 to be very serious; 22.2% consider level 4
to be serious; 11.1% consider it moderately serious; and 11.1% do not consider
this increase to be noticeable.
       By asking how administrators view violence affecting student performance,
the survey seeks to understand whether there is an awareness of the negative
effects that violence can have on students’ emotional, social, and academic well-
being, as well as on the quality of the learning environment. Of the 9 respondents,
88.9% consider that violence affects student performance to the maximum
extent, and 11.1% consider it to be at level 4.
       The study by Teixeira and Kassouf (2015) states:


                       It is not possible to state with certainty exactly how the impact of
                       violence manifests itself on academic performance. However, it can be
                       inferred that violence in schools diminishes students’ concentration,
                       reduces class attendance, and also increases demotivation and
                       turnover among teachers.


       The quote from Teixeira and Kassouf (2015) highlights the complexity of
accurately quantifying the effects of school violence on academic performance.
Although it is difficult to establish a direct relationship, the study suggests that the
presence of violence in schools can result in negative impacts, such as reduced
student concentration, decreased class attendance, and increased demotivation,
which in turn may contribute to high teacher turnover. These findings highlight the
need to understand the dynamics and consequences of violence in the school
environment in order to implement effective strategies aimed at improving the




                                                                                        396

quality of education and promoting safe and conducive environments for teaching
and learning.
       The question regarding administrators’ perceptions of teacher training
aims to assess how they view this training and whether it is aligned with the needs
and challenges related to school violence. Questions related to prevention
interventions, conflict mediation, identifying signs of violence and providing
emotional support to students may be involved in this aspect. An average of
22.2% of the 9 respondents believe that teacher training meets the needs, 55.6%
rate it at level 4; 11.1% consider the possibility to be moderate, and 11.1% rate it
at level 2, which falls short of the ability to positively meet the demand.
       In the aforementioned study, the second set of questions aimed primarily
to investigate administrators’ perceptions regarding the incidence of different
types of violence in schools. The frequently encountered types of violence that
were assessed include: verbal and physical violence, as well as bullying in its
various forms.
       When examining the type of violence present in the school environment, it
can be observed that verbal violence predominates over physical violence. Of the
9 respondents, 77.8% admit that they sometimes encounter verbal violence at
school, 11.1% frequently, and 11.1% rarely. Regarding physical violence, 11.1%
admit to encountering it frequently at school, 44.4% sometimes, 22.2% rarely,
and 22.2% never.
       Verbal violence includes insults, threats, name-calling, and other forms of
verbal aggression. Physical violence involves direct physical aggression, such as
punching, kicking, shoving, and other forms of physical violence. Bullying
involves aggressive and repetitive behavior among students, characterized by an
imbalance of power.


                      Bullying is one of the most common forms of behavior in our society, in
                      which those perceived as weaker are dominated. Men oppress their
                      partners, and older children oppress younger ones. Although bullying is
                      considered a form of violence, it is not given the attention it deserves.
                      For example, most people working in schools, including faculty, do not
                      view such behaviors as threats or oppression—that is, as acts of
                      violence. (Matos; Gonçalves, 2009, p. 4).


       Matos and Gonçalves highlight an important and troubling issue regarding
how bullying is often downplayed or ignored in our society. They point out that


                                                                                           397

bullying is a form of violence that is often devalued or tolerated, especially when
directed at groups considered weaker or more vulnerable.
      The excerpt highlights that bullying manifests itself in various contexts,
ranging from peer relationships to school and home environments. They also
emphasize that bullying can occur not only among children but also in adult
relationships, such as men’s domination over their partners. Furthermore, the
quote raises the issue of a lack of awareness and understanding regarding the
impact of bullying, especially among professionals working in environments
where it is most common, such as schools. The failure to recognize bullying
behaviors as forms of violence can lead to underestimating the severity of the
problem and consequently hinder the implementation of effective measures to
prevent and combat bullying.
      It is necessary to recognize and address bullying as a serious form of
violence that can have profound and lasting impacts on victims. Therefore,
awareness, education, and the adoption of preventive measures are fundamental
to combating bullying and promoting safer and more respectful environments.
      In the survey, bullying was reported by the 9 respondents as frequently
occurring in 22.2% of cases, sometimes in 66.7% of cases, and rarely in 11.1%
of cases. The most common types of bullying investigated are: verbal bullying,
which includes insults, derogatory nicknames, and defamation; physical bullying,
which involves repeated physical aggression, such as pushing, kicking, and
punching; cyberbullying, which refers to online harassment or intimidation
through digital tools such as social media, instant messaging, and email, among
others; social exclusion, which consists of intentionally isolating, ignoring, or
excluding a person from a social group; and other forms, which may include less
common or different types of bullying, such as racial bullying and sexual bullying,
among others.
      According to Bullock (2002), cited in Matos and Gonçalves (2009, p. 5),


                      It is considered that there are three main types of bullying, namely
                      physical or direct, psychological, and indirect. The first encompasses
                      behaviors such as hitting, kicking, pushing, stealing, threatening,
                      playing in a rude and intimidating manner, and using weapons. The
                      second refers to name-calling, teasing or picking on someone, being
                      sarcastic, insulting, or abusive, making faces, and threatening. Finally,
                      the third—which is the most covert since it is not as visible—includes
                      excluding or rejecting someone from a group.



                                                                                           398

         The quote from Bullock, cited by Matos and Gonçalves, presents a
classification of the main types of bullying, highlighting three distinct categories:
physical or direct, psychological, and indirect. Each of these forms of bullying
involves different behaviors and strategies of intimidation and violence against
the victim. Below, we will briefly address each of these types:
         1. Physical or direct bullying: This is the type of bullying that involves
aggressive physical behavior, such as hitting, kicking, pushing, stealing,
threatening, intimidating in a rude manner, and even using weapons to cause
physical harm to the victim. It is a clearly visible form of violence that can result
in physical injuries and trauma for the victim.
         2. Psychological bullying: This is characterized by actions intended to
cause emotional, mental, and psychological harm to the victim. This includes
behaviors such as name-calling, intimidation, sarcasm, insults, making hurtful
comments, making faces, and verbal threats. This type of bullying can have a
significant impact on the victim’s self-esteem, mental health, and emotional well-
being.
         3. Indirect bullying: This type of bullying is more subtle and covert, as it
does not directly involve aggressive physical or verbal actions. Indirect bullying
includes behaviors such as excluding, rejecting, socially isolating, or spreading
rumors and gossip to harm the victim’s reputation and social relationships. Social
exclusion can be just as harmful as physical or verbal aggression, in addition to
causing isolation and emotional distress in the victim.
         The categorization of bullying types proposed by Bullock and mentioned
by Matos and Gonçalves highlights the diversity of forms, such as violence and
intimidation, that can manifest in the context of bullying. Understanding these
different forms of bullying is essential for identifying, preventing, and effectively
combat this complex and harmful problem, aiming to promote safer and more
respectful environments for everyone.


                        Cyberbullying is the practice of online cruelty. With the rapid
                        development of technology, cyberbullies have begun to create many
                        other ways to torment their victims. It is more terrible than bullying
                        because the harassment is relentless, potentially occurring 24 hours a
                        day, seven days a week. The victim is attacked via text or voice
                        messages on their cell phone, secretly filmed or photographed in
                        embarrassing situations that can be posted online. The perpetrator may
                        create a fake profile of the victim on social media sites to defame them



                                                                                            399

                        or alter photos in which, for example, the victim appears as a sex
                        worker, with their phone number shared through the perpetrator’s and
                        their friends’ contact lists. (Maldonado, 2011, p. 3).


       Maldonado’s      citation   highlights    the   severity    and    complexity     of
cyberbullying, emphasizing that this form of online violence is more insidious than
traditional bullying due to the constant and continuous reach that technology
offers to perpetrators. The author explores the various ways in which
cyberbullying can be perpetrated, ranging from text and voice messages to the
manipulation of photos and the creation of fake profiles to defame victims.
       This highlights how the rapid development of technology provides
aggressors with more sophisticated means to persecute, defame, and humiliate
their victims in a severe and persistent manner, transcending the limits of physical
and temporal space. The quote also highlights the extent of the harm caused by
cyberbullying, such as the dissemination of false and defamatory information,
which can have devastating repercussions on victims’ lives, including affecting
their reputation and emotional well-being.
       Maldonado’s quote underscores the need for awareness, prevention, and
action against cyberbullying and emphasizes the importance of combating this
form of online violence, which can have profound and lasting impacts on victims.
       Matos and Gonçalves (2009, p. 4) state that “bullying is intentional
behavior, with the primary objective of harming and hurting someone, and it is
repeated over time.” This statement highlights some essential points about
bullying. First, it emphasizes that bullying is intentional behavior, that is, behavior
carried out with the intention to harm or hurt someone. This implies that the
aggressor is aware of their actions and of the negative consequences they may
have on the victim.
       Furthermore, the citation emphasizes that the primary goal of bullying is to
cause harm and suffering to the victim. Bullying is often motivated by a desire for
power, control, revenge, or simply the pursuit of amusement at another’s
expense. This aspect highlights the malicious and harmful nature of bullying,
which can have significant impacts on the victim’s physical, emotional, and
psychological health.
       Another important point addressed in the quote is the repetition of the
behavior over time. This characteristic distinguishes bullying from other types of


                                                                                        400

interpersonal conflicts or isolated disagreements. The repetition of the
aggressions amplifies the victim’s suffering and creates an environment of
intimidation and constant fear, which contributes to the worsening of the harm
caused.
       The citation highlights that bullying is not a casual or sporadic behavior,
but a systematic and intentional form of violence aimed at harming the victim in
a repeated and persistent manner. Recognizing these characteristics is essential
to understanding the severity of the phenomenon of bullying and to developing
effective prevention and intervention strategies.
       Maldonado (2011, p. 3) corroborates this explanation of bullying and
distinguishes it from cyberbullying:


                       In face-to-face bullying attacks, repetition is striking, and it is one of the
                       elements that distinguishes bullying from some pranks in poor taste. In
                       cyberbullying, powerful and destructive attacks can be carried out
                       without the element of repetition, because another factor comes into
                       play that produces devastating effects: the speed at which the message
                       spreads, reaching an audience of immeasurable proportions in just a
                       few minutes. This dramatically intensifies the shame, fear, and
                       humiliation, which leaves some people feeling trapped, to the point
                       where, in desperation, they attempt suicide.


       Maldonado’s quote highlights an important distinction between traditional
bullying and cyberbullying, emphasizing the specific elements that differentiate
these forms of violence. In the case of in-person bullying, Maldonado highlights
repetition as a key factor that distinguishes prolonged aggressive behavior from
casual pranks in poor taste. On the other hand, regarding cyberbullying, she
notes that attacks can be powerful and destructive, often occurring without the
need for constant repetition, due to the rapid and massive spread of online
messages.
       Maldonado’s analysis highlights how the instant virality of messages on
the internet can exponentially amplify the impact of cyberbullying and reach a
much larger audience in a matter of minutes. This, in turn, intensifies feelings of
shame, fear, and humiliation in victims, leading some to feel trapped and
desperate, to the point of even considering suicide as a way to escape the
traumatic situation.
       By highlighting these essential differences between traditional bullying and
cyberbullying, Maldonado underscores the need to effectively understand and


                                                                                                401

address the unique challenges posed by online violence, emphasizing the
urgency of preventive and intervention measures to protect victims and combat
the spread of cyberbullying.
        Another relevant finding that contributes to understanding the issue can be
observed in the question regarding the most common types of bullying, as there
is a consensus that 75% of respondents report verbal bullying and 25% report
social exclusion, out of the 9 respondents.
        Assessing these different types of violence and bullying is essential to
understanding the dynamics and extent of the problem within the school
environment, as it enables the implementation of effective prevention and
intervention strategies.
        When asking the cities about the measures school districts have adopted
to combat violence in schools, the 9 respondents reported the implementation of
programs involving teacher training to handle adverse situations, a permanent
policy of dialogue among school staff, students, and families, psychological
support for situations identified in the school environment; coordination with the
child   welfare   network      and    adolescents.    The       responses   highlighted
interdisciplinarity and intersectorality as key factors in addressing violence in the
school environment in these cities that serve as educational hubs.
        The approach of the cities studied reflects a comprehensive and integrated
strategy for addressing school violence, highlighting the importance of a systemic
and collaborative vision to promote safer and more welcoming educational
environments. The following were highlighted:
        1. Teacher training: investing in the training of educators to handle
situations of violence is crucial, as teachers play a fundamental role in identifying,
preventing, and intervening in such cases.
        2. Ongoing   policy    of    dialogue:   establishing    open   and   effective
communication channels between school staff, students, and families is essential
to fostering an environment of trust and collaboration, promoting peaceful conflict
resolution.
        3. Psychological support: providing emotional and psychological support
to those involved in situations of violence is essential to promote the well-being
and mental health of all members of the school community.



                                                                                   402

       4. Coordination with the support network: establishing partnerships and
support networks with social services and specialized institutions to assist
children and adolescents in vulnerable situations contributes to a more
comprehensive and effective approach to combating violence.
       The emphasis on interdisciplinarity and intersectorality demonstrates an
understanding that school violence is a complex phenomenon that requires
coordinated and integrated action among different actors and sectors of society.
This collaborative and holistic approach reflects the commitment of these
Educating Cities to promoting a culture of peace and respect, while also
highlighting the importance of considering not only educational issues but also
social, emotional, and psychological factors in addressing school violence.
       The public policies of an educating city aim to promote safe and welcoming
school environments, adopting comprehensive approaches and integrated
approaches to address violence in schools. In this regard, the research highlights
the importance of a systemic and collaborative perspective. Investing in teacher
training is crucial, as teachers play a fundamental role in identifying, preventing,
and intervening in cases of violence. In addition, a consistent policy of dialogue,
with open and effective channels of communication between school
professionals, students, and families, fosters an environment of trust and
collaboration, promoting the peaceful resolution of conflicts. Psychological
support is also essential, aiming to provide emotional and psychological support
to those involved in situations of violence to promote the well-being and mental
health of all members of the school community. Coordination with the support
network, establishing partnerships with social services and specialized
institutions, contributes to a more comprehensive and effective approach to
combating violence, especially when serving children and adolescents in
vulnerable situations. This integrated and collaborative approach seeks to
transform the school into a safe, inclusive space conducive to the holistic
development of students.
       The challenges faced by the school systems in the 9 cities surveyed in
addressing school violence are multifaceted and complex. Some of the key
issues identified include:
       1. Dialogue with parents and/or guardians: a lack of effective
communication between the school and students’ parents and/or guardians can


                                                                                403

hinder the identification and resolution of behavioral problems that lead to
violence. Parental collaboration and involvement are essential to creating a safe
and welcoming school environment.
       2. Reaching families, family engagement: Often, families may not be fully
aware of the challenges their children face at school or may not be available to
support the necessary preventive and corrective measures. Family engagement
is critical to promoting appropriate values and behaviors among students.
       3. Students’ community and social reality: the social and community
conditions in which students live can directly influence their behavior at school.
Factors such as poverty, crime, and social inequality can contribute to an
environment conducive to violence and a lack of respect.
       4. Clashes of values and coexistence: the diversity of values and
experiences among students can lead to conflicts and a lack of mutual
understanding. The school plays a crucial role in promoting values of respect,
empathy, and harmonious coexistence, but it is not always easy to overcome
existing cultural and social differences.
       5. Lack of respect among some students: a lack of respect among
students can create a hostile environment prone to conflict. It is important for
schools to implement appropriate disciplinary measures and awareness
programs to foster a culture of mutual respect and cooperation.
       In light of these challenges, it is essential that school systems adopt
comprehensive and integrated strategies that involve not only the school
community but also external partners, such as government agencies, NGOs, and
social institutions. The promotion of positive values, education for peace and
conflict resolution, as well as the implementation of violence prevention practices,
are key elements for creating a safe and inclusive school environment in
educating cities.
       To address the challenges highlighted in dealing with violence in schools,
the public policies of an educating city must adopt inclusive and comprehensive
approaches that work in an integrated and collaborative manner to overcome
these challenges. Dialogue with students’ parents and guardians can be
promoted through effective communication programs and initiatives that
encourage active family participation in the student’s school life, aiming to build
a solid partnership between the school and the community. To address the issue


                                                                                404

of family engagement, it is important to implement strategies that involve raising
awareness and
      Parental engagement in educational processes and violence prevention,
strengthening the bonds between family and school.
      Considering the influence of students’ social and community realities,
public policies can include socio-educational measures that take into account the
specific needs of each community, as well as support and assistance programs
for students in vulnerable situations. To mitigate clashes of values and
coexistence, it is essential to promote diversity, mutual respect, and the pursuit
of intercultural dialogue in schools through educational activities that foster
understanding and acceptance of differences.
      With regard to the lack of respect among students, it is necessary to
implement clear and effective school policies on coexistence, which include
awareness-raising initiatives, conflict mediation, and the promotion of values
such as respect, empathy, and cooperation, with the aim of building a safe,
healthy school environment conducive to students’ holistic development. By
addressing these challenges in a collaborative and comprehensive manner,
public policies can significantly contribute to the creation of more inclusive,
peaceful, and educational schools.
      This progress can be anchored in Maldonado’s suggestions:


                     Schools that have carried out successful bullying/cyberbullying
                     prevention campaigns have worked with students and the entire school
                     staff, seeking the partnership of families to create a culture of zero
                     tolerance for bullying and cyberbullying, establishing appropriate limits
                     and consequences for aggressive behavior, encouraging the expansion
                     of resources to empower victims, enabling perpetrators to make good
                     use of their leadership skills and increase empathy, and fostering the
                     protective role of bystanders. The result is improved relationship quality
                     and the responsible use of social media. (Maldonado, 2011, p. 6).


      The highlighted quote emphasizes that schools that have succeeded in
their bullying/cyberbullying prevention campaigns have involved students, school
staff, and families to create a culture of zero tolerance for these practices.
Establishing clear boundaries and imposing appropriate consequences for
aggressive behavior, empowering victims, and encouraging perpetrators to
developing empathy and positive leadership are key strategies. Furthermore,
raising awareness among the audience about the importance of protecting


                                                                                           405

victims is also essential. These approaches aim not only to prevent bullying and
cyberbullying but also to promote healthy relationships and the responsible use
of social media in the school environment.
      Matos and Gonçalves suggest:


                        It would also be essential to understand the school context in which
                        these phenomena occur, identifying environmental factors that may
                        prevent or exacerbate them (teachers’ attitudes, attitudes of non-
                        teaching staff, training of teachers and staff, discussion of these topics
                        in school curricula, school organization from the perspective of open
                        spaces, for example). (Matos; Gonçalves, 2009, p. 13).


      The quote from Matos and Gonçalves highlights the importance of
understanding the school context to address bullying and cyberbullying,
identifying environmental factors that may influence the prevention or
exacerbation of these phenomena. Aspects such as the attitudes of teachers and
non-teaching staff, the training of education professionals, the inclusion of these
topics in school curricula, and the physical organization of the school—including
open spaces—are identified as relevant elements to be considered.
      This approach highlights the need for a broad perspective in
understanding and addressing bullying and cyberbullying, recognizing that
factors within the school environment play a significant role in fostering healthy
relationships among students and preventing aggressive behaviors. Thus, by
taking these different aspects into account, the school can adopt more effective
measures to create a safe, welcoming environment conducive to students’
holistic development.


3. FINAL CONSIDERATIONS


      Given the complexity and impact of violence in schools, it is crucial to
understand its nature and the types prevalent in educating cities. The educational
administrators play a fundamental role in identifying and addressing these issues,
as they have the capacity to promote safe and healthy school environments.
      School administrators’ perceptions of the impact of violence on student
performance highlight the need for effective public policies aimed at preventing
and combating school violence. Qualitative and/or quantitative analysis of the



                                                                                              406

collected data provides valuable insights to inform actions and strategies aimed
at promoting safety and well-being in the school environment.
      The theoretical framework provided by the cited authors strengthens the
study’s foundation and enriches our understanding of school violence. The
study’s alignment with the guidelines of the Charter of Educating Cities
underscores the importance of local communities’ commitment to promoting
quality education and ensuring an environment conducive to students’ holistic
development.
      It can be stated that the proposed objectives were successfully achieved
in this study. Understanding the nature of violence in schools, identifying the
prevalent types of violence in educational settings, and assessing administrators’
perceptions of its impact on the school environment and student performance
provided a comprehensive and well-founded perspective on the topic.
      For future studies, it is recommended to explore the underlying causes of
school violence in greater depth, as well as to investigate effective prevention
and intervention strategies. Furthermore, it would be relevant to study the
relationship between school violence and long-term academic performance, as
well as to investigate the role of families and the community in promoting safe
and healthy school environments. Longitudinal studies tracking the impact of
intervention programs over time could also contribute significantly to
understanding and resolving this complex problem.
      Finally, the results obtained reinforce the importance of Educating Cities
investing in policies and practices that combat school violence, aiming not only
at safety but also at improved performance and the well-being of students. The
joint efforts of administrators, researchers, and educators are essential for
building more inclusive, respectful, and welcoming schools, contributing to the
formation of critical and conscious citizens in more just and peaceful societies.

CHAPTER 23
 HISTORICAL TRACES: MEDICAIS
 DIAGNOSES GO TO SCHOOL


Michele Luciana Petersen
Ph.D. candidate in Special Education, Health, and Inclusive Processes
Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS)
E-mail: michelelucianapetersen@gmail.com

Cláudia Rodrigues de Freitas
Ph.D. in Education
Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS)
E-mail: freitascrd@gmail.com


ABSTRACT: This study investigates, through historical and critical bibliographic
research, how medical diagnoses entered schools and began to speak for
Education, transforming differences into “learning disability” conditions. It begins
with a reflection on the proliferation of reports that shift the pedagogical focus
toward classificatory codes, silencing students’ unique characteristics. The
objective is to understand the historical trajectory that enabled the entry and
expansion of diagnoses into the educational field, identifying its main milestones
and problematizing the effects of these classifications on learning processes up
to the present day. The methodology examines different historical moments, from
the emergence of the first psychiatric classifications to the consolidation of the
DSM, analyzing how these discourses gradually shifted the focus from the
pedagogical to the medical. The results indicate that, by seeking out what is
lacking in the student, diagnoses erase living processes of learning, fixing the
child in narratives of incapacity. It is concluded that it is urgent to re-center the
pedagogical perspective, strengthening listening, bonding, and the construction
of alternative narratives about learning.

KEYWORDS: education, learning, medicalization, diagnostic history.

RESUMO: Este estudo investiga, por meio de pesquisa bibliográfica de caráter
histórico e crítico, como os diagnósticos médicos adentraram na escola e
passaram a falarpela Educação, transformando diferenças em doenças do “não
aprender”. Partese da reflexão sobre o crescimento de laudos que deslocam o
olhar pedagógico para códigos classificatórios, silenciando as singularidades dos
alunos. O objetivo é compreender o percurso histórico que possibilitou a entrada
e expansão dos diagnósticos no campo educacional, identificando seus
principais marcos e problematizando os efeitos dessas classificações sobre os
processos de aprendizagem até os dias atuais. A metodologia articula diferentes
momentos históricos, desde o surgimento das primeiras classificações


                                                                                 409

psiquiátricas até a consolidação do DSM, analisando como esses discursos aos
poucos, foram deslocacando o foco do pedagógico para o médico. Os resultados
indicam que, ao buscarem pela falta no aluno, os diagnósticos apagam
processos vivos de aprender, fixando a criança em narrativas de incapacidade.
Conclui-se que é urgente recolocar o olhar pedagógico no centro, fortalecendo a
escuta, o vínculo e a construção de outras narrativas sobre o aprender.

PALAVRAS-CHAVE:         educação,    aprendizagem,    medicalização,   história
