1. INTRODUCTION


        What justifies referring a student to a doctor for evaluation and diagnosis6?
What underpins the belief that a number7or an acronym can define who a student
is—or who they will not become? How did medical diagnoses become tools
capable of speaking about education? This study examines these questions, with
the aim of understanding the pathways that allowed medical discourses to enter
the educational field and their progressive consolidation over the learning
processes of schoolchildren. The intention is not to deny the existence of real
illnesses or multiple disabilities, nor the importance of medical diagnoses for
treatment and people’s quality of life. Rather, it is a matter of critically reflecting
on how certain diagnoses, upon entering the school setting, end up dictating
learning processes, as if there were a single way to learn—replacing the
pedagogical perspective and assuming responsibilities that should belong to
teachers and to education itself.
        The growing presence in schools of diagnostic reports8indicating disorders
related to learning styles has shifted the perspective on how students are
perceived: not for their individuality, but through codes that purport to translate
their ways of being and learning. The rationale for this study lies in the urgency
of shifting the focus away from the centrality of medical diagnosis to reopen space
for pedagogical agency—a movement that calls on schools to renew their
commitment to listening, building connections, and constructing alternative
narratives about learning.




6 The term “medical diagnosis” will be used to refer, broadly, to the various specialties that, in

some way, appropriate the field of learning. By adopting the term “medical,” the aim is to include
all professional categories that, through reports, diagnose so-called “learning disorders.”
7 The acronym ICD (International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health

mandatory and regulated by the Ministry of Health, and it is used throughout the public and private

of transitioning to ICD-11. Its main objective is to standardize the codes for diseases, health
conditions, and causes of death, ensuring uniformity in health records, notifications, and statistics.
Each condition or diagnosis receives an alphanumeric code that allows for its identification and
recording in documents such as medical reports, certificates, medical records, and official reports

that summarizes the evaluation and assigns a name to what has been identified, almost always
according to a standardized classification, such as the one used in Brazil, the ICD


                                                                                                  411

1.1 OBJECTIVE


      This study aims to analyze, from a historical and critical perspective, the
establishment and expansion of medical diagnoses in the educational field,
identifying their main milestones and questioning the effects of these
classifications on the pedagogical perspective and learning processes.


2. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK


2.1 FOOTPRINTS ALONG THE WAY: THE WILD CHILD


      Today, we are experiencing what Frances (2016, p. 205) calls “diagnostic
inflation—and, by all indications, we are on the verge of hyperinflation.” In
schools, this phenomenon takes on its own distinct form: it involves the
proliferation of classificatory diagnoses. Reports that bear the name of the
disorder and the ICD code, but which often end up erasing the child’s name. The
individual gives way to the number. The student comes to be defined by a code,
a label, a technical assessment that places them in the category of the “non-
student”: they do not learn, they cannot, they cannot cope! How did we get here?
How did medical diagnoses come to say so much—and, at the same time, to
silence so much—about who learns and who does not?
      To understand part of this journey, it is worth returning to an opening
scene, frequently evoked in studies of special education and psychiatry: the
encounter with the “wild boy” in January 1800, in southern France.
      The “wild boy,” named Victor, was found and sent to the Central School of
Rodez and, later, to the National Institute for the Deaf and Dumb in Paris, where
he became the subject of study by the Société des observateurs de l’homme,
[Society of Observers of Man], which included distinguished men interested in
understanding human nature. Two of them stand out: Philippe Pinel and Jean
Itard, both physicians.
      Pinel, focusing on the boy’s disabilities, produced a report that anticipated
the patterns of modern diagnoses: by describing only absences, he concluded
that he “[...] had been abandoned because he was an idiot and that there would
be no possibility of educating him” (Banks-Leite; Galvão, 2017, p. 11).


                                                                               412

       Itard, on the other hand, devised and organized an educational program
with five goals focused on social integration, sensory stimulation, communication,
and mental operations, with the support of Madame Guérin throughout the
process. Through playful activities such as the game with cups and chestnuts—
which required attention and memory—he observed significant improvements in
the boy’s concentration. He also identified signs of intelligence in everyday
responses, such as in understanding routines associated with outings and in the
spontaneous use of body language. He then proposed comparison and
classification exercises with geometric shapes, which Victor solved with ease,
even as the complexity gradually increased. Encouraged by the results, Itard
introduced metal letters, and upon observing the unique way Victor handled the
materials—stacking and repositioning the letters according to his own logic—he
recognized his inventiveness and singular way of learning, further adapting his
pedagogical approaches.
       By tracing the history of these two different medical perspectives, we find
clues about the possibility of learning for those who were believed to be incapable
of it. Victor received contradictory diagnoses. Itard’s initiative—which did not stop
at diagnosing Victor but built an educational program based on the boy’s
responses and potential—invites reflection on how we view students who, at first
glance, seem to present difficulties. Often, these difficulties do not lie strictly with
the student, but in the way he is perceived—as Pinel did when he reduced Victor
to a supposed “incurable idiocy,” disregarding his potential.
       Itard invites us to recognize that, when faced with situations often
understood as learning difficulties, there are different points of view—and this is
precisely why pedagogical possibilities become necessary. After all, it is the
school’s role to sustain the teaching process, which cannot be guided by a
medical diagnosis, but rather by principles specific to the field of education.


2.2 ALFRED BINET’S METRIC SCALE


       In early 20th-century France, a concern emerged regarding the
identification of individuals’ learning abilities. Alfred Binet, in partnership with
Théodore Simon, developed the first metric scale of intelligence in 1905. The goal
was to measure intellectual abilities and establish criteria to distinguish students


                                                                                    413

suited for mainstream schooling from those destined for special education. As
Ferreira (2016, p. 20) reports, Binet believed that every child should be in the
school system, but “[...] advocated for the creation of a specific pathway—special
education—for those who presented difficulties. To this end, he considered it
essential to measure the degree of educability of each child,” since not all would
learn in the same way or at the same pace.
       Binet founded an experimental psychology laboratory in a school and
based his analyses on the belief in a normative educational system, in which the
majority of children would be endowed with “normal” intelligence. As Ferreira
(2016, p. 21) states, this involved the “[...] prior existence of a school system so
robust that it left no doubt that the vast majority of children possessed an
intelligence considered normal and to be taken as a benchmark.”
       Binet’s work responded to hygienist demands and the ideal of academic
performance. His concern was to precisely define abnormality and its traits, for
“[...] it was very important to him to present a well-defined definition of the
concept, as it was believed that this notion was the basis for the organization of
schools and, above all, for special education” (Ferreira, 2016, p. 69). The scale
was organized as a set of 60 tests ranked by difficulty. According to Ferreira
(2016, p. 101), “[...] with regard to those considered abnormal, whether or not
they took certain tests would be illustrative for establishing their differential
diagnosis as: idiots, imbeciles, and feeble-minded.”
       In this context—marked by the attempt to measure, classify, and separate
students according to levels of intellectual performance—the conditions are set
for the emergence of what Collares and Moysés (2012) call “diseases of not
learning.” Based on this scale, designed to distinguish the so-called “normal” from
the “abnormal,” a diagnostic logic begins to take hold that transforms academic
difficulties into pathologies to be corrected. As a result, students who “cannot,”
“do not keep up,” or “do not meet expectations” are subjected to a pathologizing
logic that, far from considering the school context, individualizes failure and shifts
the responsibility for cure back to medicine. In this process, “medicine artificially
constructs these disorders and expands the demand for specialized health
services, appropriating learning without altering school structures—merely
extending its normative scope” (Collares; Moysés, 2012, p. 196).



                                                                                  414

       Therefore, the metric scale paved the way for so-called “learning
disorders” to coexist with school processes. Through it, we can recognize that the
logic of measuring, diagnosing, and classifying—used to determine who could or
could not belong in school—remains present to this day, albeit under new names
and justifications.


2.3 THE EMERGENCE OF THE DSM


       With the end of World War II, the United States faced a bureaucratic crisis
linked to the reintegration of veterans into society. These individuals needed to
receive reports to obtain benefits and certificates of fitness, but the existing
classification systems could not handle the complexity of the cases—such as “[...]
chronic brain syndromes and situational reactions” (Bezerra Jr., 2014, p. 17-18).
In response, the American Psychiatric Association (APA) created the DSM-19 ,
released with 145 pages and 106 diagnostic categories. These categories were
organized “[...] in the form of paragraphs, which highlighted aspects of subjective
functioning and relational patterns” (Bezerra Jr., 2014, p. 18). Its use was
primarily focused on hospital administration and compliance with government
protocols, without significant clinical impact.
       In 1968, the DSM-2 was published, containing 180 categories. Although
limited to the U.S., it was the first to include “[...] a section dedicated to behavioral
disorders in childhood and adolescence” (Bezerra JR., 2014, p. 20), as well as
classifying homosexuality as a mental disorder—later removed in the seventh
edition following intense social pressure.
       In the 1980s, the DSM-3 marked a break with its predecessors, adopting
a descriptive rather than theoretical approach, with objective criteria for each
disorder and distinct axes. As Bezerra Jr. (2014, p. 21) explains, the diagnosis
“[...] ceased to be viewed as a key to understanding intrapsychic or relational
conflicts or disturbances underlying the symptoms, and instead became a guide
for   detecting    visible   disorders.”    The     emphasis      on   subjective        clinical
interpretations was abandoned in favor of an approach centered on the objective
description of observable behaviors. This standardization of criteria sought to

9 The acronym DSM stands for "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders," which in

Portuguese is translated as "Manual Diagnóstico e Estatístico de Transtornos Mentais."


                                                                                             415

ensure greater uniformity in diagnoses, making them applicable in different
contexts—as Silva highlights, one of the “[...] main objectives was to expand and
standardize diagnostic processes carried out not only in the United States but
also in other countries” (Silva, 2022, p. 98). The number of categories was
expanded to 295, and according to Conrad (2015), copies of the DSM-3 sold out
immediately and were purchased by anyone with any connection to psychiatry.
       In 1994, the DSM-4 was published, coordinated by Allen Frances, with a
more rigorous approach to revision, as all methodological issues were outlined in
detail well before the work began. “There were explicit criteria for implementing
changes and a centralized method for reviewing the literature, reanalyzing data,
and conducting field experiments” (Frances, 2016, p. 207). However, Frances
himself became a critic of the excessive proliferation of categories: “[...] problems
that were once expected and tolerated aspects of life are now diagnosed and
treated as mental disorders” (Frances, 2016, p. 110).
       The DSM-5, published in 2013, took this logic to the extreme. “It contains
[...] more than 300 categories presented across 947 pages” (Silva, 2022, p. 97),
representing an explosion in classification since the two categories of 1840. The
development of the DSM-5 was described by Frances (2016, p. 207) as a “[...]
jumble of disorganized methods,” the result of autonomous working groups,
without common guidelines. The growth in categories reflected the expansion of
psychiatric logic beyond the clinical realm: ways of being, feeling, and living came
to be framed as potential disorders. This process created a paradox: in seeking
greater precision, the manual expanded the boundaries of pathology. As Frances
(2016, p. 281) warns, “[...] an accurate diagnosis can save a life; an inaccurate
one can destroy it.”
       The DSM manuals, from DSM-1 through DSM-5, show a growing
trajectory of labels and classifications in an attempt to organize human suffering,
while simultaneously expanding the scope of the medical gaze on life. As
summarized by Christofari, Freitas, and Baptista (2015, p. 11), medicine began
to produce “[...] discourses that define how we should be, what habits we should
adopt to stay healthy as long as possible; after all, being healthy is what matters.”
       It is important to emphasize that this study does not aim to delegitimize
medical diagnoses. Their value for effective treatments and improved quality of
life is recognized. However, in the educational field, caution is needed: the


                                                                                 416

medical diagnosis of “learning disorders” cannot and should not erase students’
unique characteristics and, above all, must acknowledge the diverse modes and
forms of learning.


3. METHODOLOGY


       This article constitutes a historical and critical bibliographic study, with the
aim of tracing the entry of medical diagnoses into the educational field, especially
when these began to address school learning processes. The investigation is
based on the understanding that the ways of labeling students—through
classifications, reports, and codes—are not neutral, but rather have effects on the
lives of the students who receive them, and likewise transform the ways teachers
perceive them. To this end, authors who offer fundamental contributions to this
analysis were selected, including Benilton Bezerra Jr., Ana Carolina Christofari,
Cecília Azevedo Lima Collares, Maria Aparecida Affonso Moysés, Allen Frances,
and Gisela Untoiglich, among others, whose works allow us to examine the role
played by medical diagnoses when they enter the school setting. The research is
also grounded in historical documents and successive editions of the DSM
(Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders), in order to elucidate the
transformations in diagnostic criteria and their social, cultural, and educational
ramifications.
       The methodological approach involved constructing a narrative that
connects different historical moments—from the encounter with the “wild boy” of
Aveyron in the 19th century to the publication of the DSM-5 in 2013—with the aim
of showing how diagnosis ceased to be merely a clinical tool and became a
mechanism for regulating school life. The proposed analysis is guided by an
inductive logic, which draws on historical and discursive traces to problematize
current practices, without losing sight of the tensions between the fields of
medicine and education.
       Finally, the legitimate role of medical diagnoses in healthcare, including
mental health, is acknowledged. However, this study adopts the premise that, in
the educational field, we must resist the uncritical use of these classifications as
determinants of learning trajectories, especially when we refer students for a
medical evaluation that seeks to explain why they “can’t” or “can’t handle it.” The


                                                                                   417

methodology adopted here, therefore, focuses on reclaiming agency in the face
of the complexity of the educational experience, pointing toward the construction
of other ways of understanding and supporting students in their learning
processes, beyond the meanings currently attributed to diagnostics.


4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS


       So far, we have been tracing the path of a possible trajectory for
diagnoses. But, as in any journey, there comes a moment when the paths of the
new and the lived “at home” intersect. And the school setting is our home: the
familiar and the lived-in now emerge through the stories of students who have
received a medical classification diagnosis, which has assigned them a place of
non-learning—a place that, in many cases, they themselves rebel against
occupying.
       In the school context, the diagnosis is sometimes understood as a tool that
identifies those students who stand out negatively from their peers because they
exhibit different characteristics, particularly related to behavior and learning.
       In general, schools are constrained to serve students in a standardized
manner; that is, they tend to view students by homogenizing their ways of being
and learning. There are situations in which students arrive with a pre-existing
diagnosis of learning difficulties. In others, those who stand out from the rest—
due to difficulties in learning expected content, behavior that is more expressive
than expected, or ways of being or (not) expressing themselves—end up being
referred to medical professionals, as this student “must have something wrong”
or “cannot be normal,” and this uncertain diagnosis must be identified.According
to Frances (2016, p. 106), our world “is homogenizing—we have less and less
tolerance for individual differences and eccentricities and try to medicalize them
as illnesses.” Thus, according to Christofari (2023, p. 1), “[...] there is an
increasingly common modus operandi in schools of referring students to health
services with the desire for a diagnosis.” That is, according to Christofari; Freitas;
Baptista; (2015, p. 2), “[...] isolating the subject to analyze their particularities in
detail and render them pathological. This produces a way of looking at the other
as if they were a mere sum of biological and behavioral characteristics.”



                                                                                    418

       Christofari (2014, p. 37) recounts an experience with a boy named
Valentin, who, while accepting the medical-explanatory categories of the
diagnosis, also defies them, devising strategies to escape what had been
imposed on him. According to the author, the boy “[...] struggled not to internalize
a diagnosis; he was outgoing, dressed in a peculiar way, and his movements
were almost uncontrollable, considered pathological by the school.” He went to
the doctor and was quickly assigned a pathology code, an ICD.
       He arrived at school already labeled with “learning difficulties,” particularly
in the area of writing. However, when asked to bring his texts so the new teacher
could read them, she found they were marked with comments: “improve
handwriting,” “horrible handwriting,” “incomprehensible text,” but no comments
on the process of the boy’s writing creation. In fact, Valentin had just read the
texts to the teacher, demonstrating that he had a coherent story with a certain
touch of humor. At that moment, she was able to look at Valentin and see that
there was an evident learning process in his writing, which calls into question the
initial diagnosis he had received.
       Moysés (2001), similarly, presents his research experience with 75
children who were not learning in school and who had already been seen by
various professionals. The author focused on understanding the reasons why it
was possible to determine the lack of learning and, by “[...] instead of looking for
the child’s defect or deficiency, the gaze seeks what they already know, what they
have, and what they can learn from there” (Moysés, 2001, p. 42).
       In this way, by taking a different approach, she gave each child a voice so
they could speak for themselves. Of the 75 children, 71 showed no signs of
physical, emotional, or intellectual problems. The remaining four stood out from
the group due to a special characteristic: “in three of them, the internalization of
the stigma of being sick/incapable was so intense that one cannot safely rule out
an association with some degree of developmental delay development” (Moysés,
2001, p. 45). The author described the network established through the listening
process, involving the family, the school, and the child. Thus, she listened to
everyone and made observations.
       One of the cases that stands out is that of Cícero, an eight-year-old boy
whose case was analyzed by Moysés (2001). According to the boy’s teacher, if it
were the end of the school year, he would have failed due to his “slurred speech.”


                                                                                  419

She mentioned that she had asked the family several times to take him to a
speech therapist, which did not happen. Because, in her words, “the mother is
detached” (Moysés, 2001, pp. 183–184). According to the teacher’s account,
Cícero also had a brain aneurysm, but his mother did not address it and his father
was an alcoholic. The boy’s mother explained that he wasn’t learning, but she
didn’t know why. At the same time, she echoed the teacher’s claim that he wasn’t
learning because he didn’t speak. When asked by the doctor if Cícero had an
aneurysm, the mother said she had never heard of it.
       Moysés (2001, p. 183), in giving the boy a voice, heard the following: “[...]
I don’t learn because when I do my homework, my head hurts and I forget
everything. I don’t even like looking at myself in the mirror; I’m very ugly.” After
listening to everyone, and especially the child, she concluded that he spoke well,
did not mix up or omit letters. He “[...] tells stories and draws normally, except
when he talks about himself or draws himself, revealing a severely compromised
self-image. Normal child, normal development” (Moysés, 2001, p. 184).
       In her research, the author analyzed each case individually, adopting a
detailed and personalized approach, demonstrating that although these children
had received medical diagnoses, they exhibited signs of learning throughout their
developmental process. In other words, the author, who is also a physician,
maintains that it is necessary to give voice to, and consider, the individual stories,
trajectories, progress, and ways of learning of each child, even when there are
medical diagnoses indicating pathologies.
       Of the children interviewed by Moysés (2001), several already had a long
history of navigating the healthcare system. According to Rocha and Cavalcanti
(2014), this is common, as when a diagnosis arises, it revisits a need for
confirmation. Consequently, medical and health services are frequently sought
by parents who take their children to verify and validate the initial diagnoses
received. For the authors, making a diagnosis


                      [...] has become an easy task within everyone’s reach: one need only
                      list symptoms and group them under their corresponding label. In this
                      way, legions of children described as having ADHD [Attention-
                      Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder], OCD [Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder],
                      Bipolar Disorder, and Autism Spectrum Disorder proliferate, often
                      heavily medicated (Rocha; Cavalcanti, 2014, p. 233).




                                                                                       420

       This logic of repeated validation fuels the early labeling and extensive
pharmacological treatment of children. In these contexts, students are often
referred for clinical evaluations because, as Frances (2016, p. 111) states, we
have come to set “very high goals and unrealistic expectations—especially when
it comes to children.” And thus, as Moysés (2008, p. 4) warns, a “[...] quick shift
in perspective will enable the creation of learning disorders, or rather, disorders
of not learning.” Therefore, the diagnosis is understood as a document that seeks
to affirm a place that, until then, has been hidden from the student in the school
environment. According to Christofari (2023, p. 2), “[...] the diagnosis, one of the
indelible marks on the body, tends to serve as a justification for medications and
referrals to countless treatments, exposing ‘offending’ behavior as something to
be cured, treated.” It is the definition of the presence of pathologies, of something
being within the student, and when it emerges, it simultaneously brings relief to
the school, since, “if the supposed problem lies with the student, no one is to
blame for their condition. The discourse directed at the student commonly
summarizes: this is not a matter for pedagogy, but for health” (Christofari; Freitas;
Baptista, 2015, p. 12).
       This document describes, names, and classifies each individual, creating
an impression of something bad, harmful, and unfavorable, casting doubt on
ways of being and learning, and granting the medical field permission to label a
list of symptoms and justify—or not—the acquisition of learning. For the school,
having a medical diagnosis that describes the illnesses of the non learning “[...]
implies the condition of being capable or not, according to socially defined
parameters” (Silva; Batista, 2021, p. 53).
       It has become common to find, in schools, children like Valentin and
Cícero, who arrive with multiple diagnoses, and in all these cases, the clinical
perspective takes precedence over the pedagogical one, erasing the possibility
of recognizing other legitimate ways of learning. This is a process in which the
subject’s uniqueness ceases to be understood as difference and comes to be
interpreted as a sign of deviation. As Angelucci (2015, p. 8) points out, the moral
conversion that takes place is evident:


                      [...] a personality trait, an aspect of behavior, a personal rhythm or style,
                      which, one might think, express the subject’s uniqueness, come to be




                                                                                              421

                      valued as diagnostic indicators, placing them in the realm of deviation
                      from the healthy path.


      In the face of this hasty logic of classification, Untoiglich (2006) presents
excerpts that invite us to consider a diagnosis that requires time—a time that is
not resolved by filling out questionnaires — and that presupposes dialogue
among the professionals involved with the student, possibly requiring numerous
interdisciplinary consultations. In other words, a process that demands careful
observation before arriving at any pathological classification. The author points
out that no classification is natural and that “[...] the supposedly observable data
in no way represent objective readings of reality, since they are permeated by
interpretations grounded in prior knowledge and experience” (Untoiglich, 2013,
p. 119), as such classifications are embedded in scientific aspects, but also
economic, ideological, political, and cultural ones.
      Bezerra Jr. (2014, p. 13) echoes Untoiglich by stating that “[...]
classifications are not mirrors of reality, but constructions, arrangements, that
shape a domain of reality by systematizing its multiplicity in an intelligible
manner.” For the author, when we classify, we organize information, but at the
same time, we simplify it in a way that produces a partial and superficial view of
the object in question. This bias highlights the importance of recognizing the
subjectivity present in our perceptions and analyses, understanding that reality is
not given but constructed—influenced by personal experiences, accumulated
knowledge, and cultural values.
      However, by tracing the historical trajectory of medical diagnoses, this
article aimed at more than simply reconstructing their path and entry into schools.
Above all, the intention was to shed light on the existence of other pathways—of
learning—that continue to resist classificatory logic. Amid numbers, scales, and
codes, learning processes continue to pulse, revealing themselves only when
there is space for attentive listening. Instead of focusing on what is missing or
what does not fit, we must ask: what does this student already know? How do
they learn? As Frances (2016, p. 182) points out,


                      [...] it would be better if school decisions were not so tied to a diagnosis
                      that was developed solely for relational purposes and no educational
                      hypothesis. School services should be based on needs, not on
                      diagnosis.



                                                                                              422

       Ultimately, what is being asserted here is that we need to listen more closely
to our students — for it is through this sensitive listening, which recognizes
uniqueness, that we can see learning as a living force that persists even when
everything seems to suggest otherwise.


5. CONCLUSION


       By revisiting the history of medical diagnoses and their entry into schools,
this article sought to problematize how the logic of classification came to regulate,
describe, and legitimize discourses on learning and not learning. Far from
denying the importance of diagnoses in the field of health, what is highlighted is
the urgency of shifting the pedagogical gaze away from dependence on these
classifications, reopening space for listening, connection, and the recognition of
singularities.
       The results and discussions presented show that a perspective centered
on deficiency erases the living processes of learning, transforming difference into
a problem to be corrected or treated. The history of diagnoses reveals that
classifications are not neutral: they are constructions that organize and They
simplify reality, but they also obscure what falls outside statistical parameters.
Thus, it is essential to refocus the pedagogical perspective at the center of the
debate, restoring education’s leading role in school learning—rather than leaving
it to the medical field.
       By proposing this reflection, this research contributes to society by
shedding light on practices that, under the pretext of care, crystallize inequalities
and stigmas in the school environment. For academia, it offers theoretical and
analytical insights that stimulate interdisciplinary debate between Education and
Health, without one being subordinate to the other, and proposes ways to think
about school learning from a perspective of complexity that cannot be captured
in medical reports.

CHAPTER 24
 THE BODY IN PHYSICAL
 EDUCATION CURRICULA: TRENDS
 AND APPROACHES IN ACADEMIC
 RESEARCH

ABSTRACT: The objective of this integrative review was to map and analyze
academic research in Brazilian graduate programs addressing the themes of Body,
Curriculum, and Physical Education. The study used academic works (dissertations
and theses) available on the CAPES Digital Thesis and Dissertation Library website
as its research source. The research was conducted in the following stages:
formulation of the research question supervisor, followed by the development of
keywords for the research; the PRISMA protocol; and finally, the selection of thirteen
academic works that comprised this study. The analysis process revealed a
predominance of dissertations and a geographical concentration in the Southeast
and South regions. The results indicate that studies on the body in the Physical
Education curriculum have been conducted predominantly through documentary
studies, followed by instruments such as interviews and questionnaires. This
demonstrates that the dimension of the body highlighted has been the biological one,
present in the male and white body; and that atypical bodies are strongly rendered
invisible and silenced in the training of Physical Education professionals. In this
sense, it is concluded that the patriarchal, biologistic model of current society is in
the process of being actively reproduced in the training of physical education
professionals, thereby marginalizing the atypical subjective bodies present in society.

KEYWORDS: body, curriculum, physical education.


                                                                                   426

RESUMO: Esta revisão integrativa teve como objetivo mapear e analisar a
produção científica acadêmica em cursos de pós-graduação brasileiros sobre o
tema Corpo, Currículo e Educação Física. O estudo utilizou como fonte de
pesquisa trabalhos acadêmicos – dissertações e teses – disponíveis no site da
Biblioteca Digital de Teses e Dissertações da CAPES. A pesquisa seguiu as
seguintes etapas: formulação da questão norteadora, seguida do
desenvolvimento de palavras-chave para a busca; aplicação do protocolo
PRISMA; e, por fim, a seleção de treze trabalhos acadêmicos que compuseram
este estudo. O processo de análise revelou predominância de dissertações, com
concentração geográfica nas regiões Sudeste e Sul. Os resultados indicam que
os estudos sobre o corpo no currículo de Educação Física têm sido
predominantemente conduzidos por meio de estudos documentais, seguidos de
instrumentos como entrevistas e questionários. Isso demonstra que a dimensão
do corpo destacada tem sido a biológica, presente no corpo masculino e branco;
e que corpos atípicos são fortemente invisibilizados e silenciados na formação
de profissionais de Educação Física. Nesse sentido, conclui-se que o modelo
patriarcal e biológico da sociedade atual está sendo claramente reproduzido na
formação de profissionais de educação física, marginalizando os corpos
subjetivos atípicos presentes na sociedade.

PALAVRAS-CHAVE: body, curriculum, physical education.




                                                                          427

1. INTRODUCTION


       The body is the form through which humans exist and are present in the
world. It is through the body that humans became human; whether through the
biological condition of being or through the creative power of the work performed
by the body, we have become social and cultural beings. It is impossible to
conceive of human existence without a material body (Daolio, 1995).
       Historically, no figure has been more striking than the role played by the
body in different spaces, cultures, and eras. Beyond the power of instincts
internalized in the genetics of bodies, the body is the means by which humans
became civilized as animals; it is in the body and through the body that societies
in different eras and distinct spaces inscribe their values, beliefs, knowledge, arts,
powers, and education (Soares, 2022).
       Therefore, each body is a product of its time, its space, and its culture. And
over time, bodies have undergone profound transformations, shifting from a
strictly biological body to a subjective body. A body that is constructed from the
subjective constructions of subjects; a body that exists beyond its biosystems, a
body defined by our social identities, our ways of seeing ourselves as subjects,
which in many cases conflicts with our biological condition (Souza, 2005).
       To such an extent that these productions of subjective bodies uniquely
mark contemporary societies, in all their spaces. In our personal or professional
lives, at one time or another we will experience these encounters with these
multiple bodies up close. Bodies that present as Black bodies, trans bodies,
Indigenous bodies, binary bodies, bodies with disabilities, fat bodies, elderly
bodies, among so many others (Stubs, 2019).
       The recognition and experience of bodily equity in the contemporary
landscape is a fundamental element for us to experience a society that is socially
just, politically democratic, culturally diverse, and environmentally sustainable
(Barbosa, 2025).
       Thus, the objective of this study was to analyze academic production in
graduate programs regarding how the body has been addressed in the curricula
of undergraduate physical education programs, through an integrative literature
review.



                                                                                  428

      Initially, a guiding question for the review was formulated, which served as
a starting point and guide for the subsequent phases of the study: how have
academic works—dissertations and theses—highlighted the dimensions of the
body in the undergraduate Physical Education curriculum?


2. METHODOLOGY


      To answer the guiding question of this study, we opted to conduct an
integrative literature review, which, according to Souza, Silva, and Carvalho
(2010), is a form of research that enables the gathering, analysis, and synthesis
of knowledge produced on a specific topic over a specific period.
      This type of study, as highlighted by the cited authors, offers the advantage
of developing comprehensive and consistent understandings based on different
studies conducted within a specific time frame. In this sense, the decision to
structure the research through an integrative review was based on it offers the
ability to identify trends, gaps, and recurring themes in the academic literature
regarding the body, the curriculum, and Physical Education within the works
included in the study.
      An electronic search was conducted for academic works indexed in the
Brazilian Digital Library of Theses and Dissertations (BDTD) database in October
2025. The search terms used were “body,” “curriculum,” and “Physical
Education,” separated by the Boolean operator “AND.”
      It is believed that these descriptors fully reflect the target theme of this
review, since the objective is to analyze studies on how academic works have
highlighted the dimensions of the body in the undergraduate Physical Education
curriculum. It is important to note that, in the database, the terms were entered
only in Portuguese.
      Regarding the time frame, we chose not to set a specific date for the
information search. This decision was made considering that, since the 1980s,
interest in studies on the body beyond the Health Sciences has been growing
significantly. The Humanities have devoted considerable time and research to
developing studies on the theme of the body. Therefore, we emphasize the
importance of a contemporary and up-to-date approach to the topic under
discussion.


                                                                               429

       In the process of identifying the works, 302 studies were retrieved from the
digital database, of which 240 were dissertations and 62 were theses. No time
frame was applied for the research, but generally speaking, the earliest work
found dates from 1993 and the latest from 2024. When the exclusion criteria were
applied: (a) Duplicate works in the database were excluded, resulting in 299
works remaining; (b) Works excluded after reviewing titles and abstracts that did
not focus on the discussion of the topic in higher education totaled 286; (c) A total
of 13 works were fully reviewed and analyzed.

              The objective of this study was to analyze academic output at the master’s
       and doctoral program level in Brazil regarding how the body has been addressed
       in academic works—dissertations and theses—from a historical perspective. In
       this regard, in this section, we will discuss the findings of the research conducted
       as an integrative review.
              To construct the discussions, we employed the Thematic Analysis method
       as a tool for analyzing the content identified during the research process.
       Thematic Analysis is a method proposed by Braun and Clarke (2006) and can be
       understood as a qualitative data analysis method for identifying, analyzing,
       interpreting, and reporting patterns—also referred to as themes—based on
       qualitative data.
              Thematic Analysis is a method that has been gaining prominence in the
       field of research across various areas of knowledge, such as the humanities, with
       an emphasis on Psychology, but it is also commonly used in the health sciences,
       particularly in Nursing (Souza, 2019).
              A search conducted on the website of the Brazilian Digital Library of
       Theses and Dissertations (BDTD) identified a total of 13 works that satisfactorily
       addressed the research question. Of the works found, there were 4 theses and 9
       dissertations, spanning the period from 1993 to 2024. As for the graduate
       programs where the works were produced, they were diverse, ranging from
       Agricultural Education, Science Education, Physical Education, Science
       Teaching, Public Policy, and Human Development, with a particular emphasis on
       Education. The works were produced at both public and private higher education
       institutions, distributed across all regions of the country, with the exception of
       northern Brazil; the largest volume of production is concentrated in the
       southeastern region with six works, produced mostly by men.
              After organizing the academic papers into a table and reading and re-
       reading them, we grouped the content into thematic categories. To determine
       these categories, we highlighted the themes that emerged most frequently across




                                                                                              434

the studies as a whole, as well as themes that were not discussed or presented
in the texts of the academic papers included in the review.


3.1 METHODOLOGICAL APPROACHES TO THE STUDY OF THE BODY


       The research method in a study represents the central element for the
success of any research, whether qualitative or quantitative in approach. It is
essential that the researcher have a clear understanding of the research
approach and method to be used to achieve their objective (Pádua, 2019).
       After repeated readings of the studies, it became evident in the
methodology sections that, for the most part, the studies present the analysis
documentary analysis, followed by interviews and questionnaires to understand
the dimensions of the body present in the curriculum structure of undergraduate
Physical Education programs.
       Within the context of research methodologies, documentary analysis is a
method widely used in the humanities, social sciences, and health sciences. It
basically consists of analyzing various documents to produce relevant
information, which allows for the interpretation of meanings and the construction
of knowledge.
       However, certain aspects of these research methods must be understood,
such as: it is a low-cost method, it allows access to existing information, it does
not interfere with the object of study, it enables the construction of a longitudinal
analysis, and it can serve as a complement to other studies. On the other hand,
it lacks fixed standardization, does not sufficiently problematize the subject,
requires careful interpretation by the researcher, has limited availability of access
to the material, and may present bias in the documents or incomplete documents.
       The study highlights the use of Pedagogical Curriculum Projects and
Teaching Plans as research sources to understand the emphasis placed on the
dimensions of the body in the training of Physical Education professionals.
Another instrument used to understand the body was the conduct of interviews
with faculty and students in the program, followed by the administration of online
questionnaires to students. It is worth noting that regardless of the research
instrument used, they present advantages and disadvantages in the construction
of research data.


                                                                                 435

       The interview is one of the most widely used instruments in research in
general, whether in the humanities, social sciences, health sciences, or other
fields of knowledge. It consists of asking questions directly to participants, which
may be structured, semi-structured, or open-ended (Leitão, 2021).
       In the studies analyzed during the research, the use of open-ended
questions to understand the participants’ perspectives was highlighted.
Interviews, in general, allow for a deeper exploration of the topic and possess
flexibility, direct contact with participants, the possibility of clarifying responses,
and a high level of detail. On the other hand, they are costly and time-consuming,
may influence participants, carry a high risk of socially desirable responses, and
require more complex analysis (Leitão, 2021)
       Another common and widely used method in academic studies was the
use of questionnaires, particularly in their online format, as a way to elicit
participants’ understanding of the body. Questionnaires, which are a widely used
tool in quantitative research, have the advantage of being low-cost, reaching a
large number of participants, featuring standardized questions, enabling rapid
data collection, and facilitating analysis; on the other hand, they have low
response rates, lack depth, make it difficult to clarify doubts, carry a high risk of
automated responses, limit the scope of the topic under study, and depend on
the quality of the questionnaire (Costa, 2023).
       Given this context, it is clear that academic studies have utilized
documentary analysis, interviews, and questionnaires with students and faculty
in Physical Education programs as a means of data collection to understand the
conceptions and understandings this audience holds regarding the body as a
phenomenon of study.


3.2 DECIPHERING THE DOCUMENTED BODIES


       Historically, the body has always represented a major taboo for societies,
particularly Western societies. In reviewing the literature, with an emphasis on
the discussions, the prominence of the biological dimension of the body becomes
evident; both in the documentary analysis, focusing on curricular pedagogical
projects, and in the curriculum itself, the emphasis placed on the biological
dimension of the body is evident, with the dominance of curricular disciplines


                                                                                   436

markedly centered on biology, such as anatomy, physiology, kinesiology,
biochemistry, biomechanics, and biophysics. This represents a deepening of the
understanding of the body in its biological constitution, focused on performance,
in sportsmanship, in competition, in distinction, linked to the bias of health and
body aesthetics. In the pursuit of the perfect body, the superbody, the body
capable of overcoming the limits of the human condition (Berguer, 2007).
       Only one of the studies analyzed cited Law No. 10,639/03—later amended
by Law No. 11,645/08—which mandates that the subject “Afro-Brazilian and
Indigenous History and Culture” be a required component of the curriculum in
teacher education programs and an elective in bachelor’s degree programs. In
this regard, even in the face of the law’s mandatory nature, compliance is not
evident in the vast majority of Physical Education teacher education programs,
resulting in the absence of diverse representations of bodies in the training of
these professionals (Santos, 2023).
       Consequently, the curricula of undergraduate Physical Education
programs have historically prioritized biological, white, male bodies, focusing on
an approach centered on physical performance, sports, and competition (Soares,
2017). In other words, the body depicted in the analyzed academic works merely
reproduces the structure of a historically patriarchal, sexist, and racist society.
One that denies the possibility of visibility for other bodies that exist socially but
still represent a minority economically.


3.3 PERSPECTIVES ON CONTEMPORARY BODIES


       After multiple re-readings of the works comprising the research subject, it
was possible to observe that they present different perspectives on the body.
However, the perspective that stands out most in the studies is the view of the
body in its biological dimension. The body as a collection of cells, tissues, organs,
and biosystems; the material body, the condition of being and existing in the
human world (Soares, 2017).
       Another striking perspective in the studies analyzed through interviews
and content analysis derived from questionnaires is the body as an object of
control and domination by men; it is the body as an instrument for colonizing
subjects, whether through domestication, education, or control imposed by social


                                                                                  437

rules and codes of conduct. The body as an affect of life, a site of illness and
health. The body worshipped by aesthetics, dominated by disciplinary rules, the
body as a form of recognition in societies (Castro, 2003).
      Of the works analyzed, only two discuss the conception of the body beyond
the biological dimension. They present the body as a sociocultural construction,
a product of historical, social, political, and cultural relations. The body as a
dialectic of the universe, capable of expressing ideas, emotions, desires, and
feelings. The body that expresses the culture in which it is immersed, with its
individualities, but also laden with collective expressions imposed by social
experiences (Lara, 2004).
      Modern bodies, a product of the diversity of human subjectivities in ways
of being and existing in the world, remain distant from professional training in
many fields of knowledge; this is largely because curricula in general, especially
those of undergraduate programs, still harbor within them traditionalism, content-
centeredness, and technicality, disconnected from social realities that are in
constant transformation (Moreira, 2013).
      The focus on emerging new groups arises through the construction of
identity movements characterized by social and political organization around
shared identities—such as gender, race, ethnicity, sexuality, religion, or culture.
These movements have gained strength and expanded their presence in recent
decades due to the expansion of globalization and social media; yet they remain
invisible and silenced by education and training systems that fail to keep pace
with the rapid changes and transformations significantly shaping contemporary
societies (Goellner, 2010).
      As a result, Black, Indigenous, Quilombola, disabled, female, gay, trans,
binary, and non-binary bodies find themselves marginalized in a historically and
structurally conservative society that uses every means to maintain its status quo
of patriarchy and whiteness (Costa, 2025).


4. CONCLUSION


      Therefore, given the context presented, when we seek to understand how
academic studies conducted through the scientific production of dissertations and
theses have highlighted the body in the curricula of undergraduate physical


                                                                               438

education programs, we observe that the studies included in this integrative
review reinforce our view that historically the biological body has been the central
theme of study in the curricula, and that subjective bodies and/or cultural bodies
have been strongly excluded, silenced, and rendered invisible in the curricular
training of Physical Education professionals.
       Among the main findings of these studies, we can highlight that: even in
the face of the profound transformations that marked the last century in social,
scientific,   economic,   political,   cultural,   technological,   and   educational
dimensions, the curriculum of the vast majority of Physical Education programs
—Teacher Certification and Bachelor’s Degree programs—still adhere to a
strongly traditional model, characterized by studies that emphasize the biological
body through the disciplines of anatomy, physiology, kinesiology, biomechanics,
biochemistry, and biophysics.
       A curriculum centered on the biological constitution of the body—a body
geared toward training, performance, and competition—to meet an aesthetic
imposed by society: the perfect body, the superbody, the overcoming of biological
limits, the athletic and healthy body. From this perspective, the curricula of
Physical Education programs have historically reproduced the dominant patterns
existing in society: the supremacy of white bodies, of male bodies, of the imposed
aesthetic of acceptable bodies, of the machine-like body geared toward
competition and performance. A curriculum that seeks to build elements to
prevent the body from aging, in the continuous pursuit of eternal youth and
immortality—a dream long cherished since the Middle Ages by alchemists.
       Another aspect highlighted in the studies is the invisibility and silencing in
curricula of bodies constructed from human subjectivities, or of identity-based
bodies, the result of identity movements of many historically dominated and
erased groups from the contemporary scene, such as Black bodies, Indigenous
bodies, disabled bodies, female bodies, gay bodies, trans bodies, fat bodies, and
elderly bodies, among many others. In this sense, the present study was
important for identifying these gaps in the relationships established between
Physical Education curricula and the multiple realities manifested in the
conditions of contemporary bodies.
       Thus, grounded in these studies, we need to rethink the education we have
and the training processes in games, to change these realities, and seek to build


                                                                                  439

an education, training processes, and curricula that establish equity and equal
importance among all bodies, respecting their singularities and individualities,
and upholding their right to exist in a multicultural society. Where all bodies can
experience their true citizenship.

ABSTRACT: The objective of this integrative review was to map and analyze
academic research in Brazilian graduate programs addressing the themes of
Body, Curriculum, and Physical Education. The study used academic works
(dissertations and theses) available on the CAPES Digital Thesis and
Dissertation Library website as its research source. The research was conducted
in the following stages: formulation of the research question supervisor, followed
by the development of keywords for the research; the PRISMA protocol; and
finally, the selection of thirteen academic works that comprised this study. The
analysis process revealed a predominance of dissertations and a geographical
concentration in the Southeast and South regions. The results indicate that
studies on the body in the Physical Education curriculum have been conducted
predominantly through documentary studies, followed by instruments such as
interviews and questionnaires. This demonstrates that the dimension of the body
highlighted has been the biological one, present in the male and white body; and
that atypical bodies are strongly rendered invisible and silenced in the training of
Physical Education professionals. In this sense, it is concluded that the
patriarchal, biologistic model of current society is in the process of being actively
reproduced in the training of physical education professionals, thereby
marginalizing the atypical subjective bodies present in society.

KEYWORDS: body, curriculum, physical education.

RESUMO: Esta revisão integrativa teve como objetivo mapear e analisar a
produção científica acadêmica em cursos de pós-graduação brasileiros sobre o
tema Corpo, Currículo e Educação Física. O estudo utilizou como fonte de
pesquisa trabalhos acadêmicos – dissertações e teses – disponíveis no site da
Biblioteca Digital de Teses e Dissertações da CAPES. A pesquisa seguiu as
seguintes etapas: formulação da questão norteadora, seguida do
desenvolvimento de palavras-chave para a busca; aplicação do protocolo
PRISMA; e, por fim, a seleção de treze trabalhos acadêmicos que compuseram
este estudo. O processo de análise revelou predominância de dissertações, com
concentração geográfica nas regiões Sudeste e Sul. Os resultados indicam que
os estudos sobre o corpo no currículo de Educação Física têm sido
predominantemente conduzidos por meio de estudos documentais, seguidos de
instrumentos como entrevistas e questionários. Isso demonstra que a dimensão
do corpo destacada tem sido a biológica, presente no corpo masculino e branco;
e que corpos atípicos são fortemente invisibilizados e silenciados na formação
de profissionais de Educação Física. Nesse sentido, conclui-se que o modelo
patriarcal e biológico da sociedade atual está sendo claramente reproduzido na
formação de profissionais de educação física, marginalizando os corpos
subjetivos atípicos presentes na sociedade.

PALAVRAS-CHAVE: body, curriculum, physical education.




                                                                                 445

1. INTRODUCTION


       Educational robotics has emerged as an innovative approach to teaching,
promoting the development of students’ technical and cognitive skills. This
technology is integrated into the school curriculum with the aim of enhancing
learning and making classes dynamic and interactive. The inclusion of robotics in
the school environment is not limited to teaching programming and mechanical
concepts, but also encompasses the promotion of critical thinking, problem-
solving, and collaborative work.
       The rationale for this research lies in the growing importance of
educational robotics as a pedagogical tool in an educational landscape that seeks
constant innovation to improve the teaching-learning process. Several studies
have shown that robotics can be an ally in the holistic development of students,
providing an environment conducive to the development of various skills.
Furthermore, training teachers in the use of this technology is essential to ensure
that robotics is utilized effectively and meaningfully in schools.
       The problem to be investigated in this research is to understand how
educational robotics can contribute to students’ educational development and to
teacher training. It is necessary to analyze the challenges faced in implementing
this technology in schools, as well as the strategies that can be adopted to
overcome them. Issues such as teacher training, curriculum adaptation, and the
availability of resources are fundamental to the effective integration of robotics
into teaching.
       The objective of this research is to analyze the impact of educational
robotics on students’ educational development and teacher training, identifying
the main advantages, challenges, and future prospects of this pedagogical
approach.
       The text is structured as follows: the introduction presents the topic, the
rationale, the problem, and the objective of the research. Next, the theoretical
framework addresses the main concepts and theories related to educational
robotics. The three main sections explore the impact of robotics on educational
development, teacher training, and future challenges and prospects. The
methodology describes the methods used in the literature review. In the
discussion and results section, the research findings, their implications for


                                                                               446

educational practice, and suggestions for future research are analyzed. Finally,
the concluding remarks summarize the main points discussed throughout the
study.


2. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK


         The theoretical framework is structured around three main axes: the
fundamental concepts and historical evolution of educational robotics are
presented, providing a basis for understanding the topic; next, the practical
application of robotics in the educational context is explored, highlighting the
benefits and methodologies used to integrate this technology into teaching;
finally, teacher training is addressed, discussing the necessary competencies,
available training programs, and the challenges faced by educators in
implementing robotics projects in the classroom.


3.   IMPACT       OF     EDUCATIONAL        ROBOTICS       ON    EDUCATIONAL
DEVELOPMENT


         Educational robotics has demonstrated a range of benefits for the student
learning process. According to Alexandre and Alexandria (2023, p. 2165),
“educational robotics allows for the integration of different areas of knowledge,
promoting interdisciplinary and meaningful learning.” This approach facilitates the
understanding of complex concepts and stimulates students’ interest in scientific
and technological subjects. Furthermore, Azevedo, Aglaé, and Pitta (2010, p.
348) emphasize that “the use of robotics kits in the classroom contributes to the
development of critical thinking and creativity,” skills essential for the
comprehensive education of students.
         Case studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of educational robotics
in various school contexts. Campos (2017, p. 2109) reports that “in a public
school in rural Brazil, the implementation of a robotics project resulted in a
significant improvement in students’ academic performance, particularly in
mathematics and science.” This result confirms robotics’ ability to engage
students and facilitate the understanding of content considered difficult. De
Freitas Neto and Bertagnolli (2021, p. 424) conducted a systematic review of the


                                                                               447

literature and concluded that “educational robotics projects are effective in
promoting collaborative work and problem-solving, essential skills for the 21st
century.” Analysis of these studies indicates that robotics not only improves
academic performance but also develops socio-emotional skills.
       A comparison between traditional teaching methods and the robotics-
based approach reveals significant differences. De Souza, Rodrigues, and
Andrade (2016, p. 1265) state that “while traditional methods tend to be teacher-
centered, educational robotics promotes student-centered learning, where
students are active participants in the process.” This results in greater
engagement and motivation to learn. Similarly, Ferraz (2023, p. 3215) notes that
“educational robotics facilitates the practical application of theoretical knowledge,
allowing students to see the relevance of what they are learning.” This practical
application is fundamental to consolidating learning and making the educational
process meaningful.
       Therefore, it is evident that educational robotics offers a number of
advantages compared to traditional methods. Sabatke and Costa (2023, p. 509)
highlight that “educational robotics is a powerful tool for transforming education,
promoting the integration of innovative technologies into the school curriculum.”
This transformation is essential to prepare students for the challenges of the
future. Silva (2014, p. 4021) also emphasizes that “educational robotics can be
adapted to different contexts and needs, making it a versatile and inclusive tool.”
Thus, educational robotics proves to be an effective and innovative approach to
students’ educational development.
       Based on the evidence presented, it is concluded that educational robotics
has a significant positive impact on educational development. The analysis of
benefits, case studies, and comparison with traditional methods indicate that
robotics not only improves academic performance but also develops essential
skills for the 21st century. Thus, educational robotics stands out as an innovative
and effective pedagogical strategy, capable of transforming educational practice
and preparing students for future challenges.




                                                                                 448

4. TEACHER TRAINING FOR EDUCATIONAL ROBOTICS


       Teacher training for the effective use of educational robotics is of
fundamental importance to ensure that this technology is implemented
meaningfully in schools. According to De Souza, Rodrigues, and Andrade (2016,
p. 1265), “the introduction of computational thinking into teacher training is
essential for teachers to develop the skills necessary to teach educational
robotics effectively.” This training enables educators to understand the basic
concepts of programming and robotics, as well as how to integrate them into the
school curriculum.
       Various professional development and training programs have been
created to address this need. Ferraz (2023, p. 3215) highlights that “technical
courses in agriculture, for example, have incorporated educational robotics into
their teacher training programs, aiming to prepare teachers to handle new
technologies.” These programs include both initial and continuing education,
providing teachers with the necessary tools to implement robotics projects in their
classes. Similarly, Sabatke and Costa (2023, p. 509) state that “workshops and
summer schools are opportunities for teachers to update their knowledge on new
methodologies and technologies applied to educational robotics.”
       However, teachers face several challenges in implementing robotics
projects in the classroom. Xavier and Silva (2022, p. 2006) point out that “one of
the greatest challenges is the lack of material and financial resources, which often
prevents the purchase of robotics kits and other necessary equipment.”
Furthermore, resistance to change and unfamiliarity with new technologies can
hinder the adoption of educational robotics. Freitas Neto and Bertagnolli (2021,
p. 424) explain that:


                        The implementation of educational robotics faces several obstacles,
                        including the need for adequate infrastructure, the lack of institutional
                        support, and the need for a cultural shift in teaching approaches.
                        Teachers must not only learn to use the new tools but also adapt their
                        pedagogical practices to effectively incorporate robotics. This requires
                        a collaborative effort among school administrators, governments, and
                        the educational community as a whole.


       These difficulties are compounded by the lack of time available for
teachers’ continuing professional development. Azevedo, Aglaé, and Pitta (2010,


                                                                                             449

p. 348) note that “teachers, already overburdened with their daily responsibilities,
often find it difficult to participate in additional training programs.” Thus, it is
essential that educational institutions offer support and incentives so that
teachers can dedicate themselves to their professional development.
      Therefore, teacher training is a key element for the success of educational
robotics in schools. Training programs must be accessible and tailored to
teachers’ specific needs. Despite the challenges, with the right support and
sufficient resources, teachers can become agents of change in the use of
educational robotics, providing students with an innovative learning experience.


5.   CHALLENGES         AND    FUTURE      PROSPECTS        OF    EDUCATIONAL
ROBOTICS


      The integration of educational robotics into the school curriculum faces
several challenges. According to Alexandre and Alexandria (2023, p. 2165), “one
of the main obstacles is the lack of adequate infrastructure in schools, which often
lack the necessary resources to implement robotics programs.” The absence of
specific equipment and access to quality internet limits schools’ ability to offer
meaningful learning experiences to students. Furthermore, Campos (2017, p.
2109) points out that “resistance to change on the part of teachers and
educational administrators also represents a significant challenge,” as many
education professionals are not yet familiar with emerging technologies and may
hesitate to adopt new pedagogical practices.
      On the other hand, educational robotics offers countless possibilities and
future opportunities. De Souza, Rodrigues, and Andrade (2016, p. 1265)
emphasize that “robotics has the potential to transform the teaching-learning
process, making it interactive and student-centered.” This transformation can
increase student engagement and promote the development of essential skills,
such as critical thinking and problem-solving. Furthermore, Ferraz (2023, p. 3215)
notes that “educational robotics can be integrated into various fields of
knowledge, from the exact sciences to the arts, providing an interdisciplinary
education.” This interdisciplinary approach not only enriches students’ learning
but also prepares them to face the challenges of a technological and
interconnected world.


                                                                                450

      For educational robotics to reach its full potential, significant investment in
public policies and infrastructure is necessary. Sabatke and Costa (2023, p. 509)
state that “governments must invest in the ongoing training of teachers and the
acquisition of robotics equipment for schools.” This investment is crucial to
ensuring that all students have access to the same learning opportunities. Xavier
and Silva (2022, p. 2006) explain that:


                     The adoption of public policies aimed at incorporating educational
                     robotics into the school curriculum requires strategic planning that
                     involves not only the acquisition of equipment but also teacher training
                     and the development of an appropriate curriculum. It is necessary to
                     create an environment conducive to innovation, where educators can
                     experiment with new methodologies and adapt their teaching practices
                     to effectively incorporate robotics. This process demands a
                     collaborative effort among different levels of government, educational
                     institutions, and the community.


      Azevedo, Aglaé, and Pitta (2010, p. 348) emphasize that “collaboration
between educational institutions, technology companies, and governments is
essential for the creation of sustainable and effective robotics programs.” This
partnership can facilitate the development of high-quality educational resources
and ensure the maintenance and constant updating of equipment. Furthermore,
well-structured public policies can promote equity, ensuring that all schools can
benefit from the advantages offered by educational robotics.
      In short, while educational robotics faces significant challenges, such as a
lack of infrastructure and resistance to change, its potential and future
opportunities are promising. Investments in public policies and in the ongoing
training of teachers are essential to overcoming these obstacles and ensuring
that educational robotics can contribute to students’ educational development.
Thus, educational robotics emerges as a tool for building an inclusive educational
system.


6. METHODOLOGY


      This study is a literature review with a qualitative focus, aimed at analyzing
and synthesizing existing knowledge on the impact of educational robotics on
students’ educational development and teacher training. The qualitative



                                                                                         451

approach was chosen because it allows for an understanding of the phenomena
studied without the need to quantify the data.
       The instruments used in the research included the collection of secondary
data from academic sources, such as scientific articles, dissertations, theses, and
publications in specialized journals. The selection of references was based on
their relevance and recency, seeking works that addressed the topic of
educational robotics. The procedures adopted included searching academic
databases such as Google Scholar, Scielo, and specific education and
technology databases, using keywords— related to the topic, such as
“educational robotics,” “teacher training,” “educational technology,” and
“educational development.”
       The techniques used in the analysis of the collected data included critical
reading and synthesis of the contents of the selected references. The main
concepts, theories, methods, and results presented by the authors were
identified, allowing for a cohesive and structured construction of the theoretical
framework. The information was organized in a way that provided a clear analysis
of the topics addressed, facilitating the understanding and discussion of the
results.

       The reference table used in the research contains an organized list of the

       Including the reference table after the methodology makes it easier to see

sources and topics covered. This contributes to the transparency and credibility
