7. ANALYSIS OF RESULTS OBTAINED WITH EDUCATIONAL ROBOTICS


       The analysis of the results obtained with educational robotics reveals a
varied landscape rich in implications for the teaching-learning process. Alexandre
and Alexandria (2023, p. 2165) state that “educational robotics has a significant
impact on student motivation, increasing their interest in scientific and
technological subjects.” This assertion is corroborated by several studies
showing how the integration of robotics into the curriculum can engage students
more effectively than traditional methods.


                                                                                      453

       Campos (2017, p. 2109) reports that “in a study conducted at a public
school, students who participated in a robotics project “showed a significant
improvement in their math and science grades, in addition to demonstrating
greater interest and participation in class.” This result highlights robotics’ ability
to facilitate the understanding of abstract concepts through practical and
interactive activities. De Freitas Neto and Bertagnolli (2021, p. 424) complement
this perspective by stating that “educational robotics promotes not only the
learning of specific content but also the development of skills such as problem-
solving, critical thinking, and collaboration.” The inclusion of these skills is
essential for the holistic development of students.
       However, results may vary across different studies and educational
contexts. De Souza, Rodrigues, and Andrade (2016, p. 1265) observed that “the
results of implementing educational robotics can be influenced by factors such
as available infrastructure, teachers’ level of training, and institutional support.”
This variation is important to consider when analyzing the effectiveness of
robotics in different school settings. Ferraz (2023, p. 3215) highlights that “in
institutions that have infrastructure and continuing education programs for
teachers, the results tend to be more positive.”
       Furthermore, Sabatke and Costa (2023, p. 509) emphasize that “the
integration of robotics into the curriculum must be planned and structured, taking
into account the specific characteristics of each school and the students’
circumstances.” This planning is essential to ensure that all students can benefit
from educational robotics. Silva (2014, p. 4021) clarifies that:


                      The implementation of educational robotics requires a coordinated
                      effort among teachers, administrators, and the school community. It is
                      necessary to develop an action plan that includes teacher training, the
                      acquisition of equipment, and the adaptation of the curriculum to new
                      technologies. Only through joint efforts is it possible to overcome
                      challenges and achieve the desired results.


       A comparison of results across different studies also reveals that
educational robotics can be adapted to diverse contexts. Xavier and Silva (2022,
p. 2006) observed that “in rural schools, robotics has been used as a tool to bring
students closer to technologies that are often distant from their everyday reality.”




                                                                                         454

This demonstrates the flexibility of educational robotics in meeting the needs of
different contexts.
       Therefore, the analysis of the results obtained with educational robotics
shows a promising scenario, but one that requires attention to the particularities
of each school environment. The benefits evidenced in the research, such as
increased motivation and the development of essential skills, indicate that
robotics can be an effective tool in education. However, it is essential that
implementation be well-planned and supported by public policies and adequate
investments. In this way, educational robotics can transform the teaching-
learning process and prepare students for future challenges.


8. IMPLICATIONS FOR EDUCATIONAL PRACTICE


       The results obtained with educational robotics have several important
implications for educational practice. Alexandre and Alexandria (2023, p. 2165)
state that “the inclusion of robotics in the school curriculum can transform the way
students interact with knowledge, making learning meaningful.” This suggests
that educational robotics is not merely an additional tool, but a means of
reconfiguring traditional pedagogical practices.
       The adoption of educational robotics requires a shift in the teacher’s role,
who becomes a facilitator of learning rather than a transmitter of knowledge.
Campos (2017, p. 2109) highlights that “teachers need to develop new
competencies, such as the ability to facilitate project-based learning and the
capacity to integrate different areas of knowledge.” This shift is essential to
maximize the benefits of educational robotics, as it fosters a collaborative and
interdisciplinary learning environment.
       De Souza, Rodrigues, and Andrade (2016, p. 1265) point out that
“educational robotics also requires a reassessment of the assessment methods
used in schools.” Traditional methods, based solely on written exams, may fail to
capture the skills developed through robotics projects, such as critical thinking,
creativity, and collaboration. Ferraz (2023, p. 3215) suggests that “assessments
should include criteria that value the learning process, problem-solving, and the
ability to work in teams.” The implications for educational practice are also
reflected in the need for adequate infrastructure. Xavier and Silva (2022, p. 2006)


                                                                                455

state that “schools need to be equipped with the necessary resources, such as
robotics kits, internet access, and adequate spaces for conducting practical
activities.” Without these resources, the implementation of robotics may be limited
and uneven.
           Based on these results, some recommendations for teachers and
educational administrators can be made. De Freitas Neto and Bertagnolli (2021,
p. 424) emphasize the importance of ongoing teacher training: “Teachers must
have access to training programs that not only teach robotics techniques but also
how to integrate them effectively into the curriculum.” Furthermore, it is essential
that educational administrators support these initiatives by providing time and
resources for teacher training.
           Sabatke and Costa (2023, p. 509) recommend that “educational
administrators develop partnerships with technology companies and universities
to facilitate the implementation of educational robotics.” These partnerships can
offer technical support, resources, and training, expanding the opportunities for
success of robotics projects in schools. Azevedo, Aglaé, and Pitta (2010, p. 348)
clarify:


                          Collaboration between schools, companies, and universities is
                          essential for creating an ecosystem of innovation in education. These
                          partnerships can provide not only the necessary material resources but
                          also the knowledge and technical expertise that are often lacking in
                          schools. The creation of collaborative networks allows schools to share
                          experiences, challenges, and solutions, strengthening the
                          implementation of educational robotics in a sustainable and effective
                          manner.


           Therefore, the implications of educational robotics for educational practice
require changes in teaching methods, assessment, and school infrastructure.
The adoption of recommendations that include ongoing teacher training and the
development of strategic partnerships can facilitate the effective integration of
robotics into the school curriculum, ensuring that all students can benefit from this
innovative pedagogical approach.




                                                                                             456

9. LIMITATIONS AND SUGGESTIONS FOR FUTURE RESEARCH


       The studies analyzed on educational robotics reveal several limitations
that need to be considered for a greater understanding of the topic. Alexandre
and Alexandria (2023, p. 2165) highlight that “one of the main limitations is the
variability in the quality and quantity of resources available in schools,” which can
influence the results obtained. This disparity can lead to an uneven
implementation of educational robotics, where some schools are well-equipped
while others lack the necessary basic resources.
       Campos (2017, p. 2109) notes that “there is a scarcity of longitudinal
studies that track students’ development over time following the introduction of
educational robotics.” Most research focuses on short-term outcomes, without
considering the lasting impacts on students’ learning and skill development.
Furthermore, De Souza, Rodrigues, and Andrade (2016, p. 1265) state that “the
lack of a standardized curriculum for educational robotics makes it difficult to
compare different studies and educational contexts.” This lack of standardization
prevents an accurate assessment of the effectiveness of robotics as an
educational tool.
       Another significant limitation is mentioned by De Freitas Neto and
Bertagnolli (2021, p. 424), who indicate that “many studies do not consider the
role of cultural and socioeconomic differences in the implementation of
educational robotics.” These variables can influence how robotics is perceived
and used by students and teachers, affecting research results. Azevedo, Aglaé,
and Pitta (2010, p. 348) emphasize that “resistance to change by on the part of
educators and administrators is also a limiting factor, as it can hinder the adoption
of new pedagogical practices.”
       To overcome these limitations, several suggestions for future research are
proposed. Ferraz (2023, p. 3215) suggests that “future research should focus on
long-term studies that track students’ progress at different stages of their education.”
This would allow for a better understanding of the lasting impacts of educational
robotics. Furthermore, Sabatke and Costa (2023, p. 509) recommend that “future
studies include an analysis of cultural and socioeconomic variables to understand
how these factors influence the effectiveness of educational robotics.” Xavier and
Silva (2022, p. 2006) state:


                                                                                    457

                      Future research on educational robotics should consider the creation of
                      standardized curricula that can be adapted to different contexts,
                      allowing for a more accurate comparison of results. Furthermore, it is
                      essential that studies include a critical analysis of the institutional and
                      cultural barriers that may hinder the effective implementation of robotics
                      in schools. By addressing these issues, research can provide insights
                      for the formulation of effective educational policies.


      Another important aspect is the need for more qualitative studies that
explore the experiences of teachers and students with educational robotics. De
Souza, Rodrigues, and Andrade (2016, p. 1265) suggest that “interviews and
focus groups could provide an understanding of the challenges and benefits
perceived by the school community.”
      Therefore, the limitations identified in studies on educational robotics point
to the need for a standardized approach in future research. Addressing these
limitations will allow for an understanding of the impacts of robotics on education,
providing a foundation for the implementation of innovative and effective
pedagogical practices.


10. FINAL CONSIDERATIONS


      The main findings of this research indicate that educational robotics has a
significant impact on students’ educational development and teacher training. In
response to the research question regarding how educational robotics
contributes to student development and teacher training, it became evident that
educational robotics promotes student-centered learning. This increases student
motivation and engagement, facilitating the understanding of complex concepts
and promoting the development of essential skills such as critical thinking,
problem-solving, and collaboration.
      The observed benefits include an improvement in students’ academic
performance, especially in science and mathematics. Educational robotics also
has the potential to transform teaching practice, requiring teachers to develop
new competencies and adopt interdisciplinary teaching methods. These findings
highlight the importance of ongoing teacher training and the need for institutional
support for the effective implementation of robotics in schools.
      However, the research also identified several challenges in integrating
educational robotics. The lack of adequate infrastructure, resistance to change


                                                                                            458

on the part of educators and administrators, and the absence of a standardized
curriculum are significant obstacles that must be overcome to maximize the
benefits of educational robotics. These challenges indicate that, although robotics
has great potential, its implementation requires planning and ongoing support.
       The contributions of this study are relevant to understanding the role of
educational robotics in educational development. Analysis of the results shows
that robotics can be an effective tool for improving the quality of teaching and
learning, providing an engaging educational experience. Furthermore, this study
offers practical recommendations for teachers and educational administrators on
how to effectively integrate robotics into the school curriculum.
       However, it is important to recognize that further studies are needed to
complement the findings of this research. Longitudinal studies that track student
development over time are necessary to understand the lasting impacts of
educational    robotics.   Furthermore,     research     exploring    cultural   and
socioeconomic variables can provide an analysis of how educational robotics can
be adapted to different contexts. The inclusion of qualitative analyses of teachers’
and students’ experiences can also enrich the understanding of the challenges
and benefits of robotics in educational practice.
       In summary, this research contributes to knowledge about educational
robotics, highlighting its benefits, challenges, and implications for educational
practice. Educational robotics has the potential to transform teaching and
learning, but its effective implementation requires a collaborative and ongoing
effort. Future studies are needed to deepen the understanding of the impacts of
robotics and to develop strategies that ensure its successful integration into
schools. In this way, educational robotics can fulfill its role of preparing students
for the challenges of the 21st century, promoting an inclusive education.

ABSTRACT: This research aimed to evaluate how Environmental Education
(EE) is being addressed in the Political-Pedagogical Projects (PPPs) of 8 state
schools in the municipality of Juazeiro-BA, according to the Bahia State EE Policy
(PEEA/BA) and the Bahia Reference Curriculum Document (DCRB). The need
for the inclusion of EE in the schools' PPPs is implicit in the DCRB, when it
reiterates the need to promote respect for socio-environmental sustainability.
Resolution CEE No. 11, of January 17, 2017, which provides for Environmental
Education in the Bahia State Education System, determines that EE must be
present in an articulated manner at all levels, stages and modalities of education
and included in the School Regulations, Political-Pedagogical Project, Course
Plan (PC), Course Pedagogical Project (PPC) and Institutional Development Plan
(PDI). The analysis of the PPPs (Political-Pedagogical Projects) was carried out
within the theoretical-analytical framework of Bardin's content analysis,
identifying the textual parts that addressed the environmental theme and
selecting those directly or indirectly related to Environmental Education. In
composing the corpus of analysis in the PPPs, it was possible to identify essential
information for the document, such as the didactic-pedagogical organization, the
history of the school unit, the teaching and administrative staff, infrastructure,
among other necessary aspects for its elaboration. It was concluded that there is
limited internalization of the environmental issue in the PPPs, and that proposals
and actions in Environmental Education are not adequately grounded for the
current configuration of secondary education. Regarding the theme related to
mycology, no references were found in the PPPs, demonstrating a gap that does
not adequately address this group of living beings.

KEYWORDS: education, environment and sustainability, secondary education,
fungi.

1. INTRODUCTION


       Environmental Education (EE), a topic focused on the protection and
improvement of environmental conditions, has been on the international political
agenda since the 1972 Stockholm Declaration. In Brazil, EE attained the status
of National Policy in the late 1990s and is defined in Law 9.975/1999, Article 1, in
terms of the relationships established between the individual and the community,
which encompass “the development of social values, knowledge, skills, attitudes,
and competencies focused on environmental conservation, a common good,
essential for a healthy and sustainable quality of life” (Brazil, 1999, n.p.).
Furthermore, EE must be permanently integrated and disseminated at all levels
and in all forms of education.
       Law No. 9,394/96, the Law on Guidelines and Foundations of National
Education (LDBEN), establishes the pedagogical policy project (PPP) as an
essential component for all schools (Brazil, 1996). The document contains all the
pedagogical proposals, goals, and objectives that the school seeks to achieve
during the school year, making it crucial for the school’s pedagogical policy.
Constructed collaboratively, the PPP makes it possible to restore the human,
scientific, and liberating meaning of planning, promoting changes in daily
conceptions and practices, and outlining guidelines for the educational process.
It stands in contrast to the logic of bureaucratic or purely strategic planning, which
is widespread in the more conservative spheres of education and in the neoliberal
reforms of the 1990s (Rebouças et al., 2021).
       By highlighting the reflective and transformative potential of collective
action as a pedagogical political project, Gadotti (1998) clarifies that such action
does not negate what has already been established by the school, such as its
history, its curricula, its methods, its internal and external staff, and its way of life.
A project always confronts what already exists with what can be built.
       Loureiro (2020) points out that EA is an educational and social practice
whose objective is to promote the construction of values, concepts, skills, and
attitudes that enable an understanding of the reality of life and the conscious and
responsible actions of individuals and social groups in the environment.
Contributing to the search for a new civilizational and societal paradigm, based



                                                                                      464

on a new ethic in the relations between society and nature (Silva; Schiavetti,
2012).
         Therefore, to effectively transform this structural and conjunctural crisis,
EE is, by definition, a strategic element for the development of a broad critical
consciousness that comprehends the social and production relations that situate
human insertion in nature, with the PPPs serving as a guiding document for these
practices in the school environment and the socio-environmental relations that
permeate it. Thus, education professionals must provide students with
opportunities to engage with scientific knowledge, the relationship between
humans and other living beings, and nature, fostering a worldview that allows
them to observe it from a different perspective.
         Among the content that can be linked to EA are studies of microorganisms,
particularly fungi, which are fundamental to sustaining life on the planet, as they
participate in the decomposition of organic matter, the recycling of nutrients, and
the production of various compounds beneficial to human and animal health (Reis
et al., 2024).
         Despite all their economic and environmental importance, fungi are still
little known and valued by most people, who often associate them only with
diseases and pests. It is commendable that the school highlights, in its
Pedagogical Policy Statement, a distinctive pedagogical approach, utilizing
resources accessible to students and bridging the gap between scientific
knowledge and popular knowledge, with the aim of clarifying the subject. Reis et
al. (2024) mention the lack of contextualization in the teaching of mycology in
high school, particularly from the perspective of environmental education, and
further state that an immersion in the concepts underpinning the STSA (Science,
Technology, Society, and Environment) movement is necessary for students’
critical and reflective thinking.
         The State Policy on Environmental Education of the State of Bahia –
PEEA-BA, in its Article 18, stipulates that “formal education systems must
promote the inclusion of environmental education in school regulations and in
schools’ Educational Project Plans (PPPs), at all levels and in all types of
education” (Bahia, 2011).
         To situate AE within a more specific context, the State of Bahia drafted
and validated the State of Bahia Environmental Education Policy (PEEA/BA)


                                                                                 465

through Law 12,056 of January 7, 2011, regulated by Decree 19,083 of June 7,
2019, to be implemented in all its Territorial Identity (TI) (Bahia, 2011, 2019). The
PEEA/BA is a public policy that incorporates, within its educational framework,
the principles of the Treaty on Environmental Education for Sustainable Societies
and Global Responsibility and the Earth Charter; it organizes implementation
plans within a specific territory; and it must be institutionalized as the fulfillment
of the State’s obligation to ensure conditions that facilitate society’s effective
participation in decision-making processes and public management.
       In light of the aforementioned questions and considering the PPPs as
relevant documents in the AE movement within formal educational settings, a
study was conducted to examine how AE, and its relationship with content on
fungi, has been addressed in Pedagogical Policy Projects at 8 state schools in
the municipality of Juazeiro, from the perspective of the Bahia State
Environmental Education Policy (PEEA/BA) and the DCRB.


2. METHODOLOGICAL APPROACH


       This study is a documentary research project with a qualitative approach
and exploratory nature, conducted in 2023. It consisted of an analysis of PPPs
from 8 state high schools located in the municipality of Juazeiro, Bahia. Juazeiro
is located in the far northern interior of Bahia in the São Francisco Valley
mesoregion, approximately 500 km from Salvador, the capital of Bahia, and
adjacent to Petrolina, Pernambuco, separated by the São Francisco River. It has
a population of 235,816 inhabitants (IBGE, Demographic Census, 2022).
       The study proceeded to search for and analyze the current PPPs of the
state high schools in the municipality. These documents were requested from the
Coordination of the Territorial Education Center (NTE-04) in Juazeiro, Bahia,
which promptly provided contact information for the state schools in the
municipality and issued a document to the schools, informing them of the nature
and objective of the research. The schools that provided the documents were not
identified in this study, ensuring their anonymity and confidentiality.
       Eighteen high schools in the state system were contacted via email, of
which only 8 submitted their PPPs in a timely manner for inclusion in this study.



                                                                                  466

These schools were identified as: School-A, School-B, School-C, School-D,
School-E, School-F, School-G, and School-H.
       The analysis of the PPPs was conducted within the theoretical-analytical
framework of content analysis by Bardin (2016), beginning with a pre-analysis
involving an initial, flexible reading that adapted to the flexibility with which each
school’s documents were drafted, as well as the specific nature of what the
research aims to present. This was followed by an exploratory reading, identifying
and assigning codes to relevant passages. After rereading the excerpts, the
categories of analysis were established.
       Textual passages addressing environmental themes were identified,
selecting those directly or indirectly related to EE, and after a more thorough
analysis, the excerpts were included in the results of this study in a table showing
the frequency of occurrence of the categories. The year of update for the PPPs
was also recorded, along with the frequency of occurrence of certain descriptors
related to EA, such as: “Environmental Education”; “Sustent” (ability)(able);
“Environment”; “Biodiversity”; “Socio-environmental.” Figure 1 presents the main
stages of the research.

3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION


       In compiling the corpus for analysis—specifically, the PPPs examined—it
was possible to identify information essential to the document, such as the
didactic-pedagogical organization, the school’s history, the teaching and
administrative staff, and infrastructure, among other details necessary for its
development. All analyzed documents highlighted the need for interdisciplinary
work in school activities. As an example, here is a quote from School A’s PPP:
       The contextual and interdisciplinary implementation of high school
curriculum content is achieved through interdisciplinarity, the interrelationship
between teachers and their respective subjects, and through the conduct of
extracurricular activities involving all subjects. This will ensure interdisciplinary
experiences of the curriculum content so that students can experience, in
practice, the significance of systematic studies.(School A’s PPP, p. 25).

in the EA.

directly or indirectly associated with EE.
       It was observed that the PPPs have been outdated since their creation, as
can be seen in Table 2, especially with regard to the DCRB (Bahia, 2022).
However, a concern was noted on the part of administrators and coordinators
regarding the reformulation of the documents in light of the current challenge

       The term “Biodiversity” was mentioned only by School C. The study
conducted by Rodrigues et al. (2022) concluded that “the dissemination of
scientific literature on Environmental Education and biodiversity is related to
issues that go beyond environmental concerns, contributing to social, economic,
and sustainable development aspects”; however, greater emphasis should be
placed on the importance of biodiversity conservation, including the complexity
of ecological relationships among living organisms. From this perspective, fungi,
for example, are underrepresented in terms of their ecological importance in
schools (Silva and Gown, 2021; Rizzon et al., 2017), and other potential
applications are also overlooked. Fungal bioremediation has emerged as a
sustainable alternative for remediating areas contaminated with toxic compounds
(Pesenti et al., 2023; Carvalho, 2023), as it is a process that utilizes
microorganisms—fungi—which possess metabolic versatility and the ability to
degrade complex compounds (Zeghal et al., 2021) and transform them into less
harmful or biodegradable compounds.
       Biological control is an ecological alternative to chemical pest control
methods, which can be harmful to the environment and human health; it consists
of the use of microorganisms, particularly bacteria and fungi (Dias da Silva et al.,
2023; Miranda et al., 2023). Dias da Silva et al. (2023) highlight its effectiveness
in controlling pests and diseases, reducing environmental impacts, increasing


                                                                                     469

food security, and decreasing rural workers’ exposure to toxic substances,
thereby contributing to more sustainable agriculture.
        Kramer and Estevam da Silva (2023) emphasize that fungi, due to their
ability to capture metal ions in solution through sorption, mobilization, and
adsorption, can be used in the biosorption process, accumulating high
concentrations of heavy metals in their cells, thereby enabling the removal of
these    contaminants        from     water.                         Heavy                      metals,                          because          they   are
bioaccumulative, can enter the food chain, causing physiological and biochemical
changes and posing carcinogenic risks to humans (Kramer; Estevam da Silva
2023). And in soil regeneration, with the consequent increase in agricultural
production, in addition to the recovery of degraded areas using arbuscular
mycorrhizal fungi (Prado et al., 2023; Lima et al., 2017; Soares et al., 2023).
Therefore, it is beneficial for schools to incorporate fungi as a cross-cutting and
integrative theme that can foster the development of critical environmental
education.

        The analyzed PPPs do not provide information on environmental
conditions in their surroundings, which would be essential to justify the need for
including environmental education ( ) projects and interventions; however,



                                                                                                                                                         470

environmental education projects were identified only at School-A, School-B, and
School-E. A study conducted in four state schools in Juazeiro also found a lack
of programs and projects involving the local community, as well as the “absence
of essential content and elements in the curricular Environmental Education
process” (Souza et al., 2023, p.205). However, it is worth noting that all schools
reported that they are in the process of updating and adapting their PPPs to the
new high school curriculum. The ProEASE document (Bahia, 2015) had already
warned of the limited integration of environmental issues into pedagogical policy
documents. CEE Resolution No. 11, dated January 17, 2017, which addresses
Environmental Education in the State Education System of Bahia, stipulates that
EE: [...] must be present in a coordinated manner at all levels, stages, and
modalities of education and incorporated into the School Regulations,
Pedagogical Policy Document, Course Plan (PC), Course Pedagogical Project
(PPC), and Institutional Development Plan (PDI).
      School A cites projects such as “Citizen School,” in partnership with the
State University of Bahia (UNEB), for the preservation of the São Francisco River,
and the “Vegetable Garden and Garden” project; however, although they are
mentioned in the PPE, it was not possible to find further details regarding their
objectives, implementation, or continuity. The document presents social
problems faced by the target audience and some proposals for intervention, but
we did not identify any issues related to the “Sustainable Environment” project,
as described in Figure 2:


                       Figure 2 – Excerpt from School-A’s PPP.

      Among the initiatives to foster collaboration between the school and
parents, as well as between the school and the local community, mention was
made of a visit by students to a Science Fair on the theme “Environment and




                                                                              471

Sustainability.” The 3rd Science and Mathematics Fair was held under the theme
“Respecting nature is respecting oneself.”
       According to Souza et al. (2019), the methodology for integrating
environmental education (EE) into the socio-educational context is not limited to
formal education; however, the school is viewed as the primary vehicle for
introducing the subject. This qualified discussion regarding the integration of EE
into School Development Plans (SDPs) depends on the ongoing professional
development of the stakeholders responsible for their development. However,
there are several obstacles, as mentioned in the study conducted by Nascimento
et al. (2020) at a school in Curaçá, Bahia, in which negative responses were
obtained from the surveyed teachers when asked about their participation in EA
courses offered by the Bahia State Department of Education (SEC-BA). The
study by Souza et al. (2019) also presents an analysis of the PPPs of four schools
in the municipalities of Juazeiro, Bahia, and Petrolina, Pernambuco. The authors
conclude that, in addition to the lack of preparation among professionals in
delivering EA content, elementary and secondary education programs contain
little information on the subject within their pedagogical policy documents.
       School-B submitted its PPP for the 2016–2019 quadrennium, still
following the 2012 National Curriculum Guidelines for Secondary Education,
CNE/CEB Resolution No. 2 of January 30, 2012 (BRAZIL, 2012) and Law
9394/96, the Law on Guidelines and Foundations of National Education (BRAZIL,
2017), with a work proposal for the cross-cutting themes of Ethics, Health,
Environment, Sexual Orientation, Cultural Plurality, Work, and Consumption.
       The school also presents as a goal for 2016 in its PPP the revitalization of
the interdisciplinary project “I Take Care of My Environment,” without providing
further details about the project.
       School C offers high school education integrated with vocational training,
having already submitted its updated PPP in 2019. The document highlights that:
[...] the curriculum of the courses includes knowledge related to: [...] quality
management, social and environmental responsibility and sustainability. Among
the PPP’s objectives, the following stands out: “Develop an environmental
awareness project.” In the presentation of the work areas, it was possible to
identify approaches to environmental education and sustainability. The following
excerpts from the PPP are noteworthy:

         Escola-D presents the PPP updated in 2022. The appreciation and

introduction of EA fundamentals for the development and implementation of

school projects, as presented in the following excerpt:


                     [...] there is a constant focus on the environment, seeking to foster a
                     holistic view of our students that goes beyond social issues. Several
                     initiatives have been undertaken in recent years, including
                     environmental awareness and conservation efforts starting at the

      The need to include Environmental Education (EE) in school curriculum
plans is implicit in the Bahia Reference Curriculum Document (DCRB), which
reiterates the need to promote respect for socio-environmental sustainability. EE
appears in the document as one of the integrative themes, which are a new
formulation of what were previously known as cross-cutting themes, as shown in
Figure 3.




                                                                                         474

      Figure 3 – Environmental Education as an integrating theme in the DCRB (2022).




                                  Source: Author, 2024.


       According to the DCRB (Bahia, 2022), the Integrating Themes seek to
promote the construction of a more just, fraternal, equitable, inclusive, and
sustainable society, without losing sight of the importance of secularism. They
advocate for an approach to social interaction that plays a fundamental political
and pedagogical role in formal contexts of humanization, stimulating debate on
challenges related to rights violations. The DCRB is the state regulatory
framework divided into 3 volumes, among which Secondary Education is covered
in Volume 2.
       Escola-E presents as one of its goals the landscaping of the outer
perimeter with trees and their preservation as a sustainability initiative. Structural
projects also use environmental issues as a central theme. The school also
includes, among its priority actions, the Sustainability and Environment Project –
Com Vida, which aims to:


                       [...] to raise awareness within our school community regarding
                       environmental stewardship, valuing our school grounds as well as the
                       surrounding environment, as a means of fostering an ecologically
                       healthy environment through the work carried out by our students
                       during the school year under the guidance of our dedicated faculty and
                       the democratic leadership of our innovative administration and the
                       Student Council (School-E PPP, p.24)




                                                                                         475

       School-F includes “Environment and Sustainability” as one of its
educational principles, and among its educational objectives, we can highlight
two that are associated with critical environmental education:


                      [...] Recognize the ethical and moral boundaries that have guided social
                      interaction; [...] Identify, analyze, and evaluate natural, social,
                      economic, cultural, and political transformations in their community [...]
                      (School-F PPP, p.6).


       For the new high school curriculum, the school proposes interdisciplinary
work using the STEAM approach (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, and
Mathematics), in addition to emphasizing the importance of integrating the school
with external partners such as NGOs and companies, which exposes students to
other realities and learning opportunities.


                      [...] STEAM education is an interactive, multidisciplinary, and
                      integrated teaching methodology that fosters students’ development in
                      all areas through resources that cover content in the following fields:
                      Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, Mathematics, Humanities, and
                      Environmental Awareness, where the interplay between these
                      disciplines is precisely what “resonates” with students, thereby
                      stimulating their autonomy, creativity, and cognitive abilities, among
                      other skills, through the resolution of real-world problems (School F’s
                      PPPs, p. 21, emphasis added).


       School-G presents a vision, goals, and objectives similar to those of
School-E. In the course plan for the Portuguese language curriculum component,
we highlight two competencies also related to critical EA.


                      [...] C3. Use different languages (artistic, bodily, and verbal) to exercise,
                      with autonomy and collaboration, agency and authorship in personal
                      and collective life, in a critical, creative, ethical, and supportive manner,
                      defending viewpoints that respect others and promote human
                      rights, socio-environmental awareness, and responsible
                      consumption at the local, regional, and global levels. [...] C5. Argue
                      based on facts, data, and reliable information to formulate, negotiate,
                      and defend common ideas, viewpoints, and decisions that respect and
                      promote human rights, socio-environmental awareness, and
                      responsible consumption at the local, regional, and global levels, with
                      an ethical stance regarding care for oneself, others, and the planet
                      (School-G’s PPPs, p.49, emphasis added)


       School-H states in its PPP that its curriculum includes knowledge related
to social and environmental responsibility and sustainability. Among its
objectives, the one most closely aligned with EA work was: “To foster the


                                                                                              476

development of critical and autonomous citizens capable of sound reasoning,
aware of their rights and duties toward humanity” (School-H PPP, p.17).
       The information from all PPPs identified as relating to EA was presented
here in its entirety, which highlights the superficiality with which the topic is
addressed in the documents, as also concluded by the studies by Nascimento et
al. (2020) and Souza et al. (2019) conducted with schools in the region. Nor are
there proposals or actions grounded in the new structure of secondary education,
which already offers an interdisciplinary approach to addressing current socio-
environmental issues. Furthermore, it is important to note that this document on
school identity must include the legal framework underpinning EA.


4. CONCLUSION


       Significant changes in the structure of secondary education call for the
revision of Pedagogical Project Plans (PPPs), adapting them to new curricular
concepts and organization, which must also address society’s current needs in
the face of enormous challenges to sustainability; thus, Environmental Education
emerges as the most powerful tool for raising public awareness and sensitivity.
To this end, schools will need to address the challenges of organizational
restructuring of pedagogical policy projects so that they can better align with the
DCRB (BAHIA, 2022), and from there, meaningfully integrate Environmental
Education into their interdisciplinary pedagogical projects and publicize them
through channels with unrestricted access to the entire school community.
       EA must also be integrated into the school’s pedagogical policy projects,
the organization and planning of each curricular component, in its pedagogical,
political, and ethical dimensions; furthermore, activities and projects planned and
executed during interdisciplinary sessions—which are indispensable for the
collective engagement so necessary for Environmental Education—must be
urgently internalized.
       With regard to the topic of fungi, no reference is found in the PPPs. This
absence highlights a gap that fails to adequately address this group of living
organisms, which is so relevant and present in students’ daily lives. Furthermore,
this gap may reinforce the marginalization of fungi in culture and science,
perpetuating myths, prejudices, and misinformation about these organisms.


                                                                               477

      The actions proposed in the PPPs, with regard to Environmental
Education, can and should be planned, implemented, and evaluated with the
effective participation of the entire school community and, within the applied
school curriculum, should involve all curricular components, especially Biology
and the educational pathways offered by the school. In these components, it is
essential to develop critical awareness of human action throughout the
biosphere.

ABSTRACT: The purpose of this article is to outline the profile of the school
manager from the perspective of democratic management, given the rapid
changes brought about by the evolution of information technology that have
affected the way people work and relate to each other in different aspects of their
lives. Deepen the concept of school management and what characteristics
permeate the pro-file of the school manager in organizations, in this case,
educational organiza-tions. Arguing that the director is much more than an
administrator, he is a school manager who involves several aspects within the
scope of educational processes, requiring human talent with an open vision for
the leadership of democratic management. The methodology used is a qualitative
approach, with bibliographic and documentary literature, thus contributing to
developing the ideas of the work, based on different theorists who deal with the
topic. As a re-sult, we realized that the manager seeks to reduce the
bureaucratization that permeates the school, as well as minimizing the


                                                                               482

challenges he needs to face, since the work involves the decentralization of
power and weaknesses at the administrative level, the formulation of policies and
objectives of the institution. The conclusion of the article brings an understanding
of how much the as-pects that involve the practice of school management, when
observed and de-veloped assertively and, in line with the management team,
contribute to an integral education of the human being, producing greater equity.

KEYWORDS: profile and characteristics of the school manager, decentralization
of power, practice of democratic and participatory management, leadership.

RESUMO: O presente artigo tem como propósito delinear o perfil do gestor
escolar sob o olhar de uma gestão democrática diante das rápidas mudanças
proporcionadas pela evolução da tecnologia da informação que têm atingido a
maneira como as pessoas trabalham e se relacionam em diversos aspectos de
suas vidas. O estudo busca aprofundar o conceito de gestão escolar e quais as
características que permeiam o perfil do gestor escolar nas organizações, nesse
caso, organizações de ensino. Argumentar que o diretor muito mais que um
administrador, é um gestor escolar que envolve vários aspectos no âmbito dos
processos educativos, exigindo talento humano com uma visão aberta para a
liderança de uma gestão democrática. A metodologia utilizada é de abordagem
qualitativa, com literatura bibliográfica e documental, contribuindo, assim, para
desenvolver as ideias do trabalho, embasada em diferentes teóricos que versam
sobre o tema. Como resultado, percebemos que o gestor procura reduzir a
burocratização que permeia a escola, assim como minimiza os desafios que
precisa enfrentar, uma vez que o trabalho envolve a descentralização do poder
e as fragilidades no plano administrativo, a formulação de políticas e objetivos
da instituição. A conclusão do artigo traz uma compreensão sobre o quanto os
aspectos que envolvem a prática da gestão escolar, quando observados e
desenvolvidos de modo assertivo e em consonância com a equipe gestora,
contribuem para uma educação integral do ser humano, produzindo maior
equidade. de modo que sua atuação garanta uma melhoria na qualidade
pessoal, profissional e na missão de todos os envolvidos na instituição de ensino.

PALAVRAS-CHAVE: perfil e características do gestor escolar, descentralização
do poder, prática da gestão democrática e participativa, liderança.

1. INTRODUCTION


       The purpose of this study is to outline the profile of the school administrator
from the perspective of democratic management, taking into account the intense
and rapid transformations driven by advances in information technology. These
changes have significantly impacted the way people work and interact in various
aspects of life.
       Furthermore, the study seeks to deepen understanding of school
management and the essential characteristics of the administrator as an
educational leader, highlighting their role in building a participatory school
environment aligned with the new demands of the educational landscape. More
than just an administrator, the school principal assumes a strategic role, acting
as a manager/leader who integrates different educational processes. Their role
requires interpersonal skills, a broad vision, and a participatory approach—all
fundamental to building efficient democratic management.
       For this study, we adopted a qualitative approach, utilizing bibliographic
and documentary research. This methodology allowed us to guide and develop
the ideas presented throughout the study, grounded in the work of various
theorists who discuss the topic, such as Lück (2006; 2009, 2011), Moran (2000),
and Juliatto (2007), among others. In addition, the research draws on legal
documents, such as the 1988 Federal Constitution and the Law on Guidelines
and Bases for National Education (LDBEN No. 9,394/96), which provide
normative support for the analysis.
       This article sought to contribute to a reflection on the profile of the school
administrator from the perspective of democratic management within the daily
context and trajectory of educational institutions, since this trajectory constitutes
a construction of the administrator as a mediator with positive participation in
engagement with education professionals. Such engagement encompasses
cultural,   pedagogical,   administrative,    financial,   human,    material,   and
organizational mechanisms. In this sense, Lück (2006, p. 21), in presenting the
concept of management, states that it must be considered “as a process of
mobilizing the competence and energy of people, collectively organized, in the
pursuit and achievement of educational objectives.”



                                                                                  484

      The author emphasizes that the role of the school administrator and their
competencies are not an easy task within an educational institution, as it
constitutes a process that requires engagement with the entire educational
community , which aims to achieve objectives and improvements in the trajectory
of   teaching   and    learning.   It   is   understood,   therefore,   that   the
administrator/principal must act as a coordinator across various spheres.
Furthermore, they must possess a vision for the future and planning skills
combined with a collaborative and democratic approach, always attentive to new
technological trends that can contribute to and benefit the performance of
students, teachers, staff, and collaborators.
      In fact, the administrator is responsible for coordinating and implementing
educational policies in collaboration with the teaching staff and the educational
community. Thus, it is inherent to the school administrator’s role to evaluate the
development of the pedagogical proposal and learning indicators with a view to
improving the school’s performance. Another important aspect for the school
administrator is to have a thorough understanding of the educational institution,
so that they can address potential challenges based on scientific knowledge that
enables them to refine and comprehend the political and social factors influencing
the progress of the entire school process. Given this context, the study aims to
provide historical, conceptual, and normative insights into school administration.
      It is known that, through knowledge and experience, combined with a clear
vision of their mission as a manager, they earn the trust of their staff in the
implementation and execution of their projects. This raises the following
questions: What are the essential characteristics of a school administrator’s
profile in an educational institution? What actions, in the daily school routine,
demonstrate the practice of democratic and participatory management? These
questions are fundamental to the analysis that follows.


2. SCHOOL MANAGEMENT AND THE PROFILE OF THE ADMINISTRATOR


      Throughout Brazil’s history, efforts have been made to understand the
concepts and origins of educational and school management practices. Brazilian
educational administration has been influenced by external models of public and
educational management, primarily from Europe and the United States, in


                                                                               485

addition to the particularities of each of the country’s political and economic
contexts.
      During the colonial period, public administration was based on Roman
administrative law, which incorporated Christian values and positivist ideals. The
access to formal schooling was restricted to a minority, generally composed of
men who were not firstborn sons. Furthermore, education was strongly linked to
the Catholic faith, with the Jesuits serving as the first educators in Brazil. Their
mission was to “sow the seed of faith” through educational activities, which
became a tool for conversion to Christianity (Dassoler, 2009, p. 74).
      With the emergence of the Escolanovista movement, there was a growing
concern with contemporary reality and its influences on the school environment.
This movement sought to address educational needs in a more practical, realistic
manner aligned with the principles of democratic renewal:


                      The renewal of education will be brought about within this movement of
                      transformations, which took place within societies. The vision was for
                      an education capable of responding to the challenges posed by the
                      modern society that was desired and, above all, one that aimed at the
                      social control of the masses through the selection, classification, and
                      organization of individuals to meet the demands of productive labor. In
                      this sense, the renewal of education stems from a critique of the
                      education system developed up to that point, conceived as traditional,
                      on the grounds that the education practiced in schools no longer
                      responded to the modern demands of emerging societies or, indeed,
                      that it would be shaped by the interests of a dominant elite, which saw
                      in education the possibility of realizing its intent to mold individuals to
                      the new era of progress (Gonçalves e Filho, 2021, p.7).


      Following the perspective of democracy and contemporaneity in the school
environment, educational ideals have gradually taken shape over time. It is not
difficult to see that these changes have significantly impacted school
management. In this context, it is worth highlighting the importance of the term
“management” and its relevance to education.
      Starting in the 1990s, the concept of management gained prominence in
the educational landscape, and today its use is widespread. Lück (2011, p. 21)
defines management as:


                      One way to conceptualize management is to view it as a process of
                      mobilizing the competence and energy of collectively organized people
                      so that, through their active and competent participation, they promote




                                                                                            486

                      the achievement, as fully as possible, of the objectives of their work
                      unit—in this case, educational objectives.


      Continuous professional development is essential for the role of the
manager, especially in light of technological advances, which have provided new
tools to optimize the routines of management teams. In the 21st century, the
implementation of information systems, digital tools, and online platforms has
brought greater security in communication and efficiency in school administration.
As an example, the student enrollment and re-enrollment process has been
significantly improved. With the help of integrated systems, it is possible to carry
this out online, reducing lines and streamlining the work of the educational team,
which previously had to plan, coordinate, and execute all stages manually.
       Another example is resource management, where administrators can
track necessary supplies and materials through integrated systems and
spreadsheets, which streamlines work and reduces the time spent on
bureaucratic tasks, allowing teams to integrate more effectively, since, with the
reduction and simplification of manual processes, managers can view their entire
team in a more human way and plan meetings and actions so that everyone
participates in the continuous improvement of the institution’s management and
educational processes.
       In addition to the direct benefits for school management, integration
between the institution and students’ families has also been enhanced through
the use of digital communication and interaction channels. This closer connection
strengthens the monitoring of academic performance and the school community’s
participation in the educational process.
       For students, the integration of technologies into pedagogical planning
makes learning more dynamic and engaging. Classes and activities become
more interactive and challenging, allowing students, with a simple click, to explore
new knowledge and connect with the entire world:


                      Over the past few decades, digital information and communication
                      technologies, also known as ICTs, have transformed the ways we work,
                      communicate, interact, and learn. In education, ICTs have been
                      incorporated into teaching practices as a means to promote more
                      meaningful learning, with the aim of supporting teachers in
                      implementing active teaching methodologies, aligning the teaching-
                      learning process with students’ realities, and sparking greater interest




                                                                                          487

                       and engagement among students at all stages of Basic Education.
                       (Brazil, 2018, p. 1).


        Although technological evolution brings countless benefits to the
educational system, it is essential to take a critical look at the structural conditions
of educational institutions. The physical infrastructure needs to be modernized to
support this new work dynamic, with equipment suitable for the systems and
programs essential to carrying out activities.
        Furthermore, the training of education professionals is indispensable. For
many years, the main tools used by school teams were merely paper, pens, and
pencils, and in many cases, this model still predominates. As Moran states:


                       Each teacher can find the most appropriate way to integrate various
                       technologies and methodological procedures. But it is also important
                       that they expand their knowledge and learn to master forms of
                       interpersonal/group communication as well as audiovisual/telematic
                       communication (Moran, 2000, p. 12).


        Training and ongoing professional development pose challenges for the
management team, as some professionals may be resistant due to difficulties in
using and understanding new technologies. In this context, the role of the school
administrator becomes essential, as it is their responsibility to closely monitor all
departments—both administrative and educational—ensuring that they remain
open to learning and adopting these innovations. The major challenge for
administrators is to involve the entire staff in the professional development
process, respecting the individual needs and paces of each professional.
        In general terms, school management encompasses the organization of
the school at different levels, including the educational curriculum, personnel
management, and financial administration, among other aspects. The journal
Educação em Foco (2023, p. 18) highlights that, through efficient management,
it is possible to establish clear goals and objectives, promote continuing
education, and ensure the development of the entire educational community.
        Understanding school management and defining the ideal profile of a
manager allows for the identification of the institution’s main demands, ensuring
they are met through leadership committed to education.
        Regarding the administrator as a leader, Lück (2009, p. 3) emphasizes
that:


                                                                                       488

                      [...] In the school, the principal is the professional responsible for
                      leading and organizing the work of everyone involved, in order to guide
                      them in developing an educational environment capable of promoting
                      student learning and development at the highest possible level, so that
                      students are equipped to face the new challenges they encounter.


       A good school administrator is capable of leading, motivating, planning,
communicating, innovating, and solving problems within the educational
institution. They must also possess a strategic, flexible, and accessible vision to
address the challenges and changes in the educational landscape. There are
different types of school administrators, such as principals, coordinators,
pedagogical coordinators, and pedagogical directors, among others. Each has
their own specific duties and responsibilities within the school organization;
however, all must share certain essential competencies to perform their roles
efficiently and effectively (Cardoso, 2018, p. 3).
       The Law on Guidelines and Foundations of National Education, No. 9,394
(Brazil, 1996), in its Article 12, defines the duties of educational institutions that
must be carried out by the school administrator, who represents the educational
institution. The administrator’s responsibilities begin with the development and
implementation of the educational institution’s pedagogical proposal, in addition
to managing the teaching staff, technical and administrative personnel, and
material and financial resources. With the support of the pedagogical technical
team, the administrator must ensure compliance with the teachers’ work plan, the
established school days and class hours, and the necessary resources for the
academic remediation of lower-performing students.
       Integrating the school with the family and the community is also part of the
school administrator’s responsibilities. In 2009, Law No. 2013 mandated that
educational institutions must inform students’ guardians about attendance and
academic performance, in addition to publicizing their educational proposal.
Subsequently, in 2019, Law No. 13,803 made it mandatory to notify the municipal
Child Protection Agency when a student exceeds 30% (thirty percent) of
absences relative to the limit permitted by law.
       To comply with these legal requirements, school administrators face daily
challenges, requiring empathy, effective communication, accessibility, and a
deep understanding of current legislation. In addition to these responsibilities,
Laws No. 13,663 and No. 13,840, of 2018 and 2019, respectively, expanded their


                                                                                         489

duties, including the need to implement actions to promote a culture of peace in
schools, as well as to raise awareness, prevent, and combat all types of violence,
especially bullying and drug use or dependence. This new scenario poses
additional challenges for administrators and the teaching staff, who must act
strategically and collaboratively. However, building a safe school environment
depends on the involvement of the entire society, especially families. Without this
partnership, the school alone cannot guarantee a truly safe and welcoming space
for everyone.
      Despite the importance of the administrator’s role, their profile is still rarely
discussed in the field of education. Although the National Framework Law on
Education (LDBEN) No. 9,394/1996 established democratic management for
public schools and some systems use elections to select administrators, others
still maintain the practice of appointments. Regardless of the model adopted, it is
essential that the selection process take into account the appropriate profile of
the administrator, ensuring that they are prepared to handle the multiple
responsibilities that the role demands.
      Clemente Ivo Juliatto, in his work *Educational Partners: Students,
Teachers, Staff, and Leaders* (2007, p. 189), discusses the diverse and
numerous responsibilities of the administrator, presenting a decalogue:


                      1. Embrace the institution’s mission and objectives as their own. 2.
                      Assume full responsibility for compliance with all administrative
                      procedures. 3. Represent the institution or sector to both the internal
                      and external communities. 4. Ensure and promote, by all means at their
                      disposal, the quality of education. 5. Promote the ongoing evaluation of
                      their team’s performance using reliable quantitative and qualitative
                      indicators. 6. Encourage academic productivity and demand high
                      performance from other administrators, faculty, and students. 7.
                      Support sound academic initiatives; recognize and reward the effort and
                      strong performance of other administrators on their team, faculty,
                      students, and staff. 8. Meet frequently, both formally and informally, with
                      the managers on their team and with the general administration. 9.
                      Promote the professional growth of their teachers and staff. 10. Foster
                      a cordial atmosphere among members of the academic community and
                      ensure fair and equitable treatment for all.


      In addition to the responsibilities described and the duties established in
educational legislation, there are many other un s that arise in daily school life
and require the manager to possess a wide range of skills to successfully
implement democratic and participatory management.



                                                                                            490

3. DEMOCRATIC AND PARTICIPATORY MANAGEMENT


       Democratic management is an administrative model that promotes the
active participation of all members of an organization or system in decisions that
influence its operation. Based on participation, collaboration, dialogue, and
transparency, this approach strengthens collective engagement, making
management more inclusive and effective. It can be applied in various fields, such
as education, health, politics, and the business sector.
       In   the    educational        context,   democratic   school    management       is
characterized by the active participation of the entire school community in the
administration of the educational institution. This model goes beyond the role of
administrators and coordinators, also involving teachers, staff, students, families,
and others impacted by the school. In this way, it seeks to build a more
participatory     and   pluralistic     educational   environment      aligned   with   the
community’s needs.
       Democratic school management is based on the pedagogical and
administrative autonomy of public basic education schools, the development of a
collective and participatory political-pedagogical project, the definition and
oversight of financial resources by the school community, the disclosure and
transparency of financial reporting, the institutional evaluation of the school by all
stakeholders, and the direct election of the principal. For Heloísa Lück (2006),
participatory management is a commitment that must be embraced and assumed
by all, reinforcing the importance of shared responsibility in building a more
democratic and inclusive educational environment.
       Democratic and participatory management is a model that seeks to
promote a more just, inclusive, and efficient organizational culture. It stimulates
the development of individual and collective competencies among members of
the organization or system. It also fosters the alignment of individual goals with
organizational or systemic goals. Furthermore, it contributes to strengthening
identity and a sense of belonging to the organization or system. Again, Lück
(2006, p. 41), when referring to democratic management— —explains that “it
occurs to the extent that school practices are guided by consistent philosophy,
values, principles, and ideas, present in the minds and hearts of people,
determining their way of being and acting.”


                                                                                        491

      After all, the role of the administrator is to ensure the school’s effective
performance and to find solutions to challenges that contribute to better student
learning, thereby strengthening the values that dignify human beings.
      The democratic management of public education was enshrined in the
1988 Federal Constitution and in the Law on Guidelines and Bases for Education
No. 9,394 of 1996. As Drabach and Mousquer (2009, p. 2) state:


                      recognized as an achievement of civil-democratic forces, it aims to
                      introduce a new type of school organization, based on the principles of
                      democracy, autonomy, and collective construction, in opposition to the
                      centralizing and bureaucratic character that had been guiding this field.


      However, the Law on Guidelines and Bases for National Education
highlights the need for education systems to guarantee schools pedagogical,
administrative, and financial management autonomy. This guideline has
generated numerous debates on the role of the school administrator, leading to
the following reflection: What should be the profile of the school administrator to
ensure professional, competent, and high-quality management?
      From the perspective of the collective construction of democracy in
schools—or from the perspective of holding school officials accountable for
educational outcomes—concerns regarding the training and working conditions
of school leaders become evident. After all, effective management depends not
only on autonomy but also on leaders who are qualified and well-prepared to face
the challenges of everyday school life.
      A school administrator who practices democratic and participatory
management must involve the entire school community, encouraging everyone
to participate in addressing challenges and planning the educational process.
      In this context, the profile of the school administrator is a determining factor
for the success of an educational institution. Above, we have listed some
essential competencies for a leader whose participatory and dialogic approach is
reflected in management and extends to the entire educational team (Santos
2020). These competencies are fundamental to ensuring not only efficient
administration but also a school environment that fosters student learning and the
achievement of promising results.




                                                                                           492

4. CONCLUSION


       This article sought to reflect on the profile of the school administrator from
the perspective of democratic management in the educational context. As
objectives, we developed an analysis of the relevance and clarity of the concepts
of school administrator, participatory democratic management, and the
administrator’s profile in an educational institution, drawing on various theorists.
By deepening our understanding of school management from a democratic and
participatory perspective, we highlighted some essential characteristics and skills
that, in everyday school life, define the profile of the administrator in educational
organizations.
       We argue that the administrator goes beyond the role of manager; they
are an indispensable professional whose work requires planning, reflection, and,
above all, an ethical, educational, and efficient commitment. School
management, led by the administrator, involves multiple aspects and challenges,
demanding not only technical competence but also human sensitivity and a broad
vision to lead democratic management.
       The results point to the importance of an assertive approach to education,
especially in the face of technological transformations, which introduce new tools
and methodologies capable of making teaching more attractive and dynamic.
This scenario reinforces the need for continuous training of the entire educational
team, in conjunction with the leader/manager, to ensure an innovative and
participatory learning environment.
       We believe in education as an essential instrument of transformation, as
its primary function is to promote the renewal of society. This concept requires
ongoing professional development and a constant pursuit of knowledge,
providing an education grounded in values and committed to building a more just
and equitable society.
       Education plays a central role in the social development of the individual,
empowering active and critical citizens, prepared to intervene and transform the
world in a conscious and responsible manner. In conducting this research, we
prioritized the analysis of the role of the school administrator, educational
management, and the responsibilities of each participant, emphasizing how
effective leadership can modify, improve, and maintain quality learning


                                                                                 493

environments. Such leadership must avoid both excessive authoritarianism and
neglect of the human condition of all those involved, promoting practical,
cooperative, and collaborative management, sustained by dialogue and human
interaction.
       We seek to clarify the concepts of school management and democratic
and participatory management, highlighting the importance of an administrative
model that respects and integrates the internal norms of each educational
institution. Furthermore, we present the characteristics that make up the profile
of the school administrator and that translate into educational practice, grounded
in the collective commitment assumed by professionals in the daily dynamics of
educational institutions.
       Thus, we identify that leadership in school management is realized
through participatory and dialogic actions among administrators, teachers, and
families, performing an essential function of cooperation (Santos, 2020).
       We hope that the readers of this study, whether current or future school
administrators, can draw upon the aspects discussed to enhance their
performance in institutional management and leadership. May this mission,
focused on human development through education, be strengthened daily by the
hope that drives and invigorates all educational endeavors.
