CHAPTER 28
 SEE, REFLECT, AND TRANSFORM:
 SHORT FILMS AS A TOOL FOR
 ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION


Gisele Keise Junges
Master’s Degree in Natural Resources and Sustainability
Universidade Tecnológica Federal do Paraná (UTFPR)
E-mail:giselekjunges@gmail.com .

Maristela Rosso Walker
Ph.D. in Education from the State University of Maringá (UEM)
Universidade Tecnológica Federal do Paraná (UTFPR)
E-mail:maristelawalker@gmail.com


ABSTRACT: The contemporary environmental crisis stems from a development
model based on the intensive exploitation of natural resources and unbridled
consumption, which calls for a rethinking of the relationship between society and
nature. In this context, Environmental Education (EE), which gained traction
following events such as the Stockholm Conference (1972) and the Tbilisi
Conference (1977), takes on a critical, interdisciplinary, and emancipatory
character and should be integrated across all aspects of daily school life, as
guided by the BNCC (2017). Film, especially in the form of short films, serves as
a privileged pedagogical resource because it mobilizes emotion, critical
reflection, and meaningful learning. Due to their brevity and narrative impact,
short films foster interdisciplinary debates and bring schools closer to
contemporary media culture, raising students’ awareness of socio-environmental
issues. Reported experiences show that watching, analyzing, and producing
short films contributes to students’ critical and participatory education (Menezes;
Duarte, 2007), broadening their cultural repertoires and strengthening their
ecological awareness. However, challenges such as a lack of teacher training,
inadequate infrastructure, and superficial approaches still limit their pedagogical
potential (Rosa, 2000; Napolitano, 2005). Overcoming these challenges requires
intentional planning and careful selection of materials, and integration into
interdisciplinary and community-based projects. It is concluded that the short film,
by bringing together science, art, and citizenship, serves as a transformative
resource for Environmental Education, fostering the development of critical
individuals committed to sustainability and socio-environmental justice.

KEYWORDS: environmental education, sustainability, cinema, short film,
pedagogical practices.




                                                                                497

RESUMO: A crise ambiental contemporânea decorre de um modelo de
desenvolvimento baseado na exploração intensa dos recursos naturais
e no consumo desenfreado, o que demanda repensar a relação entre
sociedade e natureza. Nesse cenário, a Educação Ambiental (EA),
consolidada a partir de eventos como Estocolmo (1972) e Tbilisi (1977),
assume caráter crítico, interdisciplinar e emancipatório, devendo estar presente
de forma transversal no cotidiano escolar, conforme orienta a BNCC
(2017). O cinema, especialmente na linguagem do curta-metragem,
apresenta-se como recurso pedagógico privilegiado por mobilizar emoção,
reflexão crítica e aprendizagem significativa. Por sua brevidade e impacto
narrativo, os curtas favorecem debates interdisciplinares e aproximam a
escola da cultura midiática contemporânea, sensibilizando os estudantes
para questões socioambientais. Experiências relatadas evidenciam que
assistir, analisar e produzir curtas contribui para a formação crítica e
participativa dos alunos (Menezes; Duarte, 2007), ampliando repertórios
culturais e fortalecendo a consciência ecológica. Contudo, desafios como a
carência de formação docente, infraestrutura precária e abordagens
superficiais ainda limitam seu potencial pedagógico (Rosa, 2000; Napolitano,
2005). Superá-los requer planejamento intencional, seleção criteriosa de
materiais e integração a projetos interdisciplinares e comunitários. Conclui-
se que o curta-metragem, ao articular ciência, arte e cidadania, constitui
recurso transformador para a Educação Ambiental, promovendo a formação de
sujeitos críticos e comprometidos com a sustentabilidade e a justiça
socioambiental.

PALAVRAS-CHAVE: educação ambiental, sustentabilidade, cinema, curta-
metragem, práticas pedagógicas.




                                                                            498

1. INTRODUCTION


       The environmental crisis that defines our contemporary era is the result of
a long historical process of unbridled exploitation of natural resources, the
intensification of production and consumption, and the consolidation of a
development model that prioritizes economic growth at the expense of socio-
environmental sustainability. Since the 1970s, global events such as the
Stockholm Conference (1972), the Tbilisi Conference (1977), and Rio-92 have
established Environmental Education (EE) as an essential dimension for
transforming social values and practices, with the aim of rethinking the
relationship between society and nature (Dias; Leal; Júnior, 2016; Loureiro,
2004). In this context, schools are called upon to play a central role in shaping
critical thinkers capable of understanding the complexity of environmental issues
and acting responsibly in the present and the future.
       The National Common Core Curriculum (BNCC, Brazil, 2017) establishes
that schools must promote the development of competencies focused on socio-
environmental sustainability, encouraging individual and collective alternatives
for a more balanced way of life. This means that Environmental Education cannot
be limited to commemorative dates or one-off activities, but must be integrated
into everyday educational practice in a cross-cutting, interdisciplinary, and critical
manner (Layrargues; Lima, 2014). In this sense, the use of artistic and cultural
languages—including cinema and, in particular, short films—emerges as a
powerful strategy for engaging students.
       From its very origins, cinema has been an art form, a cultural expression,
and a medium of communication. More than just entertainment, it functions as a
language that weaves together narratives, images, and sounds capable of
evoking emotions, reflections, and learning. As Napolitano (2005) points out,
working with film in the classroom enables schools to engage with contemporary
culture, bringing together aesthetics, leisure, ideology, and social values within a
single work. Edgar Morin (1989) adds that cinema is a “dream machine” and, at
the same time, a “social mirror,” as it reveals dimensions of human reality and
subjectivity. In this sense, watching films and short films in the classroom is not
merely a recreational activity but an opportunity for critical learning.



                                                                                  499

      The short film, due to its brief duration, accessible language, and creative
nature, serves as a prime resource for Environmental Education. In addition to
presenting diverse themes in a concise and impactful format, it allows teachers
to explore content dynamically, without the need to set aside large blocks of time
within their lesson plans. According to Rosa (2000), the break from routine
caused by showing audiovisual materials in the classroom captures students’
attention and evokes their emotions, fostering meaningful learning. Menezes and
Duarte (2007) emphasize that audiovisual resources foster students’ critical
reflection on socio-environmental issues, as they connect with their everyday
experiences and evoke feelings of belonging and responsibility.
      This article aims to discuss the pedagogical possibilities of using short
films in the classroom, especially for teaching environmental education and
sustainability. It seeks to understand how the act of “watching films” can
contribute to students’ critical development, highlighting authors who address
cinema, short films, and their interface with education— Furthermore, the aim is
to analyze experiences and propose methodological approaches that facilitate
the integration of this resource into daily school life, taking into account the
challenges faced by teachers.
      To achieve these objectives, the article is organized into sections. First, it
presents a reflection on film, education, and critical learning. Next, it discusses
Environmental Education and sustainability as foundations for pedagogical
practice. Subsequently, it analyzes the characteristics of short films and their
educational potential. Subsequently, the article addresses authors and research
that deal with the use of film and short films in the field of education, with an
emphasis on Environmental Education. It also discusses methodological
proposals and practical experiences that highlight the contribution of audiovisual
resources to teaching. Finally, it presents challenges, possibilities, and
concluding remarks that point to ways to expand the use of short films in schools.


2. CINEMA, EDUCATION, AND CRITICAL LEARNING


      Since its emergence in the late 19th century, cinema has established itself
as one of the most expressive forms of artistic and cultural language in modernity.
Initially conceived as a technological curiosity, it quickly assumed the role of a


                                                                                500

mass medium, capable of telling stories, disseminating ideologies, and
influencing social behavior (Napolitano, 2005). In the educational context, cinema
serves as a pedagogical resource capable of broadening horizons, stimulating
critical reflection, and integrating interdisciplinary knowledge.
       According to Edgar Morin (1989), cinema is both “art and industry,” but
above all, a formative experience, as it places the viewer before symbolic
representations that engage with their own experiences and emotions. For the
author, watching a film is not a passive act, but an active process of constructing
meaning, in which the viewer both recognizes and finds something unfamiliar in
themselves, experiences feelings, projects themselves onto the story, and learns.
Thus, the Showing films in the classroom enhances not only cognitive learning
but also students’ aesthetic, ethical, and social development.
       The use of film in the school setting, however, should not be limited to an
illustrative or recreational role. Napolitano (2005) warns that showing films merely
as a supplement to content or as an entertainment activity undermines their
pedagogical potential. This practice must be linked to clear educational objectives
that facilitate the connection between curricular content and students’ critical
reflection. In this sense, film helps schools reconnect with contemporary culture
by bridging formal and informal knowledge.
       Authors such as Gava and Xavier (2008) emphasize that audiovisual
media, by possessing its own everyday language, allows students to articulate
diverse worldviews in a stimulating way. Moving images, combined with sound
and narrative, engage emotion and cognition in an integrated way, enabling
meaningful learning (Ausubel, 2003). Linhares and Reis (2013) highlight that
audiovisual material facilitates discussion of scientific and social topics, going
beyond the role of a mere source of information to become a tool for dialogue,
debate, and critical inquiry.
       In the field of Environmental Education, cinema proves even more
relevant, as it engages ethical and affective dimensions related to caring for
nature and socio-environmental responsibility. Gadotti (2000) emphasizes that
Environmental Education must be critical and emancipatory, not merely
informative. To this end, films and short films serve as tools capable of raising
awareness, posing questions, and proposing new perspectives on the
relationship between human beings and the environment. By combining


                                                                                501

aesthetics and reflection, they broaden ecological awareness and promote
interdisciplinary learning. Furthermore, cinema aligns with the practices of
Freirean critical education, as it proposes a dialogical process of reading and
interpreting the world. According to Paulo Freire (1996), education must start from
the reality of the individuals involved and foster their ability to act upon it. In this
context, films and short films can be interpreted as “cultural texts” that offer
concrete situations for analysis, allowing students and teachers to engage in
dialogue about the environmental and social problems depicted, relating them to
their own experiences and contexts.
       Therefore, when cinema is purposefully incorporated into the educational
process, it ceases to be mere entertainment and becomes a powerful teaching
tool. More than simply conveying information, it encourages critical reflection,
fosters interdisciplinary debate, broadens cultural horizons, and strengthens civic
education. Based on this understanding, it is pertinent to explore the relationship
between film, environmental education, and sustainability, discussing how this
medium can contribute to transformative pedagogical practices.


3. ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION AND SUSTAINABILITY


       Environmental Education (EE) emerged as a field of knowledge and
pedagogical practice amid the intensifying global ecological crisis, beginning in
the second half of the 20th century. International discussions initiated at the
Stockholm Conference (1972) and consolidated at the Tbilisi Conference (1977)
highlighted the need to include the environmental dimension at all levels and in
all forms of education, with a view to fostering citizens who are aware of and
committed to the preservation of the planet (Dias; Leal; Júnior, 2016). Since then,
Environmental Education (EE) has established itself as a cross-cutting,
interdisciplinary field focused on transforming the relationship between society
and nature.
       According to Reigota (2009), Environmental Education should be
understood as a social practice that seeks to promote values, knowledge, and
attitudes oriented toward sustainability. More than simply conveying content
about ecology, it is an educational process that questions development models
and encourages ways of coexisting based on respect, cooperation, and collective


                                                                                    502

responsibility. From this perspective, the school is a prime setting for fostering a
critical ecological consciousness capable of addressing contemporary socio-
environmental challenges.
       Sustainability, a concept associated with the Brundtland Report (1987),
refers to the ability to meet the needs of the present without compromising the
needs of future generations. Gadotti (2000) emphasizes that this is not merely
about ecological balance, but rather a civilizational project that integrates social,
cultural, political, and economic dimensions. For the author, sustainability
requires structural changes in patterns of production and consumption, as well
as the formation of a global citizenship. Environmental Education (EE), in this
context, is a fundamental tool for raising awareness and mobilizing individuals
and communities toward a more just and balanced way of life.
       Authors such as Leff (2001) advocate for the need for a “new
environmental rationality,” capable of overcoming the instrumental and utilitarian
logic that governs contemporary society. This rationality presupposes recognition
of the complexity of the environment, understood not merely as a set of natural
resources, but as a network of relationships among ecological, cultural, and social
processes. Critical environmental education, in this sense, must challenge the
contradictions of the capitalist development model and propose sustainable
alternatives. Layrargues and Lima (2014) complement this view by presenting the
macro-trends in environmental education—conservationist, pragmatic, and
critical—emphasizing that only the critical perspective is capable of addressing
the structural causes of the environmental crisis.
       In the school setting, Environmental Education must be approached in a
cross-curricular manner and integrated into various areas of knowledge. The
BNCC (Brazil, 2017) stipulates that contemporary issues, such as environmental
concerns, should be addressed in an interdisciplinary way, connecting science,
culture, and citizenship. This means that Environmental Education should not be
limited to commemorative dates but incorporated into daily teaching as an
ongoing practice that sparks students’ interest and engagement. In this context,
the use of artistic and cultural media, such as film and short films, enhances this
approach, as it speaks directly to students’ sensibilities and imagination.
       Furthermore, critical environmental education recognizes that the
environmental crisis is also a social and ethical crisis. Jacobi (2003) emphasizes


                                                                                 503

that it is impossible to separate ecological issues from social inequalities, since
the impacts of environmental degradation fall disproportionately on different
population groups. Sustainability, therefore, can only be achieved through an
integrated approach that promotes social justice, equity, and democratic
participation. In this sense, addressing Environmental Education through short
films helps highlight these interrelationships, fostering students’ critical thinking
and encouraging them to devise collective solutions.
       Finally, it is important to emphasize that Environmental Education should
not be understood merely as a school subject, but as a broad educational practice
that involves families, communities, and social movements. Films and short films,
by circulating in both school settings and community environments, reinforce this
broad nature of Environmental Education, promoting intergenerational and
intercultural dialogues around sustainability.


4. THE SHORT FILM: CHARACTERISTICS AND EDUCATIONAL POTENTIAL


       The short film, as a cinematic genre, is characterized by its short running
time—generally less than 40 minutes according to international standards, and
up to 15 minutes under Brazilian law (Law No. 6,281/1975). This brevity, far from
being a limitation, constitutes its greatest strength, as it demands condensed,
creative narratives with a strong aesthetic and emotional impact. According to
Ramos (2004, p. 22), “the short film is a privileged space for aesthetic and
narrative experimentation, allowing for bold approaches that often find no place
in commercial cinema.”
       Historically, short films have been fundamental to the development of
cinema as a language, from the Lumière brothers’ first screenings in 1895 to the
avant-garde movements of the 20th century. In Brazil, they have also played a
decisive role, whether in independent production or as an educational and
political resource, especially during periods of social and cultural upheaval, such
as in the 1960s with the Cinema Novo movement and the film *Cinco vezes
favela* (1962).
       From an educational standpoint, short films offer unique advantages over
feature-length films. Because they require less screening time, they can be easily
integrated into regular classes without compromising the curricular organization.


                                                                                 504

Furthermore, due to their narrative conciseness, they spark students’ interest and
facilitate immediate discussion of the topics addressed. Rosa (2000, p. 39) had
already pointed out that “the break from routine caused by the presentation of an
audiovisual resource is beneficial, as it alters the classroom routine and stirs
students’ emotions.”
       Menezes and Duarte (2007) add that audiovisual materials, due to their
aesthetic and symbolic dimensions, enhance students’ critical reflection on socio-
environmental issues, as they resonate with their life experiences. According to
the authors, “short films are ideal tools for science and environmental education,
as they stimulate students’ curiosity, questioning, and engagement” (Menezes &
Duarte, 2007, p. 77).
       Another relevant aspect is that short films allow for the in-depth exploration
of diverse themes, even within brief narratives. According to Napolitano (2005, p.
11), “working with film in the classroom helps schools rediscover a culture that is
both everyday and elevated, as film synthesizes aesthetics, leisure, ideology, and
social values within a single work of art.” This synthesis is even more evident in
short films, which, by condensing ideas into just a few minutes, have an
immediate impact on the viewer.
       From the perspective of Environmental Education, this characteristic
becomes even more relevant. Issues such as pollution, deforestation, climate
change, consumption, and inequality can be presented in animated shorts or
documentaries in a playful and thought-provoking way. As Rosso and Vieira
(2011, p. 88) observe, “films and documentaries, by combining emotion and
knowledge, contribute to a critical understanding of complex problems involving
nature and society.”
       Furthermore, short films engage directly with young people’s digital and
media culture. In the age of YouTube, TikTok, and other platforms, the concise
and visual language is familiar to students. Thus, using short films in the
classroom brings the school closer to students’ cultural world, making learning
more meaningful. According to Gava and Xavier (2008, p. 55), “the language
enables students to articulate worldviews in a stimulating way, since it is part of
their daily lives and an integral part of their social experience.”
       In summary, short films are an effective educational resource for
environmental education and sustainability, as they combine brevity, impact, and


                                                                                 505

the ability to raise awareness. Their use in the classroom allows for an
interdisciplinary, critical, and contextualized approach to teaching content,
promoting learning that unites emotion, reason, and action.


5. THE USE OF SHORT FILMS IN THE CLASSROOM


       The incorporation of short films into the school environment should not be
viewed as a secondary or merely recreational activity, but rather as an intentional
pedagogical practice aimed at promoting meaningful and critical learning. For this
to occur, teachers must make informed choices regarding audiovisual
productions, establish clear objectives, and plan activities that foster reflection
and dialogue.
       According to Napolitano (2005, p. 21), “film is not merely an illustrative
teaching resource, but a language that, when deciphered, contributes to students’
cultural and critical development.” This means that short films should not be
shown in isolation, but rather integrated with discussions and activities that foster
critical thinking.
       One of the most recommended methodologies is holding discussion
groups after the screening, in which students can express their impressions,
feelings, and interpretations. According to Linhares and Reis (2013, p. 62),
“audiovisual material is an important resource for promoting discussion of
scientific topics in the classroom, going beyond its use as a supplement to
information conveyed by teachers.” This dialogic process aligns with Freirean
pedagogy, in which the act of “reading the world” precedes “reading the word”
(Freire, 1996).
       Another possibility is the critical analysis of elements of cinematic
narrative, such as characters, plot, settings, and soundtrack. This analysis allows
students to understand how cinema constructs meanings and conveys
ideological messages. Rosa (2000) argues that, when working with audiovisual
materials in the classroom, teachers should encourage students to recognize the
intentionality of images and the relationship between emotion and knowledge.
       Short films can also be used as a catalyst for interdisciplinary projects.
When discussing, for example, a short film about river pollution, it is possible to
incorporate content from Science (ecological impacts), Geography (use of water


                                                                                 506

resources), History (environmental policies), Portuguese Language (writing
argumentative texts), and the Arts (aesthetic expression). This approach aligns
with Sauvé’s (2005) proposal, which views Environmental Education as an
interdisciplinary field that integrates diverse bodies of knowledge around
sustainability.
       In addition to screening existing films, an innovative pedagogical practice
consists of encouraging students to produce their own short films. Thiollent
(2011) points out that action research, when applied to education, enhances
learning through students’ active participation. Producing a short film requires
research, planning, scriptwriting, filming, and editing, mobilizing cognitive,
technical, and socio-emotional skills. Menezes and Duarte (2007) state that
“audiovisual production by the students themselves promotes not only content
learning but also the development of authorship, creativity, and critical
awareness” (p. 84).
       Finally, it is important to select short films that resonate with the students’
sociocultural context. Gadotti (2000) notes that Environmental Education must be
context-specific and participatory, respecting local realities and encouraging
youth leadership. In this sense, animated shorts, community documentaries, or
independent productions may be more effective than major commercial films, as
they present narratives that are closer to the students’ lived experiences.
       Thus, the use of short films in the classroom constitutes a pedagogical
practice that unites art, science, and citizenship. Screening them, discussing
them critically, and even producing them with students expands the potential of
Environmental Education, transforming the school into a space for reflection,
creation, and social transformation.


6. AUTHORS AND PERSPECTIVES ON CINEMA AND ENVIRONMENTAL
EDUCATION


       The relationship between cinema, environmental education, and
sustainability has been the subject of study by various authors, who recognize
audiovisual media as a language capable of raising awareness and fostering
critical citizens. The perspectives of these thinkers highlight both the aesthetic
dimension of cinema and its pedagogical and political functions.


                                                                                  507

       Edgar Morin (1989) is one of the pioneers to highlight cinema as a
formative experience. For him, “cinema is the most powerful dream machine ever
invented” (Morin, 1989, p. 17), capable of bridging reality and imagination, reason
and emotion. This characteristic gives films—and, in particular, short films—the
ability to engage viewers beyond the rational, appealing to their emotional and
ethical dimensions.
       Along the same lines, Napolitano (2005, p. 11) argues that “working with
film in the classroom helps schools rediscover a culture that is both everyday and
elevated, since cinema synthesizes aesthetics, leisure, ideology, and social
values within a single work of art.” Thus, film should not be viewed merely as
entertainment, but as an art form that communicates values and ideologies and
that, when critically analyzed, can broaden students’ awareness of their social
and environmental roles.
       In the specific field of Environmental Education, authors such as Loureiro
(2004) advocate for a critical perspective that goes beyond isolated and purely
informative practices. According to the author, “Environmental Education must be
understood as a political-pedagogical process that contributes to social
transformation” (Loureiro, 2004, p. 38). In this sense, the use of films and short
films in the classroom becomes a tool for fostering debates on consumption,
environmental justice, and sustainability, encouraging students to understand the
structural roots of the ecological crisis.
       Reigota (2009) expands on this view by stating that Environmental
Education should be understood as a social and cultural practice, rooted in
people’s daily lives. According to the author, “Environmental Education is not
neutral, but carries values and intentions, and should promote critical and
democratic participation” (Reigota, 2009, p. 24). By showing short films that
depict local problems, such as river pollution or deforestation, teachers enable
students to make connections between their own reality and major global
challenges.
       Gadotti (2000), when discussing sustainability, emphasizes the need for
an education that fosters global citizenship. According to him, “sustainability is
not only ecological, but also social, political, and cultural” (Gadotti, 2000, p. 67).
In this context, film is a privileged resource for articulating these dimensions, as



                                                                                  508

it can represent the interdependence between society and nature through
accessible and compelling visual narratives.
       Jacobi (2003), in turn, draws attention to the inseparability of
environmental crisis and social inequality. The author argues that environmental
education should promote socio-environmental justice by valuing citizen and
community participation. By showcasing stories of communities affected by
environmental disasters or social exclusion, short films play a fundamental role
in raising awareness and mobilizing students toward collective action.
       Leff (2001) also offers the perspective of the “new environmental
rationality,” which involves moving beyond the instrumental logic of modern
society and adopting a complex view of ecological relationships. For the author,
“the environment constitutes a social rationality, shaped by behaviors, values,
and knowledge” (Leff, 2001, p. 224). Feature films and short films, by presenting
stories that connect ecology, culture, and society, can contribute to this shift in
rationality.
       Finally, Sauvé (2005) highlights the plurality of approaches within
Environmental Education, such as the naturalist, conservationist, critical, and
sustainability approaches. Each of these approaches can be explored through
short films, which, by representing different worldviews, stimulate classroom
debate.
       Thus, it can be observed that the leading authors addressing the
intersection of cinema and Environmental Education emphasize the role of
audiovisual media as a language that engages reason and emotion, culture and
politics, contributing to a critical and transformative education.


7. EXPERIENCES AND METHODOLOGICAL PROPOSALS


       The use of short films in the classroom has already been the subject of
experiments in various educational contexts, revealing their pedagogical potential
for raising students’ awareness and fostering critical thinking. These practices
show that this resource can be used both as a catalyst for reflection and as a
structuring element for interdisciplinary projects.
       One of the most common approaches is screening short films followed by
discussion circles, in which students share their impressions and discuss the


                                                                               509

issues presented. According to Rosa (2000, p. 39), “the break in rhythm caused
by the presentation of an audiovisual piece is beneficial, as it alters the classroom
routine and engages students’ emotions.” This methodology promotes
meaningful learning (Ausubel, 2003), as it connects new content to students’ prior
experiences.
        Another effective approach involves integrating the short films into
interdisciplinary projects. For example, an animated short film addressing
deforestation can be explored in Science (ecological impacts), Geography (land
use),   History   (environmental    policies),   Portuguese    Language      (writing
argumentative texts), and Arts (aesthetic interpretation). As Sauvé (2005) points
out, Environmental Education should be interdisciplinary, integrating diverse
bodies of knowledge to understand the complexity of socio-environmental
problems.
        Some schools and universities have developed short-film production
workshops with their own students. In this type of activity, students research a
socio-environmental issue, write scripts, shoot footage, conduct interviews, and
edit the material into a short film. This practice not only familiarizes young people
with audiovisual language but also fosters creativity, leadership and engagement.
Menezes and Duarte (2007, p. 84) emphasize that “audiovisual production by the
students themselves promotes not only the learning of content but also the
development of authorship, creativity, and critical awareness.”
        Another example is the use of short films in rural schools and traditional
communities, where screening films about family farming, sustainable land use,
or water conservation can serve as a catalyst for community discussions. Gadotti
(2000) asserts that Environmental Education must be contextualized and
participatory, respecting local realities and fostering global citizenship. In these
cases, short films function as a tool for cultural mediation, connecting folk wisdom
and scientific knowledge.
        Projects reported by Jacobi (2003) also demonstrate that critical
Environmental Education can be strengthened through the use of short films that
address socio-environmental inequality. Screening short documentaries that
portray communities affected by flooding, mining, or a lack of sanitation, for
example, allows students to connect local problems to structural processes of



                                                                                 510

exclusion and environmental degradation. This encourages reflection on socio-
environmental justice and the role of citizens in transforming reality.
       Furthermore, in the context of digital technologies, short films can be
integrated into virtual platforms and online learning environments. Teachers can
design activities in which students watch short films at home and participate in
virtual discussion forums, thereby expanding the scope and duration of learning.
As Gava and Xavier (2008, p. 55) point out, “audiovisual language is part of
everyday life and an integral part of students’ social experience,” which facilitates
its integration into hybrid teaching practices.
       Finally, it is worth noting that methodological proposals should be
accompanied by participatory assessment processes, in which students are
invited to reflect not only on the content they have learned but also on their
feelings, values, and attitudes toward environmental issues. As Freire (1996)
reminds us, education should be a practice of freedom, in which the student is an
active participant in the process and not merely a recipient of information.
       Thus, the experiences reported here demonstrate that the use of short
films can be incorporated into schools in multiple ways: as a teaching resource
for discussing content, as an artistic language for aesthetic interpretation, as a
tool for community mobilization, and as a practice fostering youth authorship and
leadership. All of these possibilities point toward a more critical, participatory, and
transformative environmental education.


8. CHALLENGES AND POSSIBILITIES


       Despite the pedagogical potential of short films, their implementation in the
classroom faces several challenges. One of the main challenges is the lack of
specific training for teachers. As noted by Napolitano (2005) and Rosa (2000),
many teachers have not received adequate training to work with film, which can
lead to a superficial use of the resource or to the perception of audiovisual media
solely as entertainment. For short films to fulfill their educational role, it is
necessary to invest in continuing education programs that address both cinematic
language and its integration with educational objectives and socio-environmental
themes.



                                                                                   511

       Another challenge is school infrastructure. Screening short films requires
adequate audiovisual equipment, such as projectors, screens, speakers, and
access to digital content. In socially vulnerable contexts or in rural schools, these
conditions are not always available. Menezes and Duarte (2007) emphasize that,
in such situations, it is necessary to seek creative alternatives, such as the use
of laptops, community televisions, or activities that prioritize the production of
short films by the students themselves, thereby minimizing dependence on
external resources.
       The choice of short films is also a sensitive issue. Teachers should select
works that are relevant to the curriculum, culturally appropriate, and capable of
stimulating critical reflection. As Gadotti (2000) states, environmental education
must be context-specific, respecting the local context and the students’ reality.
Short films that are too far removed from students’ experiences can lead to
disinterest or superficial learning, whereas works rooted in everyday life foster
engagement and identification.
       Furthermore, integrating the short film into the curriculum requires careful
pedagogical planning. Showing the film in isolation, without accompanying
activities or critical analysis or interdisciplinary interdisciplinary projects,
undermines the        educational potential. Napolitano (2005, p. 21) warns that
“film only fulfills its pedagogical role when it is analyzed, critically examined, and
contextualized within the educational process,” which requires time, dedication,
and integration with other content.
       Despite these difficulties, there are numerous possibilities for expanding
the use of short films in schools. Digitization and access to online video platforms
make it more feasible to screen high-quality short films, including independent
productions and environmental documentaries. Furthermore, the production of
short films by the students themselves provides an opportunity for active learning,
engaging cognitive, technical, and socio-emotional skills, as noted by Thiollent
(2011) and Menezes and Duarte (2007).
       Another possibility is collaboration with community and interdisciplinary
projects, connecting schools, families, and society. Short films can serve as a
starting point for local debates, production workshops, environmental awareness
campaigns, and the exchange of cultural experiences. This approach reinforces
the critical, participatory, and emancipatory nature of Environmental Education,


                                                                                  512

transforming cinema into a tool for citizenship and social mobilization (Jacobi,
2003; Sauvé, 2005).
       From a pedagogical perspective, challenges become opportunities when
short films are incorporated in a planned, contextualized, and reflective manner.
They enable not only the transmission of content but also the development of
critical, aesthetic, and social skills. The dialogue between film and Environmental
Education, therefore, represents a promising path for strengthening innovative
educational      practices,   interdisciplinarity,   and   student   engagement    in
understanding and transforming the socio-environmental reality.


9. CONCLUSION


       This article demonstrated that short films are a valuable pedagogical
resource for Environmental Education and the promotion of sustainability in
school settings. Their brevity, aesthetic richness, and ability to evoke emotion
and foster critical reflection allow them to be used in dynamic, interdisciplinary,
and participatory ways. As demonstrated, watching, analyzing, and producing
short films in the classroom contributes to the development of cognitive, socio-
emotional, and ethical competencies, fostering the formation of critical, conscious
individuals who are engaged with contemporary socio-environmental challenges.
       The theoretical framework analyzed shows that cinema, as a cultural and
artistic language, goes beyond entertainment. Morin (1989) and Napolitano
(2005) emphasize that films and short films are capable of articulating
imagination, reason, and emotion, bringing students closer to contemporary
culture and promoting critical learning. When integrated into Environmental
Education, these resources make it possible to address complex issues such as
pollution, climate change, deforestation, and socio-environmental inequality,
making reflection meaningful and contextualized (Gadotti, 2000; Reigota, 2009;
Jacobi, 2003).
       The pedagogical experiences reported indicate that short films can be
used in a variety of ways: as discussion starters, as components of
interdisciplinary projects, as material for critical analysis, or as products created
by the students themselves. This diversity of approaches reinforces the genre’s
versatility and its suitability for innovative educational practices (Menezes;


                                                                                  513

Duarte, 2007; Sauvé, 2005). Furthermore, the integration of digital technologies
expands learning spaces and enables closer interaction with students’ media
culture (Gava; Xavier, 2008).
       However, the use of short films in the classroom presents challenges that
must be addressed strategically. Among these are the need for specific teacher
training, the availability of adequate infrastructure, the careful selection of
materials, and alignment with clear pedagogical objectives (Napolitano, 2005;
Rosa, 2000). Overcoming these difficulties requires investment in training,
collaborative planning, and the valorization of local, community-based, and
participatory experiences.
       In short, short films offer transformative potential, enabling Environmental
Education to be critical, interdisciplinary, and context-specific. By fostering
reflection, dialogue, creativity, and active participation, this resource contributes
to the development of citizens who are aware of their role in caring for the planet
and in building more just and sustainable societies. Thus, using short films in the
classroom represents an innovative educational practice that connects culture,
art, and science and strengthens education as an instrument of social
transformation.
